articles.title: Out of office, out of service.
articles.context: Check Point patches an actively exploited zero-day tied to wiper attacks. Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability allowing attackers to gain root privileges on vulnerable appliances.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft 365 recovers from a global outage. StingyBasilisk pivots through Windows named pipes to infiltrate isolated networks. The FBI freezes billions after North Korea's Binance heist, while Pyongyang's Sapphire Sleet steals $400 million via spoofed video calls. Cupertino details Secure Exclaves for ambient sensor privacy. Operation TorNado nets 354 arrests in a global dark web crackdown. Check Point patches an actively exploited zero-day tied to wiper attacks. The wfx-loot campaign hijacks thousands of GitHub accounts to harvest cloud secrets. And civil liberties groups warn Congress against slipping Section 702 renewal into the defense bill. Our guests are Lauren Zabierek and Bob Lord, discussing the launch of the Software Safety Institute. United grounds personal AI agents over credential and compliance risks.

Today is Friday November 13th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Microsoft 365 recovers from a global outage.

If you rely on services from Microsoft, I’m betting you are already aware of today’s top story.

A major global outage disrupted Microsoft 365 services for more than twenty hours, and Redmond says a cyberattack is not to blame.

According to BBC, connectivity problems hit Outlook, Teams, and Copilot after a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable, shifting heavy traffic onto remaining infrastructure. Downdetector logged 140 thousand user reports across seventy-four countries, though total impact among Microsoft's more than 430 million users remains unclear. Knock-on disruptions have affected OpenAI, Anthropic, US courts, a Toronto hospital network, and Japanese government systems. Microsoft reports encouraging recovery progress in Europe and North America, noting earlier fixes were not taking as expected.

Prolonged cloud outages create cascading operational friction across critical infrastructure and AI dependencies, even without a threat actor at the keyboard. As Professor James Ferryman of the University of Reading notes, bringing swamped authentication servers back online requires a cautious, gradual approach to avoid triggering a fresh reconnection surge.

StingyBasilisk abuses Windows named pipes and SMB to infiltrate isolated networks.

An espionage group tracked as StingyBasilisk is abusing Windows named pipes and the Server Message Block protocol to move malware across isolated government networks, according to research from Positive Technologies.

According to incident response findings published by Positive Technologies, the group has operated since at least April 2022, masquerading as legitimate security tools. Beginning in February 2026, the attackers spread laterally over SMB and executed memory-resident payloads using Impacket's atexec tool and DLL side-loading via signed SafeNet libraries. To maintain persistence, the threat actors abused Component Object Model hijacking and modified Windows Time service providers, deploying custom implants like SilentCOM, TediousLoader, and CunningDoor. By chaining infected hosts through named pipes, the attackers reach air-gapped or segmented systems lacking direct internet access.

Abusing native Windows inter-process communication allows espionage campaigns to blend into routine administrative traffic and bypass traditional perimeter defenses. Defenders can counter this activity by restricting inter-segment SMB traffic, auditing scheduled task creation, and hunting for anomalous registry modifications.

The FBI freezes billions following the North Korean heist at Binance.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation has frozen over $2.7 billion and obtained court authorization to seize another $1.2 billion following a massive cryptocurrency theft at Binance.

According to the FBI, the October 29 cyberattack resulted in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion, most of it drained within twenty minutes. While the exact intrusion vector remains under investigation, blockchain analysts assess that attackers compromised Binance's transaction-signing infrastructure, enabling unauthorized approvals without stealing private keys. Co-CEO Richard Teng assured users that customer losses will be covered through Binance's Secure Asset Fund for Users and corporate reserves. Investigators linked the stolen funds to a prior Bitget breach, attributing the heist to the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor.

The rapid freeze demonstrates how coordinated public-private action and centralized stablecoin controls can blunt massive cryptocurrency heists intended to fund Pyongyang's prohibited weapons programs.

Pyongyang's Sapphire Sleet steals $400 million using spoofed video calls.

North Korean state-backed hackers have stolen over $400 million in cryptocurrency across eighteen months by secretly recording victims on fake video calls, according to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation.

In a campaign tracked as FaceStealer, the threat cluster known as Sapphire Sleet, or UNC1069, lures targets onto imposter versions of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet using invitations sent from compromised contacts. During the call, a fabricated technical error prompts victims to click a malicious link, infecting their devices and hijacking their accounts to repeat the cycle. Investigators seized more than nine hundred stolen webcam videos and note the group is increasingly generating artificial intelligence deepfakes of prominent cryptocurrency figures.

Weaponizing trusted social graphs alongside synthetic video bypasses traditional perimeter defenses through pure human deception.

Cupertino details Secure Exclaves architecture for ambient sensor privacy.

Apple has published technical details on Secure Exclaves, a hardware-enforced security architecture designed to isolate background camera and microphone processing from the main operating system, third-party apps, and Apple itself.

According to Apple, Secure Exclaves supports features like person recognition on HomeView, Siri Recap, and Live Rewind across new iPhone, MacBook Neo, and HomeView devices. Built on a customized L4 microkernel and enforced by the Secure Page Table Monitor, the architecture processes raw audio and video in an independent execution context before discarding the data. During ambient sensing, only strictly audited metadata—such as an enrolled user's identifier or confidence score—crosses into the main operating system. Full sensor streams are released only in active mode after an Exclave Indicator Controller verifies that on-screen pixels or hardware LEDs meet visibility thresholds.

Enforcing hardware-backed isolation and tamper-resistant indicators helps mitigate silent surveillance risks inherent in always-on ambient artificial intelligence features.

Operation TorNado nets 354 arrests across fourteen countries in dark web crackdown.

Law enforcement agencies across fourteen countries have arrested 354 dark web vendors and buyers in Operation TorNado, a coordinated crackdown spanning May 2025 through October 2026.

According to Europol, investigators targeted users linked to five previously shuttered marketplaces—Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, and Tor2Door—alongside encrypted messaging services and single-vendor shops. The United States led with 132 arrests, followed by the UK with fifty-nine, Hungary with forty-five, and Germany with forty-one. Authorities executed hundreds of searches, seizing over €210 million in combined cash and cryptocurrency, more than two hundred firearms, and nearly six metric tonnes of illicit drugs across the US and Europe, aided by Europol blockchain analysts tracing transactions.

Law enforcement's ability to exploit residual data from defunct sites demonstrates that marketplace takedowns increasingly serve as the starting point for long-term user identification, even as criminals migrate toward specialized platforms.

Check Point patches zero-day flaw exploited for root access and wiper attacks.

Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability allowing attackers to gain root privileges on vulnerable appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, the flaw stems from an unauthenticated local socket in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon. According to Check Point, threat actors compromised Mobile Access portals via the PHP2Shell bug, escalated privileges using this zero-day, deployed backdoors, and pivoted to VMware ESXi hosts to run destructive wiper malware across roughly two dozen customers.

Unauthenticated local inter-process communication exposes perimeter gateways to rapid privilege escalation and lateral destruction.

Campaign dubbed wfx-loot compromises 4,837 GitHub accounts to harvest cloud secrets.

A widespread supply-chain campaign dubbed wfx-loot has compromised 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than sixty-one thousand repositories and steal cloud credentials from at least 1,835 targets.

According to application security firm Aikido, the operation began November 10, targeting accounts linked to Fortune 100 firms, the US General Services Administration, and the French government. Attackers opened fake dependency audit pull requests to test write permissions, then injected a credential-harvesting shell script via GitHub Actions workflows or npm install hooks. The malware exfiltrated cloud tokens, artificial intelligence keys, and developer secrets—and even escalated privileges across Amazon Web Services, Azure, and Google Cloud—before reverting changes and deleting workflow logs in under a minute.

Automating secret theft across continuous integration pipelines turns compromised developer tokens into rapid, multi-cloud privilege escalation.

A Civil liberties coalition warns Congress against attaching Section 702 renewal to defense bill.

A coalition of twenty-seven civil liberties groups is warning congressional leaders against attaching a renewal of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act to the annual National Defense Authorization Act without adding a warrant requirement for searches involving Americans.

According to a letter led by Demand Progress and first reported by CyberScoop, the groups argued that slipping an unamended extension into the must-pass defense bill would circumvent bipartisan debate over constitutional rights, noting that existing court authorization allows intelligence operations to continue through March despite the law's summer lapse. Conversely, House Intelligence Committee ranking member Representative Jim Himes told The Hill that Congress should pass a reauthorization during the current lame-duck session before an incoming Democratic majority potentially imposes stricter limits next year.

The debate highlights the recurring tension between preserving rapid foreign intelligence collection capabilities and enforcing Fourth Amendment privacy safeguards through legislative reform.

United grounds personal AI agents over credential and compliance risks.

United Airlines is grounding artificial intelligence agents, blocking the digital assistants from booking flights or managing reservations on behalf of customers.

In a Wednesday press release, the carrier warned that handing account logins to third-party assistants exposes sensitive data and invites unintended purchases or rogue MileagePlus redemptions. Anyhoo, it turns out that even the smartest algorithm still cannot legally swear to the Federal Aviation Administration that your checked bag is free of explosives. United is updating its ticketing and distribution policies across its own platforms and third-party aggregators, echoing a similar password warning from Bank of America last week.

As enterprises struggle to distinguish legitimate bots from human travelers, Trua CEO Raj Ananthanpillai notes that outright bans merely delay the inevitable shift toward verified identity tokens.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Kitesurf is now open source
articles.context: Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers)
articles.full_text:
We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.

That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.

A browser built for agents

Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.

Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.

Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.

What is inside the repository?

Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:

Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.

Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.

Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).

Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.

These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.

Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.

All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.

Run your own Kitesurf

To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:

git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git cd kitesurf pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm run dev

The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.

You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:

import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core"; const browser = await puppeteer.connect({ browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser", }); try { const page = await browser.newPage(); await page.goto("https://example.com/"); await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" }); } finally { await browser.disconnect(); }

Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.

Deploy to your Cloudflare account

When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.

From the repository root:

pnpm run deploy

Help us make it better

As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution), more reliable, and efficient.

Start with the contribution guidelines if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.

Stay tuned

Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog, and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks.

And come chat with the team on Discord. We’re building a browser for agents, and we’d love your help making it better.

articles.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
articles.context: Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available
articles.full_text:
Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.

ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.

We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:

Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.

Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.

Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.

Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.

Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.

Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.

What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?

Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.

The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist

We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:

Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.

Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.

Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.

Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.

Architecture

Planning model

Built-in capabilities/execution environment

Post-exploitation capabilities

ARTEX (and forks)

Planner and parallel agents

Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target

Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

LuaN1aoAgent

Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents

Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local

Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption

Decepticon

Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents

Cairn

Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi)

PentestGPT-Agent

Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent

Run on host, can develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

Observations from the world's largest network

As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1.

As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8.

Identity-chained LLM exploitation

Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders.We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure. Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure. LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments.

ARTEX in action

As part of one incident response investigation, our team observed ARTEX gaining access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Available evidence indicated that the compromise most likely originated through a third-party hyperscaler.

We observed that a large number of new Worker scripts had been created with distinct names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, and artex-do-*. The naming of each Worker script correlated to distinct behaviors and actions it was taking, and was often postfixed by an alphanumeric identifier. We observed activity in excess of 69 requests per minute across multiple unique parts of their Cloudflare infrastructure and 400 database dump requests in an hour. We also observed attempted persistence mechanisms and attempts to validate session tokens for other third-party applications. While we believe that much of this activity was lightly guided by the human operator, this is just one example of the speed and breadth that ARTEX and similar frameworks can achieve post-compromise.

Our recommendation: the Modern Security Model

Large Language Models increase the ability of a threat actor to rapidly iterate through the Cyber Kill Chain against a target. They do this by giving the actor the advantage of speed and validation. Each step of the Cyber Kill Chain can be validated and fed into the next stage of the attack. This level of orchestration is unparalleled and effectively vaporizes legacy cyber security models. A modern model must be used against these attacks.

To help explain this model further, let’s use the metaphor of protecting a house on an estate. Each section below outlines how to defend against the threat at each step.

Fortify the front gate: implement traffic control and a WAF with advanced rules

Before anyone even sets foot on your lawn, they have to reach the perimeter fence.

On an unprotected estate, an adversary can drive an endless fleet of decoy trucks straight into your driveway, completely blocking the entrance and smashing through the barriers (Layer 3/4 volumetric floods and direct IP probing).

With perimeter gate security in place, all incoming traffic is routed through massive, distributed outer gates miles away from the main house. Rogue delivery trucks are filtered out to the highway, rogue utility tunnels trying to wiretap your property are severed, and only legitimate foot traffic ever reaches your home address.

Network traffic control serves as an important role in stopping volumetric attacks.

A security station in the foyer: anomaly detection

Once visitors arrive at the main entry, they meet a strict security station at the foyer.

Automated prowlers don't just kick the door; they disguise themselves. They attempt weird ways to get in the door — stuffing paper into the lock, trying variations like //front-door//back-room/ to trick the mechanism into swinging open.

The security guard at the door enforces clear rules:

You cannot knock 500 times in five seconds.

You cannot disguise your path with trickery.

You cannot attempt to roll a massive flatbed cart through the front hall to haul away the house's internal blueprints (diagnostic heap dumps). Suspicious behavior is turned away immediately.

Implement security keys and hardware based FIDO keys.

Web Application Firewall (WAF) serves as a key defense mechanism in stopping application exploitation through rate limits and anomaly detection.

Identify phony visitors: implement Bot Defense

A sophisticated intruder rarely looks like a masked burglar; they disguise themselves as ordinary visitors. But automated agents, headless browser scrapers, and AI reconnaissance tools don't act like real people.

They don't blink, their posture is unnervingly rigid, their cadence is mechanical, and their "identification" is often a sloppy imitation of a real visitor badge.

Bot Defense and challenges act as behavioral specialists watching the crowd through one-way glass. It flags the unnatural cadence, catches the synthetic micro-behaviors, and quietly escorts the machines off the property before they can touch a single doorknob.

Remove the back door: implement Identity-Gated Access and micro-segmentation

Many homes historically were built with side doors or a cellar hatch (internal admin panels, /actuator diagnostic endpoints, and remote gateways). Even if locked, a prowler could stand on the sidewalk, shine a flashlight on the cellar door, and start picking the lock.

Zero Trust application access does something radical: it bricks up the doorway from the outside and restricts which rooms can be entered.

To anyone wandering the perimeter, the cellar door does not exist. There is no lock to pick, no handle to rattle, and no light on inside. The only way in is with an escort who checks your biometric badge, confirms your device has a clean bill of health, and steps you directly into the specific room you need — leaving the rest of the house out of view.

For those who do enter, you have to ensure they cannot breach rooms next to the room they enter. Micro-segmentation is a highly effective strategy at stopping lateral movement. It limits compromised credentials from breaching production, test, and development systems.

Inspect deliveries: enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls

You receive daily supply deliveries to your estate — groceries, mail, maintenance parts. In digital terms, this is your incoming API traffic, which must be inspected and verified.

Intruders often attempt to bypass controls by sending unvalidated payloads or forged delivery manifests meant for restricted internal systems.

The porch protocol mandates thorough inspection and schema validation for all traffic:

Every incoming request must undergo OpenAPI schema validation to ensure it strictly conforms to expected definitions and structures.

Drivers and couriers must present validated mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates to establish trusted, authenticated connections.

Any request failing inspection or missing valid credentials is rejected immediately at the boundary.

Default-Deny Posture: Every positive security implementation ends with an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom of the ruleset.

Neighborhood watch: implement threat intelligence to gain visibility into attacks

Even with ironclad walls, an isolated property can be vulnerable if a syndicate invents a brand-new infiltration technique across town.

Threat intelligence acts as your warning network with neighboring estates. When a rogue actor sets up a new command-and-control safehouse down the road or begins deploying dynamic tunneling vans in your district, you receive an early dossier. Your estate updates its watchlists, recalibrates its sensors, and slams the gate shut before the actor ever turns onto your street.

How to get real-time help

ARTEX and similar LLM-based frameworks pose a significant challenge to legacy cyber defense models. Even the historical defense-in-depth model — which emphasizes a classic network DMZ — falls short in today's complex architectures. Tomorrow's attacks will only advance as orchestration tools become the new normal.

Securing legacy equipment and on-premises devices requires an identity-gated approach that logically makes these devices impossible to reach on the Internet. Beyond identity, slowing or making lateral movement more noisy is the goal of micro-segmentation. This architecture emphasizes a containment-first approach to security, which is essential when users are consistently losing their keys. When combined, the elements of the Modern Security Model are the answer to this vexing problem.

If you are facing an active security incident and need the Cloudforce One team on the ground to help respond to the incident or require threat intelligence support, please contact us immediately. If you need help implementing the Modern Security Model outlined here, please contact our Solutions Engineering team.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Crawls Back to Life After a 24-Hour Outage
articles.context: The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page
articles.full_text:
Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.

After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other users around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.

The outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with users reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.

The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.

“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson says in a statement. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.

As Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, users will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.

Microsoft said it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, users may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.

The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.

Ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” says Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 46 (2026)
articles.context: The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented
articles.full_text:
The Good | Authorities Dismantle Crypto Scams, Ban Illicit Exchange & Seize Malware Infrastructure

Ukrainian law enforcement partnered with German authorities this week to dismantle a network of cryptocurrency scammers that stole over €4.3 million from victims in Europe. Operating out of Ukrainian centers, the criminals used social media and dating apps to carry out romance baiting and other schemes.

After building up trust, they coerced victims into depositing funds into bogus trading platforms and attacker-controlled cryptocurrency wallets. Coordinated raids across four regions yielded hardware wallets, computer equipment, SIM cards, and over $13,000 in seized currencies. The four detained suspects remain in pre-trial custody and face up to 12 years in prison.

In the U.S., the Department of the Treasury cut off MEXC Global cryptocurrency exchange from the American financial system over extensive sanctions evasion and ties to cybercrime gangs. Between 2021 and 2026, the global platform facilitated over $16 billion in illicit transactions, according to an enforcement order from U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

Regulators identified MEXC as a key financial clearinghouse for ransomware gangs, darknet activity, and state-backed entities evading sanctions across Russia, Iran, and North Korea. While FinCEN calls out deficiencies in the exchange’s anti-money laundering and customer verification policies, MEXC states they are reviewing the order with legal and compliance experts.

Europol and Eurojust also seized 257 domains and 235 servers powering the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations. The joint takedown, part of the long-running Operation Endgame, spanned nine partner nations all targeting loaders, info-stealers, and remote access trojans (RATs) actively leveraged by cybercriminals to harvest corporate credentials and deploy secondary payloads.

Investigators uncovered over six million compromised credentials and $6.4 million victim datasets stored across the criminal infrastructure. Now, authorities are forwarding the recovered records to public breach-notification services to alert affected organizations and users.

The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers

Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented .NET cyberespionage framework dubbed Cereal to intercept communications on Microsoft Exchange servers across government organizations. Researchers began tracking the first wave of attacks in 2025 when Tulra compromised a government body in Kazakhstan before striking a Romanian state agency. In Romania shortly after, operators configured the toolset to selectively capture sensitive email correspondence involving representatives from NATO and the European Union.

Turla (aka Snake, UNC4210), linked to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), engineered Cereal for stealthy, long-term intelligence gathering. The malware avoids external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure entirely. Instead, it abuses the compromised Exchange server itself as a centralized execution hub and persistent collection point. The framework comprises eight modular components that rely extensively on data serialization and in-memory execution to conceal illicit activity from security defenders.

A primary module, named CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service process, EdgeTransport.exe. Once inside, it hijacks existing transport handlers to inspect message traffic without registering unauthorized transport agents or interrupting normal email delivery. The module automatically compresses, encrypts, and stages messages containing PDF, DOC, or DOCX attachments matching targeted sender, recipient, or subject criteria.

At the same time, a passive backdoor named CerealNeuron listens for incoming encrypted web requests designed to blend with regular Exchange traffic. Upon receiving instructions, it launches disposable CerealRunner binaries that execute memory-resident payloads to query Active Directory, extract LSA secrets, inspect mailboxes, and return encrypted results to the backdoor for exfiltration.

Security analysts emphasize that Cereal's extensive concealment strategies reflect Turla’s deep understanding of .NET execution techniques running inside legitimate processes, marking a mature offensive platform ready for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage.

The Ugly | Threat Actors Breach Railway Infrastructure to Steal Customer AI Secrets

Cloud hosting platform Railway confirmed that threat actors exploited flaws within its build infrastructure to steal decrypted customer authentication secrets, resulting in an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage charges.

The intrusion began on October 20 when adversaries exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to escape build filesystem isolation and capture internal credentials. Using these credentials, the attackers accessed stored build histories and obtained a copy of Railway's monorepo source code to identify further exploitation paths across the environment.

The attackers then exploited an improperly configured OIDC trust binding within Railway's cloud deployment system, moving laterally to compromise an orchestration server. Since that machine managed fleet workloads, it held credentials authorized to decrypt customer environment variables via cloud key management services.

Between October 20 and October 21, the intrusion escalated into a 26-hour operational contest between Railway engineers and threat actors deploying autonomous AI agents to probe systems in parallel.

Forensic investigations revealed that the attackers specifically targeted environment variables containing API keys for major AI providers, likely seeking access for resale or model distillation. The breach potentially exposed credentials across at most 1.85% of workspaces, representing approximately 100,000 customer environments, alongside linked-account tokens for 1,852 users. However, forensic analysis showed no evidence that attackers accessed customer databases. The investigation also found no indication that attackers downloaded private Git repositories.

Railway fully evicted the threat actors on October 21, isolated each build within dedicated ephemeral virtual machines, and rotated affected tokens. While the company is coordinating with AI providers to secure customer refunds, it pledged to cover any fraudulent charges that vendors decline to reimburse.

articles.title: The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World
articles.context: “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable
articles.full_text:
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.

Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.

Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.

“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.

Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.

Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

articles.title: The Green Agent POV: Formulating the Fix for an Internet-Facing Container with Sensitive Data Access
articles.context: A critical Issue was just discovered in an environment: an internet-facing container running an image with a known initial-access vulnerability, with a role attached that can...
articles.full_text:
A critical Issue was just discovered in an environment: an internet-facing container running an image with a known initial-access vulnerability, with a role attached that can reach sensitive data.

With AI speed reducing the time from discovery to exploitation, the pressure to fix it fast is intense. Yet remediation is never just about speed. Teams are forced to balance security urgency with business continuity, racing against the clock to answer three critical questions: what’s impacted, what the fix is, and who to send that fix to.

The Wiz Security Graph helps security teams answer the first question. It lays out the exact exposure path including the exposed endpoints, the deployment behind them, the image where the CVE sits, and the lateral movement path that carries an attacker from code execution to buckets holding PII.

Finding the fix and the owner, however, requires deeper investigation that security teams can’t spend hours on. They must rapidly contact the developer to deploy a fix, if it even exists, and apply mitigations in the meanwhile without disrupting production uptime.

That’s what we built Green Agent for. In this post, we’re excited to pull back the curtain and share how Green Agent investigates this exact Issue in minutes and determines the remediation strategies it recommends.

The Investigation

1. Understanding the Issue

Green Agent started by ingesting the Security Graph context to map the full attack path. This Issue represented a toxic combination centered on a single Kubernetes deployment in an AWS EKS cluster.

The Security Graph correlated five distinct risk types converging on this single workload:

External Exposure: A direct network path from the internet to the container.

Vulnerability: A known initial-access CVE-2026-111497 on the container image.

Insecure Kubernetes Cluster: A pod mounting a service account token to bridge into the cloud.

Unprotected Principal: An IAM role granting the workload access to cloud storage.

Unprotected data: Sensitive customer records residing in those accessible buckets.

Five risk types meant five distinct places where the attack chain could be broken - whether by removing the public exposure, patching the container image, unmounting the service account token, scoping down the IAM role, or purging the sensitive data.

Before it could recommend how to break the chain without disrupting production uptime, Green Agent needed to validate the ground truth behind each risk factor. It began investigating the attack path step-by-step, starting at the perimeter.

2. Validating Exposure: Is the Front Door Really Open?

Before recommending a fix, Green Agent needed to determine whether network containment was even an option. Many cloud workloads appear public in configuration tables but are actually shielded behind internal subnets, VPNs, or closed security groups.

Green Agent traced the full inbound route from 0.0.0.0/0:

The Ingress Route: Traffic flowed from the public internet through an AWS Internet Gateway, routed across an AWS Network Load Balancer, passed through the Traefik Ingress controller, and directly into the application's main container.

Unauthenticated Access: Both HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) served public endpoints returning unauthenticated 2XX status codes.

No Perimeter Defense: Green Agent inspected the hops and confirmed no Web Application Firewall (WAF) or firewall rules were in place.

This established a critical operational boundary for remediation. Because this frontend was an intentionally public production service, simply pulling the network plug - like tearing down ingress or blocking the load balancer - would cause a total production outage. Any network-level remediation plan from Green Agent would need to preserve uptime, such as introducing authentication middleware rather than severing traffic entirely.

3. Assessing Exploitability: Is the Vulnerability Running in Memory?

With the front door confirmed open, Green Agent moved to the next link in the attack chain: the vulnerability risk factor, to evaluate whether the attack path could be severed at the application layer.

It investigated the container image flaw: CVE-2026-111497 ("Broccoli2Shell"), a critical RCE in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js and cataloged in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV).

It confirmed from the Wiz Sensor that the vulnerable Brotli libraries were actively loaded in memory by the running Node.js process, verifying that code execution was a live, viable threat.

Green Agent also checked upstream advisories and verified that vendor patches (including Node.js 22.23.4 and libbrotli 1.2.1) were already available, confirming a permanent code fix was viable.

However, organizational release processes mean that rolling out a new container image through testing and CI/CD pipelines takes time. Because the attack path can be broken at any of the five risk types, Green Agent turned to the remaining links - the Kubernetes configuration, IAM role, and sensitive data - to see if the toxic combination could be severed immediately in the cloud.

4. Evaluating Cloud Identity & Data: Can the Cloud Path be Severed?

Investigating the workload's connection to cloud storage, Green Agent evaluated the three remaining risk types:

The Cluster Remediation Lever (IRSA): Green Agent examined the Kubernetes service account and confirmed it projected cloud credentials via IRSA into the container. This revealed an immediate mitigation lever: disabling token automount on the pod spec to cut off cloud access.

The IAM Remediation Lever: Inspecting the assumed IAM role, Green Agent found overprivileged s3:GetObject and wildcard s3:* permissions across three S3 buckets. This surfaced a second lever: scoping the IAM policy down to least privilege.

The Data Remediation Lever: Querying the S3 buckets revealed over 5,000 unmasked records (credit cards and PII) in files, identifying a third remediation lever: purging or masking unprotected data at rest.

Investigating these layers proved that Green Agent didn't have to wait on a code deployment to neutralize the risk. Multiple zero-downtime levers were available in the cloud right now.

5. Code-to-Cloud Lineage: Finding the Source and Owners

Cloud mitigations can sever the attack path immediately and buy critical time, but permanent remediation requires fixing at the source. If changes aren't committed to code, the next CI/CD build or Terraform apply will simply overwrite your cloud tweaks and recreate the issue. Green Agent called its Code Subagent to bridge the runtime assets back to version control, tracing the container image to its source Dockerfile, the overprivileged IAM role to its Terraform definitions, and the workload to its GitOps deployment manifests.

By inspecting commit history and metadata, Green Agent connected each fix directly to the engineers who actually maintain the code: the application developer, service owner, and infrastructure lead so security teams didn’t have to go on a search for the right owner.

6. Determining a Verdict and Creating Remediation Plans

Within minutes, Green Agent analyzed organizational context to reach a verdict that this Issue needed to be remediated and is of Critical severity. Green Agent factored in real business impact: the workload belonged to High Business Impact (HBI) production projects, formed an active breach path to 5,000+ sensitive records, and aligned with historical remediation evidence showing 100% of similar sampled issues in the subscription were successfully remediated with a 0% rejection rate.

To break the toxic combination, Green Agent determined that Mitigate and Fix plans were most appropriate to break the risk types identified, balancing immediate protection against permanent resolution:

Mitigate Plans: Immediate actions security teams can deploy right now to reduce the risk, like disabling service account token automount to instantly sever cloud access while developers work on the code fix.

Fix Plans: Permanent root-cause resolutions, like updating the base image in the Dockerfile or scoping down Terraform IAM policies.

Just as importantly, Green Agent evaluated operational trade-offs to skip unviable strategies: it explicitly rejected deleting the ingress because severing an intentionally public frontend would cause a total production outage, and skipped long-term hardening where environment prerequisites weren't in place.

Finally, Green Agent turned planning into execution by assigning each plan directly to its verified owner, ready to resolve via a one-click pull request or by handing instructions straight to a coding agent.

Why this Matters

Green Agent brought two things to this remediation that are notoriously difficult to balance in security: addressing security urgency, and maintaining the context needed to protect business continuity.

First, speed. With risks and threats moving faster than ever, security urgency demands an immediate response. A human team investigating this toxic combination would spend hours or days context-switching: security analysts verifying the public endpoint, platform engineers checking if the Brotli library is actually in memory, cloud admins auditing IAM policies, and developers tracking down which Git repository built the image. Green Agent conducted this investigation in minutes, eliminating the friction and guesswork that typically stalls remediation.

Secondly, operational intelligence. Remediation isn’t only a security team problem, it’s an organizational decision that requires understanding real-world trade-offs. Green Agent knew better than to propose deleting the ingress and taking down a public service that would impact the business. Instead, it distinguished between immediate, zero-downtime cloud mitigations and permanent code fixes, found the exact files in version control, and assigned the work directly to the engineers who own them.

That balance is how organizations can move towards autonomous remediation. Trust has to be earned before teams hand over the keys to auto-execution. That trust is built on context: when engineers see that an agent genuinely understands business trade-offs and won't break production, they can safely evolve from reviewing every action (human-in-the-loop) to supervisory oversight (human-on-the-loop).

That progression is what finally enables teams to get on a path to self-healing, while giving engineers their time back to keep building.

articles.title: MDR Pricing: Comparing Asset-Based and Ingestion-Based Costs
articles.context: Detection value How does this data support the threats we need to detect
articles.full_text:
When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment.

For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include.

Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing

Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment.

With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard.

Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership.

How to make a like-for-like MDR pricing comparison

Give each provider the same asset inventory, required data sources, retention needs, and response expectations, then ask what fits within your annual budget. Any exclusions should be visible in the proposal, so you can judge their operational consequences before committing.

For example, one proposal might accommodate endpoint and identity data while requiring you to limit high-volume network sources. Another might accommodate those sources but lack an investigation capability your team needs. Looking at an MDR price per endpoint or per gigabyte will not resolve that difference; you need to see how the service uses the available data.

Use these questions during an initial demonstration to turn the pricing discussion into a practical comparison.

Comparison area

What to ask the provider

Evidence to request

Rapid7’s approach

Breadth of collection

Which required sources fit within this budget?

A list of included sources, exclusions, and extra charges.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion, supporting native and third-party telemetry across endpoint, cloud, identity, email, and network. Confirm coverage for your required sources in the proposal.

Depth of collection

Which events and fields are collected, filtered, or summarized?

Sample records showing what reaches the investigation platform.

Rapid7 ingests and normalizes telemetry from supported technologies. Use the demonstration or proof of concept to verify which events and fields your integrations provide.

Detection value

How does this data support the threats we need to detect?

A detection walkthrough showing its data dependencies.

Investigations combine security telemetry with vulnerability and asset-risk context. Completed threat hunts show the rationale, data examined, queries, and any linked investigations.

Investigation history

How long is data retained, and how can analysts search it?

A search against older records, with retrieval costs explained.

Rapid7 provides 13 months of log retention. Confirm the history available for each data type: 3rd party endpoint alerts have different availability from log-based searches.

Response scope

What will your team do after validating a threat?

A case walkthrough and documented responsibilities.

Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response, covering investigation, containment, and threat eradication. Incident reports document findings, attacker timelines, and recommended corrective actions.

Cost variability

What changes the bill as assets or data volumes grow?

A calculation using your growth assumptions.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion removes data volume as the billing unit. Request a written calculation for additional billable assets and changes to service scope.

What Keyloop’s experience shows about MDR value

For Alan Simpson, now Rapid7’s Field CISO, the ability to collect previously restricted data made a practical difference during his time at Keyloop: "We were previously ingesting around 250 GB a day into Splunk. After moving to Rapid7, we reached 1.4 TB a day, including NetFlow, full DNS logging, and web application firewall logs. These were sources we’d previously had to limit or simply weren’t collecting, so we gained much better visibility and coverage."

The change also extended the history available for investigation, with greater certainty about how long that evidence would remain accessible: "We also moved from around 90 days of retention in Splunk to 13 months with Rapid7. Even those 90 days couldn’t be relied on, as retention depended on how much data we were ingesting at the time. Having a longer, predictable history made a real difference."

Price predictability was key as Keyloop grew through seven mergers and acquisitions, each bringing a different data profile. His experience illustrates why collection and retention belong in the buying decision, although these figures alone do not establish a like-for-like cost saving.

How to compare MDR pricing beyond log volume

Once you understand which data fits within the quote, examine what the provider can do with it. Collecting more logs can close visibility gaps, but useful investigations depend on relevant events, consistent timestamps, and enough context to connect activity to a user or system. AI-assisted investigation also depends on that foundation: a required event that was never recorded leaves an investigation gap.

Infrastructure design can improve the usefulness of that evidence. Routing access to a management interface through a controlled path, for example, creates a clearer monitoring point and helps distinguish expected access from activity requiring investigation. This is why log volume and detection-rule counts need to be assessed alongside how the environment operates.

During a proof of concept, choose a threat scenario relevant to your business and ask the provider to demonstrate the detection, evidence gathering, and response. You should be able to see which records support the conclusion and what happens if a required source is unavailable.

How will your MDR cost change as you grow?

Repeat the comparison using a plausible change, such as an acquisition, additional cloud workloads, or enabling a previously excluded log source. For asset-based pricing, calculate the effect of additional billable assets and changes in scope. For ingestion-based pricing, examine increased daily volume, applicable commitments, and retention requirements. Assuming asset counts stay the same, at Rapid7 contract renewals are capped at 5% uplift, for the contract term, not per year.

Ask both providers to document the assumptions, including implementation effort, required licenses, and work your team will continue to perform. You can then assess what the budget covers today, which evidence remains unavailable, and what it would cost to accommodate the changes you expect.

Explore Rapid7 MDR and discuss pricing based on your assets, required data sources, retention needs, and response scope.

*Referenced Rapid7 contract terms and capabilities are correct at time of publishing and are subject to change.

articles.title: BYOH: Bring Your Own Harness with Cisco IQ, for partners
articles.context: The New Question Is Not Only Security
articles.full_text:
A few weeks ago, I was brainstorming with a Principal Engineer from our Customer Experience (CX) Engineering team. We were discussing our CX transformation via AI-native workflows, specifically about the role that harnesses play in that work. During our discussion, one thing stood out: almost nobody in the team used just one harness, myself included. Most of us run several harnesses and several models, picking the one that best fits the task. Evaluations and reasoning, adversarial analysis, and deployment considerations are examples of tasks that yield better (and many times different) results when leveraging distinct harness and model combinations. Nobody told us to work that way. It’s simply how the best work gets done.

That conversation sent me back in time.

I joined Cisco in 2000, in the middle of the internet buildout. So when people compare today’s AI buildout to the late 1990s, I understand why. The capital, the speed, and the sense that everything is about to change; it’s all familiar. The one real difference is the pace. This time it moves much faster.

But I think there’s a more useful comparison to consider. The internet analogy explains the buildout. It does not explain how AI moves from our personal lives into the enterprise, from consumer to business, and from chat to agentic work. For that, don’t look at the internet. Look at the iPhone.

The Pattern We Have Seen Before

Apple debuted the iPhone in January 2007. It was a consumer device, and it set a new bar for what a personal computing experience could be. The iPad reinforced that shift. Within a couple of years, employees were walking into the office with a better computer in their pocket than the one IT had issued them. They did not ask for permission. They asked why their work experience could not be as convenient as the rest of their life.

The industry gave that pressure a name. “Bring your own device” entered workplace jargon in 2009. By early 2011, BYOD had gone mainstream. What I remember most about that time is how the corporate conversation changed. It started with “no,” but after many meaningful conversations with employees, it ended with “how.” The companies that came out ahead did not ban the devices. They made their systems safe to reach from them. That forced change and evolution on identity, policy, and device management in the workplace, among others. That experience taught me that saying “yes” safely is an architecture problem, not just a policy memo.

The Same Pattern, Much Faster

AI has already had its consumer moment. Chatbots were the Business-to-Consumer (B2C) sensation. Then something more interesting happened. During 2025, the harness arrived. A harness is the “software around the model”. It plans the work, makes the calls to tools, reads and writes files, checks its own results, fans out sub-agents for help, and keeps going until the task is done. A chatbot answers a question. A harness gets the work done. And just like smartphones, people who use a harness at home or on a side project do not want to go back. Examples today include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, and OpenCode.

So here is how I see things playing out (and the trajectory I am watching): We are about to see BYOH, Bring Your Own Harness, gain momentum. Engineers, operators, and consultants will bring the harness they already trust into their day job, as well as into their customers’ projects. In many teams, it’s already happening, sanctioned or not.

The New Question Is Not Only Security. It Is Trusted Context.

In the BYOD days, the hard question was security. Is the device safe? Can we wipe it if it’s lost?

With BYOH, the security question is still there, and it gets bigger. A harness does not just display data. It acts on it. But there is a second set of questions that BYOD never had to answer: Is the harness working from the right context? How do you keep the context consistent and up to date across different harnesses?

A harness without trusted context will sound confident, but it may be wrong about your network, your risk, and your overall resilience.

That gives us two failure modes. The first is overreach, where a harness sees or changes more than it should. The second is under-grounding, where it fills the gaps with guesses. Most AI risk discussions focus on the first. In my experience, the second is the one that quietly erodes trust.

Bringing your own harness (BYOH) also means choosing where the customer’s context travels; which model provider sees it, and under what terms, is a decision the partner and the customer should make together, not one the harness makes by default.

In other words, trusted context has become part of the security perimeter.

Where Cisco IQ Fits

During Cisco Partner Summit 2026, Liz Centoni explained why Cisco IQ is the engine and partners are the business. Vikas Butaney described the new partner operating model it enables. Bhaskar Jayakrishnan covered Cisco IQ’s design and associated principles. Here, I want to look at the pattern around it: What happens when partners bring their own harnesses, and what it means for how they work.

This is where I see Cisco IQ playing the role of trusted context for BYOH when it comes to Cisco partners. The parallel with BYOD holds up closely:

Table 1: The BYOD to BYOH parallel

With the APIs and MCP capabilities announced at Cisco Partner Summit (shown in use in Figures 1 and 2), a Cisco partner can bring their own harness to a customer project, a services proposal, or a support engagement, and connect it to generate personalized insight from Cisco IQ. The harness does not need to guess the facts. It can ask, and Cisco IQ answers with information grounded in that customer’s environment, but only the information the Cisco partner is allowed to see (as granted by the customer). Reading and changing are separate permissions, so a harness can be given the right to ask without the right to act.

Figure 1: Cisco IQ API Reference (top) and Object Explorer (bottom), showing the areas available via API and MCP Server.

Figure 2: Cisco IQ MCP Server in the open-source MCP Inspector. Each tool declares whether it reads or changes data. This account has write rights. Read-only roles see only the discover, describe, and query tools.

A typical baseline for a Cisco partner project is to understand the installed base of Cisco assets (devices and components) in a customer environment. Cisco IQ provides that trusted context upfront, from where a partner can check if some of that installed base is without support coverage and, if so, whether there is exposure to critical security vulnerabilities, increasing the customer’s risk profile even further.

Here’s an example of how the BYOH approach with Cisco IQ helps a Cisco partner with the first step in that chain (Figure 3). We have an internal demo account in the Cisco IQ production environment, which our teams use to validate and demo scenarios like this. The Cisco IQ UI shows that around 59% of the assets in that account are without support coverage, and you can click through to the full list and details.

In the example below, we leverage BYOH with Cisco IQ and ask the same question in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor: “Out of my IQ Prod environment (available via Cisco IQ MCP server, XRE account), what’s the percentage of all assets (devices and components) without support coverage as of today?”

Figure 3: The same question asked from Claude Code (in VS Code), Codex and Cursor (left to right), each answered from Cisco IQ through the MCP Server. The models used appear in each screenshot.

The point of Figure 3 is not the answer itself. All three harnesses arrived at around 59%, because they all drew from the same trusted Cisco IQ context. What differed was how they got there. Each harness and model reasoned its own way through the data and raised its own observations along the way. For the partner, that means different insights on the same facts, and new perspectives to enrich the proposal and the engagement with the customer.

MCP matters here because it is an open standard, not a Cisco invention. This way, partners are not locked into one AI vendor to work with Cisco IQ, and they can switch harnesses and AI models as the field moves.

The partner chooses the harness. Cisco IQ provides the trusted context and the guardrails. Together, they let a partner move from reacting to customer requests to acting proactively, before the customer asks, with advice shaped by that customer’s own environment, rather than generic best practice.

What I Would Do As A Partner

Three suggestions, from an architecture point of view.

Find out which harnesses your own teams already use. BYOH is probably already happening in your organization. It’s better to design for it than to discover it.

Start with read-only. Let harnesses ask questions of Cisco IQ as a trusted context source before you let them change anything. Earn the right to automate.

Treat trusted context as an asset. The value of a harness is limited by the quality of what it can reach. Customers will judge your AI work as a Cisco partner by how grounded it is, not by which model you picked.

BYOH will move faster than BYOD did. And for Cisco partners, it is less of a risk to contain than a flexibility to use. Your people keep the harness, and the models, they are most productive with. Cisco IQ gives that harness the customer’s real context, under the customer’s rules. That combination is what makes proactive and personalized service possible at the partner scale.

And if you want a place to start, the Cisco Builders Challenge kicks off early next year to reward partners who build new managed services on Cisco IQ. Bringing your own harness is a good way to build them.

ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay without seeing your card number
articles.context: Luke Gebb, who heads global innovation at American Express, called the wallet the company’s “first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration
articles.full_text:
OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Wallet, which lets ChatGPT agents pay for purchases with a stand-in card number, so the user’s card details are not shared with the agent or the merchant. OpenAI built it with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa. It runs inside dots, where a user’s dot completes the purchase on their behalf.

Merchants will have to do most of the adjusting. OpenAI says some websites may block agent purchases without meaning to, and fraud systems may flag legitimate ones, which ends in declines or cancellations. A retailer that tuned its defenses to stop automated checkout now has to tell wanted bots from unwanted ones.

How a purchase goes through

A user adds a card once. Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, the total, and the chosen card, then approves with Face ID, a fingerprint, or a similar check. The payment network then issues a token, which is a substitute card number with its own security code and expiration date, and the charge lands on the real card behind it. The card keeps its rewards and its protections for eligible disputes.

What sites need to fix

OpenAI published a Commerce Partner Playbook alongside the launch. It asks sites to set their CDN or firewall to recognize Web Bot Auth, a method for verifying signed requests from bots. It also asks them to work with their payment and risk providers on spotting agent purchases. OpenAI is working with the fraud vendors Forter, Riskified, Sardine, and Signifyd, and with the payment providers Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe. The tokens work with existing checkout flows. The risk engines sitting in front of those flows may still say no.

Luke Gebb, who heads global innovation at American Express, called the wallet the company’s “first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration.” For now, access is limited to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US who are 18 or older and hold eligible US-issued cards.
