articles.title: KnowBe4 and AWS: Behind Every AI Advancement Is Strong Collaboration
articles.context: What a Strong Foundation Makes Possible The results of the AWS collaboration brings these concrete benefits to our engineering teams and ultimately our customers: 1
articles.full_text:
Delivering AI-native security awareness training through the KnowBe4 Platform to more than 70,000 users means collaboration.

Collaboration takes many forms. Our people working together. Our departments working together. And as KnowBe4 has grown, our infrastructure, DevOps, and site reliability engineering teams have collaborated with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to streamline architectural improvements that support changing demand and simplify data sharing across products.

The Problem

As a recent AWS case study explores, the sheer size of the global employee base using KnowBe4 Security Awareness Training could lead to processing delays and backlogs. Usage peaks came at the start of the week, the month, and the business day, across the United States, Europe, and Southeast Asia.

Our engineers needed a centralized infrastructure channel to manage communication across all components and locations, enabling greater reliability and more robust integration capabilities for our customers.

What a Strong Foundation Makes Possible

The results of the AWS collaboration brings these concrete benefits to our engineering teams and ultimately our customers:

1. Two features reached production three months ahead of schedule.

2. Dozens of AI projects are now in development, each run by teams of two to four engineers supported by AI coding agents.

3. Engineering productivity on net-new development is up to 10x what it was 12-24 months ago.

Long story short: Streamlined infrastructure means lean and recurring innovation directed straight at our customers and their users.

This foundation also supports AIDA Orchestration, our autonomous AI agents that generate and deliver personalized security awareness training and personalized phishing simulations across your entire workforce, without the need for human administration.

"Building on AWS helps us ship new risk indicators faster," says Matt Duren, SVP of Engineering for AI and Data. "We're at 316 today, and the number keeps growing every year."

Keeping AI development within AWS helps our engineers get started quickly and use common development patterns across model providers. The KnowBe4 team also reinforces continuous learning through an internal certification program with incentives for engineers to earn associate-level certification within their first 12 months.

AWS AI Competency: Proof Takes a Team

Results like these are what the AWS AI Competency, recently awarded to KnowBe4, exists to recognize. The designation honors AWS Partners that demonstrate technical proficiency and proven customer success building on foundation models to automate domain-specific work.

Earning it is a collaboration of its own. The process requires a valid AWS Foundational Technical Review, evidence of AI technical controls, including a documented Responsible AI framework, and four production customer examples from the past 18 months, at least two of them public. KnowBe4's engineering, security assurance, alliance marketing, and business development teams pulled that evidence together alongside AWS partner and solutions architect counterparts.

A credential like this is a record of people on both sides asking hard questions and sharing what they know.

The Real Lesson

AWS secures the infrastructure. KnowBe4 helps secure the humans and AI agents operating within it. That is the shared-responsibility model in practice, and it only works when both sides show up.

No single vendor has all the answers, especially as AI changes how attackers and defenders work. The organizations moving fastest pair deep expertise with trusted partners.

articles.title: Microsoft Struggles to Restore Email and Other Services in a Global Outage
articles.context: “They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack
articles.full_text:
From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue.

Microsoft said the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements,” and that there was “incremental improvement in several workloads.” But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company’s services and anecdotal reports on social media.

Microsoft scrambles to recover services

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.”

The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control.

Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.

An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution.

“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote.

In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”

“Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.”

Governments, businesses from Japan to Australia affected

The British government said it is “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” are in place to minimize disruption.

British police forces said they’re unable to receive crime reports online and are urging people to call emergency responders to make any urgent reports.

The National Pharmacy Association said people could face delays getting their prescriptions because the outage is affecting the email systems of the state-run National Health Service. Hospitals urged patients to attend appointments as usual.

U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.

Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

“They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company could not receive updates from its U.S. customers throughout Outlook. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.

Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

The Philippines’ Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that officials were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

articles.title: Liz Centoni: 'Users are an essential part of the technology stack'

articles.full_text:
That gets you to start rethinking the workflow, Centoni says, since throughout most of Cisco’s history, the approach to customer engagements was to throw experts at a problem. The more complex the engagement, the more experts were needed. For customers, the priority was getting the job done correctly but as quickly as possible, yet the availability of expert engineers throttled Cisco’s ability to speed up the process.

“When I came into this business, we treated every customer we had like a bespoke model,” Centoni says. “But over the last 40-plus years, we’ve solved these problems tens of thousands of times.”

Cisco has taken 40 years of engagements to build a knowledge base and a series of playbooks that AI agents and human experts can use to help customers plan and execute deployments. Cisco can now take the information they have about a customer, including their KPIs for a project, and customize its value realization without needing to include a lot of human experts on top.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Outage Set to Ramp up Security Risks to Organizations
articles.context: ), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted
articles.full_text:
While the global outage of Microsoft 365 services that interact with Exchange Online, significantly Outlook, is not believed to be cyber-related, security teams will need to be on high alert for threats related to the incident.

As the tech behemoth grapples with the fix, cybercriminals will be poised to take advantage of the chaos by launching a surge of convincing phishing campaigns and fake support scams designed to dupe individuals and employees desperate to reconnect to M365 services.

Marie Wilcox, VP of market strategy at digital forensics firm Binalyze, said, “Just because this outage wasn’t caused by a cyber-attack, doesn’t mean attackers won’t seize the opportunity.”

In an update on November 13, the Australian National Cyber Security Coordinator Michelle McGuiness warned people to “remain vigilant and be cautious of unsolicited contact” as cybercriminals often seek to take advantage of the uncertainty.

Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre issued an update recommending everyone exercises caution around unexpected calls and messages, especially those containing links.

It is likely that threat actors will begin to send phishing messages, claiming to be the Microsoft brand in order to trick people in this time of uncertainty.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Jake Moore, Global Cybersecurity Advisor at ESET, said that this kind of disruption is the perfect excuse for cybercriminals to hit organizations with targeted calls posing as IT support.

“Affected employees are literally waiting by the phone (or scrolling on social media!), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted.

Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, said that affected businesses like banks and shops should be particularly vigilant.

“Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email,” he said.

Microsoft is one of the brands most leveraged by threat actors for phishing campaigns. In an October update, cybersecurity firm Check Point noted that in Q3 2026 Microsoft accounted for 33% of all brand phishing attempts, up from 23% in Q2 2026 and roughly four times the share of any other brand.

Read more: Phishing Dominates as Initial Entry Method for Cyber-Attacks, as Hackers Hone Evasion Techniques

Defenders Should Treat Outage as Security Incident

Binalyze’s Wilcox said that many security teams themselves will have been locked out of tools they depend on to prevent trouble, for example Microsoft Defender XDR or important alerts pushed via Outlook.

She noted that when email services return and workers are beginning to clear the day’s backlog, this is when they will be most susceptible to trusting any messages that looks like they came from Microsoft – especially fake security updates.

During the outage period it will also be easy for suspicious activity to go unnoticed while alerts were not being monitored as usual.

“A suspicious sign-in or a new inbox forwarding rule is easy to miss when everyone is focused on getting email back,” she said.

“The wisest approach is for security teams to treat the outage window as an incident in its own right. That means going back over sign-ins, mailbox rules, account changes and endpoint activity from the hours when visibility dropped, and collecting evidence directly from devices rather than relying on the platform that was down,” Wilcox advised.

At the time of writing, Microsoft’s latest update said recovery efforts are ongoing across the impacted infrastructure. “We are seeing early signs of stabilization, but service capacity has not yet returned to normal levels and health remains variable as traffic is carefully reintroduced.”

articles.title: When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?
articles.context: The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect
articles.full_text:
Suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action.

That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls.

An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents.

Turning off the model may not stop the work

An AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect.

The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received.

That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services.

When should a team contain an agent?

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context.

Signals that warrant a closer look include:

The agent calls a tool or accesses a resource outside its assigned task.

It attempts an unusual volume of reads, writes or exports.

A workflow continues after an operator believes it has been paused.

The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect.

Identity, application or network logs show activity that does not match the agent’s normal work.

The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded.

A practical response sequence

1. Pause the affected workflow

Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely.

A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow.

2. Revoke or limit the agent’s access

Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used.

Revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire quickly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it.

3. Restrict tools and network paths

Disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues.

This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations.

4. Preserve evidence and establish what happened

Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs.

Then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions.

5. Contain downstream effects

If the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes.

Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed.

Restore access carefully

Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy.

Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution.

Prepare before the incident

An incident response plan is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know:

Who owns it and who can suspend its runs.

Which identity, credentials, tools and systems it can use.

How to revoke its access and block its network connections.

Which logs show its actions and the results.

How to investigate changes and restore the workflow safely.

Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event.

An effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows.

With Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

articles.title: Apple details Secure Exclaves, isolated runtimes for camera and microphone data
articles.context: In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system
articles.full_text:
Apple published details of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture designed to protect camera and microphone data during background processing. Apple says data processed and analyzed within Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or the company itself.

The company uses Secure Exclaves for person recognition on HomeView, as well as for Siri Recap and Live Rewind. The architecture also protects the on-screen camera and microphone indicators on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators on MacBook Neo and HomeView.

Protecting background sensing

Ambient sensing uses the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. It reduces sensor streams to simple signals, such as whether a specific sound was detected or an enrolled user was recognized. During ambient sensing, raw audio and video remain protected within Secure Exclaves and are discarded once processing is complete, without reaching the main operating system.

The architecture supports two modes. In ambient mode, sensors respond to particular triggers in their surroundings, but only specific metadata can be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data can be released to the main operating system, with a secure indicator informing the user that this is happening.

Apple built the isolated environment around three requirements. Isolation prevents the main operating system from extracting or modifying data processed within Secure Exclaves. A controlled interface limits what can cross that boundary to a precisely defined set of information. Secure indication lets users see whether an active sensor session is in progress, without interference from the main operating system.

“Building a new secure runtime requires a highly secure OS foundation. For this reason, we utilized an Apple-customized version of the L4 microkernel which we originally built for some of our most security-sensitive deployments, including the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP),” Apple explained.

The microkernel uses capabilities, which are secure resource handles that identify a resource and authorize access to it.

The exclaves run in a separate processor execution context with an independent operating system. The Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), which runs at a higher privilege level than the main operating system’s kernel, enforces memory isolation.

Exclaves communicate through Secure IPC. Apple audits each interface to the main operating system to limit outgoing information to the metadata needed for ambient sensing.

The Exclave Indicator Controller allows full sensor data to flow to the main operating system only after confirming that the indicator is on and has been visible long enough. On HomeView, it controls the LED directly and ensures that it is bright enough to be visible. On iPhone, a display exclave checks that the pixels used to render the indicator meet a minimum brightness threshold and are not obscured by nearby pixels.

How HomeView recognizes people

At startup, the person recognition exclave loads enrolled face and voice models and an identity database from the secure storage exclave.

Person recognition flow on HomeView (Source: Apple)

The camera exclave detects faces and queues frames for processing, while audio exclaves handle anomaly detection and echo cancellation. They can notify the main operating system that someone may be present without sharing images or audio.

The Neural Engine exclave generates face and voice prints using isolated work queues, clearing its state after each model finishes. An orchestration service matches the prints against the identity database and combines the results into a confidence score.

Only the person’s identifier, position, and confidence level reach the person recognition daemon in the main operating system. These outputs support identity-dependent features in Calendar, Messages, Apple Music, and compatible third-party audio and video apps from an iPhone. No audio or video leaves Secure Exclaves during recognition.

What comes next

Apple said it will continue hardening Secure Exclaves through AI-accelerated vulnerability research and broader formal verification coverage. The company described the architecture as a step toward giving users greater clarity and confidence about how their Apple products respond to the world around them.

articles.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
articles.context: This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem
articles.full_text: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

articles.title: Microsoft confirms Windows activation failures after November updates
articles.context: While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates are causing Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes.

According to a Wednesday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation and licensing processes or use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter (SWbemObjectEx), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said.

"Devices that are being configured to use KMS activation might encounter errors when attempting to initiate their activation. KMS-activated devices typically remain activated for up to 180 days following successful activation."

The activation failures occur after executing the 'slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain>' and 'slmgr.vbs /ipk <key>' commands on client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) devices.

However, Microsoft added that customers with the KMS client key installed in their image and who don't use SLMGR for licensing management are unaffected.

"Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted.

While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business.

In January, Microsoft addressed another known issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because affected devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses.

This week, it also confirmed that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues.

articles.title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
articles.context: Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it
articles.full_text:
On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.”

Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure.

The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead?

A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled

Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop.

It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works.

Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue.

That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself.

The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path.

What a fallback has to do

I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover, patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name.

Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then.

The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live.

The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them.

Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals.

The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope.

How I’d build fallback-first today

If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live.

A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident.

A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it.

Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns.

A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it.

Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day.

None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone.

Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull.

Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

articles.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
articles.context: (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027
articles.full_text: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel. Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post. The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language. Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”) ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final. According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices. They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts. Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology. Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

articles.title: Suspected North Korean IT workers reached onboarding at companies with open data
articles.context: Over the year, 2,429 of them made contact, 1,100 reached an interview or later, and 27 reached onboarding, meaning offer letters, background checks, equipment requests, or...
articles.full_text:
Material Security followed suspected North Korean fake IT workers through the hiring pipelines of organizations it monitors and counted 27 personas that reached onboarding over one year. At one company where a persona got that far in the past month, about 277,000 files containing Social Security numbers were shared company-wide or by public link.

The personas are fabricated job seekers, complete with résumés and faces, applying for remote engineering roles. Over the year, 2,429 of them made contact, 1,100 reached an interview or later, and 27 reached onboarding, meaning offer letters, background checks, equipment requests, or first-day IT setup. That is roughly one in 90, a small share, but any of the 27 who received credentials walked in trusted, provisioned, and hostile from day one.

The same face at many companies

The researchers saw 41% of personas at more than one organization. Fifteen appeared at ten or more, and one appeared at 19. Of the 27 that reached onboarding, 18 were in process elsewhere at the same time, and one was finishing onboarding paperwork at one company while chasing jobs at seven others.

What the new accounts could reach

In the past 30 days, 232 suspected personas contacted 99 organizations. At 42 of them, at least one moved on to an interview or offer, and at four, a persona reached onboarding. Material inventoried the sensitive files at those four.

The first held about 15 million source-code files and 130,000 files with bank or routing numbers, shared with almost no one beyond their owners. The second held around 400,000 files with Social Security numbers and 345,000 with bank or routing numbers, and 68% of the Social Security files and 71% of the bank files were open to any account in the company or to anyone with a link. A new hire there would have needed nothing more than a login. The third had about 14 million source-code files, roughly 1,900 of them readable by anyone with the URL. The fourth, the smallest, held about 1.5 million source-code files plus files with private cryptographic keys, and 21% of its financial files and 17% of its credit-card files were shared beyond their owners.

What employers should do

Material recommends pairing hiring controls with access controls, since a North Korean hire who gets through holds valid credentials.

Flag personas early. Connect recruiting and onboarding signals with threat intelligence, so you can stop a fake identity before it gets credentials.

Check identities closely. Background checks are a chance to catch a fabricated persona. Follow up on anything that doesn’t line up.

Triage by stage. A watchlist hit during onboarding is more urgent than one at first contact. Confirm the identity and the evidence, then check whether an account or equipment has already been issued.

Keep investigating after onboarding. If an account exists, review its permissions, app grants, and activity.

Map access before you need it. Know which files, messages, credentials, and connected apps each role can reach, so responders know where to look first.

articles.title: Your pinned MCP server may not be as pinned as you think
articles.context: James Lagermann, Director of Technical Alliances at Corelight, found the drift in his company’s lab
articles.full_text:
An MCP server configured to run one fixed release on an administrator’s workstation ran with 15 different sets of dependencies over five weeks, with its configuration untouched. James Lagermann, Director of Technical Alliances at Corelight, found the drift in his company’s lab. Twenty-three of the server’s 69 packages changed versions, including the cryptography library, the JSON Web Token library and the MCP software development kit itself.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers let AI coding assistants act on other tools for a user, so they often hold that user’s credentials. On this workstation, the servers made more than 1,600 connections in a week to 11 management systems, including the firewall, the SIEM and sensor management. Code that slips into any of their dependencies runs with that access.

The pin didn’t hold

The assistants started their servers with uvx, a launcher that downloads a Python package and runs it from one line of configuration. Each entry named an exact release tag, PyPI version or Git commit. For one community server, the launcher installed from the package’s declared dependencies and skipped the project’s hash-pinned lock file, so the roughly 60 packages underneath were resolved fresh from the Python Package Index whenever the environment was rebuilt. Pinning a package’s version doesn’t necessarily pin the packages it depends on.

The assistant started one server 162 times in a week. Most launches reused a cached environment, but the cache still held 19 builds of the same release and commit, about one every couple of days. That cadence matters because a hijacked release can be live for only minutes or hours. In June 2026, a Shai-Hulud worm variant on PyPI hit MCP-themed packages and went after AI coding assistant keys.

The same pattern in the field

Corelight reviewed 35 MCP servers from two vendor catalogs and its lab. Twenty-three had a recommended install that would pull dependencies from a public registry on every launch, or on each install or image build.

Lagermann told Help Net Security he sees the same thing in the field. “I have seen the same pattern in customer environments and in other real-world deployments. So far, 100% of administrators that I’ve talked to were using at least one MCP Server with this issue.”

Freezing works, and someone has to keep it current

Corelight froze five servers: pinned to a commit, installed once from a hash-pinned lock file, launched directly, update checks off. Over the next two weeks the five were started 457 times, and each one’s installed package list matched the list recorded on install day.

Frozen code ages. When the team froze one community server, 40 of its packages were older than what the launcher would have pulled that day, some of them security-sensitive. Asked how often to re-lock, Lagermann said: “I would recommend following the MCP maintainers’ recommendation for updates. The MCP Servers I maintain are reviewed nightly for vulnerabilities. If one is found, it’s updated the next morning, with a change log.”

“For the 23 public MCP servers that I found, I notified the maintainers and/or services that share them. As a result, one company that hosts an AI agent exchange has updated its security review processes to evaluate submissions for this issue. In another case, the vendor is completely repackaging their MCP server,” Lagermann said.

Any MCP entry started by a Python or npm package runner, or tagged “latest,” can resolve new code from a public registry the next time an assistant opens a session. On Corelight’s workstation, the server’s version number stayed the same through all 15 environments.

Download: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl

articles.title: Digital sovereignty leaves enterprises chasing their own audit trails
articles.context: The report defines digital sovereignty as an organization’s ability to retain control and provide credible evidence of that control across critical AI, technology, operations...
articles.full_text:
94% of surveyed enterprises experienced at least one digital sovereignty challenge in the past three years, according to IBM’s Digital Sovereignty Index. Of those affected, 91% were required to demonstrate that they retained control during their most challenging event, and 81% had to provide formal evidence to regulators, auditors, customers or internal stakeholders.

The report defines digital sovereignty as an organization’s ability to retain control and provide credible evidence of that control across critical AI, technology, operations and data. Across these four pillars, it assesses six dimensions: responsibility, trace, constraint, intervention, exit and legitimacy.

Accountability and exit capabilities need testing

Across the six dimensions, an average of 82% of respondents were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of control. The index placed 26% of enterprises in its highest maturity tier, Leading Digital Sovereignty.

Ability of organizations to demonstrate evidence (Source: IBM)

Manual evidence collection was a barrier for 56% of respondents. Fragmented records, dependence on third parties for information, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards were each cited by 53%.

“When a business issue turns into a sovereignty risk, boards need to show real control: how they can adapt, change strategy or critical provider – where freedom to act lies. The choices they make today matter, and the stakes are high. Getting this right can help them minimize shocks, keep their options open and stay competitive,” said Jonathan Adashek, IBM Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer.

Responsibility had the largest gap between confidence and evidence across all four pillars.

During their most challenging sovereignty incident, 33% of enterprises reported being able to demonstrate exit fully and credibly, without significant follow-up. This includes the ability to replace a provider, model or system while maintaining business continuity.

AI tests enterprise sovereignty

AI-related issues affected 44% of respondents, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns.

Formal audit or regulatory events affected 38%, significant provider changes 35%, and data-access or transfer issues 33%. Government restrictions were reported by 30%. AI received the lowest score for evidence of control.

“Organisations need to be able to demonstrate where their data comes from, how it can be used, and what controls are in place,” said Debbie Lawrence, Group Head Of Data Strategy and Management at LSEG.

AI-dependent business processes require records showing what systems did, which data they used, who authorized their actions and who remained accountable. IBM recommends keeping this evidence current and accessible as systems and dependencies change.

Restrictions imposed by an external authority or provider can also affect access to an AI model, and an enterprise may need an alternative model or provider with different performance or behavior.

Continuous testing or testing through regular governance and assurance processes was reported by 63% of enterprises in the highest tier and 9% in the lowest tier. Enterprises in the highest tier reported fewer barriers to producing evidence. They were also more likely to resolve their most challenging sovereignty incident without material disruption.

articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Friday, November 13, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. This episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Bachelor's Degree Program in Applied Cybersecurity. Well and in diaries today I wrote up some attacks that we're seeing against GPUStack. GPUStack is a system that allows you to essentially make available clusters of GPU for AI workloads. As often these proxies that are in front of some of these systems have their issues and that's again sort of what hits us here. Now in this particular case we do have a special header that's being added by the proxy X-GPUStack-Real-IP. Many other proxies have similar headers and they always come with the big caveat, well it's possible for an attacker to spoof those headers. In this particular case if an attacker spoofs that the real IP is the loopback IP address, well in that case the attacker is being given access to the system and allowed to bypass authentication. So very straightforward to exploit vulnerability. Makes you wonder why it took them so long to really scan for it on a larger scale. No idea how many of these systems are actually exposed. Now a little bit tricky to sort of date this vulnerability. Apparently the fixed version of GPUStack was released back in July. The actual CVE number appears to have been assigned about a week ago. So I guess anywhere sort of in that time frame. There was also a GitHub page that had details about this vulnerability that's also sort of a couple months old. Again exploitation is trivial. No real sort of exploit really required. Just that specific header and of course an exposed system. And ConnectWise released another ScreenConnect security advisory. Now this one is less about a specific vulnerability in ScreenConnect, but more about an ongoing security investigation that ConnectWise is running given the compromise of some of their customer and partner sites. So they're looking currently at 400 compromised environments. They think they have it narrowed down to a number of third party plugins that may be responsible for some of these issues. And they disabled them now. Not really clear what the user is supposed to do here other than making sure that you do have the latest ScreenConnect client. That's version 26.6.5. That particular version does also fix a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself that is still being employed by these compromises in order to then further spread malware and compromise additional systems in your network. Remember ScreenConnect is often used by support functions to actually reach out to remote systems. And that's essentially sort of what they are abusing here. Definitely make sure that you're up to date and also take a look at this latest advisory from ConnectWise as it has additional details as to what to look for in your particular environment as well as the list of the third party extensions. And that have now been disabled. And while I already talked twice in the last week about N-able and about the patches that were released now and that are available to patch vulnerabilities that sort of had been made public without first notifying N-able. We now have exploits publicly available for at least three of these vulnerabilities. There is a GitHub repository that has the code for these. I haven't verified them yet. So as always treat them with caution. Never really know what they are doing and haven't really looked at them close enough to tell you that they're safe to the person running them. But if you're running N-able definitely you must upgrade at this point. It's kind of at the point where you probably want to assume compromise if you have an exposed unpatched N-able system connected. And Microsoft today had a significant availability event where good parts of Microsoft 365 were not reachable. This did affect Exchange, Outlook, lots and lots of different parts of Microsoft 365 that were not available.
