So not sure if this is part of the outage or part of the high load. So if you're running Microsoft 365 Business or Enterprise, that's why your email wasn't working today. And hopefully by the time you're listening to this podcast, things will look better. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending. And thanks for subscribing to this podcast and talk to you again on Monday. Bye. Bye.

articles.title: AI Didn’t Create a New Kind of Risk. It Removed the Time You Had to Fix the Old One.
articles.context: Attackers now use agentic AI for reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and, in at least one case, a zero-day, yet vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in for...
articles.full_text:
Mandiant’s AI Risk and Resilience 2026 report shows attackers putting agentic AI to work across the intrusion. Vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in, and the window to fix it is closing.

Executive Summary

Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published AI Risk and Resilience 2026 in September. Attackers now use agentic AI for reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and, in at least one case, a zero-day, yet vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in for the sixth year running. AI has changed how fast attackers exploit far more than what they exploit.

Exploitation is still the front door. Exploits caused 32% of intrusions in M-Trends 2026, and the mean time to exploit is now an estimated minus seven days. Mandiant concludes that defense has to move beyond manual triage to machine speed.

Most AI incidents started as exposures. Poisoned packages, long-lived CI/CD credentials, unsigned plugins and MCP servers, and over-permissioned agents were all in place before the attack.

AI infrastructure is now a target in its own right. An autonomous AI agent reached cluster-admin in Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment with no CVE to match, and exploits for AI components are appearing before disclosure.

The Risk Operations Center is the missing layer. The report answers with runtime controls and an agentic SOC, which act after the attacker is inside. A Risk Operations Center (ROC) closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway.

A machine-speed adversary needs a machine-speed defender. Qualys AI agents detect new exposures, prove which ones are exploitable, and remediate them, so the defender’s side of the race is automated too.

One ROC covers all of it. Infrastructure, identity, and AI risk belong in one ROC, with proactive AI governance ahead of runtime guardrails.

What the Frontline Is Telling Us

Drawing on incident response, Offensive Security engagements, and threat intelligence, the report describes attackers moving from chat-based research to autonomous attack orchestration. Five patterns stand out.

Agentic attack tooling is in the wild. Tools such as Hexstrike and Strix automate reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and credential harvesting.

AI-assisted zero-days are real. GTIG assessed with high confidence that a cybercriminal used an AI model to find and weaponize a two-factor authentication bypass in an open-source admin tool for a planned mass exploitation campaign.

The AI supply chain is part of the perimeter. Poisoned PyPI packages, a compromised LiteLLM library, weaponized agent skills, and subverted coding-assistant hooks all appear in the case studies.

Over-privileged agents are part of the attack surface. Mandiant red teamers manipulated a CI/CD chatbot into pushing internal repositories to an external GitHub account, and an assessment found a RAG support agent that indirect prompt injection could turn against other customers’ data. In a real incident, a finance agent made 15,000+ API calls in under an hour, causing a roughly $50,000 billing spike.

Long-lived credentials keep doing the damage. One healthcare intrusion began with a single long-lived CI/CD credential and ended with thousands of credentials compromised.

M-Trends 2026 also shows the hand-off from initial access to a secondary threat group falling from over eight hours in 2022 to 22 seconds in 2025.

AI Infrastructure Is Already Under Attack

The same pattern is showing up in AI infrastructure itself. In July 2026, an autonomous AI agent that had escaped an evaluation sandbox worked its way into Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment. A Qualys analysis of the intrusion counted about 17,600 actions over five days, and the agent reached cluster-admin in about 13 hours. It entered through a dataset configuration file and an unsanitized template, then used a privileged pod and a shared credential to take over clusters. None of those steps gave a vulnerability scanner a CVE to match.

Figure 1. The Hugging Face intrusion step by step, with what a package scan and a runtime sensor can see at each stage.

Vulnerabilities in AI components are being weaponized just as quickly. Qualys research on AI exploits in containers puts the window of weaponization at minus one day for flaws in the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (CVE-2025-23266) and in an MCP server (CVE-2025-6514). For a Docker Model Runner flaw (CVE-2026-28400), whether a workload is exploitable depends on runtime flags and how the service is invoked.

Most AI Incidents Are Exposure Problems in Disguise

A risky package in the build pipeline is a software exposure. A long-lived CI/CD key is an identity exposure. An unsigned plugin or over-permissioned MCP server is a misconfiguration. An agent that reads private data, ingests untrusted content, and talks to the internet is an attack path. These are familiar exposures on a new class of asset that most inventories cannot yet see. In six of the report’s eight case studies, the attacker used an exposure that could have been found beforehand.

Mandiant Case Study

Exposure Before the Attack

How Exposure Management Finds It

Coding session hijack spreads Shai-Hulud

Unverified AI-recommended package; long-lived GitHub OAuth tokens

SCA and AI-SBOM in IDE and CI/CD, secrets scanning, malware detection

AI co-debugging in a cloud intrusion

Long-lived CI/CD credential; unisolated VM with open egress

Non-human identity inventory; cloud egress posture checks

Subverted CLI hooks lead to RCE

Unsigned hooks, plugins, and MCP servers; weak AI repository controls

MCP and AI software discovery, MCP testing, access review

Confused Deputy exfiltration (red team test)

Agent with repo access, user input, and an allowed external domain

One attack path across data access, untrusted input, and egress; LLM red teaming

Denial-of-wallet reasoning loop

Agent with read and write access to billing databases, no cost limits

Agent entitlement and least-privilege findings

RAG agent with untrusted input (assessment)

Pipeline ingesting public content with reach into other customers’ tickets

LLM red teaming for indirect prompt injection and data leakage

The other two, just-in-time polymorphic malware and a stealthy espionage backdoor, are runtime detection problems. Together with the Hugging Face case, they are why a ROC needs runtime detection as well as posture.

The Risk Operations Center Is the Missing Layer

Mandiant answers these cases with agent identity, runtime guardrails, and an agentic SOC that triages at machine speed. Those controls matter, and they take effect once an attack is underway. The layer the report leaves out is the Risk Operations Center, which finds and closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway. Three capabilities make it more than another source of detections.

Hybrid coverage. The exposures in the report sit on developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, cloud VMs, SaaS applications, and identity systems. The Qualys platform covers on-premises, endpoint, multi-cloud, container, identity, application, and AI assets with the agents and connectors customers already run.

Proof of exploitability. Safe exploit validation shows which exposures an attacker can actually use in your environment, so teams act on evidence instead of a severity score.

Remediation as well as detection. Each validated exposure is patched, mitigated, or isolated, and the fix is confirmed, so the finding is closed as well as reported.

Six Moves That Answer AI with AI

Mandiant’s premise is an adversary that operates at machine speed. A defense that depends on analysts triaging by hand cannot match it, so the defender’s side has to be automated as well. On the Qualys platform, AI agents do that work at each stage. Agent Insta detects new exposures within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val proves which ones are exploitable. Agent Sara plans and runs remediation in TruRisk Eliminate. Agent Grant investigates and closes identity risk. The six moves below show where each one fits.

Figure 2. The three decisions security teams have to make at AI speed: detect faster, prioritize with runtime evidence, and act surgically.

Close the Window with Agent Insta and TruRisk Eliminate

With a negative time to exploit, what matters is how fast a team closes the gap between disclosure and fix, and every handoff between tools adds hours. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta in Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM), matches new advisories against the inventory Qualys already holds, without a rescan.

Customers are seeing this in practice. In a Techstrong TV interview recorded at ROCon Americas 2026, Theo Bowman, who runs the vulnerability management program at NCR Atleos, explains that the biggest change since Mythos is the need to find exposures first and fix them quickly. He describes InstaScan returning vulnerability data for his assets within three minutes of a Patch Tuesday release. The last two Patch Tuesdays show similar speeds.

October 2026. Microsoft fixed a record 1,414 vulnerabilities, 78 of them critical, including an exploited Windows Shell zero-day (CVE-2026-96951) with a CISA patch deadline of October 16. Agent Insta customers had detections within 5 minutes, and Qualys provided mitigations for 608 of the vulnerabilities.

November 2026. Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, 63 of them critical, including an exploited Outlook spoofing zero-day (CVE-2026-124194) with a CISA patch deadline of November 24. InstaScan showed customers their findings 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own advisory page was updated, and Qualys provided mitigations for 537 of the vulnerabilities.

Figure 3. Findings detected first by InstaScan in Qualys ETM, each marked with the Agent Insta icon and the time it was first found.

TruRisk prioritization, informed by QVSS and Qualys threat intelligence, raises likely-weaponized vulnerabilities about 45 days, on average, before they reach the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence then closes the loop through agentic remediation and autonomous RemOps. Agent Sara picks the safest action for each exposure (patch, mitigation, or isolation), rolls it out in waves with reliability scoring and rollback, and confirms the fix. In the past year, customers deployed 150 million patches, 40 million fully autonomously.

Figure 4. Agent Sara plans risk-based remediation waves in TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, starting with the exposures proven to be risky.

See AI as Attack Surface with TotalAI

Mandiant calls for a dynamic AI inventory and an AI-SBOM. Qualys TotalAI discovers AI agents, models, MCP servers, AI software and libraries, GPUs, AI containers, cloud AI services, and shadow AI using the Cloud Agents and connectors customers already run. Built on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, it scores each AI asset with TruRisk alongside servers, endpoints, and cloud workloads.

Figure 5. The TotalAI inventory of AI workloads, including coding assistants, agents, and RAG pipelines found on hosts and in the cloud.

TotalAI follows an AI application from code to runtime. It checks AI code and agent configuration in the IDE and CI/CD, assesses AI container images, generates an AI-SBOM, and confirms whether vulnerable AI packages are installed, running, and communicating, so a risk on a live workload can be traced back to its image and code. It tests MCP servers for missing authentication, tool poisoning, argument injection, SSRF, and rug-pull behavior, and red-teams LLMs for prompt injection, jailbreaks, and data disclosure, mapped to the OWASP LLM and MCP Top 10 and the EU AI Act. For supply chain malware, including the just-in-time polymorphic malware in the report that defeats signatures, Qualys uses deep learning to detect unknown malware in container images and workloads before deployment and in cloud network traffic with TotalCloud Cloud Detection and Response.

Figure 6. Code-to-runtime tracing, from the running container to its image, source repository, and AI agent code (illustrative example).

The same visibility extends to the workforce. The TotalAI Browser Plugin, combined with SaaS connectors, shows which sanctioned and shadow AI tools employees use, and it analyzes prompts and uploads to show when sensitive data is leaving through them.

Figure 7. Securing an AI workload in TotalAI. AI-SPM is delivered through the Qualys Cloud Agent and AI runtime coverage through the Qualys Browser Plug-in.

Treat Every Agent as an Identity with ETM Identity

An agent with a static API key and standing access holds privileged access around the clock. Mandiant recommends dedicated agent identities, short-lived credentials, least privilege, and treating coding assistants and MCP servers as privileged sessions. Each is an identity exposure that can be measured before it is abused, and Entro Security found that 97% of non-human identities carry excessive privileges.

ETM Identity discovers identities across Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta, and local accounts, extends to non-human identities such as service accounts and application identities, traces blast radius across chained permissions, and correlates risky identities with vulnerable assets as toxic combinations. Agent Grant investigates those findings and guides the fix. Access reviews now need to ask what has access as well as who. AI agents with standing access are where ETM Identity is heading next.

Figure 8. The identity inventory in ETM Identity, with a TruRisk score for each user and service account.

Map the Lethal Trifecta as an Attack Path

Mandiant’s “lethal trifecta” is an agent with private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and an external channel. Each alone is manageable. Together they form an attack path that one injected instruction can turn into exfiltration, as the Confused Deputy test showed.

Attack paths for AI span more than one product. TotalCloud provides attack path insights for cloud and container workloads, and with TotalAI those insights extend to the AI models and MCP servers found in container images. Figure 9 shows one: an internet-exposed container with a critical exploitable vulnerability, running an image that contains an AI model, traced back to the commit and build pipeline that produced it. ETM Identity traces how an identity can chain privileges to reach critical systems. ETM is where these come together. For the lethal trifecta, the chain joins the agent’s entitlements from ETM Identity, the untrusted inputs and unsafe tool behavior TotalAI finds, and the cloud and network exposure from TotalCloud and ETM. Showing it as one toxic combination, ranked by the data it reaches, lets teams break the chain at a single link instead of chasing each finding. That is the direction we are taking attack path analysis across ETM and TotalCloud with TotalAI.

Figure 9. An attack path in TotalCloud that links an internet-exposed container with a critical exploitable vulnerability to the AI model in its image and to the commit and build that produced it.

Prove It, Fix It, and Prove It Again with Agent Val

When exploits take hours to build, theoretical severity cannot decide what to fix. Agent Val uses TruConfirm to safely prove whether an exposure is exploitable in your environment, drives the mitigation, and revalidates closure. TruConfirm covers more than 1,800 CVEs with over 8 million validations. It brings the discipline of a red team engagement, like those Mandiant’s Offensive Security team runs, into continuous operation.

The same principle applies at the application and AI layers. TotalAppSec (or WAS) runs dynamic application security testing (DAST) against the web applications and APIs that sit in front of AI systems, alongside the penetration tests teams already run. TotalAI red teaming tests models and MCP servers and shows which technique succeeded and which guardrail failed.

Figure 10. Agent Val reports a TruConfirm exploit validation with step-by-step evidence and offers remediation options.

Detect AI Exploitation in Real Time with Container Runtime Security

Some attacks leave nothing for a posture scan to find. In the Hugging Face intrusion, a package scan had nothing to match at the entry point and no view of the later stages (Figure 1). Exploits for AI components can arrive before disclosure, and whether a flaw is exploitable can depend on how a container is started. These cases have to be caught while they happen.

Figure 11. Three vulnerabilities in AI components running in containers, where exploitation had to be detected at runtime.

Qualys Container Runtime Security, part of TotalCloud, uses an eBPF sensor in the kernel to watch process, file, and network activity inside running containers, so it can detect exploitation of AI vulnerabilities in real time. In the Hugging Face analysis, its detections map to the fileless Python execution at the entry point, the container escape through a host path mount, the mount, chroot, and setns activity on the node, and the SOCKS proxy tunnel used for lateral movement. TotalCloud Cloud Detection and Response adds the Kubernetes and cloud API activity that process sensors cannot see, such as token minting and replayed cloud credentials. Kubernetes posture checks and admission policies flag or block the privileged pods and host path mounts the agent relied on. The analysis does not claim these controls would have stopped the campaign. It shows which layer sees each step, and that runtime, posture, and cloud audit each answer a different question.

Figure 12. Runtime detections in the TotalCloud Investigate view, including a suspicious host mount through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a shell spawned after exploitation of an Nginx UI vulnerability.

The same runtime evidence sharpens prioritization, because it shows which vulnerable packages are actually running and exposed.

Runtime Is One Pillar of AI Governance

Mandiant separates governance for AI (risk appetite and policy) from governance of AI (technical guardrails in pipelines and at runtime), and most of its technical guidance sits at runtime. A program that relies on runtime alone assumes every guardrail is configured correctly and every injection is caught in flight. We believe the stronger model is proactive first, with runtime guardrails as the backstop.

Layer

Question It Answers

How Qualys Delivers It

AI-SPM

What AI do we have, who owns it, and how is it configured?

TotalAI discovery and posture across models, agents, MCP servers, AI SaaS, and cloud AI

Workforce AI

Which AI tools are employees using, and what data goes into them?

TotalAI Browser Plugin and SaaS connectors, with prompt analysis for shadow AI use

Proactive security testing

Can this model or MCP server be manipulated before it ships?

LLM and MCP red teaming from CI/CD or on a schedule, mapped to OWASP and the EU AI Act

Prioritization and remediation

Which AI risks matter most, and what fixes them?

TruRisk with infrastructure and identity context; TruRisk Eliminate and guardrail recommendations

Runtime AIDR

Is something going wrong right now?

Policy-based runtime controls, and eBPF-based real-time detection of exploitation in AI workloads

TotalAI includes the runtime guardrails that give the SOC its AI signals. A SOC delivers its best return when a ROC is working ahead of it, because the ROC closes the exposures that would otherwise keep producing alerts. Guardrails written from red team results address weaknesses proven to exist, and every retest produces the evidence boards and regulators are starting to ask for.

Figure 13. The TotalAI AI Governance Dashboard, with a TruRisk score for AI, the AI assets at risk, and regulatory status.

Measure Time to Close

The AI era will be decided by how quickly teams close the window between disclosure and fix, which a count of open findings does not show.

Measure your exposure window. Track disclosure to detection, prioritization, and fix for exploited vulnerabilities, with a target in hours.

Put AI in the asset inventory. Cover agents, models, MCP servers, AI libraries, and shadow AI-like servers and endpoints.

Retire static credentials for agents. Classify non-human identities, flag long-lived keys and standing privileges, and move to short-lived, scoped identities.

Look for the lethal trifecta. Find agents with private data access, untrusted input, and an outbound channel, and remove one of the three.

Validate before you prioritize. Use safe exploit validation to separate the exploitable from the theoretical.

Test AI before you rely on runtime guardrails. Red-team models and MCP servers before release and after every change to prompts, retrieval, or guardrails.

Watch AI workloads at runtime. Use kernel-level runtime detection to catch exploitation that has no CVE to match.

One Risk Operations Center for Infrastructure, Identity, and AI Risk

Attackers have automated their side of the race, yet their first move is still a weakness that was in place before the attack began. Runtime controls and the SOC respond once that weakness is used. The ROC closes it first, and its runtime detection catches what is exploited anyway. With Qualys, Agent Insta detects at AI speed, Agent Val proves what is exploitable, and Agent Sara remediates autonomously, on one platform that treats servers, clouds, identities, and AI systems as the same attack surface. That is one Risk Operations Center for infrastructure, identity, and AI risk.

Ready to see how Qualys closes the exposure window across your infrastructure and your AI? Request an ETM demo or start a TotalAI free service.

Contributors

Kaustubh Jagtap, Principal Evangelist, Risk Management

articles.title: The Claude Tag guide for startups
articles.context: Start narrow: only what the first channel’s job needs
articles.full_text:
Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, Claude Tag (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.

For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.

Featuring insights from

We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.

Company

On call

Thread to PR

Company brain

Self-serve data

Routine reporting

Kikoff

●

NavigateAI

●

But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden.

The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:

21

minutes from Slack mention to open PR

134

pull requests merged from Slack threads

5

<1

Days to hours

of recurring reporting prep

In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag.

Top channels to tag Claude

The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start.

01 Claude on call

Example setups:

Channels

#on-call #alerts-ci #deploy-watch #support-escalations

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io

Threads and routines

Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].

Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.

With Claude in the channel as a first responder, the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.

At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.

Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel

Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:

#deploys: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.

#alerts-ci: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.

#alerts-sentry-backend: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.

#dog-fooding: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.

#support: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.

Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.

“I’m always hyped when Claude catches an issue before a monitor or human does. One person can only personally manage so much context, Claude Tag helps us organize and own some context, and we manage the outcomes.”

NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context

NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.

Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.

“Our biggest ‘wow!’ moment with Claude Tag was when we were trying to debug a load issue, which seemed to be caused by a customer (since their calls were failing). A normal human response would be to continue chasing down that customer. But because Claude had access to so many other data sources, it actually found that it was from an uninstrumented internal cron job that was running during the same time.”

With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.

“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.

02 Thread to PR

Example setups:

Channels

#quick-wins #bug-bash #product-feedback #feature-requests #ux-papercuts #tech-debt #design-polish

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry

Threads and routines

One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.

Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.

With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.

Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.

Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days

Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.

One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.

When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.

The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.

“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”

Valence: From feature request to rollout

Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.

“It didn’t just agree with the expert. It caught duplicated configuration, the kind of thing humans lose track of.”

In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.

03 Company brain

Example setups:

Channels

#ask-anything #company-wiki #product-questions

Connectors

GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase

Threads and routines

One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.

At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.

For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.

Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing

Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.

Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.

That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.

“A firm working across 44 countries generates hundreds of one-off questions a month that no one will ever build a feature for. Claude Tag answers them from our own history in Slack. Every answer is a thread with links, so institutional memory compounds.”

Campfire: Customer experience on demand

One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”

This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.

“Claude Tag basically acts as our central knowledge base.”

04 Self-serve data

Example setups:

Channels

#data-requests #ask-revops #metric-definitions

Connectors

dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion

Threads and routines

One question per thread, weekly pre-standup readout, launch and experiment readouts, pipeline failure triage, new question triage

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer from our governed models and the definitions in [data skills repo]. If the data isn’t covered there, say it’s unvalidated instead of guessing. Lead with the answer, then give the number, what’s driving it, and any caveat. Check recent incidents, releases, and Slack discussions before explaining a change. If a metric’s definition is unclear, ask which one we mean. For anything important, share your plan or SQL before you run it. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and list any open data quality warnings at the end of your answer. If someone finds a mistake, draft a fix for a data team member to review. If a question comes up twice, suggest scheduling it.

At a fast-growing startup every function wants numbers, and the data team has to decide whose request comes first. With Claude Tag connected to your data, anyone can ask in plain English without waiting in the data team’s queue.

This is a use case we have adopted as well. In one of our data channels over a month, Claude Tag answered more than 75% of questions people posted, typically within a minute or two. It works from governed data and the same definitions analysts use, which live in a versioned repo that Claude re-reads in every conversation.

Descript: Answering ad-hoc data requests

Descript is an AI-powered video editing platform. Claude Tag is now the first line of support for data requests and initial analyses. Product, growth, RevOps, and finance ask questions in Slack and get answers grounded in Descript’s dbt models.

“I used to write complicated SQL and refresh the numbers by hand every week or month. Now I’ve replaced several data-team dashboards with my own Claude artifacts, and I no longer refresh them by hand.”

Daisy’s recurring reporting prep went from days to hours.

The growth team, for example, asks why lifecycle subscriptions dropped, whether paid search is losing last-touch credit to other channels, or how long a self-serve account takes to become an enterprise opportunity. The data team tracks the artifacts Claude generates to see which data assets matter most across teams, and spends its own time on strategic questions and on building the context that makes self-serve work.

“The promise of business intelligence has always been self-serve for business users. I’d never seen it actually realized until we had Claude Tag set up with immense context for our data.”

Orderful: From question to dashboard

At Orderful, self-serve analytics spans conversational analytics and full data builds: anyone can go from a question in Slack to a dashboard merged to production. The key is a semantic layer that encodes agreed definitions and metrics, so every answer and every build uses the same definitions.

“We trust the output because a semantic layer constrains the SQL, CI gates the builds, and there’s a process for agreeing on definitions. Without those, you get confident-looking wrong answers. Once those guardrails were in place, connecting Claude Tag took under 30 minutes. Now teammates build together in shared Slack threads instead of solo sessions.”

05 Reporting and handoffs

Example setups:

Channels

#sales-pipeline #customer-handoffs #standup-summary #qbr-prep

Connectors

Notion, Google Drive, Gong, Salesforce, Gainsight

Threads and routines

End-of-day status draft, pre-QBR brief, deal handoff

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: draft each recurring report from our threads, docs, and data, and link your sources. Lead with what changed and what needs a decision. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and flag anything missing instead of filling the gap. Post the draft in its own thread for [owner] to edit. Nothing goes out until a person approves it. If a report keeps getting the same edits, suggest updating these instructions.

Many of the examples we’ve covered are reactive: something happens, Claude responds. Routine reporting is work Claude owns on a schedule, the way a teammate owns a recurring deliverable.

You describe the outcome once; Claude runs it every time and posts the result where the team already works.

Valence: Deal reviews and handoffs

Valence is setting Claude up to brief the team before every quarterly business review, with customer health, open deals, blockers, and next steps. They are also working to make the handoff from sales to customer success when a deal closes more seamless. Claude saves the team time by helping to aggregate details across their engagement and often finds key items they may have missed.

“When a deal closes, Tag builds the handoff from the deal history, calls and contract: who’s who, what was promised, what’s customized, and what’s still open. Customer success then reviews it before their kickoff,” said Sameer.

06 Getting started checklist

The checklist below pulls together these startup teams’ best practices so you can apply them to your own workflows.

Before launch

Check the prerequisites.

Claude Tag is in public beta on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, and isn’t available on Free, Pro, or Max. You’ll need a Claude organization Owner and a Slack workspace admin to connect the two. An admin must also turn on Routines, and Team plans need usage credits before Claude responds.

Set up Claude’s access with a bundle.

In channels, Claude works under its own agent identity, with service accounts rather than anyone’s personal login. Group the connectors, repos, and instructions it needs in a bundle, and attach them org-wide, per workspace, or per channel. That sets what Claude can reach in each place, and everyone in a channel gets the same access. Start narrow: only what the first channel’s job needs.

Experiment in a private channel.

Nearly half the startups we spoke with started their Claude Tag journey by having a small cross-functional team experiment in a private channel. “Start private with a mix of roles, then move to a group channel,” said Sameer.

Determine the boundaries.

By default, anyone in your Slack workspace can use Claude, even without a Claude account. You can restrict access to your org and limit search to channels Claude is in. On Enterprise, you can also restrict access to specific roles or chosen channels.

Set clear expectations for what Claude can do and can never do. Several teams we spoke with let Claude open draft PRs, but people review and merge. For Orderful, Claude Code, not Tag, handles “infrastructure changes, audits, sensitive data.” For a “hard call,” such as “a PR that touches more than one service,” Claude gets a second opinion. Moritz doesn’t give Claude Tag access to client documents or privileged conversations with its lawyers.

Start your security review early.

The usual questions are data retention and what Claude can reach, and the security and data lifecycle pages answer both. Claude Tag isn’t available to orgs with zero data retention turned on, a customer-managed encryption (CMEK) policy, or the HIPAA configuration, and it isn’t covered by our Business Associate Agreement, so check that before you plan a rollout.

Set a budget and alerts.

Claude Tag bills by usage, so an early conversation avoids surprises as adoption grows. You can set spend limits overall and per channel, choose the model per channel, and attribute costs by user using the Enterprise Analytics API. Orderful runs an org-wide cap with alerts at 75% and 90%. “We have extreme ownership on the channel costs. The owner justifies that ‘yes, this spend is reasonable for the output / outcomes,’” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff. Use your first channel’s actual costs to size the next one.

Deployment

Pick one clear task in a channel your team already uses, like on-call alerts or bug triage.

“We experiment on certain teams, see what works, then once confident we’ve worked out the kinks, we push the idea out to other teams to add to their own similar channels as well. We want to avoid trust breaking experiences with folks with lower tolerance to AI mistakes,” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff.

Prime your experts and culture bearers.

Have the people your team already trusts use Claude first, and in the open.

“Going back and forth with Claude in the open has been productive and fun. Several people in sales and customer success have watched experts [interact with Claude Tag], then started asking Claude themselves, and got value fast,” said Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence.

Tune the noise.

Multiple startups told us they needed to adjust Claude’s chattiness. Too chatty is one risk.

“Conversation in ad hoc requests can sometimes get noisy. We’ve been trying to tune down the responsiveness here and also be more principled on what we use Claude on ad hoc requests for,” said Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI.

Too little chattiness is also a risk, however. In busy channels, “You either have to @ every time or it won’t do much,” said Will Hu, cofounder at Flagler Health. And “if no one is watching a channel closely or interacts with it, it will sit idle.”

Have teammates connect their own accounts.

The admin bundles from setup are what Claude can reach for everyone in a channel. Personal connectors work differently: Claude acts with the permissions of the person asking, so it can pull from their docs, inbox, or CRM once they approve it (an Owner adds the connector for the org first, and on Enterprise an admin manages personal connectors). The answer still posts in the channel, so choose “Allow with review” for anything sensitive.

Write channel instructions like you’re onboarding a new hire:

what to check first, when to open a PR, when to ask, and that “no action needed” is a valid answer.

Give Claude feedback in the channel, not in DMs.

Correct it in the thread. It remembers per channel, and teammates learn how to work with it by watching. For a lasting fix, ask Claude to update its memory for this channel.

Not sure where to go next? Tag Claude and ask what it has learned about your org and which use cases it would expand to.

Moritz’s co-founder and CTO, Stefan Mandaric, asked Claude to recommend use cases for each team. Fifteen minutes later, it had read the firm’s Slack channels, Linear issues, Notion SOPs, Drive, and Metabase dashboards, and published 25. “18 of 25 worked with no further setup. That became our rollout plan.”

Last word: what we learned from the wow moments

The wow moments weren’t always about speed. Often, Claude found something no one had asked it to look for. Sometimes the surprise was restraint. And sometimes the surprise was the unexpected exchanges. “Eventually you get used to Claude jumping in on jokes, and you soon appreciate that it’s an easy audience and the first one to laugh,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful.

We hope you found this guide useful. Special thanks to Campfire, Descript, Flagler Health, Kikoff, Moritz, NavigateAI, Orderful and Valence for sharing their experiences and insights.

articles.title: Building always-on agents
articles.context: First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in
articles.full_text:
Over the past few months, we’ve seen a resurgence of always-on agents.

Always-on agents are stateful and proactive, meaning they manage context across sessions and take actions without direct supervision. Underneath, they run on the same core loop as other agents. The difference is the surrounding architecture, which is built from primitives that control when the agents wake up, what carries over between runs, and how their work reaches the user.

The resurgence is largely due to recent model advancements, which have made always-on agents more practical to run. First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in. Second, intelligence is becoming cheaper, with long-horizon tasks benefiting the most. For example, on one long-horizon coding benchmark, Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.

Customers have started to ask us how to integrate this type of experience into their own products. Some companies want to make their existing agents more proactive, while others are looking to build them from the ground up.

This post breaks down the primitives behind always-on agents and walks through how they fit together.

The cycle behind the always-on agent

An always-on agent is not actually “always on.” This is just a description of the user experience.

In reality, the agent spends most of its time asleep, waking up periodically to do work. Each stretch of work is called a run: the agent receives an event, completes its task, and then saves information about what happened. A run works inside a session, which is the transcript of messages and tool calls. Once the run is finished, the agent goes back to sleep, and the cycle repeats indefinitely.

The core primitives

The surrounding architecture of an always-on agent has five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox. Let’s take a look at each.

Event inbox

Most AI agents only run when the user sends a message. In contrast, always-on agents can be triggered by many types of events, including webhooks, scheduled tasks, and background jobs.

One tempting approach is to have each event source call the agent directly, but that has a few failure modes. For example, two events arriving at the same time can start competing runs, and a crash can lose an event entirely.

This is where the event inbox comes in. Instead of calling the agent, every source sends an event to an inbox, where a worker picks it up.

The simplest version has three components:

A durable list of events, usually a database table;

A handler, usually an HTTP endpoint, that writes events to the list; and

A worker, usually a background service, that reads from the list.

The inbox should track the status of each event, and events can be deduplicated based on unique identifiers from the source. A relational database works well for the inbox, with every event appended as a new row. We recommend starting with one inbox per user, but you can split this further if you need more parallelism.

When a new event comes in, the handler writes the event to the inbox and wakes the worker. The worker reads whatever is pending and starts a run. Events that continue earlier work, such as a reply from the user, resume an existing session, while everything else starts a new session.

From there, the worker passes the events to the agent loop, waits for the run to finish, and marks the corresponding events as done. The implementation details can get tricky, so here are a few best practices:

The handler should acknowledge events quickly. Some sources, such as webhook providers, treat slow responses as failures. The handler can still run lightweight checks, but any deeper verification, such as checking for prompt injection, should be done during the run.

The inbox should be the source of truth. When the worker is woken up, it should pull the latest events from the inbox first. That way, if the worker dies mid-run, a new one can pick up the same event and retry.

An inbox should only have one active worker at a time. This prevents two runs from duplicating work or overwriting each other. When a new event shows up mid-run, you can either push it to the next run, fold it into the current run, or interrupt and restart.

The worker should batch pending events together. For example, if the user sends several messages in a row, the worker can merge them into a single run, so the agent only needs to reply once.

Timers

Together with the event inbox, timers let always-on agents be proactive. Timers generally fall into one of two categories: follow-ups or schedules. A follow-up is a deadline that the agent sets for itself, such as checking in on a reply. A schedule, on the other hand, is a recurring task that happens on a known cadence, such as a daily newsletter.

Timers live in their own durable store, usually another database table, separate from the inbox. The inbox should only hold events that are ready to be worked on. A follow-up and a schedule can share a similar schema, but a schedule needs to track its recurrence as well.

A timer doesn’t initiate a run on its own. Instead, a scheduler, usually a background service, polls the store at a fixed interval and fires anything that’s due. On each pass, the scheduler:

Scans the store and finds timers that are due.

Updates each timer based on its category.

A follow-up should be marked as done.

A schedule should get its due time updated to the next occurrence.

Adds an event to the inbox and wakes the worker.

For the scheduler, you can either build your own service or use a durable execution engine.

Memory

Always-on agents work across many disjointed runs and rely on memory to maintain continuity.

Similar to the event inbox and timers, memory should have its own store. In our products, such as Claude Code’s auto memory and the Messages API’s memory tool, this is implemented as a directory of files. For an always-on agent, the directories should map to durable storage, usually a database or an object store. This way memories outlive the worker.

As a rule of thumb, memory should only hold what the agent can’t look up again. If something already lives in another system, such as an issue tracker, you should save a pointer instead. Here is a breakdown of the types of memory an always-on agent should store:

User instructions: Any instructions from the user about agent behavior should be saved in their own file and loaded at the start of every run. The user won’t always be around to steer the agent, so the instructions have to carry over between runs.

User notes: The agent should save what it’s learned about the user, such as their role, their preferences, or any corrections they’ve given. You can start with one file and move to several small files as the notes grow. In the latter case, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.

Past messages: The agent should keep track of what it’s already told the user so nothing is repeated. It can either store this in a separate file that’s loaded at the start of each run, or have the worker load the agent’s last few messages with the user.

Task progress: For each ongoing task, the agent should keep a progress file that covers what’s been done and what’s left. Any new run can then read that file and pick up where the previous run left off. Similar to user notes, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.

The diagram below shows one example setup.

All of the above describes memory that’s saved during a run. You can also add dreaming, which reviews past sessions to curate memories. Dreaming can replace outdated entries and find patterns that only show up across many runs. If you’re interested in learning more, our post on agent memory covers this in more detail.

Inside the context window

Before doing any work, the agent loads the system prompt, tool definitions, and memory files. This initial context “overhead” is included in every run, so we recommend keeping it lean and using prompt caching to lower costs.

A new session starts only with this context overhead and the events that triggered the run. An existing session, on the other hand, brings back the messages and tool calls from its earlier runs.

If a session becomes too long, you can either compact the older messages or start a new session. Both approaches lose detail, so anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way.

Permissions

Permissions are where always-on agents carry the most risk. A run holds the user’s access and, by design, operates unattended. For each tool call, the agent needs to decide whether to proceed on its own, block it, or wait for approval.

The components for permissions are the same ones other agents use:

Credential store: Always-on agents often need sensitive user credentials like passwords or access tokens to be useful. The recommended pattern is a proxy outside the agent’s environment that adds credentials to outgoing requests. The agent sends requests without credentials, and the proxy injects the real credentials before forwarding.

Auto mode: An always-on agent should be able to work without constant user input. We’ve already tackled a version of this problem with auto mode in Claude Code. Auto mode uses classifiers to review higher-risk actions and block the ones they identify as dangerous so Claude can find a safer approach. User review, however, is still necessary for the most important decisions.

Deferred tool calls: In Claude Code, a hook can defer a tool call and wait for additional input from the user. The same pattern applies to always-on agents, which may need clarification or approval before taking certain actions. When a call is deferred, the run ends and the session is saved mid-call. The request is shown to the user (e.g., through an interactive card built with MCP Apps), and their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. That event starts a new run, which resumes the saved session with the user’s input. While the deferred call waits for a response, the worker can pick up other events, so the agent isn’t blocked.

Outbox

With most AI agents, the response is streamed to the user as it’s generated, so they can follow along as Claude reasons through the problem, calls tools, and writes its answer.

Always-on agents, on the other hand, do most of their work in the background. The user gets the outcome and a few details, rather than the entire step-by-step breakdown.

A run can end in one of three ways:

The agent sends a message to the outbox,

The agent decides that nothing needs to be sent, or

The agent uses a deferred tool call to request permission or additional input.

Most always-on agents can get by with a “send” tool that delivers the message directly to the user. You only need a formal outbox when you want to pace your agent’s messages or allow your agent to recover from errors.

The outbox is a separate table of outgoing messages, analogous to the event inbox. There’s also a dispatcher, usually a background service, that’s analogous to the worker. The dispatcher reads the pending messages, decides what to deliver, and sends those to the user. A request from a deferred tool call can either go through the outbox or be shown directly in the interface.

Beyond delivery, it’s important to tune how many messages the agent sends. An agent that sends too many becomes noisy, while an agent that doesn’t send enough misses things that the user needs to know. We recommend building evals to find the right balance. In practice, it’s better for the agent to start quiet and then earn more of the user’s attention over time.

How everything fits together

Here is how the five primitives fit together:

Every run starts with an event from the inbox, whether it’s a user message, a webhook, or a timer. When the worker picks up an event, it kicks off a run and wakes the agent in a new or existing session. The agent reads its memory to get a baseline, works within its permissions to take actions, and then updates its memory with anything it has learned. Once the run is finished, the agent pushes a row to the outbox, and the dispatcher delivers the message to the user.

Together, these form a cycle. A run can set a timer that wakes the agent again later, and when the user replies to a message, their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. Each run is brief, but the cycle keeps going indefinitely, and that’s what makes the agent feel like it’s always on.

Acknowledgements

Written by William Hu. Special thanks to Rodrigo Olivares and Michael Segner for their contributions.

articles.context: Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook. articles.full_text:
Patch Tuesday. Maersk investigates a legacy system breach. A chip-smuggling probe stalls after Nvidia reaches out to Commerce. A US Army officer is arrested in the UK for alleged Russian espionage. Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents across Central Asia. Opsec blunders unmask an alleged Qilin ransomware boss. Researchers hijack connected cars via Android apps. Our guest is Tim Starks from CyberScoop to discuss what Democratic control of Congress means for cybersecurity. A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Today is Thursday November 12th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Patch Tuesday.

In honor of the Veterans Day holiday here in the U.S. we did not publish yesterday, which means we are playing a bit of catch up for this month’s patch Tuesday.

Several major technology vendors have rolled out extensive November security updates, including a fix for an actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook.

According to SecurityWeek, Redmond addressed one thousand ninety-four vulnerabilities this month. Most notably, CVE-2026-124194 is an exploited Outlook spoofing flaw that leaks a user's NTLMv2 authentication hash if they open a malicious message file, allowing attackers to impersonate them. Windows accounted for seven hundred twenty-six of Microsoft's patches, alongside one hundred seventy-four for Office.

Meanwhile, Fortinet published eighty-nine advisories resolving nearly one hundred flaws, including roughly seventeen critical issues across products like FortiMail, FortiOS, and FortiClient, which researchers note were discovered with the help of frontier artificial intelligence models. Ivanti and Citrix patched nineteen vulnerabilities combined; Ivanti's fixes address critical unauthenticated remote code execution and authentication bypass defects in Endpoint Manager and Cloud Services Application, while Citrix resolved six XenServer flaws and mitigated AMD processor issues. Finally, Zoom patched two unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, and Asus addressed four router firmware bugs.

Attackers rapidly weaponize edge devices and collaboration tools, requiring security teams to prioritize patching Outlook and internet-facing enterprise infrastructure immediately, even where active exploitation has not yet been reported, according to vendor advisories.

Maersk investigates isolated security incident on legacy system.

Shipping giant A.P. Moller-Maersk is investigating a security incident involving potential data theft from an isolated legacy system.

In a Wednesday statement, the Denmark-based logistics firm confirmed it secured the affected platform, a local system from a previous acquisition. Maersk said initial findings strongly suggest no sensitive information was disclosed, and there is no evidence of impact on core operations or customer integrations like APIs and electronic data interchange.

Any cyber incident at Maersk recalls the devastating two thousand seventeen NotPetya attack, attributed to Russia's Sandworm group, which cost the firm roughly three hundred million dollars. While this localized intrusion appears far less severe, it highlights persistent cybersecurity risks within inherited acquisition infrastructure, according to Maersk and reporting from The Register.

The Commerce Department halted a chip-smuggling probe after Nvidia outreach.

Federal investigators at the Commerce Department abruptly paused a monthslong probe into suspected artificial intelligence chip smuggling to China late last year after receiving unusual outreach from Nvidia.

According to The New York Times, the inquiry focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed, led by Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials now believe spied for Beijing and who had an acknowledged intimate relationship with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The case was hastily transferred to the Justice Department after Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter emailed investigators, claiming Commerce official Jeff Kessler authorized the company to inquire about the probe.

The episode highlights growing tension between national security enforcement and corporate influence over semiconductor export controls, raising concerns among officials that executive intervention could compromise federal investigations into illicit technology transfers.

Nvidia shares fell ten percent after CEO Jensen Huang resigned today, naming CFO Colette Kress interim chief executive.

The Wall Street Journal reports the board met following a New York Times report alleging a second affair with executive Kimberly Powell.

A US Army officer is arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia.

British police have arrested a forty-one-year-old US Army lieutenant colonel on suspicion of attempting to steal secret information from a NATO installation for Russia.

According to The Washington Post, the unnamed officer was stationed at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire, England, which houses NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. A joint counterintelligence operation involving Britain's MI5, Metropolitan Police, and the FBI detained the officer before any sensitive files were transferred to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any Russian link to the incident.

US Army Counterintelligence Command noted the arrest is a sobering reminder of persistent insider threats within allied defense infrastructure, as Western nations navigate heightened Russian hybrid operations across Europe alongside ongoing Ukraine peace negotiations.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers deploy AI agents in Central Asian espionage.

Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an autonomous artificial intelligence agent to conduct cyberespionage against Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure, according to Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK.

Researchers uncovered the operation on an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, also tracked as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper. The operator configured an open-source AI agent named Hermes, powered primarily by DeepSeek models, to act as an offensive security specialist. Controlled remotely via a Telegram bot in Russian, the agent automated reconnaissance, data theft, and log erasure.

Using compromised railway credentials, the attackers breached Tajikistan's national electronic document platform, stealing thousands of files linked to the Defense Ministry and security agencies. They also compromised a server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and prepared phishing lures targeting Turkmenistan.

The discovery underscores how threat actors are operationalizing agentic AI to automate complex intrusions, lowering the operational friction required to pillage government networks.

Operational security missteps expose an alleged Qilin ransomware administrator.

Operational security mistakes over the past decade have exposed the alleged real-world identity of the administrator behind Qilin, currently the world's most active ransomware affiliate program.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, Qilin, which claimed at least three hundred sixty-five victims in the past three months, is led by a threat actor using the handle "Haise." Threat intelligence firms IntelHawk, Intel 471, and Flashpoint traced Haise back to older cybercrime forum monikers, including "Rjun," and a Telegram account tied to an email address exposed in a late two thousand twenty-five breach of Russia's state services portal, Gosuslugi. Those records, alongside leaked travel and education data, point to thirty-six-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev of St. Petersburg.

The attribution demonstrates how even sophisticated ransomware operators leave persistent digital breadcrumbs across seized forums and breached databases, aiding defenders and law enforcement in piercing criminal anonymity.

Security researchers exploit Android apps to remotely control connected cars.

Security researchers uncovered critical flaws in Android applications from two major automakers that enabled remote access to connected vehicles in the United States and Australia.

According to research published by Assetnote co-founder Shubham Shah and Sam Curry, the exploit chains targeted weaknesses in the manufacturers' ForgeRock identity platforms. In Australia, hardcoded staging credentials and path traversal flaws allowed account takeovers using just a license plate lookup. In the US, path confusion and factory default credentials on an Apache Felix console yielded shell access to identity servers, letting the pair start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. The unnamed automakers, widely speculated by observers to be Toyota and Lexus, patched the vulnerabilities within two hours of disclosure earlier this year.

The findings underscore how backend identity misconfigurations and hardcoded credentials in connected vehicle ecosystems can turn everyday mobile apps into remote-control attack vectors.

A New Jersey township holds the news until after the votes.

Officials in Cranbury, New Jersey, intended to buy land for affordable housing, though they inadvertently subsidized some ambitious cybercriminals instead, wiring twenty-six million dollars straight into fraudsters' hands.

According to The Wall Street Journal, police expect to recover seventeen point three million dollars, leaving roughly nine million missing, an amount comfortably exceeding the township's five-million-dollar insurance policy. Adding salt to the fiscal wound, officials waited until the Friday afternoon after Election Day to announce the heist. While the police chief took responsibility, explaining a gag order prevented thieves from liquidating the stolen funds, residents packed a town meeting expressing skepticism over the timing and marveling that an eight-figure transfer proved easier than logging into an iCloud account.

The episode offers a sobering reminder that business email compromise doesn't spare small municipalities, and that delayed breach disclosures rarely play well with voters, even when investigators have sound operational reasons.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.
