articles.title: EY Cyprus recognized as the winner of 2026 Microsoft Partner of the Year
A Single Branch No Longer Operates in A Single Place
articles.context: Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools
articles.full_text:
Branch Traffic Has Changed. Security Has to Follow.

A traditional branch was simple in nature: a location that connects back to headquarters where applications, data, and security controls were housed. Today the landscape is wildly different. A branch may connect directly to SaaS apps, clouds, data centers, the open internet, and other locations within the enterprise. And while all those connections are being made, often many at one time, employees expect video calls and cloud applications to perform just as well in the office as they do at home.

The branch itself has become more complex, too. Connected devices can range from printers and ‘smart building’ systems to specialized IoT equipment. Employees may also access AI applications and services directly from the network. And many branch locations are expected to manage all of this without dedicated security personnel on site.

Routing all that activity back through headquarters can introduce unnecessary latency and cost. However, without the right controls you’re opening yourself up to new exposure. The modern branch needs connectivity, protection, and resilience to work together.

Now is the Time for Connectivity to Adapt to the Application

Not every application needs the same network path.

Video calls? Highly sensitive to latency and packet loss. Large backup transfers? Often prioritize cost over speed. Internal business applications? Might need an encrypted route back to a data center.

Software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN) gives organizations more control over those decisions because, rather than relying on one fixed route, SD-WAN can evaluate available connections and steer traffic based on the application, business policy, and real-time network conditions.

Multiple links can add another layer of resilience. If one connection degrades or fails, traffic can move to a healthier path automatically. But branch continuity depends on more than WAN alone. Firewall clustering and hardware redundancy can help keep both connectivity and protection available when individual components fail.

For businesses that depend on real-time transactions, voice and video, cloud apps, or always-on access to corporate resources, that resilience helps keep a local issue from becoming a larger business interruption.

See how Hybrid Mesh connects security across the distributed enterprise. Download Our CISO Guide

The Branch Has Become A Bigger Security Surface

Direct internet access improves performance, but it also changes where traffic needs to be inspected and protected. Branch firewalls increasingly need to secure traffic locally while supporting the same high-bandwidth applications they are helping accelerate.

And the risk now extends well beyond internet traffic: printers, cameras, building systems, medical devices, and industrial equipment can all expand the internal attack surface. Many of those devices were never designed with modern cybersecurity in mind, making visibility, segmentation, and threat prevention increasingly important inside the branch as well as at its perimeter.

And of course AI adds another consideration entirely. Employees may use third-party AI applications, agents, or connected tools directly from the branch. Security teams need visibility into that activity and the ability to apply policy, including controls that help prevent sensitive data from being shared through prompts. Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools. Branch security therefore needs strong prevention at the point where traffic is already being inspected, rather than relying on another, additional layer.

Every Branch Should Be Easier to Operate

A distributed enterprise may have dozens, hundreds, or thousands of locations. Managing each branch as its own network creates complexity that grows exponentially with every new site that needs to fit within the existing architecture.

Centralized policy, zero-touch provisioning, network-health monitoring, and unified visibility can make branches easier to deploy and manage while keeping protection more consistent across locations.

That matters especially when there is no security specialist sitting at every branch. Centralized management allows teams to deploy and maintain protection across large numbers of sites without turning every new location, policy change, or connectivity issue into an on-site project.

Bring Connectivity and Security Together at the Branch

Hybrid Mesh Network Security connects the branch with the security architecture protecting data centers, clouds, applications, and users across the enterprise.

AI security at the firewall adds visibility and policy controls for employee AI usage, while centralized management and zero-touch deployment help maintain consistent protection across distributed locations.

Integration with Check Point SASE extends that approach beyond the branch, helping connect users and locations to the applications and resources they need while keeping branch security part of the broader enterprise architecture.

Organizations who prefer a hybrid security approach can benefit from a hybrid SASE deployment. This way, they can cater to remote users with cloud-based security (SSE) connected to on-prem SD WAN, and also protect office users through network firewalls embedded with SD WAN for optimized branch connectivity.

articles.title: When Coding Agents Inherit Your Pipeline’s Permissions
articles.context: Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds
articles.full_text:
What you will learn

How coding agents borrow the permissions of your CI/CD pipeline, why enforcement is thinnest in those environments and how to scope agents to the task, treat pipelines as privileged identities and check each action at runtime.

A coding agent working in PocketOS’s staging environment hit a credential error, found an unrelated API token and used it to delete the production database and the backups stored alongside it.

Nobody attacked anything, and according to the founder, all it took was nine seconds.

Most of the conversation about coding agents is about the code they write, but engineering and security leaders need to be able to say what an agent can set in motion, and whose authority it uses when it does.

Enforcement is thinnest where AI agents do their work

In Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition, 2,254 IT and security leaders told us where AI access is checked at the moment of action, before the action runs. CI/CD pipelines came in at 35% and Kubernetes at 28%, the lowest of the six environments we asked about. And 47% of organizations lack enforcement at the moment of action across at least two of the six.

Those are the environments developers hand off to agents first, and they're where deploy roles, cluster permissions, and production credentials live.

The agent doesn’t need the prod credential

Say you ask an agent to bump a service in staging. It updates the deploy workflow and opens a pull request. On GitHub, a pull request from a branch in the same repo runs the workflow as modified in that PR. If the workflow can pick up the pipeline’s cloud role, and that role reaches prod as well as staging, the agent’s edit now has production authority behind it.

The agent never touched a prod credential. It borrowed the pipeline’s.

Over-scoped CI roles were a problem long before agents showed up. Workflows branch too, but someone wrote and reviewed every branch. An agent can write a new one and trigger it in the same session.

Permissions that were safe for a predictable job become much broader once the identity using them can improvise

Identity has to follow the action

Security teams already know how to limit privileged access. Agents need those same controls applied to each action because they decide what to do next on their own.

Scope the agent to the task, not the person who launched it. You might be allowed to query the production database, but your agent shouldn’t inherit that because you started it. A policy that can tell the two apart lets your query through and stops the same query when the agent sends it.

Treat the pipeline as a privileged identity. The deploy role is what actually touches prod, so it deserves the scrutiny you’d give an admin account: one role per environment, and a human review before anything reaches production.

Keep enforcing policy after access is granted. Authentication only checks who's connecting, so a command an agent runs 40 minutes into the session goes through unchecked. Access should exist only while the task needs it, and each consequential action should be checked against policy before it runs.

Where Delinea fits

Delinea extends Privileged Access Management from the point of access to the moment of action. For the connections it brokers, including databases, servers, Kubernetes and MCP tools, access is granted just-in-time for the task, and in a brokered session the credential is injected at the proxy so it never reaches the agent. Each query, command and tool call is checked at runtime, and one that’s out of scope doesn’t run.

Start with one agent-assisted workflow

Pick one agent-assisted workflow and trace it to production. List each identity it touches, from the agent to the runner to the deploy role to the cluster, and what each one is allowed to do. Then find the point where a production action from a staging task would be stopped. If the answer is “we’d catch it in the logs,” you’ve found your gap.

Explore the findings in Delinea’s 2026 Identity Security Report, Fall Edition: The AI Enforcement Gap.

Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police.

The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg.

articles.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
articles.context: NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to...
articles.full_text: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic. ®

articles.title: Beyond Storage: Your Repository as Software Inventory
articles.context: But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job
articles.full_text:
Repositories give teams a managed source for build inputs. They proxy public registries, host internal components, and cache packages.

That work remains essential. But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job.

A typical build may pull in open source packages, container images, internal libraries, build tools, and models. Those inputs can enter in several ways:

A developer selects a package or library.

A pipeline retrieves a component.

An AI agent adds a dependency while changing code.

A package manager resolves additional components required by another library.

Because many requests happen automatically, teams need to understand what is available through the repository path and manage the inputs that pass through it. A repository used as a common source can provide that operational inventory.

From Artifact Storage to Software Inventory

A repository inventory describes the artifacts available through a managed source: the formats and versions present, and the assets associated with them.

Sonatype Nexus Repository gives teams a shared view of components available through managed repositories.

That view can help answer questions such as:

Which packages, containers, models, and build artifacts are available through managed repositories?

Which versions are hosted or cached?

Do developers, pipelines, and agents have a common route to obtain software?

Can teams apply consistent policies and block known malicious packages before they are served?

Consider a routine library update. An engineer needs to know which versions are available through the team's standard source. When groups rely on separate proxies or caches, that information may be scattered. A shared repository gives teams a common place to check.

Know What the Repository Inventory Covers

A component appearing in Nexus Repository does not necessarily mean it is included in a deployed application. It means the component is managed or available through the repository. Build records or software bills of materials (SBOMs) identify what went into a specific application or release.

These views answer different but related questions. The repository inventory helps teams manage the shared supply path, and build records help them understand a particular application's inputs.

That distinction also gives teams a place to start an investigation. If a package is flagged, they can check whether it is managed or available through Nexus Repository, then consult build records to determine if a specific application included it.

Software Delivery Starts With What Teams Pull

Most applications depend on components their teams did not write. A developer might add a framework, then a package manager resolves its dependencies.

Each component can affect the application in different ways:

Compatibility: Dependencies may conflict or require specific versions.

Maintenance: Older or unsupported components create upgrade work.

Security: A malicious component requires investigation and response after it enters development.

When these issues surface after development begins, replacing a component can mean code changes, retesting, and release delays.

AI tools can add or update dependencies while changing code, increasing the pace of these choices. A faster request does not tell a team whether or not a component is compatible, maintained, or appropriate for the application. Teams need enough context to assess those choices before they create work downstream.

Make Centralized Access the Trusted Default

A shared repository gives teams a consistent place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs their workflows need. Developers and pipelines can use a managed route that supports their existing package managers and build tools, instead of relying on separate collections of external sources.

In day-to-day work, that shared route gives teams a common way to:

Retrieve components and resolve dependencies through the organization's configured source.

Manage the software supply chain used by multiple groups, rather than having each team create its own process.

Route AI agent dependency requests through the same access and intake controls used for other development activity.

Configure supported formats in a shared repository, giving new projects a starting point instead of another one-off source.

Centralizing access does not automatically cover packages downloaded directly from a public registry or through an unconfigured source. Teams need to route the requests they want managed through Nexus Repository. Then it can serve as a common point for understanding the inputs it handles and applying controls to them.

Block Known Malicious Packages Before They Reach the Build

Nexus Repository sits between upstream sources and the developers, pipelines, and agents requesting software. In the Pro+ and Enterprise editions, malicious package protection and configurable policies can block known malicious packages when requests pass through a protected repository path, before Nexus serves them downstream.

If a malicious package reaches a development environment, teams may need to remove it from the repository if it is still available, then:

Identify which developers, pipelines, or agents retrieved and used the package, and assess what systems or data may be affected.

Assess which systems or credentials it could access.

Determine whether builds or releases incorporated it, and assess downstream exposure.

Blocking the package at the repository can prevent that specific input from becoming part of a downstream investigation. Developers also do not have to identify every suspicious package name or track each campaign themselves. Protection applies where component requests already flow.

Repository protection does not address every dependency or application risk. A component can cause compatibility problems without being malicious, so teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. For dependency decisions and remediation, Sonatype Guide brings intelligence into developer and AI coding workflows to inform component choices and help automate dependency upgrades.

Within the broader Nexus One platform, Guide complements repository protection: developers and agents get support for choosing and updating dependencies, while Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can block known malicious packages and packages flagged as suspicious, even before they are confirmed as malicious at the repository request point.

Make the Repository Part of Delivery Infrastructure

A reliable software supply chain depends on more than where artifacts are stored. Teams need a consistent way to find the components their workflows can use, manage the route those components take, and keep known malicious packages out.

Nexus Repository provides a shared source for the software inputs it manages. Its Pro+ and Enterprise editions add protection that can block known malicious packages at the point where components enter the managed path. Together, these capabilities give teams both a clearer view of available inputs and a way to stop a known threat before it reaches a build.

As developers and AI agents make more requests, that combination becomes more useful. Teams can make software available through a common route, apply consistent controls to incoming requests, and understand the limits of what the repository inventory shows.

Know what your teams can get through the repository. Make trusted access the default. Block known malicious packages before they become part of the work.

Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027: Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline

November 12, 2026

Kyle Koppe

BLOG

5 min.

Have you been wondering what the prevailing cloud security best practices for 2027 might be? Unlike years past, 2027 is set to center around the data-to-AI pipeline. Data platforms, AI services and autonomous agents now run side by side across multiple clouds and the data moving between them carries the most business value and the biggest security risk. Organizations planning their 2027 security programs need practices that protect that entire movement, not just the environments on either end.

TL;DR – A critical cloud security best practice for 2027 is going to center around securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system, with protection and access policies following data from collection through model training, deployment and agentic AI use.

Key takeaways:

Own the configuration. Under the shared responsibility model, organizations are responsible for securing the AI and data services they use and default settings need tuning to each environment.

Enforce through architecture. Policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code and automated guardrails turn security strategy into controls that hold up at scale.

Start with a baseline and build from there. Assess, plan and engineer pipeline security as a holistic motion, starting from wherever you are and building toward a scalable architecture that’s ready for what comes next.

Six Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027

Data teams and AI teams often work on different platforms with different priorities. Similarly, security programs have traditionally treated data security and AI security as separate disciplines. Moving into the coming year, organizations that secure the pipeline end-to-end will allow protection and access policies to carry forward as information moves between environments. This strategy allows them to enable new AI workloads to come online quickly without sacrificing security.

By following six interconnected practices, organizations can strengthen each individual layer of the cloud environment and then connect them into a cohesive, policy-driven foundation.

1. Treat Shared Responsibility as an AI Practice

Under the cloud shared responsibility model, the customer owns the security configuration of services such as Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker and Google Gemini Enterprise (Vertex AI). These services ship with default settings designed for broad use. Organizations should review and tune access controls, content filtering and model permissions to match their own data, risk tolerance and compliance obligations.

2. Classify Data Before AI Consumes It

Sensitive data discovery and classification work best when they happen early. Data security posture management (DSPM) gives teams visibility into where sensitive information lives, who can reach it and how it moves, so they can apply protection before data reaches a model or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application.

3. Enforce Policy as Code

Documented policies only reduce risk when they are enforced. Policy-as-code and infrastructure-as-code let teams define security requirements once and apply them consistently across every environment, pipeline and deployment, which keeps controls aligned as cloud footprints grow.

4. Govern Every Identity, Human and Non-Human

AI workloads and agents act as identities in the cloud and they can accumulate permissions quickly. Mapping entitlements, enforcing least privilege and reviewing privileged access for data and AI administrators help limit the reach of any single account or agent.

5. Build Compliance Into the Architecture

AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and the CSA AI Controls Matrix sit alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS. Aligning architecture to these frameworks from the start creates audit-ready governance and reduces rework as new regulations take effect.

6. Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline as One System

This is the practice the others point toward. Before data reaches a model or agent, teams copy, combine and transform it across databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines. At each stage, organizations need to preserve data integrity, understand sensitivity and origin and limit access to sensitive information.

GuidePoint Security’s new Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI bring together assessments, platform advisory and cloud engineering to secure the full pipeline, from collection and preparation through architecture, development, deployment and secure agentic and generative AI use. GuidePoint cloud experts translate governance requirements into enforceable controls such as encryption, access policies, content filtering and model access restrictions.

AI Services: Strengthen AI platform configuration, machine learning operations (MLOps) pipeline integrity and policy enforcement across native AI solution and third-party AI SaaS platforms.

Every engagement scales to the organization’s maturity, risk posture and AI roadmap:

Health Check: Baseline security posture across platform configurations, data exposure and AI operational readiness so remediation starts with what matters most.

Advisory: Align security investments with regulatory and business requirements through data protection strategies, governance frameworks and roadmaps.

Engineering: Turn strategy into production infrastructure with secure databases, automated pipelines, policy-as-code enforcement and infrastructure-as-code foundations designed to scale with continued AI innovation.

GuidePoint Security brings vendor-objective, hands-on experience across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and major SaaS ecosystems, including native tools such as Microsoft Purview, Amazon Macie, Google Cloud DLP and Oracle Data Safe. Engagements also connect with complementary GuidePoint services, including Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), Application Security, Identity and Access Management and threat simulation.

Get Started

Check out our Secure Cloud Platform for Data and AI datasheet. Then, schedule a Secure Cloud Platform Health Check to establish a clear view of data platform configuration, pipeline security and AI readiness and to identify where to focus first in 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top cloud security best practices for 2027?

Key cloud security best practices for 2027 include owning the security configuration of cloud AI services, classifying data before AI consumes it, enforcing policy as code, governing human and non-human identities, building compliance into the architecture and securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system.

What is the data-to-AI pipeline?

The data-to-AI pipeline is the path data takes from collection and preparation through storage, transformation, model training, deployment and use by generative and agentic AI applications. It typically spans databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines across multiple clouds.

Why is securing the data-to-AI pipeline a cloud security best practice?

AI models and agents are only as trustworthy as the data they rely on. Securing the pipeline end to end preserves data integrity, tracks sensitivity and origin and keeps access policies in place as data moves between environments and new AI workloads are introduced.

Who is responsible for securing cloud AI services like Copilot, Bedrock and Vertex AI?

The customer is. Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure, but the customer owns configuration, access controls, content filtering and model permissions for AI services. Default settings are designed for broad use, not your risk profile.

What is policy-as-code?

Policy-as-code is the practice of writing security rules as machine-readable code that deploys automatically with infrastructure. It eliminates manual configuration and ensures every environment gets the same controls from day one.

What is DSPM and how does it support AI security?

DSPM continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud environments. For AI security, it identifies which data AI models can access, flags overexposed training sets and tracks data lineage from source to model.

Which AI regulations and frameworks should cloud security programs plan for in 2027?

Organizations should plan for AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and state AI legislation, alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS.

What are GuidePoint Security's Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI?

London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
articles.context: ” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams
articles.full_text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways

Neither flaw is in your application code. Every app and API on a vulnerable runtime inherits the risk.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1.

Both are on the CISA KEV list. PHP2Shell was added on October 26. Node2Shell followed on October 27.

Qualys TotalAppSec tests the application and the APIs with four non-intrusive QIDs for detection of vulnerabilities and two intrusive QIDs for verification of the fix.

Patching fixes the runtime. A rescan confirms the fix worked and the application is no longer exposed.

On October 21, fixes came out for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two critical flaws in the runtimes beneath your web apps and APIs. Five days later, PHP2Shell was on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and Node2Shell followed the next day. Attackers had been probing PHP2Shell four days before a patch even existed.

With a timeline that short, the standard response of finding hosts, upgrading, and closing the ticket is not enough. Patched is a claim about a server. However, attackers really connect to the applications and APIs running on them. The question for application security teams is not whether PHP and Node.js were upgraded. It is whether an attacker can still reach the flaw through any application you run, and how you would know.

This post covers how the two flaws impact your application estate, where most response plans break, and how Qualys TotalAppSec turns a runtime flaw into a finding you can fix and verify.

A Runtime Flaw Is an Application Risk You Inherit

Neither flaw is in your application code, which is why code scans, reviews and tests won’t flag them. Every application and API running on a vulnerable runtime inherits the exposure.

PHP2Shell is a wide-scale problem. Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers and found 167 million PHP installations. Of the 156 million where the PHP version could be identified, 73% are on internet-facing assets. About 71% of the same 156 million run end-of-life or end-of-support versions that will likely never get a vendor patch, and only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js) hides in plain sight. Apps can be exposed even if they never call a Brotli API, because frameworks or dependencies may decompress attacker-controlled data. Node.js fetch() and Express 5 request-body parsing are examples of such attack vectors. As with PHP, end-of-life Node.js lines, including 25.x, 23.x and 20.x, get no fix and must move to a supported release.

In practice, the exposed estate includes customer portals, CMS-powered sites, microservices and the APIs that connect them. It also includes anything that fetches or accepts compressed content.

Attackers are not waiting for your patch cycle

Details of PHP2Shell leaked before the coordinated release. Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped, though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits. Then it escalated. CISA added PHP2Shell to its catalog on October 26 and Node2Shell on October 27.

Confirmed code execution: a researcher’s honeypots recorded confirmed remote code execution with usable memory disclosure against Apache mod_php running PHP 8.4.26.

Scale of attacks: Delft University’s Threat Intelligence Lab tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries.

Node2Shell: Public exploit code is available, and exploitation attempts have been observed in the wild.

What’s at stake: Researchers have shown that PHP worker memory can be disclosed without authentication, exposing passwords, authentication tokens and API keys.

To be precise: CISA hasn’t said which organizations were compromised, and the confirmed PHP exploit was on a deliberately favorable single-worker setup. The safe reading is that attackers have working exploits and are scanning widely, so treat any unpatched internet-facing app as a target.

Find, fix and verify PHP2Shell and Node2Shell across your apps and APIs with TotalAppSec.

Where Most Response Plans Break

Most plans follow the same path: inventory hosts, upgrade, restart, close the ticket. That works until one of three gaps appears. In each case, the fix was applied in one place, but the attacker reaches the application through another.

The application nobody owns

You can’t test or patch what isn’t in your inventory. Forgotten microsites, acquired apps, and shadow APIs can run old runtimes, and they are the ones nobody is watching.

A version string is a hint, not proof

Proxies can strip the headers that reveal a PHP version, so a version-based check can miss a vulnerable app. Distribution builds can carry a backported fix under an older version number, so the same check can flag a fixed one. Neither a version banner nor a package list tells you how the application behaves when an attacker sends a request.

Patched on disk is not patched in production

Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until services such as PHP-FPM or long-running Node.js apps restart. Servers can also carry more than one PHP copy, so upgrading one leaves another. The fix only counts if the patched runtime is the one serving requests.

A response built to end in proof

An industry-neutral response has five steps, and the fourth is the one most teams skip.

Find every runtime and application. Inventory the web apps and APIs behind your internet-facing services and the runtimes under them. Include end-of-life versions, containers, vendor-bundled runtimes and apps nobody owns.

Scan, then rank by exposure. Start with internet-facing apps. Most teams can’t tell which apps use Apache mod_php or decompress untrusted Brotli data until they scan, so test first and rank the confirmed findings.

Fix, then restart. Upgrade to a fixed version or your distribution’s backported build, and restart every service that loads the runtime. If you can’t patch yet, apply the vendor’s interim mitigations and restrict access to the service.

Prove it from the outside. Retest the same applications and APIs, and treat any remaining finding as an incomplete fix. Also check for signs of compromise from before the patch, since exploitation began early.

Make it repeatable. The next trending CVE will start the same race. A standing process beats a scramble.

How to detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell in web apps and APIs with TotalAppSec

Qualys TotalAppSec brings AI-powered, unified risk management to web apps and APIs. For PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, it tests the application itself over HTTP, the same path an attacker uses, not just the host. Six new QIDs cover both web applications and APIs.

Two kinds of evidence: Potential findings (QIDs 520310 and 520404) read PHP version signals from response headers and application cookies. Confirmed findings (QIDs 533086 and 533203) observe behavior in the live application: how PHP handles a session ID with an invalid character, and how Node.js handles a crafted Brotli payload. Four of the six checks are non-intrusive and can be safely used in production.

A safe way to verify: The two intrusive checks (QIDs 533068 and 533085) stress the application and can crash an unpatched one. Run them in a QA environment or on a patched production system, through the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile, so verification is a deliberate step with approvals and a maintenance window.

A ready starting point for the next one: TotalAppSec includes two system-generated option profiles for scanning trending CVEs such as PHP2Shell and Node2Shell. To run a PHP2Shell and Node2Shell web application scan, choose a profile, select your apps by name or tag, and launch. The product tour below walks you through each step. Your scheduled scans may already include the four non-intrusive QIDs, because they are part of the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles and of AI-powered scans.

Each finding attaches to a named application or API, so its owner can act on it. After the fix and restart, rescan the same applications. If a QID still reports, the patched runtime isn’t the one serving those requests.

TotalAppSec shows what is exposed at the application and API layer. The runtime underneath lives on hosts, in images and in cloud workloads, where Qualys VMDR, TotalCloud and Container Security find vulnerable PHP and Node.js components. The Qualys Threat Research Unit covers that side in the PHP2Shell and Node.js blogs.

See It in Action with This Interactive Product Tour

The Next Runtime Flaw Is Already On Its Way

PHP2Shell and Node2Shell showed how quickly a flaw in the layer under your applications can become an application risk. The pattern will repeat. The next critical runtime flaw may also sit outside your own code, and attackers will again move faster than most patch cycles.

The teams that cope best aren’t the ones scrambling hardest in the first week. They already know which web apps and APIs they have, can see which are exposed, and can confirm a fix actually worked. Patched is a claim about a server. Proof is a finding about an application. Qualys TotalAppSec gives you that application-level view, with ready-made trending vulnerability profiles to start from.

Know Your PHP2Shell Exposure and Mitigate It with Qualys

Our free service finds PHP2Shell across your internet-facing assets, proves which servers attackers can exploit, and gives you a patch or mitigation path for each one, including versions PHP will never fix.

Get Our Free Services

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Which option profiles include the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell QIDs?

The four non-intrusive QIDs (520310, 533086, 520404 and 533203) are in the Trending Vulnerability Options profile, and also in the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles. The two intrusive QIDs (533068 and 533085) are only in Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options.

Does an AI-powered scan test for the new QIDs?

Yes, for the four non-intrusive QIDs. The two intrusive QIDs are not part of AI-powered scans, so run them separately with the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile.

When can a scan miss PHP2Shell or Node2Shell?

Version-based checks (QIDs 520310 and 520404) can miss an app when a web server or proxy strips response headers and hides the PHP version. The confirmed checks (QIDs 533086 and 533203) test how the application responds instead of reading version headers.

How do I confirm a fix worked?

Upgrade the runtime, restart the affected services, then rescan the same applications with Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options on patched systems or outside production, with approvals and a maintenance window. If a QID is still reported, the fix is incomplete, so check that the patched runtime is serving requests.

articles.title: The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
articles.context: No vulnerability needs to be exploited
articles.full_text:
For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production. An agent can reach systems that previously required deliberate human intervention, often using permissions granted for an entirely different purpose. Unlike conventional software, an agent may take different actions when presented with the same task because its context and decisions change. CISOs now face a fundamentally different challenge: governing autonomous software that already holds active pathways into production.

The security control we never recognized was human judgment

Where human developers and coding agents diverge most sharply is in judgment, not technical capability.Developers understand what state their code is in, whether it’s something they’re testing or something that’s production-ready. They understand what their credentials permit them to do, but also when and how those credentials should be used. There’s an implicit compartmentalization between having access and exercising it.An AI agent is much more single-minded. If an available credential helps accomplish the task, the agent uses it. Agents don’t recognize the distinction between what is technically possible and what policy permits.Consider an agent asked to troubleshoot a failing application. It discovers production credentials on the developer’s laptop and determines that querying the live database is the fastest way to diagnose the problem. It might modify production data while attempting a fix, even though the developer intended only to investigate a local issue. No vulnerability needs to be exploited. The agent simply uses available authority to pursue its assigned objective.Traditional development pipelines weren’t designed around software that independently decides which systems to access and what actions to take. Security controls must now account for behavior that can’t be fully anticipated from the original request.

A sandbox can contain an agent without containing its authority

Sandboxing has emerged as an obvious response to the risks of autonomous agents. By isolating execution inside a container, virtual machine or microVM, organizations can limit an agent’s ability to interfere with its host or other workloads.Strong isolation is essential, particularly when agents execute untrusted code or interact with potentially malicious tools. A microVM with its own guest kernel can provide a stronger boundary than a conventional container sharing the host kernel. But isolation answers only part of the security question.An agent sandbox that blocks all external access is as useful as a computer encased in cement at the bottom of the ocean.An agent doesn’t have to escape its sandbox to cause a security incident. It can misuse perfectly legitimate permissions, send sensitive information through an authorized network connection or make destructive changes using credentials deliberately provided to it.Isolating execution is useless unless you also precisely control what that workload can reach. A secure sandbox containing unrestricted credentials still leaves an enormous attack surface.

Can you revoke an agent without disabling its developer?

Security professionals are familiar with least privilege, but agentic development exposes the limitations of conventional identity and access management.Consider a developer who authorizes an agent to modify one GitHub repository. If the agent uses the developer’s personal token, it may inherit access to every repository that developer can reach. That could include merge permissions, CI/CD environments and downstream credentials associated with those systems.This is ambient authority: the ability to perform actions beyond the particular task for which access was originally intended. Even a relatively narrow token may authorize repeated actions when the agent only needed permission to perform the action once.When an agent operates under a developer’s credentials, revoking its access can also mean disabling the developer. Security teams need to separate autonomous workloads from human identity.Agents should have independently defined identities, with permissions delegated for specific purposes. That makes it possible to track what each agent did, investigate where something went wrong and revoke an individual agent’s authority without disrupting its developer.

The missing link is a trusted broker

One of the most interesting developments in agentic security is the emerging idea of a trusted broker that sits between an agent and the systems it wants to access.Some approaches are described as MCP proxies. Others use authorization services, gateways or different architectures. What they’re circling is the same fundamental problem: how do we decide which agents can access which resources, under what circumstances and for how long?Crucially, the agent cannot be responsible for deciding the limits of its own authority. Those decisions must be enforced by a separate system that can authorize individual operations without surrendering the credentials that make them possible.Imagine asking an agent to fix a GitHub issue. Instead of granting unrestricted repository access, the developer authorizes the task once. A trusted intermediary could then permit the agent to read the repository, push changes to a designated branch and open a pull request. Those permissions could expire after an hour, without exposing a broadly reusable developer credential.This is the core tension agentic security has to resolve. Grant too little access and developers abandon the controls. Grant too much and isolation becomes irrelevant to the damage an authorized agent can cause. The goal is to make secure delegation as frictionless as unrestricted access.Agentic security may be approaching a comparable architectural moment. Developers, open-source projects and commercial vendors are experimenting with approaches to identity, delegation, authorization and policy enforcement. Some organizations are building their own controls around existing IAM systems. Others are exploring dedicated intermediaries that evaluate requests before allowing agents to reach external resources.The trusted broker is not yet a universally defined component, and there’s no guarantee one implementation will become the equivalent of Kubernetes. Questions about policy decisions, credential custody, latency, availability and auditability remain open.But the missing function is becoming clearer. We need a dependable intermediary that translates human intent into narrowly defined, enforceable authority for autonomous software.

MCP servers have become a new software supply chain

MCP is one of the principal ways agents connect to external tools and information. That makes it both an important integration mechanism and a security boundary.A malicious MCP server can become an indirect route into an agent’s workflow. If servers or tools execute with access to shared filesystems, processes or credential stores, a compromised component may be able to read secrets belonging to another tool.But credential theft isn’t the only concern. A compromised server can return manipulated information that influences an agent’s subsequent actions even before the agent uses the tool. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise the agent—only the context it consumes.The familiar disciplines of provenance, signing and build integrity need to extend to MCP servers, agent tools and model weights. Organizations should know where these components originated, whether they’ve been modified and what authority they receive when introduced into an environment.The answer is layered security: strong isolation, independently managed identities, narrowly scoped permissions, controlled network access and sufficient observability to understand what agents actually do.

Why agent security belongs in the execution path

Containerization demonstrated that security works best when guardrails are baked directly into developer platforms without stripping away speed. Kubernetes eventually made it possible to enforce common security and operational policies across distributed workloads without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure expert. Agentic development needs a comparable shift.The longer-term opportunity is to move from granting persistent access to delegating task-specific authority. Developers need a way to authorize an agent to fix one issue or open one pull request without surrendering standing keys.Laptops are production endpoints now, and they won’t revert back to safe sandboxes. Security teams must protect developer speed by embedding the boundaries that human judgment used to handle manually directly into the infrastructure.

Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
articles.context: The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment
articles.full_text: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, November 12th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10176, (Thu, Nov 12th)
articles.context: Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 12, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich. We're recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. And as so often after a Patch Tuesday, we have a bit of a cleanup episode here today covering issues that we may have missed. Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. The vulnerability allows for remote code execution. The problem here is that during stream processing, the assign_headers function is used to assign request headers to specific streams. That's where a heap overflow happens. And well, that of course, then could potentially be used to trigger remote code execution. No working exploit has been made public yet. Disabling HTTP/2 can be used to mitigate the issue. Of course, you may run into other issues. If you, for example, have proxies translating to HTTP/2, you have always to be careful with HTTP request smuggling in this case. And Fortinet published 89 different advisories addressing more than 100 different vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. 17 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical, FortiMail being sort of the product with the most critical vulnerabilities being addressed in this update. Now, several of the critical issues may lead to arbitrary code execution without authentication. Too many vulnerabilities really to talk in detail on about each particular vulnerability. But well, if you have Fortinet products in your environment, there's probably a patch that you must apply. And now for these product. And as listeners probably expect when they hear about that many vulnerabilities all of a sudden popping up. Yes, AI took a part in discovering these vulnerabilities. And Ivanti also released its November 2026 security update. Now in this update, there is one patch for another SQL injection vulnerability, in Endpoint Manager. This SQL injection vulnerability may be leveraged to accomplish remote code execution. And then we also have a vulnerability in Ivanti CSA that allowed altering trusted EPM Core certificates without authentication. And then we got another, well, Saturday, Wednesday after patch Tuesday, thanks to Nightmare Eclipse. Nightmare Eclipse released what they're calling SignDrop. SignDrop is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Windows Common Log File System. What makes this kind of interesting is that about a year ago, Microsoft added HMAC based authentication to CLFS log files to make it harder to abuse them in response to some of the vulnerabilities in this overall system. While SignDrop abuses exactly that new feature with some symlink and timing tricks, a regular user can escalate to system on Windows 11, 26H2 and Windows Server 2025. A proof of concept exploit has been posted to GitHub. So far, Microsoft has not confirmed the issue. There is no CVE number. I have not seen any reports of it being exploited. And as tempting as it may be, disabling CLFS log authentication is probably not a good workaround. Again, that was specifically established to prevent other security issues. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced. And a quick follow up to the N-able N-central story from earlier this week. N-able has now released the 2026.4 hotfix 2 for N-central. And with that release notes explaining what they're fixing here. They're identifying three different CVE numbers that are addressed in this update. Now, if you remember N-able shut down actually its own sort of cloud -based infrastructure in response to these vulnerabilities being reported to N-able. And yes, now we get the patch for it. The initial news release, I think, talked about like 30 vulnerabilities. So not sure if these are just the sort of the critical ones they're patching here. They're actually being exploited right now. Or if they sort of consolidated some of these vulnerabilities. There are some reports that attackers are already probing for vulnerable paths that were leaked. Of course, there have been a lot of issues with N-able N-central in the past. This could be also some older stuff. The good news, many of you appear to have listened. Shadowserver's count of exposed N-central servers dropped from about 1,338 to around 148. So almost like a factor of nine or 10 here. If you run N-central on premise, apply the hotfix before you bring the server back online. And probably still avoid exposing it if you can help it. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye. You

articles.title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
articles.context: 5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and...
articles.full_text:
Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks.

If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which can then offset much of its higher price per token.

Here's how the current models compare:
