articles.title: TiffInTech explains the server room problem
Default Admin Password Let Researchers Unlock and Start Cars
articles.context: Test Car Unlocked and Started From a Hijacked Account In early 2026, the researchers bypassed the web application firewall (WAF) in front of the login servers and found the...
articles.full_text:
Researchers been able to take over customer accounts at two car brands. They then demonstrated how they could remotely unlock and start a test car after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password.

Security researchers Shubham Shah and Sam Curry detailed the work in a write-up published November 7. Customer logins for both brands ran on OpenIDM, identity management software from ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity. The brands were not named, at the automakers' request.

The researchers reported the flaw to the two automakers and pointed to ForgeRock's hardening guidance to remove or protect the console before deployment.

Test Car Unlocked and Started From a Hijacked Account

In early 2026, the researchers bypassed the web application firewall (WAF) in front of the login servers and found the console still accepted its documented default credentials. From there they ran their own code on the identity servers and changed the email address and password on a test account.

Logging in as that customer through the normal app, they unlocked and started the test car with its owner present. The session also exposed the vehicle's location and telemetry.

The researchers wrote that they could have created a session for any customer account on the affected deployments. Changing an account's login details also left the owner's existing app session active, and the researchers could divert the app's notifications away from the owner's phone.

Both automakers fixed the issue about two hours after the flaw was reported and rotated affected credentials, according to the write-up.

Read more on default passwords in connected systems: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks

Australian Systems Exposed Through Hardcoded Credentials

In a companion post, Shah described a separate chain against one of the automaker's Australian systems, researched in July 2026.

The chain could start from a car's number plate. Hardcoded administrator credentials, a WAF bypass and a misconfigured multi-factor authentication (MFA) step then allowed account takeover and remote unlocking.

The exposed data included customers' names, phone numbers and password hashes. Together, the write-ups covered vehicles in Australia, the US and Canada. The researchers wrote that they tested only on cars they owned or had permission to use.

Shah's post does not say when the Australian findings were reported or whether they have been fixed. Neither post reports malicious use or says whether the researchers checked for it.

Shah's post also does not mention when the Australian findings were reported or whether they have been fixed. Neither post reports malicious use or says whether the researchers checked for it.

Ping Identity was contacted for comment but did not respond by the time of publication.

articles.title: Your Artifact Repositories Need a Firewall
articles.context: Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise
articles.full_text:
Most organizations spend a lot of time looking for vulnerabilities in the software they build. But what about the malicious packages that enter before development even begins?

Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise. Malicious packages can run code during installation, when a developer or build system may already have access to source code, tokens, cloud accounts, or publishing credentials.

CI pipelines and AI agents add to the volume of package requests. They can resolve and install dependencies automatically, often without a human reviewing each request. That makes the point where packages enter the development workflow an important place to evaluate risk.

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests against threat intelligence and policy before components reach developers, agents, or builds. The protection depends on the quality of that intelligence and where the firewall can evaluate a request.

Recent Attacks Show How Much Can Hide in a Package

In October 2026, a hijacked release of the TensorLake TypeScript SDK used an install hook to search for credentials and accept remote commands.

Sonatype's analysis found code that could modify repositories accessible to the compromised account and could expose collected data through a GitHub fallback. The investigation did not confirm that data was published, repositories were modified, or downstream systems were affected.

Other campaigns used different routes into the same workflows:

Hijacked packages and new malicious packages: Six npm packages delivered the same malware. Three appeared to be hijacked legitimate packages, and three were published with the malicious payload already included. The malware used Ethereum transactions to find infrastructure hosting additional payloads.

Large-scale package flooding: Sonatype identified nearly 850 components in the Flooding Dropper campaign. The packages downloaded and launched additional payloads on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Credential theft and propagation: The Mini Shai-Hulud wave affected more than 2,200 component versions. Malicious releases of legitimate packages used install hooks to steal credentials and, where publishing access was available, compromise more packages.

Install-time execution: Miasma waves abused binding.gyp and node-gyp to execute during installation, rather than relying only on familiar lifecycle scripts. The Leo Platform compromise report tracked 23 malicious package versions.

These incidents show why package risk is not limited to suspicious names or newly created projects. Malicious code can arrive in a familiar package, run as part of installation, and act with the access available to the developer, build, or agent that requested it.

What a Repository or Package Firewall Does

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests as they pass from a development environment toward package sources. It evaluates a requested component against security intelligence and, depending on the product's capabilities and configuration, can block or quarantine components that appear malicious or violate policy.

Once a package has been installed, teams may need to investigate the affected machine, identify exposed credentials, check for persistence, and determine whether the package reached other systems. Blocking a known malicious package at the point of entry can help prevent that cleanup from starting in the first place.

A firewall is one layer of software supply chain protection. It does not replace endpoint security, code review, or other controls. It addresses a specific risk: malicious or policy-violating components entering through package requests. And like any control, its coverage depends on which developers, pipelines, agents, and package sources route through it.

What to Look for in a Package Firewall

A repository or package firewall should do more than sit between a repository and a registry. As you evaluate options, consider whether or not it can:

Block malicious components before download, at the point where a package is requested.

Use current, in-depth threat intelligence that can help identify more than known vulnerabilities or suspicious package names.

Protect requests from developers, CI pipelines, and AI agents that can access public package sources.

Fit your repository tools and package sources without requiring a change to established workflows.

Cover the package ecosystems your teams use, and make clear which registries, mirrors, and private sources are included.

Strong firewall protection helps teams stay ahead of threats by identifying and blocking malicious components before they enter the development process. By evaluating package requests at the point of intake, it can reduce the risk of compromised builds and the investigation and rework that follow, while helping teams keep development moving.

How Sonatype's Intelligence Informs Firewall Decisions

A firewall's decision is only as useful as the evidence behind it. Sonatype Firewall combines machine-learning signals with AI-powered analysis, alongside the expertise of Sonatype's security research team, to identify suspicious packages and investigate if they contain malicious code.

By analyzing release behavior, examining package contents, and correlating findings across multiple sources, Sonatype can detect threats earlier, uncover additional affected packages, and turn new discoveries into actionable intelligence that informs Firewall's blocking and quarantine decisions.

That work can involve several kinds of analysis:

Activity and release patterns can help surface packages that behave differently from their project's history or from typical ecosystem activity.

Behavioral analysis can flag unusual signals around a package or release. Researchers can investigate those findings to confirm whether a component is malicious.

Payload analysis examines what the code actually does, including behavior such as credential theft, code injection, or downloading another payload.

Secondary expansion follows the code beyond the original package. Advanced Binary Fingerprinting can help identify embedded or renamed code that may not appear in a package's declared dependencies. In one investigation, Sonatype researchers found code associated with the flatmap-stream incident in 12 additional npm components.

Together, these methods provide context that a package name or manifest alone cannot. That context helps a firewall make a more informed decision about whether to allow, block, or hold a request for review.

Give Every Package Request a Safer Path

Every dependency starts with a request. A developer adds a package, a pipeline pulls it into a build, or an AI agent selects it for generated code. That request is an opportunity to assess a component before it becomes part of your software.

Sonatype Firewall helps teams bring security and development together at the moment open source enters the software supply chain. Backed by Sonatype's research and designed to work with supported repository environments, it helps organizations block malicious components earlier before they reach developers or workflows. That gives teams a chance to stop known threats at the point of entry, reduce avoidable disruption, and keep development moving with greater confidence.

Even if your existing repositories support secure component selection, malicious packages can still make their way into development. The difference comes down to how threats are identified, how quickly new malicious activity is detected, and whether that intelligence can stop a package before it's downloaded. Sonatype Firewall is that difference. Since it's designed to work with a wide range of repository managers, you can add an additional layer of protection to block known risks and avoid downstream work.

See how Sonatype Firewall can help protect your repositories from malicious packages.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
articles.context: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that...
articles.full_text: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register. Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI." As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years. AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens." "The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited. "So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out." Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general. "We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

articles.title: Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data
articles.context: It’s the reason we have detections in the first place
articles.full_text:
At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

After the alert

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Data vs. data

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:

Are full transaction details provided or just a summary?

Is packet content or file extraction available?

How far back can we search, and how fast?

Can I follow a connection across hosts and time?

AI <3 data

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

Unfamiliar territory is the test

When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

Look at the transactions behind the alert

Ask what packet content or extracted files are available

Follow the activity backwards and forwards in time

Ask a question that wasn’t anticipated

These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

About Corelight:

Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. Learn more about Corelight at https://corelight.com/cp/elitedefense

articles.title: Bitdefender Threat Debrief | November 2026
articles.context: Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest
articles.full_text:
N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

This edition of the Bitdefender Threat Debrief covers the latest events in the ransomware threat landscape, including the claims surrounding the rise of the new ransomware group N0n, a former affiliate that turns on The Gentlemen, and news concerning BYOD ransomware.

As ransomware continues to evolve, our goal with this monthly Bitdefender Threat Debrief is to help you stay ahead of the curve. To do this, we combine information from openly available sources (OSINT) - things like news reports and research – with data we gather by analyzing Data Leak Sites (DLSs), websites where ransomware groups post details about their victims. It is important to remember that we can't independently verify all of these claims but are confident in the trends we see over time.

For this month's report, we analyzed data from October 1 to October 31, 2026, and recorded 1,072 claimed ransomware victims. Note that when excluding some of N0n’s victim dataset (126 victims) from October’s total victims, the actual number of victims reported is actually 946.

Featured Story: N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

What Happened?

In mid-September, the ransomware group N0n emerged. The group hosted a data leak site with more than 100 victims, divided into categories including pending, exposed, leaked, and honors (where NOn claims to have honored the promise to destroy victim data in exchange for a ransom payment).

Several weeks later, information about N0n’s operations became plainly visible due to N0n’s failures to maintain strict operational security measures. N0n’s Python file server was left accessible on the open Internet. This presented visitors with the opportunity to go to the web address and navigate through directory structures to view contents of the server. This exposure allowed cyber defense and research teams to determine with greater confidence that N0n’s image as a potentially significant threat is just that: a false depiction. N0n is a newcomer to the ransomware landscape, relying on AI tools for foundational hacking tasks.

What Information was Disclosed in N0n’s Exposure?

N0n’s file server address is associated with a location in Sweden. Several types of information were disclosed in the aftermath of N0n’s exposure. All information types revealed make it highly unlikely that N0n is a ransomware group capable of competing with other leading threats. N0n;s actual victim count (rather than their published/perceived victim population) and their use of open-source AI dismantles their apparent trend of continuous growth. According to the data obtained from N0n’s file server, the group targeted just over 20 victims. Duplicate or false entries may have emerged due to weaknesses in maintaining the site and polling potential targets.

N0n also uses an open-source AI platform, OpenCode, to manage different AI models and write scripts. N0n invested more than $7000 in Generative AI to assist them in building common scripts that are maintained to perform actions necessary for scanning and reconnaissance activities. While an encryptor was also identified, debate remains over whether N0n consistently uses ransomware. Their reuse of encryption keys and weaknesses in OPSEC may point towards hesitancy for the group to execute ransomware code more frequently.

The exposure of N0n’s server also revealed that N0n references the same encryption keys that are used across different victim campaigns. This means that the group was leveraging the exact same ransomware code and keys to lockdown systems for different targets. Cybersecurity teams supporting victims with access to those hardcoded encryption keys can then analyze them and identify patterns needed for decryption.

What Actions are Recommended for Organizations?

As opportunistic ransomware groups continue to adopt AI into their operations, it is important for organizations to remember the following:

Data theft claims often initially lack any validity. Keep an inventory of your assets, including critical data that may be found in open repositories. Do not assume that any data stolen is from a current dataset or usable by the threat actor without supporting evidence.

Harden remote access controls to secure systems. This includes enforcing VPN access, restricting access via RDP and also requiring MFA authentication.

Enforce a strong password policy and regularly rotate credentials.

Regularly document breach cases predating current operations and check for additional exposures.

Maintain backups in a location separate from critical infrastructure and test them regularly to ensure backup data can be restored.

Request and review intelligence on an ongoing basis to evaluate the threat actor’s behavior and current indicators of compromise

Other Notable Ransomware News

Now, let’s explore the notable news and findings since the last Threat Debrief.

Azazel, an affiliate of The Gentlemen, turns on their operator: Azazel has accumulated more than 6 terabytes of stolen data. Despite their affiliation with The Gentlemen, the group broke away from them after stealing data in an RaaS campaign and keeping the profits for themselves. Azazel published the stolen data on a data leak site under the name Leakned. Notably, Azazel has leveraged a technique that differs from other ransomware groups. They used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to establish a connection between an AI coding assistant and a reverse shell. This connection allows Azazel to use the AI assistant as a command and control channel, executing commands on compromised machines. Azazel has engaged in primarily in data theft and credential theft, extracting credentials from GitLab and other pipelines.

BYOD ransomware claims university that provides healthcare services: BYOD, a ransomware group that emerged in September, has claimed enterprise organizations across both North America and Southeast Asia. The group recently claimed a university clinic that provides healthcare services to patients. Within 24 hours of their claim, BYOD expressed that they did not realize the systems they targeted were used specifically to support direct patient care. BYOD announced they would make decryptors available to the victim organization for free; and, the affected victims are encouraged to reach them and submit a payment of $2,500 to ensure their data is destroyed. These claims are identified as potential ploys to extend the compromise and/or collect additional payment.

Booba Team claims more victims and hits government organizations: Booba Team has claimed more than 9 government organizations at the time of this release. According to Booba Team’s data leak site, this accounts for more than 800 GB of stolen data. Booba Team’s total victims claimed in the government sector in October surpasses the totals in the same period for both Qilin (who claimed 6 victims) and The Gentlemen (who claimed 3 victims). Unlike Qilin and The Gentlemen, who have broadened their victim populations to include government victims in Western Europe and Southeast Asia, Booba Team has continued to claim victims in a limited number of regions, including North America (specifically the US) and South America. The group has been known to deploy ransomware and conduct data theft.

New brands continue to make their entry into the ransomware ecosystem: More than 17 ransomware groups have emerged in the last two months. Several newcomers were identified in October, including but not limited to: aoqin, everstake, shiba, whitearmor, hyflock, umbra, vypr, and scarlettgroup. While some groups emerge out of a necessity to commit acts of organized crime, with limited influence from other threat groups. However, the largest variables that contribute to new ransomware groups include law enforcement takedowns, feuds and factions among ransomware groups and affiliates, and operational failures. Bitdefender will continue to track further developments in ransomware takedowns, rebrands, and evolutions.

Top 10 Ransomware Families

Bitdefender's Threat Debrief analyzes data from ransomware data leak sites, where groups publicize their claimed number of compromised organizations. This approach provides valuable insights into overall RaaS market activity. However, it comes with a trade-off: while it reflects attackers' self-proclaimed success, the information comes directly from criminals and may be unreliable. Additionally, this method captures the number of victims claimed, not the actual financial impact of these attacks.

The Top 10 ransomware groups in October include N0n, The Gentlemen, Qilin, Akira, and Booba Team. Note that due to several indicators of N0n misrepresenting their operations and victims, Bitdefender has high confidence that N0n is not in actuality a group that has the means to maintain a ranking in the Top 10 Groups.

Top 10 Most Attacked Regions

Ransomware gangs prioritize targets where they can squeeze the most money from victims. In many cases, this means focusing on developed countries with higher projected growth rates. Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest.

Taiwan rejoins the Top 10 Regions: Taiwan ranked 10th in October; most of the region’s industries affected by ransomware attacks are in manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

Victims based in South Korea rise due to N0n’s claims: The number of ransomware victims based in South Korea rose to 18 in October. N0n claimed 11 victims based in South Korea; all of these victims are organizations in the transportation industry. However, due to the high level of scrutiny cast on the validity of N0n’s claims, this increase should not be viewed as an accurate pattern of behavior. Ransomware groups have not claimed a total number of victims based in South Korea surpassing 10 per month since September 2025 when Qilin executed the Korean Leaks campaign.

Top 10 Most Attacked Industries

Ransomware gangs may target organizations in critical infrastructure sectors, select other organizations that offer services tailored to consumers, or attack organizations that fall into both categories. Understanding the trends and ramifications associated with specific industries, and how specialized services and clientele are impacted is crucial for assessing risk. Here are the Top 10 industries affected by ransomware attacks.

Healthcare rises to second place in the Top Industries

In October, there was an increase in the number of victim organizations represented in the manufacturing and healthcare industries. Healthcare rose to the second rank. And, the transportation industry moved from the 10th rank to the 6th rank in the Top Industries with N0n claiming a total of 20 transportation victims.

About Bitdefender Threat Debrief

The Bitdefender Threat Debrief (BDTD) is a monthly series analyzing threat news, trends, and research from the previous month. Don’t miss the next BDTD release, subscribe to the Business Insights blog, and follow us on Twitter. You can find all previous debriefs here.

Bitdefender provides cybersecurity solutions and advanced threat protection to hundreds of millions of endpoints worldwide. More than 180 technology brands have licensed and added Bitdefender technology to their product or service offerings. This vast OEM ecosystem complements telemetry data already collected from our business and consumer solutions. To give you some idea of the scale, Bitdefender Labs discover 400+ new threats each minute and validate 30 billion threat queries daily. This gives us one of the industry’s most extensive real-time views of the evolving threat landscape.

We would like to thank Bitdefenders Stefan Hanu, Mihai Leonte, Gabriel Macovei, and Andrei Mogage for their help with putting this report together.

A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
articles.context: Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning...
articles.full_text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.
