articles.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
articles.context: An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and...
articles.full_text:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.

For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.

Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6. Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;

A technical report explaining the details of our system;

A (Claude-written) protocol specification document;

Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and

Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.

Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

Challenge 3: text provenance

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

Challenge 4: model approval

Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

Our system: FlashProve

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:

In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase.

In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:

The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

Guarantees

A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:

A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier.

A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden.

A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure.

Evaluation

We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

Prover. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report, the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.

Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.

Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

Engineering the system

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

The prover's work is proportional to the experts that actually ran. In a MoE model a token uses ~17B of the 400B parameters, and the prover's work per token is proportional to those ~17B instead of all parameters (the proof still hides which experts were chosen).

Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request.

The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices.

Post-hoc versus in-line

When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.

Trustworthiness from formal verification

Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?

The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:

Completeness: if the statement is correct, the resulting proof is accepted by the verifier.

Soundness: any fake proof is rejected by the verifier (except with negligible probability).

Zero knowledge: the proof reveals no information about the weights of the model, beyond what the verifier can infer from the response itself.4

These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.

Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.

Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.

For soundness, we only need the verifier code to be correct (the entire value of having “proofs” is that you can fully distrust the prover if you trust the verifier). We provide an executable Lean verifier, alongside the C++ verifier. The Lean verifier runs more slowly, but Lean proves that it accepts only what the verifier in our soundness theorem accepts. Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests.

For completeness, the threat model does not assume adversarial attacks (the prover and verifier are honest). Therefore, a Lean verifier lets us gain confidence through standard software testing that the honest prover produces accepting proofs: run the prover on a correct statement, and then the Lean verifier on the resulting proof.

For zero knowledge, we only need the prover to be correct. However, unlike the verifier, the prover is an expensive procedure, and it would be impractical to run a Lean prover. We do not provide facilitations here: we expect that any prover that wants to hide the weights of a model they are serving has access to enough resources for careful agentic and/or human security audits to ensure equivalence to the Lean prover.

Prior work

Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.

Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. In 2025, zkGPT reduced GPT-2 to 21.8 s (≈0.05 tok/s), zkPyTorch proved Llama-3 8B at ~150 s per token on one CPU core (≈0.007 tok/s), and ZKTorch proved GPT-J (6B) in about 20 minutes (≈0.001 tok/s). VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. DeepProve, a current peer-reviewed state of the art, certifies an entire generated sequence with a single forward pass. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100.

Recently commercial efforts have reached impressive numbers, with Attestable proving Gemma 4 31B at 53–77 tok/s on a single H100; at the time of writing, Attestable has not released a corresponding open source library.

The above numbers speak to the precipitous progress of provable inference in the past years. They should update our priors on what it is possible to prove in zero-knowledge.

In 2024, zkLLM proved a 13B model at about 2.5 tokens/second on one A100. The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify.

FlashProve proves the same model at 110 tokens/second on a single H100, with 19 MB proofs that can be verified in seconds. Attestable independently reports 53–77 tokens/second for a dense 31B model.

We believe that the progress should transfer to more models and architectures, yielding a flexible and powerful tool with overhead over native computation of roughly 2 orders of magnitude (about 70 to 95 times in our measurements), much less than previously expected.

Limitations

This release is a research prototype, and has the following technical limitations:

No formal guarantees on fast executable code. We provide a Lean implementation of the protocol (including an executable “slow” Lean verifier), along with security properties proved in Lean. The paper and the fast executable code are derived from the Lean protocol, but we do not guarantee that all three (Lean, paper, code) match each other.

The proof is about an integer model under greedy decoding. We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved. The integer version is generally expected and empirically tested to be within some small error rate of true floating-point inference generically (even taking into account non-determinism of floating-point computations), though this does not cover adversarially designed prompts.

Architecture hiding. Our system assumes the served model uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, in which each transformer layer’s feed-forward block is replaced by multiple expert sub-networks and a router that activates only a small subset of experts for each token and our system uses the MoE structure for efficiency gains. Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model.

Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release.

Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens).

articles.title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
articles.context: With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT)
articles.full_text:
Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions.

How message threads works

A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT).

With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%.

To use message threads, add the thread parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.

Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including:

Long-running coding agents, where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation.

Computer use agents, where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn.

Document and image-heavy workflows, where requests are made smaller.

The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token.

Getting started

Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the documentation to get started.

articles.title: Kubernetes Security Monitoring & Threat Detection with Behavioral AI
articles.context: [2] While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent...
articles.full_text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Credit to Emma Foulger, Sam Lister, Dylan Evans, Moishe Tajtelbaum

By pure timing coincidence, the Proton CEO's AI @ Proton, Engineering Manifesto made headlines around the same time as this week's video. The guy's management style and choice of language have really rubbed a lot of people up the wrong way, and deservedly so, IMHO. However... this section of his screed really resonated with me:

Your job has fundamentally changed. It is no longer to write code, and LLMs are not here to help you write better code faster. Your job is to help the LLM write better code faster.

Dev jobs as we know them are gone. Dead. And if you disagree, you're in for a shock in the very near future. But at the same time:

I don't remember the last time tech has been this exciting. It's white hot right now. Anyone who loves technology and computers is probably having a great time right now.

— Jack Rhysider 🏴‍☠️ (@JackRhysider) October 30, 2026

Yes! This! Not handwriting code "old school" isn't something to lament; rather, our unprecedented ability to innovate, create and build things that are meaningful to us is something to be enormously excited about. Anyway, on that topic:

articles.title: The long road to root. [Research Saturday]
articles.context: " A Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Red Heron exploited a critical Gitea remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-60004, within days of its public disclosure,...
articles.full_text:
Today we are joined by ⁠⁠Subhajeet Singha⁠⁠, Senior Security Researcher at ⁠⁠Acronis⁠⁠ Threat Research Unit, discussing their work on "Red Heron exploits Gitea n-day flaw in multinational campaign, exposing new Linux rootkit." A Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Red Heron exploited a critical Gitea remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-60004, within days of its public disclosure, compromising organizations across five countries and stealing source code, credentials, and sensitive infrastructure data.

The campaign involved deploying persistent backdoors and a newly identified Linux implant called JITTERLY, which contains an undocumented rootkit, SIXZUT, capable of hiding files, processes, and network connections while protecting the malware from removal. Acronis assesses with moderate confidence that Red Heron operates within a PRC-linked context, highlighting how quickly attackers can weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities and turn exposed development platforms into gateways for broader network compromise.

The research and executive brief can be found here:

⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Red Heron exploits Gitea n-day flaw in multinational campaign, exposing new Linux rootkit⁠

articles.title: “Black October” for AI Developer Platforms
articles.context: While there is no single vulnerability or dependency linking these attacks, the overall picture is strongly aligned with recent reports on two fronts: Agentic Attacks, which can...
articles.full_text:
At least nine AI Developer Platforms have disclosed incidents over the course of the month:

Fireworks AI (Oct 6)

Andromeda (Oct 9)

Zeabur (Oct 14)

Lightning AI (Oct 15)

OpenCode (Oct 16–17)

Railway (Oct 20)

Warp (Oct 23)

CommandCode (Oct 28)

Northflank (Oct 30)

Wiz customers can refer to our relevant Threat Intel Center advisories for more information on the Railway Platform Breach, Lightning AI Security Incident and the overall campaign.

Fireworks, OpenCode, and Warp have all reported indications of an “agent swarm” attack. Andromeda’s incident report calls it part of an "industry-wide attack." OpenCode and CommandCode have explicitly attributed their incidents to an attempt at “distillation.”

Any other month, and this would be the top security story. However, with all the ongoing incidents, few reports are connecting the dots across these attacks (Cloud Security Alliance as a notable exception).

The Pattern in these Attacks

Currently, most of these security incidents are still being analyzed, and detailed technical information is not available. Zeabur has shared a full write-up, and the company will be shutting down due to this incident. Railway has released a preliminary report and timeline.

However, there are some indicative details. Fireworks, Zeabur, and Lightning all attribute their incident root causes to credential access. Lightning was previously impacted by a supply chain attack within the Mini-Shai Hulud campaign. Railway so far has shared they believe the initial access was via “privilege escalation in our build infrastructure,” while Warp has suggested the root cause was a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode attributes it to a “legacy system.”

All public reports highlight targeted exploitation, explicitly hunting stored environment variables, with a focus on those granting AI access. While there is no single vulnerability or dependency linking these attacks, the overall picture is strongly aligned with recent reports on two fronts:

Agentic Attacks, which can enable threat actors to compromise victims faster and more efficiently.

The rise of LLMJacking, and the associated infrastructure of LLM Brokers. These create a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials. Distillation, notably alleged against Chinese AI labs, drives demand as well.

Impact and Follow-on activity

Reports on the impact of these attacks have so far been limited to anecdotal reports on social media, which include:

Alleged theft of cryptocurrency, to the tune of ~$371,000, using crypto keys stored in Railway

Abuse of stolen AI access, such as those from OpenCode, resulting in consumer bills in the hundreds to thousands of dollars

However, Wiz has been able to observe downstream abuse of enterprise credentials, whose compromise we can attribute to one of these vendor breaches. We will discuss an exemplary pair of such cases.

In both cases, we see abuse of keys that previously were heavily used from the infrastructure of a compromised vendor.

They shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach. It was a single InvokeModel from a residential IP address, in a one-minute sweep that tested stolen keys across multiple organizations. The call asked for Claude Fable 5.1, failed, and fell back to Opus 5.5, which worked.

In the days after this initial validation, both keys saw only a trickle of traffic: 14–120 calls a day from the same small Go client. The calls on the two keys ran in lockstep, about a minute apart. This indicates a single ongoing verification job checking that the keys remained valid.

Case A

Four days after the initial validation, a rotating proxy pool ran a catalog probe across dozens of addresses, sending one call per model across vendors: Amazon Nova, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, GLM, Kimi, Grok, GPT-6 Astra and older Claude models. Every call worked except Fable. A few hours later, a boto3 script on a residential address enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. Twenty-two seconds after that, bulk traffic started from the same address. Within the next half hour, a second host mapped quotas and model availability across regions, making more than a thousand calls in under a minute.

The Flood

Over thirty hours, after which the key was remediated, the actor made approximately 800k Bedrock calls, and about 90% of them succeeded. The bulk ran first from the residential address and then, overnight, from a Level 3 hosting address. The key's policy allowed global.* cross-region inference profiles, and the actor routed every call through them. Because global routing spread the load across regions, only about 6% of calls were throttled. Traffic leaned heavily on Opus: Opus models were three quarters of successful calls, led by Opus 5 (36%), Opus 5.5 (22%) and Opus 4.8 (10%).

Case B

Unlike Case A, this key was restricted. Seven days after the initial validation, it surfaced in an apparent reseller pool. Over four hours, thousands of failed calls came from rotating hosting addresses, each active for about 15 minutes. The calls failed because the key's policy allowed Bedrock only through us.* cross-region inference profiles, and the pool requested global.*.

Early the next morning, a checker on a shared VPN exit identified the working us.* model IDs. Two hours later, a boto3 script on a Level 3 address retested global.* and us.* and enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. It was the same script, down to the version string, that had probed Case A. Within minutes, the floodgates opened.

The Flood

Over thirteen hours, after which the key was remediated, that single Level 3 address made approximately 1.7 million Bedrock calls, with over a million successful. Nearly all of the rest were throttled: without global routing, the traffic ran into the account's regional quotas. Traffic was spread across a dozen Claude models and was less Opus-heavy than Case A. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 5 made up three quarters of successful calls.

The Stolen Tokens

In both cases, the token usage profile resembles resold coding-agent traffic. A typical call sent only a handful of uncached input tokens, the signature of prompt caching, and got back a few hundred tokens of output. A long tail of calls carried tens of thousands of uncached input tokens, consistent with many different end users behind a reseller. At list price, these two cases alone likely ran up over $100k in usage.

What we see from these Attackers

Our research has been able to link the usage of the keys in the cases above overt reselling organizations. While we are not able to definitively establish the relationship between these reselling organizations and either the initial compromise or the “flood” token abuse documented above, the actors had access to the compromised keys and tested them from their infrastructure. The use of the keys by multiple actors suggests a robust market for this type of credential.

“momo” - Resale (and compromise?)

Wiz Research identified an actor centered around 23.106.46.239 who appears to refer to themselves as “momo” who had access to the keys used in Case A and Case B and is tied to an overt LLM resale site. Infrastructure linked to this IP address goes back to 2025 and has hosted multiple sites with titles related to LLM resale, including the site llm-routing.com which is currently active and advertises discounted access to frontier models, while accepting payment in USDT. This IP has also hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October and was publicly named by Zeabur as being part of their compromise. While we cannot definitively tie this operation to the “flood” of abuse documented above, the operator did have access to the stolen keys.

The site momo.skin resolved to 23.106.46.239 in early 2026 and another site tied via passive dns (direct.465415.xyz), used the title "Moの自建网盘" ("Mo's self-built cloud drive").

In March of 2026, this actor begins advertising LLM related services, hosting sites with titles such as "ChatGPT Team 席位兑换" ("ChatGPT Team seat redemption"), and "ChatGPT 号池管理" ("ChatGPT account-pool management").

On October 8, 2026, a subdomain (artex.nhhh.de) resolving to 23.106.46.239 hosted a page with the title “ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台" ("ARTEX — autonomous penetration testing console"). This is four days before Zeabur’s timeline identifying that IP address targeting their infrastructure (Oct 12 - 14).

In late October the 23.106.46.239 address conducts api key checks on the keys used in cases A and B and attempts a PutAccountDataRetention call using the Case B key.

“Xingjiabi” - a second resale hub

Wiz also identified a second resale operation that was leveraging stolen keys. This one is publicly available at xingjiabiapi.org where they offer access to a wide range of frontier models for discount prices. Infrastructure tied to this site (38.246.114.118) was identified conducting permission checks on the keys used in both cases A and B. In both cases the checks were conducted after the high volume abuse of the key from unrelated ip addresses had already begun, suggesting that there is an active resale market for these keys.

A subdomain of the main site, s3.xingjiabiapi.org resolved to 38.246.114.118 beginning on September 10, 2026. This 38.246.114.118 IP address enumerated the key used in case A, listing the inference profiles and models per region, paging through every bedrock quota. It also conducted a manual test of the key being used in Case B.

One interesting note about this actor is they seem to be attempting to guard against distillation. Their domain was snapshotted hosting a page titled “蒸馏检测监控” (Distillation behaviour detection) that was designed to score users across three categories and attempt to sort them into “high risk”, “watch” and “normal”. This may indicate that the attackers are attempting to avoid being associated with distillation, potentially due to that activity leading to accounts being suspended.

IOCs

These IPs were used to test stolen keys and are suspected to be linked to LLM token abuse and resale. We do not have evidence that links them directly to the “Black October” attacks mentioned in this blog.

Indicator

Observed Activity

Reported by Zeabur and later used for credential checking

10/26 - 10/29

38.246.114.118

Checked permissions on several stolen keys

10/25 - 10/29

Checked permissions on several stolen keys

10/19 - 10/30

Identified using multiple stolen keys

10/18 - 10/25

articles.title: Crypto's biggest withdrawal.
articles.context: Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts.
articles.full_text:
Binance suffers a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. Russian disinformation targets U.S. elections. Treasury sanctions North Korean IT worker operations. A cyberattack halts Polymarket trading. GCHQ loses track of thousands of storage devices. An abandoned Mac app leaves security risks behind. Japan Airlines reports a third-party breach. An AI-powered command-and-control framework emerges in the wild. Our guest is Josh Devon, Co-founder & CEO of Sondera, winner of the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

Today is Friday October 30th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Binance suffers the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered a staggering $6.3 billion theft, reportedly the largest cryptocurrency hack on record. Researchers at TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the October 29 attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation. Attackers moved funds across ten blockchains, with most of the theft occurring in just 20 minutes. Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which may have provided access to systems authorized to move funds. The company found no evidence that private wallet keys were stolen. Instead, attackers apparently manipulated transaction-signing infrastructure, including an Ethereum feature that allowed them to automate withdrawals. Cryptocurrency issuers and networks have frozen billions in stolen assets, but estimates suggest attackers still control between $2.4 billion and $3.3 billion. Binance has promised to reimburse affected customers, while significant questions remain about the security controls protecting its wallets.

A maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA has added the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler, allowing attackers to execute malicious code through specially crafted CI/CD configurations. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts. The Shadowserver Foundation reports nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable. The latest discovery follows several serious GitLab security issues this year, including another recently exploited vulnerability that could expose sensitive credentials and other secrets.

A Russian disinformation group targets U.S. elections.

Researchers say a covert Russian influence operation is targeting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas with fabricated allegations of misconduct. Analysts at Alethea and Clemson University attribute the campaign to Storm-1516, a Russian disinformation group that spread similar false accusations during the 2024 presidential election. The latest attack involved videos that researchers at Graphika believe were AI-generated. Initially attracting little attention, the videos gained traction after several influential accounts on X amplified them. One received more than 850,000 views in its first 24 hours. U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Russia has recently intensified its election interference efforts, particularly in competitive Senate races. While much of the activity targets Democrats, intelligence officials haven’t concluded that Moscow is explicitly favoring either party.

Treasury officials sanction Russian and North Koreans over fraudulent IT worker operations.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russian and North Korean nationals and companies accused of supporting Pyongyang’s fraudulent IT worker operations. Two Russians allegedly laundered millions in cryptocurrency earned by North Korean operatives working remotely for American companies. Treasury also targeted North Korean managers overseeing IT workers in Russia, along with a company accused of using artificial intelligence to help operatives secure U.S. jobs. The broader scheme involves North Koreans using stolen identities to obtain lucrative technology positions, then funneling earnings back to Pyongyang. Some workers have also stolen sensitive information and extorted employers. U.S. officials say the proceeds help fund North Korea’s weapons programs. The sanctions follow a Justice Department operation targeting laptop farms used to disguise workers’ overseas locations.

Polymarket suspends trading following a cyberattack.

Prediction market Polymarket temporarily suspended trading Thursday after a cyberattack involving a third-party service provider disrupted its international platform. The company says trading has resumed and promises to reimburse affected users, but hasn’t disclosed the extent of the losses or identified the attacker. Blockchain security researchers traced more than $2.1 million in suspected cryptocurrency theft to a single account. Security firm Hudson Rock identified the compromised provider as website performance company DebugBear, which separately acknowledged a security incident and urged customers to remove its embedded code. Researchers discovered malicious code apparently designed to identify cryptocurrency wallets and transfer their assets to an attacker-controlled account. Polymarket removed DebugBear’s code from its website. There’s currently no evidence that other DebugBear customers were compromised.

GCHQ laments missing storage devices.

Britain’s intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of storage devices potentially containing sensitive information. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner says USB drives, hard disks, and memory cards remain unaccounted for years after the problem was first identified. Some devices may contain intercepted communications and other highly sensitive intelligence data. The watchdog expressed frustration over GCHQ’s slow investigation. The agency acknowledged shortcomings in its tracking system but says it has implemented corrective measures. Officials are still determining how many devices are actually lost.

An abandoned Mac app causes security headaches.

An abandoned version of the once-popular Popcorn Time streaming app left hundreds of thousands of Macs potentially vulnerable to attack. Researchers at Eye Research discovered that Time4Popcorn installed a persistent update checker that could download and execute code with elevated privileges, even years after users stopped opening the app. With the developers long gone, attackers could potentially hijack expired update domains to distribute malware. Researchers found no evidence of exploitation, but estimate 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. They took control of an abandoned domain and used the update mechanism itself to disable the vulnerable checker on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. Other vulnerabilities remain, however, and some update domains are still uncontrolled. Researchers recommend uninstalling Time4Popcorn entirely.

Japan Airlines suffers a third-party data breach.

Japan Airlines says a breach at its technology provider, Amadeus IT Group, exposed personal information belonging to 92,000 customers. Compromised data includes names, reservation codes, and flight details. For approximately 2,000 passengers, attackers also obtained passport numbers, contact information, and frequent flyer numbers. The airline says payment card information and flight operations were unaffected.

The disclosure comes amid a wave of cyber incidents in Japan, including breaches affecting millions of customers at a Sony-owned internet provider, Burger King Japan, and gaming company Capcom. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called for emergency cybersecurity measures, warning of growing risks from stolen personal information. Japanese and American defense officials have also discussed strengthening cooperation against cyber threats as the country grapples with the recent attacks.

An AI-integrated command-and-control framework is found operating in the wild.

Cisco Talos researchers have discovered an AI-integrated command-and-control framework called NIK C2 operating in the wild. The Windows-based malware combines credential theft, keylogging, surveillance, and remote access with direct access to OpenAI’s API. Attackers can use AI to analyze stolen information during an active intrusion, potentially accelerating their operations. The malware can even use a victim’s own OpenAI API key, potentially charging them for the attacker’s AI requests. NIK C2 also includes screen-locking ransomware that demands cryptocurrency payments without encrypting files. Its capabilities extend to lateral movement, security evasion, and persistent access. Talos observed active infrastructure and multiple versions of the malware, suggesting ongoing development. Researchers warn that integrating AI directly into malware could significantly reduce defenders’ opportunities to detect and interrupt attacks.

We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

We say goodbye today to Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.

His was a remarkable life. From a difficult childhood in a working-class Yorkshire home, he found his way to the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he spent decades mastering his craft. And then, approaching 50, he took a chance on a science fiction television series that he wasn’t entirely convinced would succeed.

And in doing so, he became Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

For those of us who grew up with Star Trek, it’s difficult to overstate what Patrick Stewart brought to that role. Picard was thoughtful, principled, intellectually curious, and deeply committed to the idea that humanity could become something better. He valued diplomacy over violence, reason over impulse, and the dignity of every individual. He was a leader who listened, who questioned his own assumptions, and who understood that having the authority to give an order didn’t necessarily mean it was the right order to give.

And there’s something else worth remembering. Star Trek inspired generations of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technology professionals. People who watched those shows as kids and went on to build the technologies that shape our world today. The communicators, the tablets, the voice-controlled computers, the extraordinary networks connecting people across unimaginable distances. For countless young viewers, Star Trek wasn’t just entertainment. It was an invitation to imagine what technology might make possible, and then go out and make some of it real.

Patrick Stewart helped make that future feel worth pursuing.

He also reminded us that intelligence and kindness weren’t mutually exclusive, that leadership could be compassionate, and that even in a universe filled with extraordinary technology, the most important questions were still fundamentally human ones.

Now, you might reasonably ask, “What does this have to do with cyber security?”

Well, as it happens, Captain Picard was something of an early adopter of multifactor authentication. Whenever the Enterprise’s auto-destruct sequence needed to be activated or canceled, the ship required authorization codes and confirmation from multiple senior officers.

Even in the 24th century, apparently, you couldn’t just blow up the Enterprise with a single password.

Sir Patrick Stewart gave us many wonderful performances over a long and extraordinary career. But for generations of us who looked to the stars and imagined a better future, he’ll always be our captain.

Thank you, Sir Patrick.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 44 (2026)
articles.context: Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026
articles.full_text:
The Good | Global Response Continues for PHP2SHELL Exploit Attempts & Defenders Dismantle Global Cybercrime Rings

This past week, cyber defenders responded to a cluster of vulnerability disclosures and security incidents collectively dubbed “Black October,” spanning flaws in PHP2SHELL, Node.js, GitLab, and Brotli, a software supply chain attack in LiteLLM, and compromised certificate authority keys at eMudhra.

Despite PHP2SHELL affecting roughly 70% of websites worldwide, mass, internet-wide exploitation of the kind seen with Log4SHELL hasn’t materialized. PHP2SHELL lacks a universal offset, since heap layouts, memory alignments, and worker states differ by PHP version, build, and SAPI configuration, and attackers must craft specific request streams to line up memory blocks before triggering the underlying out-of-memory error.

That complexity hasn’t stopped targeted compromises against systems, but it has kept broad, automated attacks from succeeding at scale. CISA added both PHP2SHELL CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a remediation deadline of October 29 for federal agencies.

International law enforcement this week also delivered major blows against cybercrime syndicates. Authorities extradited Chinese national Zheng Zhao from the Netherlands to California over an alleged multimillion-dollar cryptocurrency investment scheme that defrauded 174 American victims through fake trading platforms.

A U.S. federal court sentenced Ukrainian national Artem Stryzhak to 70 months in prison for conspiring to deploy Nefilim and Hive ransomware against hospitals, law firms, and other targets.

Finally, an international law enforcement coalition seized the domain of Virtualine, a “bulletproof” hosting provider that marketed itself to criminals for “all illegal/black hat activities”. Court records tie the seizure to Virtualine hosting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and non-consensual intimate imagery despite repeated takedown notices, plus money laundering that concealed the proceeds. Virtualine had also offered to quietly migrate a customer’s infrastructure to a shell company after law enforcement made contact.

The Bad | Threat Actors Chain Fragnesia Linux Flaw with PHP2SHELL to Root PAN-OS Firewalls

As part of Black October, researchers are warning that a high-severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw is being actively chained with the PHP2SHELL vulnerabilities. Tracked as CVE-2026-46300 and dubbed “Fragnesia,” the flaw stems from a logic defect in the Linux XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that leaves stale page-cache writes exploitable for root access. Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026.

In response to active in-the-wild exploitation, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV Catalog and mandated federal agencies patch affected systems under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, noting that threat actors are pairing it with the PHP2SHELL RCE flaws: exploiting PHP2SHELL first to implant a web shell, then using Fragnesia to escalate from that shell to full root control.

Security researchers uncovered a complete attack operation featuring custom weaponized exploit chains, target lists, detailed activity logs, and roughly 40 custom post-exploitation scripts. The campaign successfully rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers, whose web interface runs on PHP, across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

Chaining an unauthenticated web flaw with a local kernel privilege escalation means patching either one alone isn’t enough. Closing the web shell’s entry point still leaves the root escalation path open on any system running a vulnerable kernel.

The Ugly | Silent Fix for Brotli Decoder Exposes Node2Shell Vulnerability

Security researchers uncovered a critical memory corruption vulnerability in the open-source Brotli compression decoder used across much of the web. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 with a CVSS score of 9.2, the flaw, variously named Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Broccoli2Shell by the researchers who worked on it, stems from an out-of-bounds write when handling invalid stream block switches during decompression. It affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, reaching major language runtimes and web frameworks including Node.js, Python, and .NET.

The flaw’s timeline stretches back further than its public disclosure. Upstream developers quietly fixed the underlying code on February 27 without a security advisory or CVE, and the vulnerability wasn’t publicly identified until a researcher team reported it in October.

Coordinated disclosure landed October 21, and fixes followed in waves: Python’s package registry shipped updates October 22 and 23, a Ruby gem update followed October 24, and .NET received an out-of-band patch on October 25, the same day researchers demonstrated working code execution on x86-64 against Node.js. Separate research into FFmpeg the same day produced a reproducible crash rather than confirmed code execution. Edge and hosting providers rolled out interim firewall mitigations within hours of the initial disclosure.

CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog on October 27, requiring federal remediation by November 10. Because proxy-level filtering doesn’t protect outbound client requests or file-based attack paths, closing this gap means upgrading the underlying Brotli library and rebuilding affected applications, not just patching at the network edge.
