articles.title: Snyk UNFILTERED: Inside Our First-Ever Customer Summit
articles.context: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job Detection is no longer the bottleneck
articles.full_text:
What happens when you bring security leaders from some of the world's most forward-thinking organizations into one room, close the doors, and invite them to speak candidly about what's working, what's breaking, and what they’re still working out?

That’s what we set out to find with Snyk UNFILTERED, our inaugural Customer Summit. Held in San Francisco ahead of the launch of Evo Agentic AppSec and the AI Security Summit, Snyk UNFILTERED was designed to feel nothing like a conference.

We brought together a small group of security leaders from our customer community for an afternoon of candid discussions, interactive debates, and peer-to-peer exchanges. With no traditional presentations, product demos, or carefully rehearsed talking points, the summit gave attendees the freedom to share their experiences without attribution. What followed was an open exchange of ideas about the challenges and opportunities shaping the future of AI security. Leaders compared notes on real rollouts, real roadblocks, and real questions they have not yet figured out, with a level of transparency that is hard to find at traditional industry events.

From the growing backlog of vulnerabilities to the governance of autonomous agents, attendees challenged assumptions, compared real-world experiences, and explored questions the industry is still answering. And that's where the most valuable conversations began.

Five key takeaways that stuck with us

Five themes kept resurfacing over the afternoon, across every table and every discussion:

1. When AI writes the code, who owns the risk?

If an engineer prompts an AI tool to build an agent skill and that skill causes an issue later, who is at fault? The room kept coming back to the importance of guardrails: clear controls and ownership that hold up even when no human typed the line.

2. The AI conversation has grown up

Just a few months ago, the questions were about cost and token usage. Now leadership wants to know the return on investment, what AI is really costing, and where to set budget caps. AI has moved from experiment to line item with scrutiny to match.

3. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job

Detection is no longer the bottleneck. The questions have moved to how teams fix issues, how fast they can fix them, and how they reduce human error within the loop. Fixes that stall in review, testing, and merge were a shared frustration.

4. Risk can come from anywhere

When everyone on a team has access to AI, vulnerabilities can come from anywhere. Democratizing AI also spreads responsibility, and attendees talked about how to keep everyone accountable without slowing anyone down.

5. Humans can only do so much

Teams are limited by how much people can review and approve. Leaders are open to trusting agents, but only with controls that an agent cannot bypass, and with governance designed for machines rather than adapted from processes built for people.

From UNFILTERED conversations to the future of AI Security

Snyk UNFILTERED was just the beginning of an important week in San Francisco. The challenges discussed behind closed doors at UNFILTERED reflected a broader shift happening across the industry: security teams are moving beyond simply identifying risk toward enabling organizations to build, innovate, and operate safely at AI speed.

The next morning, we launched Evo Agentic AppSec, and the AI Security Summit brought builders, researchers, investors, and CISOs into the same building. The questions from the customer room about fixing at speed and governing agents were carried straight into those conversations. Hearing those challenges directly from customers shapes what we build next.

The best conversations don't end when the event does

The leaders in the room are navigating enormous change. They’re balancing innovation with accountability and securing technologies that evolve faster than the processes designed to govern them. What made the afternoon valuable was their willingness to talk openly about what they haven’t solved yet. Spaces like that are rare, and we plan to keep creating them.

Snyk Unfiltered is part of our commitment to bringing our customer community together through candid conversations and shared learning, and this was the first of many.

articles.title: Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude Enterprise
articles.context: The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate...
articles.full_text:
In-app surveys capture feedback

In-app surveys add the team's own perspective on that work. The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate should copy, and, if the team lost access tomorrow, what would break or slow down first. Admins can customize or remove questions and choose who receives a survey, when it runs, and where it appears. Members see it as a short card after a reply in the tool they’re already working in.

Responses appear on the survey page as they arrive, and admins can export them to a spreadsheet. In-app surveys can now be enabled for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, and for organizations that set one retention period for all data, surveys and their responses are deleted on that schedule.

In-app surveys are treated as your data, so Anthropic accesses them only as necessary to operate the service.

Pooled group budgets put spend where the work happens

Pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly budget, so people who use Claude heavily are less likely to hit an individual limit early in the month while others leave budget unspent. Member limits still work as a guardrail against unusually high individual use. Every request counts against both, and a member stops at whichever runs out first. When someone hits a limit, they can request more from inside Claude, and the request goes to admins for review. The setup suggests an amount based on the group's recent usage, and admins with billing permissions receive email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of a budget.

Getting started

Smart reports, in-app surveys, and pooled group budgets are generally available today for Claude Enterprise. Availability varies by configuration, including for organizations with a HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys. Visit the Help Center for eligibility and detailed setup steps.

articles.title: IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the company
articles.context: IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today
articles.full_text:
IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today. IDC Quanta gives customers access to IDC’s trusted and validated forecasts, market data, research, and more, and now, they can ask questions in Claude to get answers enriched with IDC’s insights in minutes. IDC has also rolled Claude out across the company, where teams use it every day.

Applying market research has traditionally meant reading through long reports to get to the answers a customer needs, such as a vendor shortlist or a competitive brief. Now, an IDC customer describes the market, strategy, or purchase they're working on, and the IDC Quanta MCP connector for Claude returns finished analysis built on IDC's trusted forecasts and data.

What customers can do with IDC Quanta in Claude

IDC Quanta, an AI-powered technology intelligence platform that helps customers do better work, faster, with credible, verified intelligence from IDC’s proprietary data and research. In Claude, IDC Quanta enables customers to benchmark performance, size markets, choose vendors, and shape strategy. It’s as simple as a customer describing the question they're working on, and Claude answering it using IDC's intelligence.

The questions that users ask vary by role, but they tend to look like this:

Competitive briefs: A corporate strategy lead asks Claude for a competitor brief. Claude returns the competitor’s positioning, market share, product capabilities, and recent acquisitions, cited to IDC's research. A job that used to take a day’s worth of research is complete in minutes.

Vendor shortlists: A CIO evaluating procurement software asks Claude which vendors are the best fit based on her existing architecture and unique business requirements. Claude returns the top three by IDC's procurement database and MarketScape research as an Excel scorecard, ready for the evaluation team to act on.

Analysis of their own numbers: A CFO uploads next year's IT budget, and asks how it compares to IDC's forecast. Claude returns where the two differ, and by how much, while updated data stays private to the customer.

IDC Quanta works wherever the customer already uses Claude, including the Claude app on desktop and mobile, Cowork, and the Microsoft Office add-ins. It gives Claude the same data and definitions an IDC analyst works from, so a market share or growth rate matches what IDC would publish, and each answer cites the IDC document or dataset it came from.

How IDC uses Claude internally

IDC has also put Claude to work across the company, where its engineers, product, marketing and sales teams are using it daily to build, plan, and sell. A clear example of the difference it's making is in engineering: IDC's engineers rebuilt the internal data repository its analysts use for research in three weeks instead of an estimated three months, and since they began using Claude Code for testing, bugs in the code they ship have come down significantly.

Engineering was the first team to adopt Claude, and the rest of the company has followed. Here's how they're using it:

Building and testing software: Product managers use Claude Code to build working prototypes before engineering starts, which has cut the time it takes a feature to reach engineering from months to weeks. Engineers use it to run tests in parallel, and a code review that once filled five days is done in about 30 minutes.

Planning and strategy: Product teams give Cowork their research and internal files, and it writes the first draft of the plan. Planning sprints that took three weeks now take three days. Writing a new test to check that code works now takes about 20 minutes, down from days.

Optimizing sales: IDC's sales team runs a tool built with Claude that reads an export from the company's CRM. In minutes, it tells each rep which of their deals have stalled and which are worth chasing.

Producing marketing content: IDC's content marketing team built an assistant in Claude to draft much of its marketing content. It optimizes the content for search and AI answer engines (SEO/AEO), and checks it against buyer personas and IDC's own research. From there, the team edits, proofs, and publishes the work, publishing content faster than it could on its own

“Assessing the impact of a competitor’s acquisition used to mean a market intelligence professional spending hours pulling multiple reports, synthesizing the findings, and turning them into an executive-ready brief. Now, they can open Claude, ask what that acquisition means for their business, and get a board-ready analysis in minutes, grounded in IDC’s research and more than 15 billion data points,” said Lorenzo Larini, CEO, IDC. “We brought IDC Quanta into Claude because that’s where many of our customers already work, giving them a faster, more intuitive way to put IDC’s trusted data and research to work.”

“IDC has spent 60 years helping leaders make better technology decisions, and now it’s using Claude to rethink how its teams work and how it delivers value to its customers,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic.

Getting started

IDC Quanta customers who use Claude can add the IDC Quanta connector from within Claude. Others can contact IDC or book a demo. To learn more about Claude for Enterprise, visit anthropic.com/enterprise.

articles.title: The strategy behind the shield.
articles.context: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats. CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known...
articles.full_text:
CISA unveils its 2030 cyber strategy. PHP2Shell exploits are in the wild. HHS preserves healthcare security requirements. Microsoft offers buyouts amid its AI spending spree. A cyberattack disrupts New Mexico hospitals. Google’s Finnish data center plans hit an environmental roadblock. Blue Initiative tracks maritime vulnerabilities. A Chinese national faces charges in a $37 million cryptocurrency scam. Our guest is Cal Al-Dhubaib, host of the new Authorized Intelligence podcast. Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Today is Tuesday October 27th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA plans to defend, harden and prevail.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats.

The plan rests on three pillars. Defend focuses on securing networks, operational technology, software supply chains, and emerging technologies, including quantum computing and advanced AI. Harden emphasizes turning threat intelligence into action, improving risk prioritization, and accelerating incident response. Prevail seeks to strengthen national resilience through regional partnerships, emergency communications, and coordinated planning.

The strategy also prioritizes resilient 5G and 6G networks and satellite communications.

CISA will review its existing capabilities within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan within 180 days, and report on its progress within a year.

PHP2Shell is officially under active exploitation.

CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell, to its catalog of actively exploited flaws. The bugs could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

Researchers observed widespread exploitation attempts before patches were released October 21, though early attempts reportedly failed. Subsequent honeypot activity confirmed successful exploitation in the wild.

Federal civilian agencies have until Thursday to patch their systems.

HHS scales back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements.

Federal health regulators have scaled back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements for electronic health records, following widespread objections from healthcare providers and industry groups.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ final rule eliminates 14 health IT certification criteria, down from the 34 originally proposed. All 13 core privacy and security requirements will remain intact, including standards for authentication and access controls.

Commenters warned that eliminating those safeguards could shift security responsibilities onto healthcare providers, particularly smaller and rural organizations with limited resources.

However, the rule does eliminate transparency and risk-management requirements for AI-powered clinical decision support tools. Those provisions required developers to disclose information about their systems’ capabilities, limitations, and potential risks.

HHS says the changes will save health IT developers more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs.

Most provisions take effect December 28, with others following in January.

Microsoft offers buyouts amidst AI-driven growth.

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, roughly 27 percent of its workforce, as it balances soaring AI infrastructure spending with efforts to control costs.

The offers cover eligible workers in the United States, Canada, India, and Britain, including some employees at the vice president level.

Microsoft expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the September quarter, driven largely by data center investments supporting AI services.

The company previously offered voluntary retirement packages in April and announced 4,800 layoffs in July.

Some engineering, sales, and marketing teams are excluded from the latest program. Eligible employees have until early December to decide, with departures scheduled for December 31.

Microsoft says the initiative will provide flexibility as the company reshapes its workforce around AI-driven growth.

New Mexico hospitals divert patients following a cyberattack.

A cybersecurity incident disrupted operations across the University of New Mexico Health System on Monday, forcing ambulance diversions, canceled appointments, and temporary restrictions on hospital access.

The disruption affected New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center, leaving the state without its highest level of emergency trauma care. Other healthcare providers stepped in to accommodate additional patients.

Employees reported hearing messages broadcast through hospital computers claiming that student, employee, and patient information had been stolen. Those claims have not been verified.

The health system declined to discuss the incident’s nature or scope, citing an active law enforcement investigation. The FBI confirmed it was assisting.

Hospitals and clinics began gradually resuming operations Monday afternoon, although the full extent of the disruption remains unclear.

Cleared trees halt development of a Google AI data center in Finland.

Google’s massive AI infrastructure expansion in Finland has run into an environmental backlash after the company cleared hundreds of thousands of trees without completing required environmental assessments.

At one site in northern Finland, an estimated 250,000 trees were removed across 815 acres. Conservationists estimate another 150,000 were felled at a second location.

Finnish regulators have ordered work stopped at both sites. Google has apologized, saying it acted according to its understanding of local regulations.

The controversy threatens to complicate Google’s €13 billion investment in Finnish data centers, part of a broader AI infrastructure boom attracted by the country’s cool climate and abundant energy.

Supporters point to jobs and tax revenue. Critics question the environmental costs, electricity demands, and limited economic benefits.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding tighter regulation and compensation for affected communities.

Google says it will comply with regulators and plans to replant trees.

Blue Initiative tracks vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

A coalition of cybersecurity and maritime organizations has launched Blue Initiative, a free public database tracking vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

The project helps operators identify and prioritize security risks across IT and operational technology systems.

The database currently contains nearly 30,000 vulnerabilities, including more than 2,000 rated critical and over 580 known to be exploited.

Users can search, filter, and receive alerts about vulnerabilities, while researchers and industry partners review entries and contribute new findings.

A Chinese national faces federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam.

A Chinese national has been extradited from the Netherlands to face federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam that defrauded at least 174 Americans of nearly $37 million.

Prosecutors say 44-year-old Zheng Zhao participated in an international fraud network operating partly from scam centers in Cambodia.

The scheme allegedly involved contacting victims through social media, dating sites, and text messages, building relationships, then persuading them to invest through fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms.

Investigators say the stolen money moved through American bank accounts to the Bahamas, where it was converted into Tether cryptocurrency and transferred to wallets controlled in Cambodia.

Eight alleged co-conspirators have already pleaded guilty.

Zhao faces a money laundering conspiracy charge carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Anthropic is preparing to go public, and its pitch to investors comes with an unusual warning: the company’s products could potentially threaten human civilization.

In its 335-page IPO filing, Anthropic devotes 93 pages to potential risks, ranging from employee retention and computing costs to AI systems developing beyond human control.

The company warns that increasingly autonomous models could conduct cyberattacks, spread misinformation, help develop dangerous weapons, or take harmful actions without human intervention.

There’s also the possibility that AI development could outpace Anthropic’s ability to evaluate and safeguard its own technology.

And then there are more conventional business concerns, including expensive data centers, regulatory scrutiny, and dependence on major customers.

Anthropic argues that its commitment to AI safety makes it uniquely positioned to manage these dangers.

So, the investment proposition is essentially this: help us build extraordinarily powerful AI, and we’ll do our best to keep it from ending civilization.

Not your typical prospectus.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: AWS becomes first CSP in Canada to complete the Cloud High profile assessment with 172 services and features in scope
articles.context: We continue to expand the scope of our assurance programs at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and are pleased to announce the successful completion of our first ever Cloud High (PBHH)...
articles.full_text:
We continue to expand the scope of our assurance programs at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and are pleased to announce the successful completion of our first ever Cloud High (PBHH) security assessment with 172 assessed services and features. Completion of this assessment, effective September 18, 2026, makes AWS the first cloud service provider (CSP) in Canada to meet this high security bar and provide assurance to our valued customers. This assessment also reaffirms our commitment to helping public and commercial customers achieve and maintain the highest-grade security standard for workloads with increased sensitivity.

What is the Cloud High assessment and why is it important?

The Cloud High security profile (that is, PBHH) seeks to enhance the integrity and availability of customer organizational workloads that are considered to have an increased level of sensitivity. These are systems that the Government of Canada (GC) and its service providers use to support delivery of services at a national scale or that are determined to be significant for handling sensitive information. The profile is based on the Security and privacy controls and assurance activities catalogue (ITSP.10.033). The Cloud High (PBHH) profile includes all controls and enhancements contained within the Cloud Medium profile (PBMM), with additional controls and enhancements to address higher integrity and availability requirements. The Cloud Medium and Cloud High profiles establish baseline security requirements for cloud services. These services support GC workloads and information processing up to the Protected B level.

As of September 18, 2026, there are a total of 172 AWS services and features that were assessed by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) under Cloud High security assessment. The assessment covers services and features that are available in both the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) AWS Regions.

How can you access the assessment?

The summary assessment is available through AWS Artifact. You can also learn more about the Cloud High and Medium assessment on the AWS CCCS assessment compliance webpage.

AWS strives to continually bring services into scope of its compliance programs to help you meet your architectural and regulatory needs. Please reach out to your AWS account team if you have questions or feedback about the Cloud High and Medium assessments.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, refer to AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.

Naranjan Goklani

Naranjan is AWS Compliance, Security Assurance and Privacy (CAPS) Lead for Canada. He has experience leading audits, attestations, certifications, and assessments across the Americas. Naranjan has more than 16 years of experience in technology risk management, customer security assurance, and technology audits. He previously worked in the Big 4 accounting firms and supported clients from the financial services, technology, retail, and utilities industries.

articles.title: Part 3 – Cybersecurity journeys: The work behind the work
articles.context: Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come...
articles.full_text:
The most important work I’ve done in cybersecurity would make for terrible television. There were no countdown clocks and no frantic typing, just a lot of careful reading, a lot of hard conversations, and the occasional quiet moment where everything finally clicked. That’s the part I want to show you this week, because the three people I talked to have built their entire careers on the work that happens off-camera, and it’s the part that decides who lasts in this field.

This is a four-part series following 11 AWS security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. In Part 1: I didn’t plan this, I shared how three of them found their way in, and in Part 2: What even is this job?, we looked at roles most people don’t know exist. This week is about what the day-to-day actually feels like, told through three AWS security professionals whose work rarely makes it into the trailer but is the reason any of it holds together.

Unlimited ammo

Brandon Caldwell, Mgr, Security Engineering

Ask most people to picture an application security engineer at work and they’ll imagine someone hunched over a terminal breaking into systems. Brandon Caldwell‘s actual days (reviewing software while it’s being built so the flaws never ship) look almost nothing like that. He spends them in conversation: sitting with the engineers who built a product, walking through how it works, and asking question after question until he understands it well enough to see where it could break. “This job is at least 50 percent people,” he tells the folks he hires. “You have to people a lot.”

The hardest part of the day isn’t technical, it’s human. Brandon’s team has to hand builders news they don’t want to hear, and he’s blunt with new hires about what that really feels like.

“Our job is to go tell someone their baby is ugly. I use that phrase because it is meant to draw out empathy. This is the thing they love and spent time on, and you show up at the end and say that thing is ugly. Of course they are going to react.” – Brandon Caldwell

Learning to deliver that message without crushing the person across the table is, in his telling, the actual craft of the job. It’s why he prizes empathy, and why he says the engineers who struggle most in application security are the ones who got into tech specifically to avoid talking to people. The rest of the day is the patient, unglamorous work of reading someone else’s code closely enough to find the one flaw they didn’t know they’d left, then explaining it in a way that lands as help rather than judgment.

That explaining is more than a conversation. So much of security work gets written down: the finding documented so an engineer can act on it, the advisory that tells customers what to do, the policy that sets the bar for everyone who comes after. The ability to write clearly, to turn something messy and technical into a few sentences a reader can actually use, is one of the quiet differentiators as you move up in this field, and it’s a skill worth building long before anyone asks you to.

None of this is where Brandon started. He’s been curious about breaking things since he was a kid hex-editing the game Doom for unlimited ammo, taught himself reverse engineering (taking apart finished software to understand how it works) before it had a name, and spent years as an IT admin and then in incident response at Microsoft back when cybersecurity barely existed as a job title. What pulled him off the breaking side was noticing—after watching the same handful of mistakes scroll past again and again (things like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, two of the most common ways attackers exploit a poorly built website)—that he’d rather help teams avoid the break-in than perform it. Application security, he says, is his natural place.

As for breaking in yourself, Brandon’s advice follows straight from how he spends his days: practice interviewing and asking the right questions and spend real time around builders so you understand what goes into the thing you’re critiquing. When he hires, certifications are the last thing he looks at; he wants to see capture-the-flag competition results (hacking contests where you solve security puzzles to earn points) and public GitHub projects, because those prove you’ve done the work. Build something, break something, and get comfortable talking to the people who build.

Forget that

Kurt Heath, IT Support Associate

Kurt Heath‘s chosen corner of the work is offensive security: penetration testing (getting paid to legally break into systems to prove where they’re weak) and, eventually, red teaming. The day-to-day of getting good at it is far less cinematic than the label suggests. It’s hours of hands-on practice against deliberately vulnerable targets, reading about a technique and then trying it until it works, and the slow accumulation of the layers the job actually rests on: operating systems, networking, software development, and security fundamentals, all applied at once. He’s the first to say pen testing is “the sexy thing” that gets advertised, and the first to warn that it shouldn’t be anyone’s first stop, because of how much quiet groundwork sits underneath it.

A big part of his real workday now is deciding how, and how much, to lean on AI. Kurt treats it as a tool rather than a crutch: he uses it as a coding assistant when he has to work in an unfamiliar language, and to sort through large volumes of information quickly, but he won’t let it think for him. He still fills out forms like this blog’s questionnaire by hand, keeping a personal touch on his own work, and he’s wary of letting AI pull the trigger during an engagement, since an overzealous tool can act on a network however it sees fit, cause unintended operational damage, or wander out of scope and create a legal problem. The way he sees it, security is fundamentally a human problem: automation keeps getting better at the systematic parts, but thinking outside the box the way an attacker does stays stubbornly human.

How Kurt got here matters less to the day-to-day than how he keeps going, but it’s worth knowing that he’s largely self-taught. After a community college program didn’t work out, he taught himself from scratch, finishing shifts at an auto plant and then spending nights with YouTube and a search bar learning how computers and networks actually worked. The hardest part, he told me, was self-motivation, and what carried him through was a mix of sheer want and, eventually, other people: the friends and community he found in Discord servers, security podcasts, and interest channels who helped him turn raw drive into real focus. He even got a tattoo as a reminder that there is no plan B.

“There is no other option. There’s no what if. This is it. This is life now, and I’ll figure it out some way, somehow, no matter how long it takes.” – Kurt Heath

If you’re drawn to the same offensive work, Kurt’s advice is to resist starting there. Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come after the groundwork is solid. Progress in this field—in his experience—is measured less by the title you land than by how much you grow and who you grow alongside.

The comfort lock

Seth Jeacopello, Mgr, Security Engineer

Seth works in application security too, but if Brandon’s days are mostly about people, Seth’s are mostly about code, which makes the two of them a useful picture of how differently the same job can look. When Seth Jeacopello gets stuck on a hard problem, he doesn’t stare at it harder, he picks up a lock. An actual physical lock with pins and tumblers, because he’s a serious lock-picking hobbyist, and over the years he’s learned that the best response to hitting a wall is to set the problem down and pick what he calls a comfort lock, one he knows well and can open easily. It isn’t about the lock; it’s about giving his brain a small win so he can return to the hard thing with fresh eyes.

The comfort lock exists because Seth’s actual day-to-day is easy to get lost in. In application security, a big part of the job is reading enormous amounts of someone else’s code looking for the one flaw that matters, and as a lifelong developer he genuinely loves reading code, which is exactly what makes it a trap. He described the pull of it to me: you convince yourself the vulnerability is just behind the next function, and the next, and suddenly two days are gone. The skill he’s spent decades sharpening isn’t finding things, it’s knowing when deep enough is deep enough and when to step back, which is where the lock comes in. After 26 years, the meta-skill of managing his own attention is as much a part of the craft as anything technical.

That longevity goes back a long way. Around 1999, still in his teens, he landed a software quality assurance internship, was hired as a developer by 17, and gravitated toward the security-flavored work from the start before moving into network security tooling, rising to chief architect and then chief technology officer along the way.

“We’re like three or four guys off the street coming in with a product, and this huge company was like, yeah, you three, go for it. That was probably one of the coolest things.” – Seth Jeacopello

His advice for building the instincts the daily work demands is refreshingly concrete: set up a deliberately vulnerable practice machine, break into it, and then go read the logs it generated, so you learn not just how an attack works but what it looks like from the defender’s side. That single exercise builds both the offensive and the investigative muscle at once, and it’s the kind of patient, repeatable practice that the day-to-day of this field actually rewards.

The thread

There’s a version of cybersecurity that makes for great television, fast-paced and full of eureka moments, and those moments do exist. But the three people I talked to this week live in a different version of the field, one built on patience, repetition, and a kind of stubborn care that doesn’t photograph well. For Brandon, the real work is the hard, human conversation of telling a builder their work is flawed without making an enemy of them. For Kurt, it’s the unglamorous hours of hands-on practice and the discipline to use AI as a tool without letting it think for him. For Seth, it’s reading one more page of code and knowing when to stop, with a comfort lock on the desk for when he can’t.

None of that makes a great action sequence, but all of it is what a security career actually looks like, and the good news for anyone starting out is that these are learnable habits, not inborn talent. Notice how much of the real work is human: empathy, patience, judgment, and knowing how your own mind works. The analytical, interpersonal, and self-management skills you already have are not a consolation prize, they are part of the job. If you want to begin building the rest, here are a few places to start:

TryHackMe and Hack The Box let you stand up deliberately vulnerable machines, break in, and study what you triggered, exactly the exercise Seth recommends

The OWASP Top 10 explains the most common application security flaws, including the ones Brandon saw on repeat

The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series turns those flaws into practical, task-level guidance on how to build and review software securely; the daily bread of Brandon’s and Seth’s work

The Darknet Diaries podcast tells the human stories behind real security incidents, and it’s a good way to hear what the work actually feels like

And if you want to build cloud security skills specifically, AWS has free and hands-on resources to help you start:

AWS Skill Builder offers more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans you can start today

AWS Builder Labs lets you practice in a real AWS console on hands-on security labs, the stand-it-up-and-try-it approach Seth recommends

In Part 4: What I’d tell myself, we close the series with the advice and hard-won lessons these professionals would hand to someone just starting out.

Doing the work behind the work? These three want you to know it counts. Share your story on LinkedIn!

Shannon Brazil

Shannon is a senior security engineer, managing a team on the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), specializing in digital forensics and cloud security investigations. Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

articles.title: Securing Vercel at Scale: From One Team to Every Team
articles.context: Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget)
articles.full_text:
On Thursday, a customer marketing manager vibe codes a community portal where customers can sign in, post questions, and search past answers. By Friday it’s live on Vercel, with a custom domain, an OPENAI_API_KEY for the AI search saved as a plain config variable, and a database full of customer names, emails, and support threads.

No ticket. No code review. No security sign-off. Nothing broke, so nobody looked.

Vercel has the settings to prevent every part of that. The harder question belongs to the security team: how do you know those settings are on, for every team, across the whole company?

The builder population just changed

Vercel used to be where front-end engineers shipped Next.js apps. Now it’s where AI ships apps for everyone else. Vercel’s v0 has crossed 4 million users (SaaStr), and CEO Guillermo Rauch says more than 60% of activity on Vercel is now driven by coding agents (The Stack).

Many of those apps belong to companies, not hobbyists. Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget).

Why your current tools only see part of it

Vercel isn’t a cloud account, a repo, or a typical SaaS app. It’s a control plane that sits between all three, so each tool you already own sees only part of it:

CNAPP sees the AWS, Azure, or GCP accounts DevOps provisioned. Vercel isn’t one of them.

AppSec scans the repos you point it at. An app built from a prompt may never pass through one.

SSPM checks SaaS sign-in and access settings, but rarely Vercel’s deployment and firewall settings.

Vercel’s own Security Dashboard, free on every plan since August 2026, is the best place to start. It scores a team on settings like MFA, owner count, token expiry, and secret storage (Vercel). But it covers one team at a time, a fixed list of checks, and only Vercel.

These settings are configured in Vercel, team by team, usually by whoever created the team: access tokens, environment variables, custom domains, deployment protection, SAML enforcement, firewall rules. That person usually isn’t on the security team.

Vercel’s dashboard tells one team how its settings look. Security teams need every team, more checks, and one place to work them next to the rest of their risk.

What Orca adds beyond Vercel’s dashboard

The integration supports Vercel Enterprise. You connect it with a Full Account access token created by a dedicated service user with the Enterprise Viewer and Security roles, so Orca’s access stays read-only. Set an expiration on the token and rotate it (Vercel access tokens). If your organization enforces SAML, connect each team with its own team token instead. There’s no agent to install, nothing to deploy in Vercel, and no change to how anyone builds.

Orca inventories every team the token can reach, including teams added later: projects, deployments, domains, members, access tokens, firewall settings, and environment-variable metadata, never the values. Each Vercel team shows up as an account in Orca, so you see every team in one place instead of one dashboard per team.

Orca runs a variety of detections out of the box. Some overlap with Vercel’s dashboard.

Area

Orca adds

Also covered by Vercel’s dashboard

Identity and access

SAML configured but not enforced, invitations pending more than 14 days

Members without MFA, tokens with no expiration, too many owners, long-lived credentials that could use OIDC

Network exposure

Production deployments without protection, custom firewall (WAF) disabled, no bot blocking, no IP blocking rules, overly permissive bypass rules

Public preview deployments

Data protection

None

Secrets saved as readable Config variables, Git fork protection disabled, variables exposed to the browser

Best practices

Unprotected source maps, unverified Git commits

None

Neglected assets

Access tokens unused for 90+ days

Environment variables older than 90 days

Four misconfigurations that AI-built apps make by default

These four issues come up most with AI-built apps. None is a mistake anyone makes on purpose. Each is a default, or a step builders skip because nothing breaks without it.

Production URLs with no login. Vercel’s Deployment Protection covers preview URLs by default. Production is a separate setting. Builders rarely change it, because the app works fine either way. The result is a public, indexable production URL with nothing in front of it. The fix is free: since September 2026, every plan can put Vercel Authentication in front of production and make it the team default (Vercel).

Secrets saved as readable Config variables. Since August 2026, Vercel stores each variable as Config (readable) or Secret (write-only) (Vercel). Values are encrypted at rest, but a STRIPE_SECRET_KEY saved as Config stays readable to anyone with project access. The name is the giveaway, and that’s what Orca flags.

SAML connected but not enforced. The identity team links the IdP to Vercel. Nobody turns on enforcement, so members can still reach the team without a SAML session (Vercel).

Long-lived and forgotten access tokens. A Full Account or Team token carries the role of the person who created it. Tokens set to never expire, or unused for 90 days, are standing credentials nobody is watching. Orca flags both. Project-scoped tokens limit any one token to a single project (Vercel).

One queue for every team

A dashboard per Vercel team works for the person who owns that team. It doesn’t work for a security team responsible for dozens of them.

In Orca, Vercel findings show up alongside your AWS, Azure, and GCP findings, in the same risk scoring, alert workflows, and ticketing integrations your team already uses. Each finding shows which Vercel team owns the project, so it reaches someone who can fix it. New teams are covered as soon as they’re created, without anyone registering them.

Vercel findings land prioritized in the same queue as your cloud findings in the Orca Platform

Vercel is one part of the AI-built app

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security covers these parts in one platform instead of one tool per vendor. Today that means Vercel, where AI-built apps run, and Claude Enterprise, where many of them start, in the same inventory and the same queue. More platforms are coming.

The goal isn’t to slow builders down. They keep the tools they picked. Security gets enough visibility to say yes instead of no.

Want to see your Vercel teams in Orca? Book a demo today.

About the Orca Platform

Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Trusted by hundreds of organizations, including SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, and Digital Turbine, Orca is backed by leading investors including Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, and Redpoint Ventures.

articles.title: The platform approach to becoming Frontier
articles.context: Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There i
articles.full_text:
Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There is no path where this notion of infinite cognitive compute replaces human purpose. Frontier Transformation is an opportunity for a wholesale reinvention of how you think about your unique ideas coming to life and how your organization can thrive in your industry.

Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. We are taking a platform approach toward enabling the same: Copilot as the place to call home for interacting with AI to empower human ambition; the Microsoft IQ platform to compound and amplify your intelligence from within while protecting your unique differentiation; and Agent 365 to enable Trust and Observability at every layer of the stack so that you can govern, manage, secure and get business value and return out of the capabilities you deliver.

Our latest earnings are another important marker on that journey. Behind the numbers are thousands of customers, partners, developers and employees putting AI to work in meaningful ways. We have so many inspiring stories from our customers that highlight these outcomes, and below are some of our favorites.

Empowering human ambition with Copilot

Volkswagen has scaled Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees as it expands the role of AI in decision-making and knowledge-based processes across the enterprise. Building on Copilot Chat adoption that reached more than 300,000 monthly active users, employees are now using Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced scenarios, bringing greater organizational context to decision-making and knowledge-based work. Volkswagen is also working with Microsoft to further scale its Intelligent Data Foundation on Microsoft Fabric to make data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. With this investment, Volkswagen is demonstrating how companies have evolved from using Copilot as a productivity tool to an operating system to empower human ambition.

Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000. Copilot usage has surpassed 90%, and the company is using the tool to connect employees with specialized agents and business systems. AI agents are already automating roughly 75% of initial responses and triage for a service desk that receives nearly 300,000 inquiries annually, while new agents are supporting work across sales, systems engineering, procurement, finance and accounting. As customer zero, Fujitsu is using Copilot as the front door to a multi-agent work environment and using insights from its own AI adoption to better serve its customers.

KOHLER is using GitHub Copilot to transform software development, with one organization improving code releases by 25% and reducing error defects by 75%. These engineering breakthroughs are part of a broader effort to embed AI processes across the company, spanning IT, finance, marketing, supply chain and operations. Microsoft Copilot has reached 98% adoption, saving an average of 2 to 5 hours per month as employees are making informed decisions and getting answers faster in the flow of their work. Employees across the company have also created more than 3,000 agents to date, with hundreds active daily.

At Krafton, Microsoft Security Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR are helping the security team respond to a growing volume and complexity of threats. The global gaming company automated key parts of security operations, from alerting and investigation to reporting, combining Microsoft Security solutions with its own systems and data to quickly gather context that helps distinguish real threats from false positives. This approach is having immediate results: security alert recognition time has fallen by approximately 95% to less than one minute, investigation work that previously took tens of minutes now takes about three minutes and roughly 95% of report creation has been automated. By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.

To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot. NASA employees are using Copilot to sift through massive amounts of academic literature and streamline daily tasks, and specialized assistants are helping researchers navigate complex Earth science data through natural language, extending access to information that once required significant technical expertise. Hydrology Copilot, for example, can analyze variables like precipitation and soil moisture to help communities better understand water conditions, prepare for droughts and anticipate flood risks, while automatically performing calculations and analyses.

To transform frontline work, Williams, a US natural gas company, is using Microsoft Copilot to help employees spend less time searching documents and completing manual processes, and more time on critical field operations. Copilot helps teams generate plans, interpret procedures, assess regulatory requirements, troubleshoot issues and complete safety reporting, while employees can create agents tailored to their own workflows. Demonstrating that the person closest to a problem is often the best one to solve it, one operations technician built an anomaly detector using Copilot that compares equipment data against baseline statistics and alerts teams to potential issues before they become costly or dangerous. Since deploying Copilot, AI adoption at Williams has grown from single digits to more than 90%, helping employees accelerate operations, improve reporting and compliance and identify equipment issues earlier.

Bristol Myers Squibb has rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 25,000 employees, reaching 96% adoption, and is now putting AI agents to work across everyday use cases such as document review and project management in support of the company’s mission to bring more medicines to more patients faster. One agent, called RABIT, analyzes meeting transcripts, surfaces action items and delivers insights directly within employees’ workflows.

Facing rising patient demand and financial pressures, Brown University Health is using Dragon Copilot to give clinicians more time to focus on patients. The health system adopted Dragon Copilot, and an early pilot across 420 clinicians found users spent less time on after-hours documentation and reported lower cognitive burden. Building on that experience, Brown University Health deployed Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio across departments, which led to the creation of more than 24 AI agents to support clinical workflows, hospital policies, patient access and operations. These AI solutions are not only supporting clinicians in the flow of their work but also helping to improve the patient experience and access to care.

Microsoft IQ compounds and protects your intelligence

BNY has made AI part of how its employees work through Eliza, its in-house AI platform built with Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot – with plans to add Work IQ. More than 300 solutions now run on Eliza, ranging from inquiry management to client onboarding, and 100% of employees have been trained on the platform. Across the bank, that scale is translating into meaningful results: client transaction inquiries are being resolved 80% faster and AI-assisted client onboarding is 20% faster on average. Through the Microsoft CEO Co-Innovation program, BNY also worked with Microsoft to develop an AI research capability with Foundry that investigates complex data issues, analyzes context across multiple sources, identifies likely root causes and recommends next steps, bringing AI-assisted reasoning into processes that have traditionally relied on human investigation alone.

Docusign is helping 1.9 million customers across 180 countries turn agreement data into actionable business insights. The company built an Intelligent Agreement Management platform on Microsoft Azure and used Microsoft Foundry to shift from general-purpose models to a system of task-specific models that better understand context. This change allows Docusign to process more than a million agreement documents in a single day, with up to eightfold greater throughput and 90% lower AI processing costs. Foundry also supports a model lifecycle designed for continuous improvement, where processes are fine-tuned before deployment and monitored in production, while also providing the governance and traceability needed to meet enterprise requirements for compliance, visibility and control. Now agreement content is structured data that compounds from within, so organizations can use it to make decisions and automate workflows, knowing their IP is protected.

To help marketers create more effective content, Kantar turned decades of proprietary advertising intelligence into action with Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry. Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market. The new approach can process and score large volumes of videos 20x faster while reducing platform operating costs by 4x, helping customers move from insight to action in minutes rather than hours. By bringing its unique intelligence into a continuous loop of observation and improvement, Kantar is creating new ways to help marketers turn insight into better creative and business outcomes.

Kinaxis, a Canadian supply chain software company, runs Maestro, its AI-driven supply chain orchestration platform, on Microsoft Azure. Maestro helps businesses make better decisions faster amid constant disruption. It brings together traditionally disparate business data like sales orders, inventory and production capacity with external signals like weather, market shifts and breaking news to give planners a near real-time view of their supply chains. With this unified data foundation, planners and analysts can use predictive AI and optimization models to anticipate demand shifts, evaluate constraints and recommend action, while generative AI agents act as assistants to ask questions, explore scenarios and automate parts of the planning process. With this intelligence in one platform, businesses can understand how disruptions ripple across their interconnected operations, weigh trade-offs and adjust plans as conditions change.

Moody’s is making more than a century of credit and risk intelligence directly accessible through Microsoft Copilot, giving customers trusted, protected context for complex decisions. Through a federated connector built using Model Context Protocol, customers can access live, decision-grade Moody’s intelligence through Researcher in Copilot and within Word, Excel and Teams, without copying or exporting the underlying data. A single question can synthesize information across credit ratings, company financials, ownership information and physical risk models, helping customers reach insights in minutes instead of spending hours or days on research and analysis. This brings trusted, connected intelligence directly into workflows where customers make complex decisions.

To turn conversations into actionable intelligence at global scale, Plaud, an AI hardware and software company, is using Microsoft Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models and Azure Speech in Foundry Tools to power transcription, summarization and AI inference across long-form audio and multilingual scenarios. Serving more than 2 million users worldwide, Plaud increased transcription accuracy and processing speed by 35% and improved inference performance by 30%, helping professionals turn spoken content into structured outputs and insights. Even as its user base doubled, the company used Foundry’s elastic scaling and flexible deployment models to reduce overall compute costs by 35%, while strengthening its ability to meet security, privacy and compliance requirements across global markets.

Rockwell Automation built a Maintenance Copilot using Microsoft Foundry to put decades of manufacturing expertise in the hands of employees. The AI assistant brings together expert knowledge from veteran engineers, manufacturing data and machine manuals, allowing technicians to quickly identify likely causes of equipment issues, see how colleagues have solved similar problems and access step-by-step troubleshooting guidance. At its Singapore factory, the approach has helped reduce machine downtime by 33% and cut servicing and spare-part costs by about 25%. Rockwell estimates it has also reduced the time it takes new workers to learn to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three months.

With 1.5 billion passengers riding its elevators and escalators every day, TK Elevator knows that every minute of downtime affects how people move through airports, hospitals and offices. Building on a decade of connected-equipment data on Microsoft Azure, the company created AI agents with Microsoft Foundry that brief service technicians before they enter a building, telling them which elevator, which floor, what the issue is and which tools to bring. After each job, a voice agent records the technician’s account of the work in their own words, with no typing, and adds that expertise to a shared record. With 25,000 technicians caring for 1.4 million units worldwide, TK Elevator is turning each technician’s know-how into compounded intelligence every colleague can draw on.

Telstra partnered with Microsoft Frontier Company to deploy an AI-powered Migration Payment Agent that helps simplify one of the most complex aspects of customer migration: reconciling billing and payments across legacy and new platforms. The agent uses intelligence across these systems to proactively identify inconsistencies, recommend corrective actions and create enriched cases for human review, combining AI-driven insights with human-in-the-loop validation to maintain operational trust and governance. Already supporting more than 272,000 service migrations and delivering recommendations at 95%+ accuracy in production, the solution demonstrates how Telstra is applying agentic AI at enterprise scale to transform complex operations, improve customer outcomes and build reusable AI capabilities while compounding and protecting Telstra’s operational intelligence.

Agent 365 observes AI solutions across the stack

To advance its transformation into an AI-powered organization, Manulife is adopting Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite, expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 30,000 employees and leveraging Microsoft Agent 365 to govern, manage and secure AI agents at enterprise scale. With Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry supporting its global enterprise AI platform, Manulife is building a foundation for teams to develop and deploy AI and agentic solutions while maintaining standards for quality, security and cost efficiency. AI is already delivering impact across the business, from generative AI solutions supporting more than 110 million customer calls annually to developers increasing productivity by 30% with assisted and autonomous AI capabilities. With agentic solutions and AI-powered workflows already in production, Manulife is creating the foundation to scale AI responsibly across its global operations and accelerate its next phase of enterprise transformation.

Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale. As a Microsoft customer zero organization for Agent 365, Insight Enterprises is quick to adopt new capabilities internally and pass those learnings on to clients. With Microsoft engineering, it tested how Microsoft and third-party agents could be observed, managed, governed and secured through a unified control plane. To date, Insight Enterprises has discovered 9,734 agents with visibility into which are active, what data they can access and how to monitor their activity over time. The experience has helped Insight Enterprises build practical AI governance expertise it can bring to customers, including organizations in highly regulated industries.

KPMG is adopting Microsoft Agent 365 to manage and secure AI agents across its global organization, providing centralized observability and control as it scales agentic AI. Agent 365 will also strengthen KPMG Workbench, its multi-agent platform built on Microsoft Foundry that coordinates agents across client service delivery platforms. At the same time, KPMG is expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 276,000 professionals worldwide, helping embed AI more deeply across audit, tax and advisory services. Together, these capabilities are giving KPMG the confidence and security to move agents from experimentation into enterprise-wide deployment, while helping clients do the same.

Operating in one of the most highly regulated industries, where protecting sensitive customer information is essential, Truist Financial Corporation is using Agent 365 to manage, govern and observe more than 13,000 AI declarative agents across its organization. Truist manages its agent ecosystem with discipline: every agent has an accountable owner and agents are automatically disabled after 45 days of inactivity. That rigor is driving strong retention and adoption, with more than 8,000 agents active each month. Building on this trusted foundation, Truist has advanced its broader AI strategy through their investment of more than 50,000 Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite seats.

—

Every quarter gives us an opportunity to step back and look at the progress we are making with our customers and partners around the world. What continues to strike me is not simply the pace of change, but the ambition we see from organizations using technology to achieve aspirations that simply weren’t possible before. We look forward to working alongside you on the path to becoming Frontier, and we hope to see many of you at Microsoft Ignite this year in November to share the latest innovations that will enable you to reach that destination.

Judson Althoff is the chief executive officer of the commercial business at Microsoft. He is responsible for the product strategy, sales, services, support, marketing, operations and revenue growth of the company’s commercial business, which operates in more than 120 regional and national subsidiaries globally.

The post The platform approach to becoming Frontier appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.title: The Identities Nobody Is Governing Are About to Rotate Every 47 Days
articles.context: IDC research sponsored by GuidePoint Security found that abused non-human identities are now tied as the top entry point in confirmed breaches and only a fraction of...
articles.full_text:
The Identities Nobody Is Governing Are About to Rotate Every 47 Days

October 27, 2026

Mark Whitesell

BLOG

5 min.

TL;DR – Public Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate validity drops to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days by 2029. Certificates are non-human credentials and organizations that lack full discovery and automated lifecycle management will face recurring outages, compliance gaps and tougher cyber insurance renewals.

Three takeaways:

Certificates are identity, not infrastructure. If your certificate program is not part of your identity governance framework, you have a blind spot that shrinks with every validity reduction.

Most organizations only track what their primary CA issues are. Certificates from cloud providers, containers and shadow IT teams sit outside that view.

March 2027 is an automation deadline, not a compliance checkbox. At 100-day validity, manual renewal processes break at enterprise scale. Organizations that invest in discovery and automation now will absorb the transition. Those that wait will spend Q1 in reactive mode.

It’s Wednesday morning and your VP of Engineering pings the security channel: a production API gateway is rejecting connections. So the team runs through the usual checks: Traffic is flowing. DNS is clean. Firewall rules haven’t changed.

Forty minutes later, someone finds the source. A Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate on an internal service expired overnight. It was issued eleven months ago by a team that has since reorged and it was never added to your renewal tracker.

This outage is not unusual and the root cause is always the same, a credential no one was watching. That scenario plays out today with certificates valid for a year or more. Now compress the timeline.

The Timeline is Already Moving

March 15, 2026: the CA/Browser Forum’s Ballot SC-081v3 took effect, capping public TLS certificate validity at 200 days. This is the current state.

March 15, 2027: the next milestone drops the maximum to 100 days. Manual certificate management breaks at this cadence.

March 15, 2029: every publicly trusted certificate tops out at 47 days. There is no opt-out. Every publicly trusted certificate authority is bound by this schedule.

SC-081v3 applies specifically to publicly trusted TLS certificates, but the operational implications extend across your entire Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) environment. Organizations managing TLS renewals manually are almost certainly managing internal certificates, code signing and machine identities the same way. The validity reduction is a TLS mandate. The readiness gap it exposes is a PKI-wide problem.

For organizations still managing certificates manually, the math is unforgiving. At 47-day validity, a single certificate requires nearly eight renewals per year. Multiply that across hundreds or thousands of certificates, many of which have never been inventoried and the operational burden becomes unsustainable without automation. Organizations need to adapt now or timelines will catch up.

This is Not a Web Certificate Problem

It is tempting to treat shortened certificate lifecycles as a web server issue, something your infrastructure team handles during routine maintenance windows. But that framing misses the scope of what is actually at stake.

Certificates authenticate actions on behalf of humans and non-human identities, including service accounts, API connections, cloud workloads, CI/CD pipelines and AI agents. Every time one of these identities establishes trust with another system, a certificate is doing the work.

When a certificate expires untracked, it does not generate a security alert. It generates:

An outage

Authentication chains break

Automated workflows stop

Production systems go offline

And the team that gets the 2:00 AM call spends hours tracing the failure to a credential that was issued once, never inventoried and never assigned to an owner.

At 200 days, that risk is manageable in small environments. At 47 days, it becomes a recurring operational failure for any organization without automation.

The Discovery Gap

Organizations assume they know how many certificates they have because they track what their primary certificate authority issues. That view misses certificates issued by cloud providers, embedded in containers, baked into legacy applications or managed by individual engineering teams outside of central IT.

The gap between “what we think we have” and “what actually exists” is where both outages and risk concentrate. You cannot rotate what you can’t see and you cannot assign ownership to something you don’t know about.

IDC research sponsored by GuidePoint Security found that abused non-human identities are now tied as the top entry point in confirmed breaches and only a fraction of organizations run continuous discovery across their non-human identity landscape. Certificates are non-human credentials. If organizations are not discovering service accounts and API keys, they are almost certainly not discovering every certificate in their environment either.

That’s the disconnect shortened lifecycles will force into the open. Organizations that treat certification management as a separate infrastructure function (detached from their identity governance program) are building a slot spot at the exact same moment that the rotation window is shrinking.

What Shortened Certificate Lifecycles Mean for Cyber Insurance

Cyber insurance carriers are tightening underwriting requirements around security hygiene and cryptographic infrastructure is part of that evolution. Expired or mismanaged certificates create two categories of risk that underwriters care about:

Attack surface exposure (man-in-the-middle, impersonation)

Operational liability (outages, compliance failures, downtime)

If you are approaching a cyber insurance renewal, expect more pointed questions about how you manage certificate lifecycles, whether rotation is automated and whether you can demonstrate control maturity across your cryptographic environment. The ability to answer those questions directly affects coverage of those terms.

What to Do Before March 2027

The 100-day milestone is less than six months away. Here’s what you need to do before March 2027:

Run a certificate discovery assessment

Map every certificate to an owner

Evaluate automation readiness

Connect certificates to your identity program

Pressure-test your incident response

Assess your post-quantum cryptography readiness

What to Do Before March 2027

If you’re not starting to plan for March 2027 now, you will spend Q1 scrambling to get a hold of your environments. Those that take the time now to discover what they have, automate what they can and assign ownership for the rest, will operate with few outages, less risk and a stronger security posture.

Your certificate infrastructure is your trust infrastructure. The countdown is already running.

Ready to assess your certificate landscape? Schedule time with our identity team to get started.

FAQs

Why are TLS certificate lifecycles getting shorter?

The CA/Browser Forum passed Ballot SC-081v3, which reduces public TLS certificate validity to 200 days (2026), 100 days (2027) and 47 days (2029). Every publicly trusted certificate authority is bound by this schedule. Shorter validity windows reduce the time an attacker can use a compromised certificate.

Why are certificates considered non-human identities?

Certificates authenticate machines, services and workloads the same way passwords authenticate people. They are credentials assigned to non-human entities like APIs, containers and CI/CD pipelines. Managing them outside your identity program creates a blind spot that becomes more dangerous with every validity reduction.

How does certificate automation reduce outage risk?

Automated certificate lifecycle management handles discovery and renewal without manual intervention. At 47-day validity, a single certificate needs nearly eight renewals per year. Without automation, each renewal is a manual task where human error can cause an outage.

What happens if you don't automate certificate renewals before March 2027?

At 100-day validity, manual renewal processes break at enterprise scale. Expired certificates cause outages, break authentication chains and stall automated workflows. Organizations without automation will spend Q1 2027 in reactive mode instead of operating normally.

How do expired certificates affect cyber insurance renewals?

Carriers are tightening underwriting requirements around security hygiene. Expired or mismanaged certificates create two categories of risk: attack surface exposure and operational liability. The ability to demonstrate automated certificate lifecycle management directly affects coverage terms.
