articles.title: Cybersecurity awareness month:
The Impact of AI on CVEs: Industry Challenges
articles.context: AI Shortens the Path from Disclosure to Exploitation AI is not only accelerating vulnerability discovery; it is also reducing the time and expertise required to turn...
articles.full_text:
Integrating artificial intelligence into cybersecurity has fundamentally changed vulnerability research – and not necessarily for the better. For decades, discovering and verifying Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) required deep technical expertise, creating a disciplined process that kept disclosure volume relatively manageable. Today, Generative AI has obliterated that barrier to entry.

While AI empowers seasoned security researchers to uncover complex zero-days at unprecedented speeds, it simultaneously enables a flood of low-effort, AI-generated vulnerability reports. The result is a fractured ecosystem struggling to stay afloat. The signal-to-noise ratio in vulnerability intelligence is plummeting, open-source maintainers are drowning in hallucinated “slop“, and foundational institutions like the American National Vulnerability Database (NVD) are buckling under the sheer volume of submissions.

In Part 1 of this series, we explore how the AI era has weaponized scale in CVE research. We examine the real-world toll on maintainers, the growing danger of severity inflation, the rise of fabricated security advisories, and the cost of keeping up with it all.

The CVE Surge in Numbers

The JFrog security research team has collected data about CVEs published since 2021. Below is a graph showing the steadily climbing increase in the volume of CVEs in recent years.

Due to AI the volume of CVEs is growing at an alarming rate

The data shows a sharp increase in total CVEs, driven by two AI-related trends: experienced security researchers can now identify vulnerabilities faster and more easily, while lower skilled researchers can leverage AI to bypass traditional technical barriers, flooding systems with noise and real CVEs alike.

This surge caused major changes in how CVEs are being assessed and the quality of those assessments.

The Boy Who Cried Wolf

In January 2026, the consequences of this growing verification burden culminated in a stark milestone: Daniel Stenberg, creator of the widely used curl utility, announced the end of the project’s bug bounty program. According to Stenberg, an explosion of AI-generated submissions in 2025 contributed to a flood of invalid reports, and the share of submissions confirmed as vulnerabilities fell below 5%.

Just six months later, Michael Catanzaro, then the security coordinator for the GNOME project, announced changes to the GNOME security tracking system. Catanzaro stated he would no longer forward security reports to GNOME maintainers who had explicitly opted out of receiving AI-generated content. Because the overwhelming majority of incoming reports in 2026 utilized LLMs, he explained, the project was forced to operate under the assumption that the overwhelming majority of vulnerability reports now contain AI-generated material. To manage this new reality, Catanzaro also slashed GNOME’s vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 days to 30 for issues reported on or after August 1, 2026. Noting that some other projects, notably the Linux kernel, have implemented an immediate full disclosure policy for reports that seem to be AI-generated, GNOME adopted the shortened window as a compromise to accelerate the pipeline without crushing maintainers.

The National Vulnerability Database’s Policy Change

The deluge of CVEs has also led NIST to change how it prioritizes NVD analysis. In an April 2026 announcement on NVD operations, NIST said that starting April 15, 2026, it would prioritize CVEs in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, software used by the federal government, and critical software. NIST also moved backlogged CVEs published before March 1, 2026 to “Not Scheduled.” In our view, this leaves many published CVEs without NVD enrichment and pushes more of the verification burden onto enterprise security teams.

AI Shortens the Path from Disclosure to Exploitation

AI is not only accelerating vulnerability discovery; it is also reducing the time and expertise required to turn vulnerability information into a working exploit. In one May 2026 case involving CVE-2026-46529, which affects GNOME’s Evince document viewer and its forks, a researcher used Claude to help develop a weaponized, single-click code-execution exploit. Controlled research from PoCGen and Anthropic has demonstrated similar capabilities, showing how attackers could exploit the period between public disclosure and widespread patching.

Severity Inflation

Not every vulnerability labeled Critical represents a critical real-world threat. Severity inflation occurs when a rating is based on a theoretical or reasonable worst-case outcome without adequately accounting for the conditions required to enable it in the wild.

These conditions may include whether the vulnerable code is exposed, whether an optional feature is enabled, whether a particular configuration is present, or whether exploitation requires an unlikely sequence of events.

Annual number of CVEs segmented into Critical, High, and other severities

This distinction is built into CVSS itself. The official FIRST CVSS v4.0 User Guide states that CVSS Base scores are designed to measure the severity of a vulnerability and should not be used alone to assess risk. Nevertheless, scanners, dashboards, and remediation policies frequently treat the Base score as a universal measure of urgency.

At JFrog, we provide additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, allowing customers to prioritize vulnerabilities and define policies using trusted JFrog severity scores instead of relying solely on external Base scores.

The Cost of Scoring at Scale

The scale described earlier matters because vulnerability assessment does not expand automatically with vulnerability volume. Each score may require reviewing the affected code, reproducing the issue, inspecting its fix, and understanding how the component is deployed.

When thousands of records must be processed quickly, assessors may instead rely on short CVE descriptions, the general vulnerability class, or default worst-case assumptions. Volume alone does not make a score incorrect, but it increases the likelihood that important technical details might be missed.

Severity Dissonance: The curl Case

A clear illustration of severity inflation emerged in a recent four-month window involving the libcurl project. Since June, the maintainers have published 27 CVEs with assessed security impacts ranging from Low to Medium. However, when CISA evaluated these same vulnerabilities, nearly all were escalated to High or Critical scores.

When the JFrog Security Research team investigated this striking dissonance, we found that the assigned CVSS vectors had failed to reflect the vulnerabilities’ technical reality. For instance, flaws assigned Critical scores were often merely client-side crashes or required niche client configurations outside an attacker’s control. In several cases, client-side use-after-free bugs were miscategorized as network-based memory corruption threats, resulting in a Critical rating that, in our assessment, did not reflect the actual attack vector and practical security impact.

Faux CVEs: The Rise of AI Generated Slop

Generative AI is remarkably adept at mimicking the authoritative tone, formatting, and technical jargon required for a security advisory. The result is a growing wave of slop vulnerabilities that sound terrifying but either do not exist at all or are nowhere near as severe as they are presented.

Case Study: The SQLite Slop Advisories

A clear example of this systemic breakdown is the research we published at JFrog in July 2026 regarding a wave of critical advisories. A newly created GitHub repository published over 50 security advisories, a batch containing reports targeting SQLite alongside various other open source projects. The reports appeared polished and authoritative, detailing complex Use After Free (UAF) memory corruption flaws. They were swiftly assigned high CVSS scores, up to 9.8 Critical, and CISA’s ADP program agreed..

However, when our security researchers analyzed the target codebases to verify the claims, the reports completely fell apart. The technical details appear to have been hallucinated by an LLM:

Nonexistent code: The advisories cited functions like exprComputeOperands() and jsonBlobEdit() that were not present in the targeted SQLite versions.

Impossible line numbers: One advisory pointed to a vulnerability at line 3555 in a file containing only 2706 lines.

Ghost fixes: Another claimed a fix was committed in a newer release, but source diffs showed zero changes to the referenced files.

Because the current CVE pipeline is overwhelmed by volume and does not require a working POC before scores are issued, these reports slide directly into downstream feeds. Out of 55 advisories published by that account, 54 were completely fabricated, yet reports like these can flow into GHSA, enterprise scanners, and developer alerts.

The Cost of Keeping Up

When a Flood of Fixes Arrives

The pressure becomes especially clear when a large number of fixes arrive together. According to Oracle, its July 2026 Critical Patch Update, its largest security release to date, addressed 1,434 distinct CVEs with 1,449 patches across 334 products. Oracle attributed the scale partly to AI-powered identification of actionable security findings. For customers, however, receiving more fixes does not make deploying them any simpler. Each organization still has to identify the affected systems, decide what is most urgent, test the relevant updates, and fit them into its release schedule.

AI is also uncovering bugs that were not detected even after years of conventional research. A security agent developed by depthfirst reported 21 zero-day vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, several of which had remained in the code for 15 to 20 years despite extensive fuzzing and manual review.

The Gap Between Discovery and Patching

AI can find vulnerabilities faster than developers can fix them. As AI increases the number of findings entering remediation queues, maintainers still have to verify each report, understand which versions are affected, develop and test a reliable fix, and prepare a release. Those steps do not become faster simply because discovery does. Rushing them can produce an incomplete patch or introduce new problems.

CISA has connected this pressure directly to AI-assisted discovery, stating that AI is vastly increasing the pace at which new vulnerabilities are found while defenders are already struggling to keep up. According to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, as cited by CISA, , organizations fully remediated only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog during 2025, down from 38% the previous year, while the median time for full resolution rose to 43 days. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre has issued a similar warning, saying that AI-assisted discovery could create a vulnerability patch wave, with an influx of updates across all severity levels that organizations will need to deploy more frequently and at greater scale. Together, these sources show the practical effect of higher volume: even when teams improve their processes, a larger queue can still leave fixes waiting longer.

Stay Tuned…

AI has increased both speed and uncertainty across the CVE ecosystem. Finding vulnerabilities is no longer the only challenge, as verifying, prioritizing, and fixing those that pose a genuine risk has become equally important. In Part 2 of this series, The Impact of the AI-Era on CVE Research: PROTECTION STRATEGIES, we recommend best practices, demonstrate JFrog’s AI-assisted libheif exploit chain and show how JFrog Xray and JFrog Advanced Security help teams assess their actual exposure.

To gain a better understanding of how JFrog provides additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, schedule a demo with our team.

Examples and outcomes are illustrative; actual results may vary depending on your environment and use case. articles.title: Keep Cyber Threats Out of Play: Five Cybersecurity Tips for Golf Facilities
articles.context: Helping PGA of America Golf Professionals address those questions is part of the Association’s partnership with LevelBlue, the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of...
articles.full_text:
Originally published by the PGA of America.

Operating a golf facility means keeping track of a lot more than what’s happening on the course. Tee times, lesson schedules, payroll and vendor payments all depend on technology working as it should. Keeping those systems secure is easy to put off when everything is running smoothly, but it’s worth making time before a problem interrupts the day.

October’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month is a good opportunity to sit down with your team or technology provider and ask a few questions: Who has access to your accounts? How do employees flag a suspicious email? What’s the plan if your booking system goes down?

Helping PGA of America Golf Professionals address those questions is part of the Association’s partnership with LevelBlue, the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of America, PGA Championship and KPMG Women’s PGA Championship through 2028. LevelBlue provides services to help protect the Association’s technology and flagship events, while also bringing cybersecurity education to the broader golf community.

Discover why LevelBlue is the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of America.

Learn More

“Our PGA of America Members have a lot on their plates, and cybersecurity may not be their area of expertise,” said Kevin Scott, Chief Technology Officer, PGA of America. “Working with LevelBlue helps us bring them practical information they can use when talking with their staff and technology providers.”

Five places to start

Check your logins. Use a different password for each account and a password manager to keep track of them. Turn on multifactor authentication, which requires another verification step when you sign in. Start with email, financial systems and accounts with administrative access.

Give staff permission to pause. An email asking for an urgent payment or new banking details should prompt a phone call to a number you already trust. Make sure employees know whom to ask when something seems off, even if the request appears to come from the boss.

Ask who handles updates. Your reservation software, shop computers and other devices need regular security updates. Confirm with your providers who installs security updates and how quickly they’re applied. Don’t assume someone else has it covered.

Remove access when people leave. When a seasonal employee finishes or a vendor relationship ends, removing their access should be part of the process. For current staff, check that each person has access only to what their job requires.

Talk through an outage. Decide how staff members would handle check-in and other essential tasks without access to your usual systems. Keep your technology provider’s contact details handy, ask about backups and recovery, and practice the plan with your team.

You don’t need to tackle everything in one meeting. Pick a starting point, assign someone to follow up and put time on the calendar to check progress. Revisit the discussion when you bring on new staff, change providers or add a system.

Learn more about LevelBlue’s partnership with the PGA of America.

articles.title: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026
articles.context: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic
articles.full_text:
The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event.

In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters.

Disruptions at a glance

Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption.

In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five.

Power failure was a leading cause of disruptions

The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns.

In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3.

Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%.

Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country.

Cloudflare Radar - Traffic volume by autonomous system

On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. As discussed in more detail below, geopolitical conflict remains a major driver of Internet disruptions. These incidents also show how conflict, energy infrastructure, and Internet connectivity are fundamentally intertwined.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Also of note: on August 13, a cooling system failure at a data center in the U.S. city of Phoenix caused a near-total drop in Internet traffic from Namecheap (AS22612). Outages such as these will be important to watch as the role of cooling systems becomes increasingly critical.

Beyond the larger outages in Cuba, Honduras, and Ukraine, power-related disruptions also appeared across a wide range of countries, including Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Some of these events were caused by sudden failures, while others, such as planned load-shedding in Eswatini, reflected deliberate efforts to manage constrained power supply. Their scale and duration varied, but together they point to the same underlying dependency: when power systems become unstable, Internet connectivity often becomes unstable with them. In total, Radar observed 14 power-related disruptions across 10 countries during the quarter.

The physical world takes the virtual world offline

Last quarter, Radar reported on the impact of Super Typhoon Sinlaku, as it moved through the Mariana Islands, knocking out power and, in turn, Internet connectivity in Guam, where HTTP traffic took four days to return to typical levels.

Super Typhoon Bavi followed Sinlaku by less than three months, giving Guam two major storm-related connectivity disruptions in a single year. Officials appeared to take earlier preparedness steps ahead of Bavi, including declaring a state of emergency before peak storm conditions. Even so, the storm caused widespread power outages. The Guam Power Authority reported that strong winds brought down key transmission lines, leaving only about 25% of distribution feeders online at one point. From a connectivity perspective, the outcome was familiar: widespread power outages, downed transmission lines, and a multi-day recovery period for Internet traffic.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

In Japan, an earthquake of similar magnitude, 7.1, prompted evacuation orders affecting roughly 150,000 people in Kumamoto. The impact on Internet connectivity primarily appeared in desktop traffic, while mobile traffic remained largely unaffected.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP requests time series for Kumamoto, Japan

In Colombia, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in August caused building collapses, injuries, mass evacuations, and a four-and-a-half-day Internet disruption. Damage to fiber-optic infrastructure, compounded by the wider earthquake aftermath, drove a significant drop in traffic from Colombia Telecomunicaciones (AS3816).

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Finally, in Nepal, sudden flash floods swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, affecting communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The flooding damaged homes, infrastructure, and essential services, including power, which in turn disrupted regional Internet connectivity. The outage recorded on Radar lasted two hours, during which HTTP traffic dropped by up to 18%.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Exam shutdowns continue in Iraq

Government-directed shutdowns were the largest cause of disruptions in Q3, the majority of which occurred in Iraq with separate scheduled shutdowns occurring throughout the quarter. The shutdowns took place on a strict schedule 03:30–04:00 UTC, lasting about 15-90 min each. The majority occurred between August 26 and September 28, with three occurring between July 1 and 8.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Per Internet Society Pulse, “In a video message, Minister Mustafa Sanad, Iraq's Minister of Communication, confirmed the shutdown and vowed to develop a digital system that would eliminate the need for centralized exam distribution and, by extension, the need to shut down Internet access on exam days.” Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor the country’s networks as the development of the new system progresses.

Notably, Syria and Sudan, two countries that have also frequently used exam-related Internet shutdowns in recent years, did not record similar disruptions this quarter. However, this likely reflects differences in exam calendars rather than a clear shift in policy. Radar will continue to monitor whether future national exam periods bring renewed shutdowns in either country.

Disruptions coincide with political events

In Ethiopia, renewed conflict in the Tigray region was accompanied by a government-directed Internet shutdown that lasted 10 days. Traffic dropped by 100%, signaling a full-scale shutdown.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

The disruption revived memories of the extensive blockade imposed during Ethiopia’s civil war from 2020 to 2022, when Tigray was largely cut off from telecommunications, electricity, banking services, fuel, and humanitarian aid (France24), which the World Health Organization described as a “de facto blockade.” Although this latest outage appears to have remained localized to Tigray, its impact was still visible in country-level traffic, with HTTP traffic falling by up to 30%.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

On September 19, during nationwide elections, fiber-optic cable damage in Russia’s Far East caused regional connectivity disruptions affecting Chukotka, Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka Krai, and Sakhalin Oblast. Rostelecom described the incidents as deliberate damage to backbone fiber lines and said connectivity was restored using backup channels. Radar data alone cannot determine whether the cable damage was related to the elections, but the timing is notable.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

A quarter shaped by shutdowns and power outages, but also resilience

Across Q3 2026, government-directed shutdowns were the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by Iraq’s exam-related shutdowns. Power outages were close behind, affecting networks across Cuba, Honduras, Ukraine, Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Natural disasters and conflict added another layer of disruption, reminding us that Internet resilience depends on far more than routers and cables. It depends on electricity, physical infrastructure, policy decisions, and the ability of networks to route around failure.

Radar also observed outages inside individual networks, including One Communications (AS19863) in Guyana following a cable cut, MEO (AS3243) in Portugal following a reported “mass attack”, Digicel Haiti (AS27653), TurkNet (AS12735) in Turkey, and Fanap Telecom (AS206065) in Iran.

Each of these events demonstrates the Internet’s fragility, but also its resilience. Many disruptions were brief: 14 saw traffic return to typical levels in under an hour, and 16 recovered in less than three hours. But short outages can still have real consequences for the people affected, especially during storms, earthquakes, conflict, or political unrest. Access to the Internet is often access to information, coordination, safety, and help.

Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor Internet disruptions around the world and share what we see from Cloudflare’s global network. Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

articles.title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
articles.context: The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure,...
articles.full_text:
AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools.

In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern.

AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster.

A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance.

Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch center, and then attempt to move laterally toward the bigger target.

When one of those weak links fails, the consequences can reach well beyond the breached agency: halted 911 dispatches, disrupted water service, exposed resident data, and more.

AI is further complicating the picture.

State, local, and education (SLED) organizations are adopting AI quickly to improve efficiency, employees are building applications with it informally, and adversaries are using it to speed up reconnaissance. Each of those developments is making it harder for security teams to protect SLED agencies.

In this fourth and final blog in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we focus on what that expanding AI attack surface means for state, local, and education cybersecurity leaders responsible for critical infrastructure, and how whole-of-state cybersecurity can help them stay ahead.

Why SLED critical infrastructure is a prime target

SLED organizations operate critical infrastructure, such as water treatment plants, transportation systems, public hospitals, schools, and emergency communications, across many of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors categorized by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

State technology leaders are concerned about protecting these critical infrastructure facilities and services from cyber attacks, as “The Expanding Cyber Perimeter” report, published in September by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), found.

Here are five key findings from the report, which drew on the 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey, the 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte Cybersecurity Study, and interviews with state CISOs:

Nearly 90% of state CIOs rate cyber attacks on critical systems as a high concern. The rest rate them as moderate.

State CIOs report low confidence in local governments’ cyber practices. The report’s authors also say it’s unclear how states should help local governments and independent local government entities, like special districts.

Water and wastewater plants, dams, hospitals, and transportation services face the greatest cyber risk.

Many systems run on aging or proprietary operational technology (OT) with no upgrade path, and broad remote access increases their cyber risk.

Small communities and special districts often have limited cyber staff, aging equipment, and complex OT with few controls. With hundreds of such entities in a single state, attackers have plenty of entry points to try.

Responsibility is also murky. According to the NASCIO-GDIT report, it’s often unclear which agency is responsible for responding to an attack on critical infrastructure, especially where legal authority, governance, or partnerships aren’t in place.

Cyber risk extends beyond technical and geographical boundaries. When an attacker breaches systems of a county water utility or a school district, the incident can have widespread consequences.

State and local officials and their CIOs and CISOs should stop treating these incidents as one city’s or one county’s problem. Robert Beach, then CTO of the City of Cocoa, Florida, and a member of the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) executive committee, told StateScoop last year that an attack on critical infrastructure “is an attack on the nation.”

Insiders add another layer of risk. Another MS-ISAC report, “Strengthening Critical Infrastructure: SLTT Progress & Priorities,” published in August 2025, flagged excessive access to system controls as a vulnerability. The report recommended agencies review who can reach their networks and disable credentials promptly when employees leave.

The 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte study underscores the risk, noting that attackers exploit compromised credentials and former employee accounts, so regular access reviews and prompt offboarding remain essential.

Recent cyber attacks against water systems have made the threat very real. On July 30, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned that water and wastewater sector utilities in at least seven states had reported cyber attacks, leading in some cases to degraded water operations.

That same day, the CISA said it had observed “a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers” in the water and wastewater sector.

“Threat actors targeting exposed PLCs have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” the CISA alert reads.

A week earlier, CISA and several federal agencies had published a joint advisory warning critical infrastructure organizations in the government, water, and energy sectors of “ongoing cyber exploitation of internet-connected OT devices.”

Tenable researchers recommend removing internet-exposed PLCs and setting their mode switches to “Run”, among other steps. The U.S. government is also tightening cybersecurity regulations for water and wastewater utilities.

Federal and state leaders are mobilizing, too.

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Texas Cyber Command Chief Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White launched Project Watershed at a roundtable in San Antonio, Texas, which I was honored to attend. Project Watershed is a joint effort aimed at strengthening the cybersecurity of Texas water and wastewater systems against threats from hostile foreign adversaries.

Governor Abbott said that through the project, “our communities and water systems will be better secured from the onslaught of cyber-attacks.”

Protecting the water systems Americans rely on every day is a shared responsibility, and Project Watershed shows the kind of public-private collaboration a whole-of-state approach depends on.

How AI expands the attack surface

AI has moved from pilot project to operational reality in state government. NASCIO’s 2026 research shows AI overtaking cybersecurity as the top policy priority for state CIOs, the first time in more than a decade that cybersecurity loses the top spot.

AI adoption is good news for service delivery, but it also increases SLED agencies’ cyber risk. Three forces drive the rise in cyber risk:

Employees build and adopt AI tools on their own. As we covered earlier in this series, non-technical staff can now use AI tools to generate working applications using natural-language prompts, often without permission from the IT and security departments. In a government setting, those unsanctioned apps can access resident data, case management systems, and internal credentials, all without testing, patching, or monitoring.

AI shows up inside the software SLED agencies already own, as vendors quietly add AI features and connectors to their products, which can expand data access and permissions without the awareness of the IT and security teams.

Attackers use automation to move faster. The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure, as the window between when an exposure appears and when attackers exploit it keeps shrinking.

For critical infrastructure operators, the stakes rise further. Their aging OT systems with broad remote access are already a soft target. Unvetted AI apps, over-permissioned connectors, and automated scanning by attackers quickly multiply the number of paths an attacker can chain together.

The key for SLED agency CISOs is to see their exposures across IT, OT, cloud, identity, and AI as one connected picture, and to prioritize and act on the ones an attacker could realistically exploit to reach systems that matter to public safety. An exposure management program can help SLED agencies address this cyber risk with comprehensive visibility, prioritization, and AI-assisted action.

What a whole-of-state approach looks like

A whole-of-state approach treats state agencies, local governments, schools, and utilities as one defensive perimeter instead of a collection of individual, siloed organizations.

The state government should share governance frameworks, visibility of IT/OT assets and security findings, and cybersecurity capabilities so the smallest entity doesn’t have to defend itself alone.

As Tenable’s Matt Kucik explains in the blog, “Whole-of-state cybersecurity: Uniting SLED agencies for maximum impact,” success starts with leadership and vision, open communication, and an actionable plan.

The model is gaining ground. The NASCIO-GDIT report found that 73% of states responding to the 2026 State CIO Survey include critical infrastructure cyber protection in their whole-of-state plans. It calls these models the main framework emerging for statewide resilience. Maturity varies widely, though. Four building blocks separate strong programs from weak ones:

Governance and clear roles. CISA’s state cybersecurity governance case studies highlight Georgia and Virginia, which use formal structures to treat cyber risk as a collective priority. They have proactively defined who is in charge of prevention, who is in charge of responding, and who is in charge of generating incident reports.

Shared visibility. You can’t prioritize what you can’t see. A statewide view of assets and exposures lets a small water district benefit from the same insight as a large state agency.

Shared services. In Utah, its federally funded shared services program offers endpoint protection, patching, training, and incident response to roughly 80% of local government entities in the state. The state secured an additional $1.5 million for water-sector cybersecurity.

Trust earned through results. What local partners need from the state is faster remediation, lower costs, and fewer surprises. New Jersey CISO Michael Geraghty made this point in the NASCIO-GDIT report: Telling local governments you’re from the state and here to help doesn’t earn their trust. Results do.

It’s also key to share information quickly. Terry Loftus, CIO of the San Diego County Office of Education and an MS-ISAC committee member, told StateScoop that many districts learn of attacks when they receive a ransomware demand.

State cybersecurity agencies should build channels that proactively push threat intelligence and exposure data to every entity in their state, to increase the chances of preventing attacks.

Five steps SLED agencies can take to boost their cyber defenses

Here’s Tenable’s advice on where to start, whether you lead a state agency, a county IT shop, a school district, or a municipal utility:

Create and continuously update a complete inventory of your critical infrastructure assets, including OT systems, remote access paths, and AI tools and apps. Start with the systems that affect public health and safety.

Prioritize by exploitability and impact. Don’t chase every finding. Focus on the exposures an attacker could realistically chain together to reach water, power, health, or emergency systems. Removing internet-exposed controllers and securing any remote access paths to them should be the highest priority.

Share visibility across jurisdictions. Give small entities access to the same insight larger agencies have, whether through statewide tooling, shared services, or regular information-sharing forums.

Govern AI use before it sprawls. Set clear policies, approved-tool lists, and training for employees who build with AI.

Check if State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP) funding is still available in your state to help fund these priorities.

How Tenable can help SLED agencies

Tenable One gives security teams unified visibility, insights and action across their organizations’ attack surface, including IT, cloud, identity, AI, and OT.

Tenable One OT Exposure capabilities extend that visibility, insight, and action to the OT and extended internet of things (xIoT) devices used by many critical infrastructure organizations.

With Tenable One, SLED teams can see what they have, understand which exposures matter most, and take prioritized actions, maximizing staff and grant dollars to drive down cyber risk.

The City of Raleigh in North Carolina, for example, uses Tenable to ensure the safety and sustainability of its public water systems. To see how Tenable supports statewide programs, explore our state, local, and education solutions and learn how Tenable helps meet SLCGP requirements.

Looking ahead

The attack surface is growing, a trend that AI is accelerating. Federal funding is shrinking, and its future is uncertain. Yet the fundamentals of resilience stay the same: know your assets, understand your exposures, share what you learn, and act together before an attacker forces your hand.

No single state or jurisdiction has solved this, and no single tool will. A whole-of-state approach gives SLED organizations the best chance to stay ahead of the threats facing the critical services residents rely on every day.

articles.title: Simplify User Access Management with SCIM on Rapid7 Command Platform
articles.context: Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes
articles.full_text:
Managing access to security tools shouldn't require another manual process. As organizations grow, keeping user accounts and permissions up to date becomes increasingly complex. Employees join, change roles, and leave, creating a constant need to update access across applications.

When these processes rely on manual administration, delays and oversights can introduce unnecessary work and security risk.

Rapid7 Command Platform now supports System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), enabling customers to automate user provisioning and deprovisioning through their existing identity provider (IdP).

This helps organizations reduce administrative overhead, maintain more consistent access controls, and manage identity at scale.

Automate user access throughout the employee lifecycle

SCIM is an open standard that enables identity providers, such as Okta, to automatically manage user accounts in connected applications.

With SCIM enabled, Rapid7 Command Platform customers can:

Automate provisioning: Create accounts when employees join or need access.

Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes.

Simplify offboarding: Automatically deactivate accounts when users no longer require access.

Manage groups at scale: Synchronize group membership to help streamline access administration.

Rather than manually updating accounts in Command Platform, administrators can manage supported identity lifecycle changes through their existing IdP.

Less administration, more consistent access control

Consider a common scenario: An employee leaves the organization. Without automated provisioning, an administrator must remember to deactivate that employee's access across their applications. If an account is missed, it could remain active longer than intended.

With SCIM, changes made in the organization's identity provider can automatically trigger corresponding account updates in Command Platform.

By introducing SCIM at the platform level, Rapid7 helps organizations:

Reduce operational overhead by eliminating repetitive account-management tasks.

Strengthen access governance by reducing stale accounts and keeping user information aligned with identity provider policies.

Scale more efficiently by centralizing identity lifecycle management for supported Command Platform applications.

For organizations with security and compliance requirements, these capabilities also help support consistent onboarding and offboarding processes.

Get started with SCIM

SCIM support is now available to Rapid7 Command Platform customers.

Platform administrators can configure SCIM through Command Platform's SSO settings using their existing identity provider. SCIM is disabled by default and requires configuration before automated provisioning begins.

For prerequisites and setup instructions, visit the Command Platform SCIM integration documentation.

articles.title: Cato AI Endpoint secures browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents on every endpoint
articles.context: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware
articles.full_text:
AI used to live in a browser tab. Today it also runs inside the apps employees use every day, like Copilot in Word, in dedicated apps like ChatGPT and in coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Coding agents work differently from chat apps. A chat app answers a question and waits. A coding agent is given tools and takes actions on its own, with the developer’s access.

So every endpoint is becoming an agentic endpoint. Your security team now needs to know what the AI on those endpoints does and whose data it touches.

Cato AI Endpoint is a lightweight client that secures AI in the browser, AI in desktop apps and the coding agents developers run locally.

Separate point products leave blind spots on the endpoint

Take two employees on an ordinary afternoon. Sam, a developer, asks a coding agent to tidy up a build.

The agent opens the project files and reads the passwords inside. Then the agent pulls in a tool or a skill your security team never approved.

Maya in finance pastes a customer list into the ChatGPT app because she wants a summary before her next meeting. Neither Sam nor Maya means any harm.

Most of today’s security tools miss both. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware.

The web filter watches the browser, and network tools see what leaves the endpoint.

Sam’s agent works inside the endpoint, so much of what it does doesn’t cross the network at all. Maya’s prompt does leave, but some AI desktop apps lock their connection to their own certificate (certificate pinning), so network tools can’t look inside their traffic. The customer list goes out, and your security team doesn’t see it.

Each of those tools still does the job it’s made for, but network security can’t see enough of the endpoint to control agentic AI.

Skills and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are add-ons that give agents extra abilities, and skills and MCP servers that sit installed but unused still widen the attack surface. An employee installs a skill once and forgets it, but the agent decides when to use it. If that skill can make web requests, the agent can use it to send data anywhere without asking.

Adding another point product for each kind of AI doesn’t close the gap either. Each product leaves its own blind spots and splits policy enforcement across more tools.

Secure browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents together

Cato AI Endpoint protects local agents, desktop apps, embedded AI assistants and web AI traffic with a lightweight client, so teams deploy and manage fewer tools. Protection starts with knowing which AI is already on your endpoints.

Discover Shadow AI and Agents. Shadow AI is AI that employees use without approval. Cato AI Endpoint can find the AI applications, local agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints, so your security team knows what is in use and what to govern first.

Protect Prompts and Responses Inline. When Sam’s agent calls the unapproved tool, Cato AI Endpoint can block the tool before it runs. The rest of the agent’s work carries on.

Cato AI Endpoint doesn’t act while Maya types or pastes. When Maya sends the prompt, Cato AI Endpoint can inspect and block the prompt on the endpoint before the customer list reaches the AI model. Maya sees a pop-up saying company policy blocked the prompt, and her session carries on.

The same user interaction rule applies to AI in the browser and desktop apps, with no extra configuration. When a prompt is sent, the rule can monitor it, block it or anonymize it by swapping names and other sensitive data for placeholders. Coding agents get monitor and block controls, and your team manages browser, desktop and coding agent protection from one dashboard.

Add AI security without replacing your existing stack

You’ve invested in EDR, in SSE (the cloud security service that includes your web filter) and in a VPN, and you can’t afford to disrupt them. You also need AI protection now.

Cato runs alongside the existing security stack. Only AI application traffic goes to Cato, and all other traffic stays on your existing tools, so you can see the AI in use within weeks.

The Cato AI Endpoint client goes out through device management like any other app. Finding the agents on an endpoint requires no network change. If another SSE client already runs on the endpoint, your team sets up both clients to run side by side.

Catch risky agents and prevent unsafe actions

Blocking Sam’s tool stops one unsafe action. Your security team also needs to know which other agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints are risky.

The Cato AI Endpoint client gives each skill a risk finding with a block, monitor or allow recommendation. Verified remote MCP servers get a badge. Cato can also flag risky agents, MCP servers and skills before they act, so teams can fix the riskiest first.

A week later, when someone asks which AI touched customer data, your team opens one dashboard and finds Sam’s blocked tool next to Maya’s blocked prompt. Each shows the user, endpoint and data behind it. Endpoint and network AI events sit in the same platform and data lake, so they share context.

Sam gets a tidy build without the unapproved tool, and Maya’s customer list stays inside the company.

articles.title: The Confidence Gap in Application Access Governance | Report
articles.context: Sixty-eight percent of organizations say more critical applications are in scope for access governance or SOX compliance than two years ago, and 60% say the number of critical...
articles.full_text:
What you will learn

Why 95% of leaders feel audit-ready while 26% see the same access findings return, how AI agents that act inside critical business applications add risk and which controls to examine first to close gaps for good.

Business application estates are growing, creating more places for risk to hide. Sixty-eight percent of organizations say more critical applications are in scope for access governance or SOX compliance than two years ago, and 60% say the number of critical applications in use but outside that scope has also increased.

Those out-of-scope applications expose the organization to unmanaged risk.

As a number of critical line-of-business applications increase for companies, application access governance (AAG) must keep pace with more users, permissions and connections between systems. Finance, IT, audit and compliance leaders need to analyze access risk across a growing number of ERP, CRM, and HCM applications, and demonstrate that controls remain effective as people change roles and AI tools and AI agents become part of critical business processes.

In Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report, finance and finance technology leaders reported confidence that their access controls would hold up to an audit. The findings tell a different story.

High confidence in access controls, yet audit findings persist

When surveyed, 95% of respondents say they are confident their access controls for business applications would withstand external audit scrutiny today. Yet 26% say the same or similar access findings have recurred in consecutive years, and 25% say findings have remained open for three or more years.

Strengthening application access governance takes time and resources. The growth in scope of business applications is translating into heavier workloads for teams responsible for governance. Sixty-eight percent of respondents reported greater effort to complete user access reviews (UARs) and 58% reported longer remediation times for access-related audit findings.

That additional work resulted in substantial expenditures to remediate risk. In the US, 46% of respondents spent $251,000 or more in the past 12 months remediating access-related audit findings. In the UK, 42% spent £201,000 or more.

What to examine: Are the same access-related findings recurring year after year, and can you show why prior remediation didn’t hold? What would it take to close an audit finding permanently rather than reopening it at the next audit?

AI adoption is outpacing oversight in business applications

Of organizations surveyed, 88% reported they already use AI tools or AI agents within critical business applications.

What is more surprising, 35% of respondents said they have deployed AI agents that perform actions that go beyond read-only analysis and recommendations. That distinction matters when it comes to critical business processes like payroll and procurement. An AI agent that can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions needs extra guardrails around what access it holds and which decisions require human approval.

Oversight hasn’t kept up. Fewer than half of organizations using AI in critical business applications have full, centrally tracked visibility into AI agent deployment, access, permissions, ownership and approval. Fewer than half consistently apply common governance controls across all their AI tools and agents.

This gap is causing observable problems. Eighty-four percent of organizations using AI in critical applications report at least one in the past year. Respondents reported the following AI-related issues, in order of prevalence:

What to examine: Which AI agent actions require approval, which permissions are restricted, is each action authorized and can every consequential action be traced to an accountable owner?

Excess privileged access goes unchecked

As organizations expand their portfolio of business applications, and adopt AI agents within business applications, foundational access controls become even more important. Yet the survey found that 52% of respondents do not continuously monitor and remediate excess access.

Automation helps teams make access risk management continuous, and it is becoming common across access governance activities. Access controls like segregation of duties (SoD) risk analysis and UARs have been around for quite some time, yet for many organizations manual work remains part of the control equation. When asked to what extent common access governance activities were automated, nearly two-thirds of respondents said each activity was mostly or fully automated. Only about one-quarter reported full automation.

Manual work leaves the door open for risk to show up in everyday operations. 91% of respondents reported at least one access-related condition. Respondents reported the following access-related issues, in order of prevalence:

What to examine: Do role changes, departures and emergency-access expiry reliably trigger access removal? Can you demonstrate that rejected or unnecessary access was removed, including when an audit has already identified it?

articles.title: First ISC2 AI Security Certification Expected for Early 2027
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The preliminary phase of the certification benefitted from the input of 10,000 volunteer professionals worldwide through Job Task Analysis surveys.

From October 26, ISC2 is opening a pilot exam phase, giving cybersecurity professionals, employers and the global cybersecurity community insight into the domains and topics the exam is designed to assess.

The nonprofit is now looking for 3000 volunteers to enrol in a beta version of the exam in December 2026. Volunteers have until November 4 to submit their interest.

Six Key Domains to Shape the AI Security Exam

The pilot exam will assess candidates’ knowledge, skills and abilities across the following areas of professional practice needed to secure AI-enabled environments:

AI concepts and security fundamentals

AI governance, ethics, risk and compliance

AI data management, privacy and model security

Secure AI architecture, engineering and identity and access management (IAM)

Secure AI operations and incident response (IR)

AI threats, testing and lifecycle management

Each domain includes topics and subtopics to help candidates understand the AI security expertise the exam is designed to evaluate.

In a public statement, Casey Marks, COO of ISC2, said this pilot phase aims to provide “critical evidence to evaluate whether the examination measures AI security competence reliably, fairly and defensibly, which are all key facets of the rigor essential to certification integrity and to employers’ and professionals’ trust in what earning the credential represents.”

If the pilot exam phase is successful, the certification will be available to take from the first quarter of 2027, and maybe even as early as January, Beale estimated.

Eligibility Requirements for the New AI Security Certification

This new AI security credential will be available to both ISC2 members and non-members. It will be open to professionals who hold existing ISC2 credentials as well as those who do not.

It is primarily intended for professionals responsible for securing the design, deployment and maintenance of AI and machine learning (ML) systems throughout the AI lifecycle.

This includes managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI-enabled services and extending beyond technical defense to governance, ethics, risk-based guidance and enterprise collaboration.

In addition, candidates who wish to pass this certification must meet certain criteria, including having a minimum of four years of cumulative, paid full-time experience in cybersecurity or AI-related fields, with two years in cybersecurity and one year in two or more of the domains of the AI security certification exam outline.

Candidates holding active CISSP, ISSAP, ISSEP, ISSMP, CCSP or CSSLP credential may be substituted for the entire AI security certification experience requirement.

In his Security Congress opening speech, ISC2’s CEO Beale also said that AI questions are currently being “incorporated across all other ISC2 current certifications.”

“We’ve significantly increased the amount of certificates, webinars, events and professional development capabilities in the AI safety and security space over the past six months,” he told Infosecurity.

One example is the launch of the Cyber AI Workforce Coalition, announced on October 20.

articles.title: Watchdog Urges Police and Fire Service to Improve Cybersecurity
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The cyber threat to UK police forces and fire and rescue services is growing rapidly and demands a more urgent response, an independent assessment has warned.

The Cybersecurity in Police Forces and Fire and Rescue Services report from His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) was published on October 27.

It was compiled from a three-phase inspection carried out between January and May 2026, and involved dozens of interviews, “reality testing,” and scrutiny of over 260 police service and fire and rescue service documents.

“While there have been gradual improvements, many forces and services still need to urgently redouble their efforts to respond to the increased risk of cyber-attacks,” warned Michelle Skeer, His Majesty’s inspector of constabulary.

“Cybersecurity should be viewed as a core organizational priority and not solely a technical risk. Leaders need to prioritize and invest in their cybersecurity arrangements to improve their organization’s ability to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from attacks.”

Read more on threats to policing infrastructure: Government Updates UK’s National Risk Register with Cyber Warnings

The report highlighted multiple areas of weakness:

Legacy ICT systems identified as a “strategic risk” due to difficulties with patching and integration

Exposure to third-party risk, especially ICT suppliers that manage sensitive police data, and human error when using external services

Underdeveloped preparedness and resilience, including backups and incident response

Basic control issues, including access management, authentication and provisioning/deprovisioning

A lack of accountability at a senior level, with several police and fire leaders claiming cybersecurity isn’t part of daily operational decision-making

Poor coordination at a national level, leading to uneven levels of cyber maturity across the various forces and fire/rescue services

A Plan for Improvement

HMICFRS made 13 recommendations for improving the cybersecurity posture of the nation’s police forces and fire and rescue services.

These include:

Introducing baseline cybersecurity standards to improve maturity across the board (ie Cyber Assessment Framework)

Third-party assessment of cybersecurity capabilities

Improving procurement and contract management of third-party ICT suppliers (including mandatory Cyber Essentials certification)

Enhancing collaboration between government and policing cybersecurity leads

Promoting the use of the Police Digital Service’s National Management Centre, and creating a similar national capability for fire and rescue services

Improving the preparedness of services to respond to an attack (eg backup and restore and incident response exercises)

Improving learning and development for senior leaders and cybersecurity staff

“The government’s program of police reform and local government reorganization could offer both sectors opportunities to improve and better co-ordinate the approach to cybersecurity,” said Skeer. “These opportunities to strengthen cybersecurity cannot be missed. Protecting systems and data is essential to protecting the public.”

articles.title: How Maven Central Builds Trust Into Dependency Delivery
articles.context: The team expects the component to be what its coordinates say it is, the metadata to help its build tool resolve the right version and related components, and the download to be...
articles.full_text:
When a development team adds a dependency, it is placing trust in more than a file.

The team expects the component to be what its coordinates say it is, the metadata to help its build tool resolve the right version and related components, and the download to be available when the build runs, wherever that build happens. Often, all of this happens automatically, without anyone having to contact the publisher or check that the service is working.

That trust is easy to overlook because the process is routine. But a public registry is part of the path between a publisher and the teams that depend on its software. How it handles publications, metadata, delivery, problems, and long-term availability affects how much confidence people can place in that path.

A registry does not establish that every component is secure or suitable for every use. Its role is to provide a dependable way to identify, publish, find, and retrieve software. That is an important part of trust in the software supply chain.

A Dependable Source Matters

For many development teams, Maven Central is the default source for Java dependencies. That default reduces friction. Developers and build tools know where to look, and publishers have a widely understood way to make release-ready components available.

Defaults also carry an expectation. Teams expect to retrieve the component they requested, with metadata that lets their tools resolve it correctly. They expect the service to be available during a local build, a CI run, or a scan. A registry that can meet those expectations consistently becomes part of the development infrastructure organisations rely on every day.

This kind of confidence is built through operational work. It begins when a publisher submits a release.

Publication Needs to Be Predictable

The registry needs to check that a submission meets the requirements for publication and can be handled consistently.

That includes:

The component's coordinates.

The structure of the files being published.

The metadata used to identify and resolve the component.

These checks support predictable publication and retrieval. They do not determine whether the software is secure, well designed, or appropriate for a particular product. Those questions depend on the component itself, how it is maintained, and the context in which it is used.

Still, predictable publication is a foundation for trust. A team needs to know that a request for a particular component and version will resolve to the files associated with that release. If information is incomplete or inconsistent, a component can be harder to discover, resolve, or use. A small problem at publication time may become a confusing failure much later, in a build pipeline far from the original publisher.

Metadata Makes Components Understandable

A registry stores files, but consumers also rely on information that describes them. Metadata helps build tools understand a component's identity, its versions, and its relationships to other components. It helps developers and automated systems find what they need.

That information has to be processed and made available alongside the files. Indexes need to be maintained so components can be searched and queried. As new versions are published, the registry needs to keep its view of the ecosystem current.

For a developer, this often feels like a simple lookup. A build tool asks for a component and gets an answer. Behind that request is work to represent, update, and serve published information in a form that clients can use.

Trust Is Becoming a Practical Requirement

This work is taking place as organisations face growing expectations to understand the software they use and how it enters their products and services.

For example:

The EU Cyber Resilience Act places due diligence responsibilities on manufacturers that integrate third-party components into products with digital elements.

NIS2 requires supply-chain security measures from entities within its scope.

DORA requires financial entities to manage ICT third-party risk as part of their wider ICT risk management.

These laws have different scopes and requirements. They do not mean that every package registry is automatically subject to the same obligations, or that using a registry makes a component compliant or secure. But they point to a broader expectation: organisations need to understand their dependencies, the sources they rely on, and the risks involved in using them.

A dependable registry can support that work by making components identifiable and reliably available, and by maintaining the information that build tools use to resolve them. It cannot make a manufacturer's risk assessment on its behalf. Confidence in a component also depends on its origin, maintenance, known vulnerabilities, and the way it is used.

Trust in the registry and trust in the component are related, but they are not the same thing. Both matter.

Availability Takes Continuing Work

Once a release is accepted, it needs to remain accessible. The registry has to manage growing volumes of files and requests, and make components available to consumers in different locations and environments.

Replication is part of that operational picture. A registry needs to make content available across the systems that serve requests while keeping files and metadata consistent. It also needs to monitor capacity and performance as usage changes. Demand is not limited to people actively writing code. Builds, test jobs, scanners, and other automated systems may all request the same component, often repeatedly.

One build fetching a dependency is unremarkable. The same request repeated across thousands of short-lived build environments becomes part of the registry's daily workload.

The service has to handle that demand while remaining dependable for everyone using it. Reliability is not something a system achieves once and then keeps automatically. It depends on continued work to operate, monitor, and improve the service.

Problems Need a Response

No shared service can assume every request will be expected or every interaction will work as intended. Registries need ways to identify and respond to abuse, unusual traffic, and operational issues. They also need people who can investigate problems and communicate with publishers and consumers when something goes wrong.

Some problems are deliberate. Many are not. A misconfigured tool, an overly aggressive automation job, or a workflow that repeatedly requests the same information can create load without anyone intending to cause harm. Understanding what is happening takes operational visibility and, sometimes, conversations with the people running the systems involved.

Support is part of that work too. A publisher may need help understanding why a release did not complete. A consumer may be trying to work out whether a failure comes from its own configuration or from the service. Clear guidance and timely responses help people resolve these issues, and help the registry team see where its processes could improve.

Dependability Has a Long Horizon

Teams build software that depends on components released years ago. They expect to resolve those dependencies as their own systems change and as new versions of build tools and operating environments arrive.

That expectation brings long-term responsibilities: retaining published files, maintaining the systems that make them discoverable, and continuing to operate the service as the ecosystem grows. A registry's role does not end when a file has been uploaded and stored.

This is easy to miss because the service often works quietly. A developer adds a dependency, a build completes, and the team carries on. The registry becomes visible when a component cannot be found, a release behaves unexpectedly, or a build fails while trying to retrieve what it needs.

By then, the work behind the service has already shaped the outcome.

Central Is Part of the Development Path

Maven Central's value comes in part from being a dependable, familiar source for Java components. Developers can build on published software, and publishers can make release-ready components available to a broad ecosystem. That convenience rests on confidence in the service and the work required to maintain it.

The more organisations rely on public registries, the more important it becomes to understand them as operational infrastructure. They receive and validate publications, process metadata, maintain indexes, serve files, respond to abuse, support users, and preserve access over time.

Maven Central should continue to make community open source broadly available. Keeping that promise means caring for the infrastructure that makes it possible, and being clear about the work on which that trust depends.

Written by Paul Horton

Paul Horton is the OSPO Global Director at Sonatype and a Core Maintainer of OWASP CycloneDX, with more than 20 years of experience spanning software development, DevSecOps, open source governance, and software supply chain security. He is an active open source contributor who helps organisations improve software transparency and translate complex security and compliance challenges into practical solutions.

articles.full_text: As the news from last week has settled down, it would seem this headline was pretty spot on. The foretold apocalypse didn't eventuate, and there were no internet-destroying outages. In fact, it took days before I could find a single story of PHP2Shell being reliably attributed back to a breach. And I don't think we can say the relatively benign outcome was only achieved because we did take it so seriously either; there's a massive trove of sites out there that have been left to rot and would have every opportunity to be pwned by a bug of this magnitude that was readily exploitable, yet here we are. Which is good 🙂
