Maintaining security

If your organization has already approved Claude chat, this builds on the enterprise controls you already use, including single sign-on (SSO) and the Compliance API. Anthropic still encrypts data in transit and at rest and doesn’t use it for model training by default.

Claude does agentic work in cloud sessions, each running in its own isolated virtual machine with network egress off by default for Claude Enterprise and connector credentials kept outside the sandbox. Because that work runs in one environment that Anthropic manages, your security team gets central visibility and controls over it. The security best practices guide on the Anthropic Trust Center covers the full architecture.

Managing cost

Claude Enterprise pricing stays usage-based. The newest Claude models are more efficient than their predecessors: billed through usage, Claude Opus 5.5 costs 40% less to run than Claude Opus 5 on typical workloads, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs up to 30% less than Claude Sonnet 5 for most work.

Depending on the task, agentic work can use more tokens than a quick chat. Claude Enterprise admins have four controls for managing this usage. Efficient mode is a new setting that keeps the unified Claude experience on Sonnet and Haiku models. Model entitlements set which models each role can use. Spend limits apply at the organization, group, and member level, and pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly amount to draw from.

Getting started

The unified Claude experience is generally available today for Claude Enterprise plans. Admins can manage the rollout in Organization settings. Organizations that use zero data retention for Claude Code, a HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys stay on their current configuration.

See the admin setup guide for details. If you're an existing Claude Enterprise customer, you'll receive an email about the rollout for your organization.

articles.title: Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
articles.context: If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your...
articles.full_text:
Claude Duet (opens in new tab) is an agent, currently in research preview, that uses a cloud-based computer to do work for you. It can use all the apps and services you've chosen to connect to Claude, and it runs continuously even after you close the app. It can read your inbox, draft replies, book things, and run routines while you are away. Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day.

We built Claude Duet on three principles to guide the agent's behavior:

Your information, and what other people share in your connected apps, is handled with discretion, using a new classifier that checks messages Claude Duet drafts before they go out.

You stay in control of what it does on your behalf.

Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, sign-in tokens, or other credentials.

Claude Duet is new but the thinking behind it is not. In 2025 we published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. Since then, we have written about why no single defense is enough (opens in new tab) and why protection inside the model can’t stand alone (opens in new tab). We also build and operate the infrastructure businesses use to run agents in production through Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), and Claude Duet keeps credentials separate from the agent in the same way. It builds on this work, adding the protections that an agent acting for you needs. This post walks through what we added and what we’re still working on.

You approve important actions

An agent that acts while you’re away has to know when to stop and ask for permission before proceeding, and to do it at the right cadence. Before Claude Duet does something like sending a potentially sensitive message, paying for something, or deleting anything, it shows you the action, the destination, and the content, including every recipient. It then waits for you to approve the action.

A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code (opens in new tab) and extended for Claude Duet. It assesses whether the action matches your intent. The check runs outside the model doing the work so instructions hidden in a page cannot affect the outcome.

Some actions stay off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities, banking actions such as moving money between accounts, and accessing someone else's account. Some other steps aren’t covered by a "don't ask me again" rule, however often you have approved them, like paying or sending money, deleting an order, or creating an account. The routines that run while you are away have the same safeguards.

We spent a lot of time calibrating how often Claude Duet asks for approval. Approval fatigue is a serious issue, because too many requests teach people to tap through them, sometimes without adequate consideration. We will continue to adjust this calibration over time.

For purchases, Claude Duet pays with a one-time card from a wallet like Link from Stripe, limited to that merchant and amount. You see the item and the total, and you approve the purchase in your Link app. Your real card number isn’t shared with Claude Duet or the merchant.

Your information is handled with discretion

An agent that reads your email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where different types of information should go. If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your performance review conversations.

To address this, we built a new safety classifier that runs separately from the main model and checks whether each message Claude Duet is about to send contains potentially sensitive information. We categorize this information into two tiers:

Never share: We give the most sensitive protection to information like sign-in credentials, full card and bank account numbers, and government ID numbers. Claude Duet is instructed never to share these with anyone, even if you ask.

Needs consent to share: Claude Duet will share other private information, such as health or finances, only if you’ve explicitly approved it. Your own request counts as consent, so “send a note to my dentist about my tooth pain” generally won’t need additional approval.

If Claude Duet is blocked for either reason, it can decide to rewrite the message without the sensitive information and share with you for approval.

Claude Duet is still in research preview and these safeguards will occasionally miss something or flag a harmless message. That’s why they work alongside the approval mechanisms above, which are designed to keep you in control of what Claude Duet sends on your behalf. We expect to continue iterating on our classifier as we learn more about how people use Claude Duet.

You have visibility into tasks and connected apps

You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing in its task list, where each task has its own page, and steer it mid-task. Claude Duet keeps your conversation history and its memory so it can carry context between tasks, until you delete your history or reset it. Deleting your account wipes everything Claude Duet has stored.

The apps you have connected to Claude carry over to Claude Duet, and switching an app off in one place switches it off in both. Disconnecting an app stops new access from that moment, but what Claude Duet already learned from it stays until you reset its memory, which you can do anytime from the app’s settings. Claude Duet also uses the memory from your Claude account, so details Claude remembered from your earlier chats are visible.

Credentials and the browser are isolated from the model

Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, or the sign-in tokens for your connected apps, and it can’t save them to its memory. They only ever pass through separate machines the model can’t access, and the approvals and safety checks that govern what it does run there too.

Passwords

When a site asks for a password, you type it into a form inside the Claude app. The form encrypts it with a single-use key that exists only on our secure cloud browser machine, for that one single use. It passes the encrypted password unopened to the browser, which types it into the site. The model doesn’t see the password and can’t save or repeat it. Soon you will also be able to sign in with 1Password; Claude Duet will ask for a credential, you will approve that request in 1Password, and the credential will go to the browser without passing through the model.

An agent that signs in for you changes phishing in two ways. On one hand, Claude Duet doesn’t hold credentials for you so it can’t be phished for a password, and no hidden instruction can make it reveal a secret it doesn’t have. On the other hand, the sign-in form is itself a target, because anything that asks for a password can be imitated. So Claude Duet’s sign-in form only appears inside the app, during a sign-in you asked for. It never arrives as a link, a text message, an email, or a website other than claude.ai. If something that looks like Claude Duet asks for your password anywhere else, it’s not legitimate.

Sign-in tokens

When Claude Duet works in a connected app, it follows our Claude Managed Agents design (opens in new tab) so credentials stay out of reach of the agent’s work. Credentials that the agent uses on your behalf, such as a sign-in token for a connected service, never enter the machine where the agent works. A placeholder for the credential sits there instead and a proxy outside that machine puts in the real value only as a request is made.

The browser

Your browser in Claude Duet runs in its own dedicated virtual machine in the cloud, separate from the model and from the cloud computers the agent works on. The agent drives the browser only through a fixed set of commands: open this page, click here, type this. Whatever a site runs stays on the browser machine (opens in new tab). The site’s code and cookies don’t reach Claude Duet’s memory or your connected apps, and none of the agent’s commands can read cookies out of the browser. What does come back is the page's text and downloads, because the agent has to read them to do its job. That’s why the other checks exist, and why Claude Duet also uses the prompt-injection safeguards described in our browser-use research (opens in new tab). Files it uploads through the browser get the same sensitive-information check as its messages.

Claude Duet is also designed to identify itself as an agent. Today, requests that its web browser sends include a distinct User-Agent header, and we publish the public IP addresses it browses from, so sites can recognize it and decide how to treat it. Before launch, we also contacted several large websites and gave them the option to prevent Claude Duet from visiting their sites, and some chose to. We’ll keep refining how Claude Duet identifies itself as we learn from the research preview.

How we tested Claude Duet

Testing started well before the research preview and continues now. Our Safeguards team built evaluations from routine-shaped tasks, each in three variants: an innocent version, one with injected instructions, and one that tempts the agent to do more than it was asked. Those run alongside shadow traffic from real use.

Red teams further tested whether Claude Duet would leak information, act without approval, or follow malicious prompts. We built a threat model of the whole system, across the repositories and trust boundaries it touches. An external penetration-testing firm tested Claude Duet with access to our source code, and a follow-on engagement covering the cloud browser and the sign-in form is running now. Each new credential feature is red-teamed on an isolated rig before it ships to anyone.

Claude Duet is also in scope of Anthropic’s public bug bounty program, which rewards valid reports and offers safe harbor for good-faith research, under our responsible disclosure policy. If you find a security vulnerability, we want to hear about it: report it through Anthropic’s bug bounty program on HackerOne (opens in new tab).

Building this with you

We’re releasing Claude Duet as a research preview because we want to learn what you value in a personal agent, including the protections and controls you’d like to see next. Some of what’s described here is still changing: how often it asks for approval, how you sign in, and how well the sensitive-information checks tell what’s private from what’s harmless. Tell Claude Duet in plain words what you’d like to see or what went wrong, and it will file a report for our team.

articles.title: Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3
articles.context: On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be...
articles.full_text:
What happened?

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be derived from their public certificates. The derived private keys can be used to issue certificates for any domain, and software that trusts the eMudhra root will accept them.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Cloudflare have blocked the affected intermediates. Mozilla has removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from its trust store, and Chrome will remove it on October 27, 2026. eMudhra has revoked the intermediates.

Okta’s response

Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and the eight affected intermediates across our services.

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across Okta’s production environment. The change is continuing to roll out across Auth0 production.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Only if Okta or Auth0 connects to a server you control and that server's certificate chain includes the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Inbound access to Okta and Auth0, including sign-in, is not affected.

The case to check is a non-browser connection or webhook that calls your own API, such as an Okta Inline Hook or Event Hook, or Auth0 Action, Custom Database connection, or Auth0 Federated Connection.

These connections may not have shown you any error before now. Run

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <your-host>:443

and look for "emSign" in the chain. If you find it, replace the certificate with one from another trusted CA. Connections to that endpoint will fail once our change is applied to your tenant.

References

eMudhra Statement on distrust of select Global TLS Intermediate and one Root CA

Google - Protecting Chrome and Android Users from Compromised eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates

Mozilla - Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates

articles.title: Do Your Security Tools Actually Work Together? Assessing Your Zero Trust Readiness
articles.context: They purchased one tool to address an immediate threat, added another to meet a compliance requirement, and introduced others as the business adopted cloud services, supported...
articles.full_text:
LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review helps organizations uncover security gaps and get more value from their existing investments.

One of the first questions I ask security leaders is simple: Do you know whether all your security tools work together?

The answer is rarely a straightforward yes.

Most organizations have built their security environments over many years. They purchased one tool to address an immediate threat, added another to meet a compliance requirement, and introduced others as the business adopted cloud services, supported remote work, or completed an acquisition. Each decision may have made sense at the time, but few organizations have had the opportunity to step back and evaluate the environment as a whole.

That is why we developed LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review. In roughly three days, one of our Solution Architects evaluates an organization’s security posture across identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and visibility. The review is aligned with the NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture framework, and the organization receives a written report identifying potential gaps and opportunities to get more value from its existing security investments.

There is no cost, no obligation, and no predetermined platform to adopt. The organization owns the findings and decides what to do with them.

More tools do not necessarily mean better security

When I talk with security teams, I often find that the challenge is not a lack of technology. In many cases, the organization already owns many of the capabilities it needs.

The harder question is whether those capabilities are configured correctly, connected where they need to be, and supported by processes that allow the team to act on the information they produce.

For example, one tool may identify suspicious activity, while another contains the information needed to determine whether that activity is truly a threat. If the tools do not exchange information, or if the right team does not receive it quickly enough, both technologies can be working as designed while the organization still lacks the visibility needed to respond effectively.

Take the first step toward Zero Trust with the LevelBlue Readiness Review.

Learn More

We also see organizations paying for overlapping capabilities or leaving valuable features unused. That does not necessarily mean they made poor purchasing decisions. Their business, technology environment, and risk profile may simply have changed since those decisions were made.

The problem is that these inefficiencies and gaps can be difficult to recognize when every tool is evaluated individually. Security leaders need to see how the entire environment functions together.

Zero Trust is not something you can buy

Another question I frequently hear is: What product do we need to implement Zero Trust?

My answer is that Zero Trust is not a product. It is an architectural approach based on continuously evaluating access according to identity, context, risk, and the sensitivity of the resource involved.

No single platform can establish that model on its own.

An effective Zero Trust strategy depends on how identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and security visibility work together. A weakness in any one of those areas can undermine otherwise strong controls. Even sophisticated technology can fall short when policies, integrations, and operational processes do not support it.

That is why I believe a Zero Trust review should begin with the environment an organization already has, not with a predetermined list of products it is expected to purchase.

Some of the most useful questions are also the most practical:

Can you consistently verify who and what is requesting access?

Are access decisions informed by device health, user behavior, and other relevant context?

Can your security team connect related activity across the environment?

Are applications and data protected according to their sensitivity and importance to the business?

Do your existing tools share the information needed to detect and respond to threats?

Are you paying for redundant capabilities or leaving valuable features unused?

These questions help establish a realistic view of where an organization stands today. The objective is not to declare that an organization has either “achieved” or “failed” Zero Trust.

It is to identify the gaps that matter most and determine what practical improvements should come next.

The next investment may not be another tool

Security teams are being asked to reduce risk while operating under tighter budget and resource constraints. In that environment, buying another product should not always be the first response.

Sometimes the fastest way to improve security is to enable a capability the organization already owns. It may be correcting a configuration, connecting two systems that currently operate separately, or improving the process for investigating and escalating alerts. In other cases, a review may confirm that a genuine capability gap exists and that a new investment is warranted.

Both outcomes are valuable. The point is to make that decision with a clear understanding of the existing environment.

I also encourage security leaders to consider how they will communicate the findings outside the security organization. A technically accurate assessment has limited value if it cannot help the CISO explain risks, priorities, and investment needs to other executives or the board.

That is why our Zero Trust Readiness Review concludes with a written report in plain language. It provides a practical summary of where the organization stands, why the identified gaps matter, and which actions could have the greatest impact.

Start with a clear view of where you are

Zero Trust is a continuing process, not a one-time project. Technologies, business requirements, and threats will continue to change, and an organization’s security architecture must evolve with them.

But before security leaders can determine where to go next, they need an honest view of where they are today.

My advice is to begin by looking at what you already own. Understand how your tools work together, where visibility breaks down, and whether your current investments support the outcomes your organization needs. That foundation will help you focus your resources, establish defensible priorities, and make future decisions with greater confidence.

Ready to see how your security tools work together? Book your free Zero Trust Readiness Review.

The Zero Trust Readiness Review is not a compliance audit, certification, or attestation against NIST SP 800-207.

articles.title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
articles.context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
articles.full_text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Check back next week when we’ll finish our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series with a blog about the cybersecurity challenges of state and local governments. Read the first two blogs in the series:

How to mitigate the risk from AI-generated apps built by your '‘citizen coder’ employees

Critical infrastructure orgs face heightened cyber risk from nation-state groups, AI threats

To learn more about shadow AI and how Tenable can help you address this issue, check out the following resources:

What is shadow AI? (guide)

Introducing Tenable One AI Exposure: A new standard for securing AI usage at scale (blog)

Security for AI: A strategic framework for closing the AI exposure gap (blog)

Mastering AI security risks with unified exposure management (on-demand webinar)

Tenable Hexa AI: Automating exposure remediation with agentic routines (blog)

What is AI security posture management (AI-SPM)? (guide)

What is an AI acceptable use policy (AUP)? (guide)

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed
articles.context: How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially...
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On 21 October 2026, PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution. Cato’s self-evolving CVE mitigation agent helped turn the investigation into concrete research output by creating a proof of concept and generating an IPS signature in minutes. The agent connects vulnerability analysis, controlled lab testing and protection generation. Validation feedback and researcher corrections inform improvements to its skills and workflows, while security researchers review proposed protections before release. Cato has put PHP2Shell IPS protections in place, connecting fast agentic research with cloud enforcement to help customers reduce exposure on inspected traffic while they update affected applications.

Why Cato AI native SASE enables protection at machine speed

Speed matters because attackers can study the same patches defenders use. Our AI-native SASE approach connects our self-evolving agentic CVE mitigation researcher with centralized cloud inspection and enforcement. The researcher helps turn vulnerability analysis into candidate signatures, with validation and security researcher review before release. We can then deliver protections through our cloud without customers installing a separate signature package on each PHP server. This shortens the path from disclosure to protection while application owners complete remediation.

What happened

The flaws affect PHP core rather than a single application or plugin. PHP identifies installations serving web requests as at risk, including PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The highest demonstrated risk is in Apache mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs. A login page therefore does not reliably shield the vulnerable processing.

CVE-2026-109618 concerns out-of-memory handling that can interrupt initialization and leave invalid request data for cleanup to process. CVE-2026-109619 concerns request-owned state retained after its memory is freed and later accessed by the same worker. These failures can lead to code execution. Sensitive process memory may also be exposed. Exploitability depends on the runtime integration, configuration and reachable behavior.

The UK NCSC urged immediate action to identify PHP installations and apply updates. NHS England’s alert highlights code execution and sensitive memory exposure, while Canada’s Cyber Centre also calls for assessment of products that bundle PHP. These official advisories reinforce the urgency of remediation.

The business risk

Public research also shows unauthenticated code execution on tested WordPress, Drupal and Joomla deployments, and separate disclosure of PHP worker memory. These examples illustrate runtime exposure. Exploitability varies by deployment.

For a business, code execution could expose application data, allow content changes or disrupt customer-facing services within the PHP process’s permissions. Memory disclosure could reveal passwords, tokens and API keys even without code execution. Usable credentials could extend the risk to connected services. Prioritize systems by exposure, sensitive data and the business processes they support.

How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes

Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially different from the publicly circulated alleged exploit. This prompted additional research before finalizing the signatures. The discrepancy did not establish whether that material described another issue or an incomplete attack path.

Our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent created a proof of concept (PoC) and generated an IPS signature in minutes. The new signatures address the alleged scenario and the patch-analysis findings, with coverage bounded by the attack paths tested.

Our agentic researcher combines vulnerability intelligence, patch analysis and controlled testing to develop candidate IPS protections. Its self-evolving workflow uses validation feedback, execution traces and researcher corrections to refine the skills and workflows used in subsequent investigations. Our security researchers review proposed protections before release, bringing expert judgment to the path from generated signature to customer protection. Figure 1 shows this workflow from patch analysis and PoC creation to signature validation, researcher review and cloud enforcement.

Figure 1. Self-evolving CVE mitigation from patch analysis to PoC, signature and enforcement.

PHP2Shell from PoC to signature in minutes

In Figure 2, the upper pane shows the local PHP2Shell test completion message, while the lower pane shows runtime monitoring and test events. This capture comes from the investigation in which our agent created a PoC and generated a signature in minutes. Detailed outcomes are redacted.

Figure 2. PHP2Shell PoC test and runtime monitoring. Results redacted.

Cato protection

Our infrastructure assessment found that Cato’s production systems are not exposed to PHP2Shell. This finding concerns the infrastructure we operate.

For customer environments, we have added PHP2Shell IPS signatures covering the alleged scenario and additional behavior identified through patch analysis. These protections help block matching exploit requests on traffic inspected by our cloud when the applicable signatures are enabled in blocking mode. Customers should also assess and update affected PHP applications and third-party products in their environments.

The connection to Agentic Threat Prevention (ATP) is the speed of turning evidence into enforcement. Our CVE mitigation researcher uses vulnerability evidence to create signatures after disclosure. ATP evaluates related host activity as an attack develops and activates prevention policies to restrict its next steps.

In our separate controlled demonstration against an agentic attacker, ATP used shared context and inline controls to prevent progression to full domain compromise. The PHP2Shell response described here delivered CVE-specific IPS signatures. Together, these examples show how AI-native SASE can accelerate both the creation of protections and adaptive enforcement during an intrusion.

Our initial response telemetry showed scanning, with no exploitation attempts identified against customers.

The attacker path and where we block it

Figure 3 illustrates a hypothetical PHP2Shell attack and how our IPS protection would apply. It places an attacker on the left, our cloud IPS in the center and a vulnerable PHP service on the right. The crafted request represents an attempt to exploit the PHP runtime. The red stop mark shows where a matching request would be dropped when payload inspection and the applicable blocking protection are active. Some exploit paths involve multiple requests.

Figure 3. Illustrative PHP2Shell attack path and IPS prevention.

The diagram illustrates our protection model rather than documenting an observed customer attack. Traffic must pass through our cloud with its payload visible to inspection and the applicable signature enabled in blocking mode.

Close coverage gaps

Identify PHP services outside our inspection coverage. Extend our inspection coverage and blocking where supported. Protect remaining gaps with an appropriate application-layer control, such as an inbound WAF configured for PHP2Shell. Continue updating affected PHP runtimes.

The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed appeared first on Cato Networks.

articles.title: Chief data officer strategy for a data-driven enterprise
Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

articles.full_text:
Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.

You can submit a proposal for a project here.

Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.

We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.

We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.

We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.

We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.

Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.

This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

articles.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
articles.context: Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)
articles.full_text:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

articles.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
articles.context: While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs
articles.full_text:
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa AgrawalEvyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai ZeldovichNicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;

The exact theorem statements that were proved;

The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

Proving more than memory safety

Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

Other formal verification case studies

Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA.7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We then measured the adherence to CPython’s behavior empirically, running over 1.7 million randomly generated Python programs, finding identical behavior with CPython in 99.95% of tests, with remaining test differences as unsurprising known corner cases.

We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year.

See the Appendix for more details on some of these efforts.

This is just the beginning

One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.

Newer models need fewer tokens

We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

Proofs can be reused

When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).

This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib, a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).

As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.

This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

Limitations

In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

Conclusion

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

Read the full appendix.

Customers using the Anthropic managed offering also get access to the Claude Console, Anthropic’s development environment for observing and managing agents with Claude. The Console includes tools to write prompts and configure agents, run them on hosted environments, monitor usage and costs, and manage access and security per workspace.

Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are available, with new models shipping on the Anthropic managed offering as they launch.

Two paths to build with Claude

There are two ways to build with Claude on Google Cloud.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is built for customers who want day zero access to all beta and generally available Claude Platform features. It’s best for customers who want full Claude Platform feature parity, accessed through Google Cloud. Anthropic operates the service and acts as the data processor.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed) remains the best choice for customers who need Google Cloud as the data processor, have strict regional data residency requirements, or want native Google Cloud integrations like Model Armor or Agent Engine.

Get started

The Anthropic managed offering is generally available today. To get started, open Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) (opens in new tab) or explore the documentation (opens in new tab).

If you have an existing discount, please contact your Anthropic or Google Cloud account executive before getting started with the Anthropic managed offering, to ensure your discounts are applied correctly. Discounts cannot be applied retroactively to usage.

articles.title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
articles.context: However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main...
articles.full_text:
If you’ve built an agent in Claude Platform that includes multiple subagents, see which may make sense to fold into the main agent loop using our migration kit. It runs a guided workflow to identify your patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. It includes a demo that you can try on a mock system before running on your agent.

Subagents – agents with their own context window, tools, and instructions, orchestrated by a coordinator – are a core component of agent design. They are effective at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning. We use them in many of our own agents that we build using Claude Platform, for example our multi-agent research system.

However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main agent loop. In our comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task.

For example, one company found the dozen of specialist subagents within its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience.

We also often see proposed agent designs that follow a familiar progression: an intent classifier, a fixed multi-step reasoning pipeline, user-segment buckets, separate recommendation branches, and a multi-agent orchestrator on top.

In these cases feedback is often that most of this structure was doing work the model no longer needed done for it, and that one clear system prompt, 4-5 thin data tools, and firm output guardrails would cover most of the use case.

To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier. Use them when:

A single agent loop hits measurable performance degradation from context bloat, or

Multiple tasks need to be tackled in parallel with fresh context windows that can be discarded once the task is done, or

A single agent struggles to select appropriate tools or there are conflicting instructions in the system prompt.

But too often we see enterprises give each team or problem type its own subagent, with the agent architecture becoming a copy of their org chart (Conway’s law at work).

This post explains when to consider folding subagents into your main agent loop with best practices we’ve learned from building agents in large organizations.

Agent building failure modes for large organizations

Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:

Context management: You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.

Subagent sprawl: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.

The Frankenprompt: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.

Unvetted, overly localized evals: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.

Latency: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.

Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:

Shared context produces better answers: for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window.
