An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs.

Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat: this technique allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80% which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools.

Models are more capable: starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.

The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.

One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.

If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.

How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:

One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.

Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.

The loop stops when the model answers or hits a budget. A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer.

The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.

Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:

A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.

Ordering and domain procedure move into skills.

Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the tools.

Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.

This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.

The suggestions below are how a team could get from a multi-agent system to a single agent loop in stages, and how several teams can keep contributing to that agent along the way.

Task-completion evals

The first step is to create an eval set that can help you determine whether you should fold a subagent into the main agent loop. The eval structure we’ve seen work is one shared end-to-end set owned by a central team with smaller eval sets shipped with each skill by the team that owns it. Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.

Grading the agent's final message against a rubric is a good starting point for tracking answer quality. While you still have an orchestrator, you should also track routing accuracy (did it pick the right subagent?). Once a subagent is folded in, check instead whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.

This can be complex in environments where internal systems are difficult to replay and user engagement is difficult to simulate. One approach that has worked for us internally is to record timestamps on important events, so they can be replayed later to run as targeted evals.

Reducing subagents over time

Evolving toward a single agent loop involves folding the subagents into tools and skills. This can be done by merging domain subagents, calling them as tools, or replacing them with skills and tools.

Combining domain agents

Build a small end-to-end eval before the first merge. Then fold in by shared context starting with subagents that have the most use.

Merge specialists that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.

Subagents called as tools

When one of the three conditions above applies and you keep a subagent, it can be effective to have the main agent call subagents as tools so it can continue holding the conversation with the user.

We’d only recommend a full handoff, where the subagent takes over the conversation, when it needs to talk to the user directly. Everything else can be a skill plus tools in the main loop.

This will allow you to define a shared response schema for subagents, verify the conclusion against real data with the main agent, and trim the input to any final synthesis step. This is a good first step, as you don’t need to rewrite the subagents. It also gives you a baseline on the task-completion eval before deciding to fold any subagents into the main agent.

However, some failure modes will remain:

Each specialist has its own prompt, context, owner team, and evals

Each call still hands back a lossy summary

Every call is a nested model loop that adds latency

Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

When you compare, don’t just examine the final score, take a look at which tasks flipped. When we tested this on a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency, but also broke a process that had been passing. The main agent was holding the order lookup tool and answering on its own, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date.

Before each change, make sure your eval has a task for every chain of agents that runs together in production and for every rule the agent must not break, and run each task more than once, since a break like this one only showed up in one run out of two.

How several teams can contribute to a single agent

Domain reasoning can be retrieved from knowledge bases, skills, and MCP tools. Individual teams can shift their ownership from agents to skills and tools, with one small central team keeping ownership of the system prompt and end-to-end quality. This involves vetting new skills, tools, and evals before they ship.

MCP tools

Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

Use tool search with deferred loading, limit hard preconditions, and move any needed ones into the tools. For example, if Y needs X's output, Y's tool checks for it and returns an instruction the model can act on. Per-user permissions work the same way. Each tool checks what the calling user may see or do and returns a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop can serve users with different access without a separate agent per permission level.

Skills

Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

Our approach to growing skill libraries is to give the maintenance work back to the people writing the skills. Claude can do the heavy lifting with skills that can build, test, and prune other skills.

To prevent skill sprawl, you can have DRIs per team own their skills and make sure they are well crafted, distinct, and shipped with appropriate evals.

/skill-creator allows you to author new skills that start well-formed, and audit existing ones to trim, deduplicate, and restructure them.

/skill-doctor allows you to see what each skill in your library costs and how often it’s actually used, and delete dead weight.

Knowledge bases

Knowledge bases are the right fit for reference material the agent only needs some of the time. Facts and reference material (policies, metric definitions, product specs) can sit behind a search or lookup tool the model calls, or ship as reference files inside a skill. Avoid having code retrieve and paste this context into prompts.

Tools to accelerate this work

We recently released a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our migration kit chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:

/claude-api build-eval: can help create a first end-to-end set owned by the central team or small evals each team ships with its skill

/claude-api prompt-audit: can flag instructions written for older models in your prompts, skills, and tool descriptions and propose fixes as a diff. This can be run on your system prompts to find any rules that were added for an earlier model and are now making the agent slower or more rigid. Each team's DRI can also run it on their own skills and tool descriptions.

/claude-api hillclimb: can iteratively improve an app against an existing eval. This can be used for the "folded in vs kept" comparison (after folding one subagent into a skill plus tools, let it iterate on the skill and tool descriptions and see if the folded version matches or beats the subagent), as well as your system prompt.

/claude-api cost-optimize: profiles where your calls go and proposes savings from options such as prompt caching, trimming unneeded input and output tokens, effort, and model choice, one change at a time. This can help bring cost and latency down on a given design.

As models evolve, our understanding of how to best use them and guidance around best practice evolve as well. That makes any one architecture less important than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up.

This is one of those cases. As models get more capable and agents get longer running, more of your subagents can be skills and tools. You don’t have to make that move in one step, though. Build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, then rinse and repeat.

articles.title: Okta's Response to PHP2Shell
articles.context: Okta tested the publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits against Okta Access Gateway in its default configuration, and none achieved code execution
articles.full_text:
On October 21, 2026, industry-wide third-party critical PHP pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed, both with CVSS scores of 9.2.

Okta tested the publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits against Okta Access Gateway in its default configuration, and none achieved code execution.

Okta’s Response

Cloud services: Not affected. Okta and Auth0 cloud service platforms are not affected by these vulnerabilities.

On-premise software: Okta Access Gateway (OAG) requires a patch. Customers should upgrade to Okta Access Gateway version 2026.44.0.

Action for Okta Access Gateway (OAG) Customers

Customers running Okta Access Gateway appliance versions prior to 2026.44.0 should upgrade to version 2026.44.0. For complete vulnerability details and remediation guidance, refer to the Security Advisory:

PHP Runtime Vulnerabilities Affecting Okta Access Gateway CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619

Action for Auth0 and Okta SDKs users

For actions required and developer guidance, please refer to the appropriate KnowledgeBase article:

PHP Critical Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)

articles.title: No time to PHP around.
articles.context: Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.
articles.full_text:
Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Weak certificates from an Indian authority spark a global security scramble. Investigators probe a U.S. consulting executive’s alleged ties to ShinyHunters. SafePay ransomware hits at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations. Researchers find troubling security biases in Chinese AI-generated code. A $10 million initiative bolsters cybersecurity for small U.S. utilities. An American pleads guilty to stealing from thousands of servicemembers and veterans. Leo Scott, Managing Director of DataTribe, is talking about their upcoming Cyber Innovation Conference and the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

Today is Wednesday October 21st 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

PHP vulnerabilities put millions of web sites at risk.

PHP is a widely used, open-source programming language that powers the behind-the-scenes functionality of websites. It runs on web servers, handling tasks like processing forms, managing user accounts, interacting with databases, and generating web pages. Popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla rely on PHP. Because it’s so widely used, a serious PHP vulnerability can potentially affect millions of websites.

Now, PHP administrators are bracing for two potentially critical vulnerabilities that could put millions of websites at risk. PHP maintainers have announced plans to release patches for two flaws, each carrying a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.

The warning follows leaked, but unverified, details of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, reportedly capable of executing code on servers running popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento.

Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.

One researcher estimates that 1.3 million internet-connected hosts may be affected.

Administrators are being urged to inventory their PHP applications, prepare backups, and arrange emergency maintenance windows. Patches are scheduled for release at 14:00 UTC, though maintainers warn they could arrive earlier if exploitation is detected.

Given PHP’s enormous footprint, the potential consequences extend across much of the web.

An Indian cert authority unlocks a global security headache.

Security teams worldwide are scrambling to contain a potentially massive Internet security problem after researchers discovered eight digital certificates with private keys so weak that attackers could use them to impersonate virtually any website.

The certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra. They’re intermediate certificates, meaning they can be used to issue other certificates that browsers and applications automatically trust.

Normally, cracking their encryption would be practically impossible. But these keys were astonishingly weak, containing as little as three to eight bits of entropy. One researcher described the situation as “bonkers.”

Major browsers and several applications have already blocked the certificates, and there’s currently no evidence they’ve been maliciously exploited. But cleaning up the broader Internet could take years.

Cryptography expert Filippo Valsorda compares the challenge to the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability, warning that this recovery could be even more complicated. Linux systems, embedded devices, forgotten servers, and Internet of Things equipment may require individual updates.

The immediate concern involves attackers intercepting encrypted communications, particularly VPN connections. Exploitation requires positioning oneself between communicating parties, something that’s easier for attackers controlling local networks or possessing sophisticated surveillance capabilities.

Most modern browsers have implemented protections, although Microsoft’s Edge on Windows 10 reportedly remained vulnerable in some circumstances.

The incident exposes a fundamental weakness in Internet trust: even the strongest encryption depends on the security of the organizations issuing certificates.

And when one of those organizations gets the fundamentals spectacularly wrong, the cleanup becomes everybody’s problem.

Investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters.

Federal investigators examining the ShinyHunters hacking group are scrutinizing executives at two ransomware negotiation firms over their alleged relationships with the cybercriminals.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters’ extortion website, which pressured nearly 100 victims to pay ransoms.

Authorities have also arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky on extortion-related charges. Investigators reportedly uncovered communications linking him and other negotiators to ShinyHunters after Dutch police arrested a suspected group member and accessed his Signal messages.

The investigation raises troubling questions about conflicts of interest in the ransomware negotiation business. Some firms reportedly collect fees based on the size of ransom payments, creating financial incentives that may favor the criminals over their victims.

The allegations remain under investigation.

SafePay ransomware has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide.

The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since emerging in August 2024, according to a joint advisory from U.S., German, and British authorities.

SafePay has become one of 2026’s most active ransomware operations, targeting organizations across four continents.

The group gains access through stolen credentials, brute-force attacks, vulnerable VPNs, and exposed network devices. Once inside, attackers escalate privileges, move laterally using legitimate administrative tools, disable security software, and steal sensitive data before encrypting systems.

SafePay employs double extortion, demanding cryptocurrency payments in exchange for decryption tools and promises not to publish stolen information.

The group also reportedly calls victims directly to pressure them into paying.

Authorities are urging organizations to strengthen defenses against SafePay’s increasingly widespread operations.

New research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

The United States has banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, citing national security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security says DeepSeek’s China-based infrastructure could expose sensitive American data to Chinese authorities.

Beijing condemned the restrictions and warned of possible retaliation, adding another complication to already strained U.S.-China technology relations.

Meanwhile, new research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

Cybersecurity startup Hirundo tested Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder and found it produced significantly more vulnerable applications for American defense contractors than Chinese ones. Seventy percent of applications generated for U.S. contractors were exploitable, compared with 59 percent for Chinese contractors.

Applications built for a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group were also more likely to leak secrets.

Hirundo says the discrepancies disappeared after researchers modified the model to remove what they characterize as Chinese Communist Party political alignment.

The findings suggest that AI coding assistants may introduce security risks influenced by their training and underlying model behavior.

A $10 million initiative looks to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute are launching a $10 million initiative to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

The new nonprofit Community Cyber Resilience Foundation will initially provide free cybersecurity technology, hardware, deployment assistance, and training to as many as 500 water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities.

The announcement follows a surge in cyberattacks affecting more than 100 American water systems across over a dozen states.

Eligible utilities must have annual revenues below $100 million, a threshold covering more than 50,000 organizations nationwide.

Participants will receive access to Dragos security technology, Accenture implementation support, and SANS operational technology training.

The initiative aims to address a growing cybersecurity divide between large infrastructure operators and smaller utilities struggling with limited budgets, aging equipment, and staffing shortages.

An American pleads guilty to an identity theft scheme targeting U.S. service members.

A 45-year-old American has pleaded guilty to orchestrating an identity theft scheme that targeted thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr. operated from the Philippines, using stolen personal information to access victims’ bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits between 2014 and 2019.

Prosecutors say Boling obtained sensitive records from a former U.S. Army medical records contractor stationed in South Korea.

The operation relied on dozens of money mules in the United States who received stolen funds and transferred portions of the proceeds to the Philippines.

Boling was deported to the United States and arrested in May. Two accomplices have already been sentenced, while two others remain fugitives.

Boling faces up to 40 years in prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering.

Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

A Brazilian electronics distributor is looking for nearly half a million dollars’ worth of missing graphics cards, and it’s taking its search to Instagram.

Oderço says two pallets of high-end Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, then apparently vanished.

After getting nowhere with official inquiries, the company turned to social media, saying nothing like this has happened in its 38-year history.

The missing shipment is valued at roughly $470,000, although the company hasn’t disclosed exactly how many cards disappeared, or when.

The timing is particularly unfortunate. RTX 5090s are already in short supply, with retail prices reaching thousands of dollars per card.

Whether the shipment was stolen, misplaced, or swallowed by some bureaucratic black hole remains unclear.

For now, Oderço is hoping the internet can help locate its missing hardware.

Which is perhaps fitting, considering how many people have already been searching the internet for an RTX 5090.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music and sound design by Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
articles.context: This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs
articles.full_text:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

Create a trust anchor.

Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.

Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.

Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] }

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632

Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

Event

Channel

Threshold

Enabled

CA certificate expiry

CloudWatch, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

End-entity certificate expiry

EventBridge and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

Solution deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.

Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.

Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.

Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

Parameters for this deployment are shown in the following table:

Parameter

Required

Default

Description

TrustAnchorCertificateBody

Yes

—

PEM-encoded X.509 certificate of your CA (includes BEGIN and END markers)

WorkloadSubjectCN

No

WorkloadA

Subject CN from the workload certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadIssuerCN

No

MyCompany CA

Issuer CN from the CA certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadSANCN

No

WorkloadA

SAN CN from the workload certificate, provides additional identity assertion

SessionDurationSeconds

No

3600

Maximum session duration in seconds (900–43200)

NotificationEmail

No

(empty)

Email address for certificate expiry notifications. When provided, creates an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and an EventBridge rule

Important: The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

For additional deployment guidance, see Planning for your IAM Roles Anywhere deployment, which covers end-to-end deployment planning including network architecture, monitoring, and operational considerations.

If you have questions, you can start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

Abhishek Avinash Agawane

Abhishek is a Security Consultant at Amazon Web Services with more than 8 years of industry experience. He helps organizations architect resilient, secure, and efficient cloud environments, guiding them through complex challenges and large-scale infrastructure transformations. He has helped numerous organizations enhance their cloud operations through targeted optimizations, robust architectures and best-practice implementations.

Manoj Gupta

Manoj is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, based in San Francisco. With over 4 years of experience at AWS, he works closely with customers to build optimized AI/ML powered solutions and cloud infrastructure. His primary focus areas are data, AI/ML, and security, helping organizations modernize their technology stacks. Outside of work, he enjoys outdoor activities and traveling with family.

articles.title: What’s New in GravityZone October 2026 (v 6.78)
articles.context: This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response
articles.full_text:
Bitdefender rolled out new functionality in Bitdefender GravityZone, a unified cybersecurity platform that provides prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities for organizations of all sizes. These features, aligned with our multi-layered security strategy, are designed to reduce the workload for security analysts, administrators, and users.

What’s new for Security Analysts

As attackers increasingly blend into legitimate activity, security analysts must uncover signs of sophisticated attacks and make the invisible visible. This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response.

CLAIRE AI Assistant Enhancements (Early Access)

When an analyst opens an incident and needs to decide on containment, the assistant now starts from that page’s context instead of a blank prompt. CLAIRE, previously named GravityZone AI Assistant, is a conversational assistant built into the Control Center. It applies large language model (LLM) reasoning to Bitdefender Support Center documentation and to data from your GravityZone environment to answer questions, issue recommendations, and initiate selected response actions.

CLAIRE is available through a controlled Early Access Program (EAP). It now has its own entry in the GravityZone navigation menu, with a Chat page and an Advisor briefing page.

On the Incidents, Network, and Policies pages, a new chat opens with page-specific prompts, and coverage extends to the rest of the interface. As the conversation continues, CLAIRE suggests follow-up prompts. When asked to isolate the endpoints associated with an incident, CLAIRE builds the endpoint list for review, and isolation runs only after the analyst refines the list and clicks Isolate. Outside incident work, the Advisor briefing page lists proactive posture recommendations. Each recommendation’s details page explains why CLAIRE chose the issue, summarizes the top affected items, and suggests remediation actions.

The chat window also adds a Stop button that cancels a prompt before the response is generated. A message now appears when you reach your usage limit, and all chats now follow a 30-day retention period.

Attack Path in GravityZone Exposure Management

Attackers rarely reach a critical asset in one step. They chain a misconfiguration on one asset to an exposed account or vulnerability on the next. Attack Path is now available as part of the new GravityZone Exposure Management license. It correlates endpoint risk findings, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) data, and External Attack Surface Management (EASM) asset records to determine the most likely paths an attacker could take to compromise your assets.

Each attack path under Risk Management > Attack Path shows a graph and an asset list that mark potential entry points, exploitable vulnerabilities, and misconfigurations along the route. The graph can highlight the shortest path to the target asset, showing where a single remediation action breaks the largest portion of the chain. Risk factors such as Public exposure and Critical asset appear in both the graph and the asset table. When an asset also has a Risk Management entry, the asset details panel includes a button that opens the matching Risk Management > Resources or Risk Management > Accounts record.

Four new widgets on Monitoring > ASM Dashboard track attack paths across the environment:

New attack paths: lists newly created attack paths for Last 24 hours, Last 7 days, or Last 30 days.

Open attack paths over time: charts New and Resolved attack paths, with a trend line, for Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or Last 90 days.

Top 5 attack path destinations: lists the five assets that attack paths target most often.

Top 5 attack path entry points: lists the five assets that most often serve as attack path entry points.

For detailed information about Attack Path, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

AI Visibility and Control Enhancements

Unmanaged AI tools on endpoints are now a routine part of an organization’s attack surface, and assessing that exposure requires seeing it alongside other risk data. AI Visibility and Control (AIVC), is a discovery and risk layer that reports which AI software is installed and running on managed endpoints and assigns a risk score to each finding. This release extends AIVC data to the ASM Dashboard, the AI Services page, and Risk Management > Resources.

Monitoring > ASM Dashboard now includes a dedicated AI Visibility and Control smart view with an overview of AI usage and risk exposure across the organization. Its widgets show the overall AI risk posture, compare risk across AI categories, list the affected users and endpoints, break findings down by AI category, and list the discovered AI services. AIVC widgets can also be added to custom dashboard smart views.

On AI Visibility and Control > AI Services, each discovered AI service now shows its associated finding or finding count, in both the grid and the service details. From there, analysts can open the AI Findings page to investigate. AI-related findings also appear in Risk Management > Resources, so an endpoint’s AI exposure sits alongside its other risk data. From there, analysts can move between the affected resource, its findings, and the associated AI services.

For comprehensive insights into AIVC, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EASM Enhancements

External Attack Surface Management builds an attacker-centric view of an organization’s internet-facing exposure. This release adds classification detail to similar domain findings, and maps discovered public IP addresses back to the managed servers that use them.

Similar domains flagged as potential brand impersonation attempts now identify the typo squatting technique used to construct them — misspellings, alternative top-level domains, and substitutions involving visually similar or keyboard-adjacent characters. EASM also highlights public IP addresses used for external communication by servers managed by Bitdefender Endpoint Security Tools (BEST), with the managed servers using each address viewable alongside it. Analysts can identify which addresses to add to the EASM scan list, giving Attack Path additional context on potential entry points into the organization’s network.

For comprehensive insights into EASM, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EDR and XDR Enhancements

GravityZone Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) give security analysts the tools to detect, investigate, and respond to threats across managed endpoints and connected sensors, with raw event telemetry that supports historical querying and incident investigation. This release changes how search is organized and shared and adds detail to incident and alert data.

Search and investigation

Separate menu entries: Historical search and Live search now appear as separate entries in the left-side menu of GravityZone Control Center.

Shared smart views: Smart views created on the Live search page can now be shared with other users in the company, with read-only or editable permissions. Company Administrators can edit, delete, rename, or make editable for any shared smart view, regardless of who created it or what permissions it has. Other users can delete, rename, or make editable only the views they created, and can edit only those they created or have edit permissions for. Shared smart views appear in a separate section of the Queries panel. Each one has a banner showing its access rights, creator, last update date and time, and the user who last modified it. Create, edit, and delete actions are logged on the User activity page, in the Live search area.

FQDN search: Historical search now supports searching and filtering raw events and alerts by endpoint-submitted fully qualified domain name (FQDN) values. The fqdn field is available in the query editor helper under the Other category, and other.fqdn can be added as a column in the results table and viewed in the event details panel.

Incidents and alerts

Entity type filter: A new Entity type filter under More filters on the Incidents page narrows incidents by the types of entities they contain. It supports multiple selections, and its options are populated from the entity types present in your incidents.

Self Protect attribution: In alert details for Endpoint incidents, alerts generated by the Tamper Protection module now show Self Protect in the Detected By field.

MITRE ATT&CK tactics: XDR and EDR incident and alert details now also support the Resource Development, Stealth, Defense Impairment, and Reconnaissance tactics. Activity previously classified as Defense Evasion may now be reported as Stealth or Defense Impairment, depending on the detection context.

Timestamps with seconds: Timestamps throughout Incidents and Historical search now include seconds as well as hours and minutes.

For analysts reconstructing an intrusion, the new tactics and second-level timestamps work together. A sequence in which an attacker disables a security service and then clears event logs within the same minute can now be ordered precisely, with each step mapped to Defense Impairment or Stealth.

For comprehensive insights into detection and response with GravityZone EDR and XDR, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

What’s new for Administrators

With administrators constantly juggling numerous tasks and responsibilities, they appreciate tools that make their daily work easier. This section describes new functionality designed to simplify managing features responsible for prevention, protection, and detection in a defense-in-depth security architecture.

Extended Email Security Enhancements

Bitdefender Extended Email Security (EES) offers flexible deployment models (Gateway, API-based, and Unified) to provide a comprehensive defense against sophisticated spear-phishing, brand impersonation, and supply chain fraud. This release adds outbound data loss prevention rules, distributor-level console access, and a confirmation step for identity provider sign-in.

DLP rules in Extended Email Security now also cover outbound email for the Gateway and Unified deployment models, which require Outbound Smarthost. Rules inspect the subject, headers, body, attachment types, URLs, and sensitive data patterns, including credit card numbers, International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), and Social Security Numbers (SSNs). Matching outgoing messages are sent to Quarantine or deleted with Delete. You can apply enforcement globally or target specific customers, domains, or users.

Distributors and higher-level partners can now access the Extended Email Security consoles of the downstream partners they manage directly from the Extended Email Security section, across nested partner hierarchies, without Extended Email Security being provisioned for their own company. Console visibility follows the existing Your Bitdefender partner can assist you with security management settings, and the available actions are determined by Extended Email Security permissions within each accessible company. For detailed information, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

In addition, users who sign in with GravityZone credentials and open the Extended Email Security console now see a confirmation prompt. The prompt asks them to approve the automatic switch to the GravityZone identity provider (IdP) before proceeding.

For comprehensive insights into Extended Email Security, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Data Lake Single Sign-On

Security teams that use Security Data Lake alongside GravityZone can now sign in to both with the same corporate credentials. Bitdefender GravityZone Security Data Lake combines SIEM operations with scalable data lake storage and advanced analytics, collecting and correlating data from multiple organizational sources for proactive threat hunting.

Security Data Lake now supports single sign-on (SSO) through GravityZone IdP Proxy, so users authenticate with their organization’s identity provider. GravityZone IdP Proxy supports SSO using SAML 2.0 and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) to manage and verify digital identities across the GravityZone ecosystem.

With Security Data Lake added, sign-in to it is now handled by the organization’s existing identity infrastructure, the same as for the other GravityZone services connected through IdP Proxy.

Network Enhancements

The GravityZone Network inventory gives administrators a consolidated view of all managed endpoints, containers, and network assets across their environment. This release adds two network identifiers to the Network page and refines one filter option:

Public IP column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s public IP address, separately from the existing IP column and filter, which show the local IP address. The filter supports text matching with starts with or contains, so partial IP addresses also return results. Endpoints imported through integrations such as Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID, VMware vCenter, or Amazon Web Services (AWS) do not display a public IP address.

MAC addresses column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s MAC address information with the same text-matching options. Devices with multiple network interfaces show all their MAC addresses in a single cell, and the filter matches any of them.

Golden Image role option: The Golden Image option in the Role filter now appears only when the feature is turned on for your company.

With public IP and MAC addresses searchable directly in the grid, administrators can locate an endpoint from a known address, match devices against data exported from external network or security tools, and narrow large endpoint inventories even when only part of an address is known.

Compliance Manager Enhancements

The Compliance Manager in GravityZone maps endpoint findings against regulatory and industry compliance standards, giving administrators a structured view of their organization’s compliance posture across managed assets.

This update adds two new compliance standards, now available across the Findings, Identity risks, and Compliance manager pages:

BNM RMIT 2025 (MY): Issued by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM), the Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) policy document sets out requirements for financial institutions on technology risk management, covering technology governance, cybersecurity management, and operational resilience.

CSA Cyber Trust 2025 (SG): Issued by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), Cyber Trust is a risk-based certification mark for organizations with extensive cybersecurity measures and practices. The 2025 edition extends coverage to cloud, operational technology (OT), and AI security.

In addition, a new Notes column and filter on the Compliance manager page let administrators add and view notes for individual controls, such as justifications, context, or links to external documentation. Control notes can also be included when exporting compliance reports in PDF or XLSX format.

For comprehensive insights into Compliance Manager, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Telemetry Enhancements

Organizations that correlate endpoint activity in their own Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform depend on the range and naming of the events they receive. Security Telemetry forwards raw operating system events from endpoints running BEST to a third-party SIEM. Administrators configure it in the Policy under General > Security Telemetry, where they select the event types to send. This release groups all events by category, adds descriptions for every category and event, and extends coverage with additional event types.

The Security Telemetry page now lists event types under named categories. Each category and event has a description, so administrators can see what an event captures before turning it on. The following categories and event types are now available:

Service: Added, Change status, Modify.

Scheduled task: Create, Delete, Modify.

Account management and authentication: Create local account, Delete local account, Logon failed, Settings changed.

Shell and script activity: Command Prompt command, PowerShell command, PowerShell script block logging, Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) buffer.

Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) job activity: Add file, Create, Delete.

Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) activity: Execution method, New activity, New binding.

Device and driver: Driver module load, Hardware mount, Hardware unmount.

BEST agent: Agent uninstall request.

Audit policy: Change Windows audit policy.

Process: Injection.

Existing event types now sit within the new categories under shorter names:

Process: Create and Terminate, previously Process creation and Process deletion.

File: Create, Delete, Modify, Move, and Read, previously File creation, File deletion, File modification, File move, and File read.

Registry: Create key, Delete key, Modify value, and Delete value, previously Registry key creation, Registry key deletion, Registry value modification, and Registry value deletion.

Account management and authentication: Logon, and Logout (renamed from Logoff).

Network: Connection and DNS query.

With command-line, PowerShell, and AMSI buffer events added next to service, scheduled task, and WMI activity, a SIEM can now correlate script-based execution with the persistence mechanisms that commonly follow it. Examples include a PowerShell command that registers a scheduled task, or a new WMI binding created shortly after an AMSI buffer event.

Firewall for macOS

Organizations that run mixed Windows and macOS fleets can now apply the same network traffic controls across both platforms. The GravityZone Firewall gives administrators granular control over network traffic, including which services and applications can communicate. The module, previously available on Windows servers and workstations, now also supports deployment and management on macOS endpoints.

Also, macOS support for the Firewall module carries through the Control Center areas that already handle Firewall on Windows: policy settings, installation packages, Threats Xplorer, Executive summary, Network, Reports, Dashboard, Health dashboard, Notifications, User activity, and the public API. The module requires BEST for Mac version 8.26.10.2000xx or later.

Policy rules now account for the platform they target:

Platform column: The Policies > Firewall > Rules table includes a new filterable Platform column that shows which operating system each rule applies to.

Existing rules: All rules previously defined in a policy are automatically set to Windows as their default platform.

Protocol support: The complete list of macOS-supported protocols is available on Bitdefender Support Center here.

The rollout of the Firewall module on macOS endpoints will take place in phases, so availability in individual environments may follow the console update.

Service API Keys

Automated integrations such as SIEM connectors, ticketing systems, and orchestration scripts often run on API keys tied to an individual user account, so the integration’s access depends on that user’s account and permissions. GravityZone now introduces dedicated service API keys and associated service accounts that manage automated integrations and API access independently of user API keys.

Service API keys are managed from the new Accounts > Service API keys page, with options to create, edit, clone, suspend, activate, and delete keys. You can configure each key with specific API module permissions, a target company and folder scope, and an expiration period of 1 to 365 days. Access to the page is controlled by the new Manage service API keys permission, available in the user account settings under Accounts.

Key lifecycle events are recorded in the User activity log, and administrators can receive email and Control Center notifications before keys expire. This keeps integration access auditable and scoped to the companies and API modules each integration needs.

More information about service API keys can be found on the Bitdefender Support Center here.

API Enhancements

Bitdefender Control Center APIs enable developers to automate business workflows. These APIs are exposed via the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol. You can find usage examples and documentation in our Support Center, located here.

This update introduces new methods, push events, and response parameters to support incident assignment and tracking, service API key permissions, scan task visibility, network inventory, and macOS package configuration.

Incidents: The new assignIncident method assigns and reassigns Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) incidents to eligible GravityZone users in bulk, and also removes assignees. All assignment changes are recorded in the Incident history panel and on the User activity page in GravityZone Control Center. Actions performed by Managed Detection and Response (MDR) analysts are attributed to an MDR Service account.

Event Push: Six new Event Push API events report EDR and XDR incident updates: incident-status-changed, incident-assignee-changed, incident-priority-changed, incident-note-created, incident-note-updated, and incident-note-deleted. They are turned on through the existing setPushEventSettings method. The Task Status push event payload now also includes the parentTaskId parameter for correlating parent tasks with their child subtasks.

Companies: The getCompanyDetails method now returns the status of companies undergoing migration between partners instead of a generic error.

Accounts: Accounts API methods now support the manageServiceAPIKeys permission, which corresponds to the Manage service API keys permission described in the Service API Keys section above. The createAccount, updateAccount, getAccountsList, and getAccountDetails methods now accept and return the updated role identifiers used with service API keys.

Network: The getTaskStatus response now includes the subTaskId (unique child task identifier) and scanType parameters in the subtasks object for scan tasks (Type 1). This identifies the scan type: Quick Scan, Full Scan, Custom Scan, Network Scan, Memory Scan, or YARA Scan. The getEndpointsList and getNetworkInventoryItems methods now also return the endpoint’s public IP address in the publicIp parameter.

Packages: The createPackage, updatePackage, and getPackageDetails methods now support configuring and installing the Firewall module on macOS endpoints.

For comprehensive insights into the GravityZone API, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Where Can I Learn More About Bitdefender GravityZone?

To learn more about the Bitdefender GravityZone platform, contact us or a Bitdefender partner for more information. You can also start a free trial by requesting a demo here.

The Bitdefender GravityZone unified security platform offers a one-stop solution for all your organization's security needs. As the digital landscape evolves, Bitdefender stays ahead, providing prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities to help keep organizations of all sizes worldwide safe.

articles.title: Human Expertise at the Speed of AI: SentinelOne Names LevelBlue its Global Exclusive Delivery Partner for Wayfinder
articles.context: Today, SentinelOne named LevelBlue its global exclusive delivery partner for Wayfinder, SentinelOne’s suite of AI-powered managed security and threat detection services
articles.full_text:
Today, SentinelOne named LevelBlue its global exclusive delivery partner for Wayfinder, SentinelOne’s suite of AI-powered managed security and threat detection services.

LevelBlue will deliver Wayfinder managed detection and response (MDR), threat hunting, incident readiness and response (IRR), and SentinelOne’s professional services for organizations around the world.

It’s a milestone for our teams, and it reflects something we believe deeply about security in the AI era.

AI changed the speed. People still make the call.

AI has changed the speed of both attack and defense. SentinelOne’s Autonomous SOC detects, investigates and responds at machine speed, and that matters when attackers move in minutes.

But speed alone doesn’t resolve an incident. Someone has to validate what matters, decide what to do next, and stand with a customer when the pressure is on. That human layer is what Wayfinder provides, and it’s what LevelBlue’s practitioners do every day.

This partnership brings the two together: the AI, platform, and intelligence behind Wayfinder, and LevelBlue’s global scale, security operations, and frontline incident response expertise. SentinelOne continues to lead Wayfinder’s technology and direction, and LevelBlue gives Wayfinder global scale and reach.

Wayfinder will sit alongside, not replace, the MDR services LevelBlue already delivers with a wide range of technology partners. All of them connect through the LevelBlue Indigo Security Platform™, which brings intelligence and operations together across our services, so our clients keep the freedom to choose the technology that fits them.

Discover why LevelBlue is the SentinelOne preferred global partner.

Learn More

What it means for customers

For already-stretched security and IT teams, Wayfinder delivered by LevelBlue means:

Experienced practitioners, around the clock. Day-to-day detection, response and incident work handled 24/7/365.

Coverage for today’s attack surface. Specialized protection across endpoints, cloud workloads, identities and AI.

From detection to decision. Help turning detections into informed decisions and coordinated action, from investigating threats to containing incidents and supporting recovery.

More organizations, in more countries

This agreement significantly expands the reach of Wayfinder’s expert-led services. SentinelOne and LevelBlue are expanding joint commercial and go-to-market efforts to bring Wayfinder to new regions and emerging markets, including organizations that haven’t had access to these services before.

A relationship built step by step

Today’s news is the latest chapter in a partnership that has grown throughout 2026. In March, at RSAC, SentinelOne named LevelBlue a preferred global partner for MDR and managed SIEM, and a preferred provider for incident response. In August, at Black Hat, we became SentinelOne’s premier remediation partner for Wayfinder Frontier AI Services. Together, LevelBlue and SentinelOne now bring customers:

Integrated MDR and AI SIEM operations. Our newest offering with SentinelOne combines SentinelOne’s AI-driven analytics and SIEM with LevelBlue’s intelligence-led operations, surfacing higher-fidelity alerts while reducing tool sprawl and operational overhead.

Remediation for Wayfinder Frontier AI Services. As SentinelOne’s premier remediation partner for Wayfinder Frontier AI Services, LevelBlue turns Wayfinder’s confirmed-exploitable findings into a prioritized remediation and resilience program, then verifies the fixes. Wayfinder Frontier AI Services finds it. We fix it.

Wayfinder delivery. And now, SentinelOne has named LevelBlue its global exclusive delivery partner for Wayfinder services.

AI Security Services. Also at OneCon, LevelBlue was named SentinelOne’s MSSP launch partner for its new partner-led AI Security Services, helping customers secure their use of AI and build toward an Autonomous SOC.

As Sundhar Annamalai, LevelBlue’s Chief Strategy Officer, put it: “Being named SentinelOne’s global exclusive delivery partner for Wayfinder reflects the trust our teams have built working side by side for customers.”

The threats are moving faster, and so are we. Pairing AI with experienced people at global scale is how we help more organizations investigate threats, contain incidents and recover with confidence.

Learn more about LevelBlue and SentinelOne, and read the full announcement here.

articles.title: How Tenable brought multi-language support to security detectors with agentic translation
articles.context: AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection
articles.full_text:
AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection. Here’s how Tenable trained our threat detectors to process nine additional languages and understand thousands more, without the need for a translation model, which increases costs and slows down processing.

Key takeaways

Tenable One AI Exposure’s detectors, covering AI threats, harmful content, and other policy risks, were originally English-centric. To assess threats written in other languages, our product translated them into English, a slow, expensive, and often imprecise approach.

Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that generates high-fidelity, label-preserving training and benchmark data across nine languages, guarded by a multi-judge quality gate, a refinement loop, and a model-refusal handling fallback.

This single multilingual model detects threats natively in all 10 supported languages. Compared with our previous process of translating threats into English, this model is roughly 20-800 times faster per item and is less expensive by an order of magnitude, bearing a one-time cost that does not grow with usage traffic from our customers.

Why your AI security tool should support multiple languages

A prompt attack against an AI model written in Spanish, Arabic, or Hindi is every bit as dangerous as one written in English, which is why an English-only AI security detector will leave your organization at risk from non-English attacks.

To address this issue in our product, Tenable first adopted a “translate-then-detect” process:

Identify the language.

Translate the input to English with a large translation model.

Then run the English detector.

This process works, but it has four downsides:

Latency. A large, autoregressive translation model that runs before every non-English detection needs hundreds of milliseconds for short inputs, and seconds to tens of seconds for long ones.

Cost. Every non-English request pays for a full translation pass.

Operational overhead. You have to serve, scale, and maintain another heavyweight model.

Lost signal. Meaning and intent blur in naive translation, which degrades the tool’s ability to detect threats.

How Tenable turned our AI security tool into a polyglot
