JACK: She had no idea her son was living this double life, bringing in anywhere from $100,000 to a million dollars from victims. But having all this Bitcoin was pointless unless Ricky could spend it, and this is where he had to be careful. Crypto exchanges require KYC, which stands for ‘know your customer’. They want your full name and picture of your ID before they will let you exchange cryptocurrency for cash. So, that wasn't going to work. His Bitcoin wallet was likely marked as fraudulent, and if he used an exchange and gave them his name, then they would probably call the cops on him. So, he needed a new plan, a way to cash out Bitcoin without using an exchange, and basically he just found another person in the world who would do it. Like, he would send them the Bitcoin and they would hand him cash. He met them through localbitcoins.com. RICKY: I had a guy in the Tampa area. If I needed $20,000 cash or less, I can go to him, or if I needed more, I had a guy that was in Miami, and he never scammed me, but I would send him the crypto and he would mail me the cash. JACK: Yeah, let’s talk about both of these, right? So, when you go to meet someone, how does this meet go down? RICKY: Typically it was at a McDonald’s or something. We would just go sit in the booth. I would send him the Bitcoin. We would wait for the confirmations and for him to get it in his account, and he would give me the cash. Prior to that, though, we had the deal locked in at a certain amount, 'cause Bitcoin would go up and down. But I would typically just lock in the deal, and I’d be — okay, we’ll meet at 7:00. This is where we’re going. He would send me an address, and I would just go there. JACK: And then he’d just hand you an envelope? RICKY: Yeah, or just straight cash or an envelope and whatnot. But it was always a public place. It was never in a dark alley or anything crazy like that. JACK: That’s the classic way LocalBitcoins worked; you meet someone in person, you send them the Bitcoin, and they hand you the cash. Of course, they’d take a percentage for doing this deal. Maybe they'd give Ricky 95% of the money and keep 5% for themselves for the trouble of having to launder these Bitcoins. So, he actually had a lot of people making decent money on LocalBitcoins just buying crypto off people. But eventually Ricky needed to cash out bigger and bigger amounts, and this person he was working with wasn't able to cash out what he needed, so Ricky had to find someone new, and this new person was like, send me the Bitcoin; I’ll send you the cash in the mail. RICKY: It typically would just come in a vacuum-sealed, clear envelope wrapped in another envelope kinda thing. Sometimes it would be inside of a book, like a big Harry Potter book or something like that, and the pages would be cut out and the money would be in there. What's funny is I lived with my mom, so packages are coming to the house, but I’m eighteen years old. She’s not going through my mail. So, she would just take the envelope, put it on my bed, and she’d be like, hey, the mail came for you. She had no idea what was inside of it. JACK: Alright, so you're loading it up in crypto here. Things are coming in, $100,000, $1 million at a time. So, you're leading a double life here. You're living with your mom. Does she have any idea that you're doing any of this stuff, involved with this? RICKY: First of all, she doesn't really understand what the hell crypto was, and she was like, Ricky, what are you doing? How do you have all this money? I bought a $100,000 F-250 Ford truck, I had jet skis, I had side-by-sides. I had a lot of toys and stuff like that. DEBBIE: It really got my attention when he came home with the truck. I said, what is going on? RICKY: I would just lie to her. Like, yo, I invested back then. At the time when I started, Bitcoin was a couple hundred dollars, and now it’s, let’s say, $3,000, $6,000. So, I made a lot just from that, that little growth. So, I was able — but that’s what I told her. Meanwhile I’m stealing it, but — so, she has really no idea the severity of it. So, my mom, she believed me. She believed that I was saying there’s no reason for her not to believe me. DEBBIE: He never gave me a reason not to believe what he was doing was wrong, 'cause he wasn't that kinda kid. JACK: Ricky’s crypto investment explanation wasn't a total lie. He did have Bitcoin investments, and Debbie didn't have any reason to question it. After all, her own mother, Ricky’s grandmother, dabbled in Bitcoin, too, so she knew it was real. Ricky also had a young kid at home, and Debbie thought why would he do anything to throw his life away? DEBBIE: I was a single mom. I did the best I could growing up with him. He was a very honest child, never got in trouble, never was in the principal’s office. He didn't get in fights. So, when he came home with the truck, I just said, I don't know what you're doing or what's going on, but that’s not normal, and all I know is if you get in trouble, there’s not much I can do. I mean, I — and I said — at that time it was just his daughter, and between the mom and my son being the parents to this child, they were both younger, and I was fairly involved with my granddaughter. I just said to him, it’s just not your life anymore. You have a child involved here. JACK: Debbie believed her son and was proud of him, and had no reason to think he would lie to her. In fact, she thought Ricky’s crypto savviness could actually help others. At the time she worked as a nurse in the Pasco County Jail, and one day she overheard some sheriff’s deputies yapping about crypto. DEBBIE: I assumed at this point my son was doing really good with crypto, 'cause that’s what — the vision I was getting. I kinda went into work and was saying, yeah, my son does crypto, Bitcoin, and he’s done really well, and they've matured. I remember one of the deputies was really interested. He’s like, really? RICKY: They were like, oh, we’d love to talk to him. DEBBIE: I was like, yeah, he’s doing really good with it. One of the guys, one of the deputies, wanted to get with him and speak with my son. RICKY: So, next thing you know my mom is having me call these police officers and they're coming to the house to ask me about crypto. They're asking me about investing. They're asking me like, what do I think? I just went along with it. Like, yeah, crypto’s great. This is what I recommend. I recommend Bitcoin or Ethereum. I think XRP was actually blowing up at that time, too. I think I made a lot off XRP, actually, which — not legitly, but I used my dirty money and put it into XRP, and XRP blew up. I was telling them about that, and they were loving it. So, they were just like, okay, cool, thanks for chatting. They had no idea I was stealing it. JACK: And how were you feeling inside? RICKY: Oh, I’m nervous. I’m like, mom — that’s when I told her. Like, yo, never again. Don't tell people what I do. DEBBIE: [Music] I said to Ricky, and you let this deputy come to the house and talk to you? JACK: By 2018 the walls started closing in on Ricky. He says he has a hunch of when it all started to unravel. One night he was doing a SIM-swap, a crypto heist with some other guys online, his crew. One of the guys was a younger kid, and this younger kid was posing as an AT&T employee trying to social engineer someone into doing the SIM-swap for him. But little did this kid know, his mother was listening through the door, and she heard him trying to scam someone on the phone. That kid’s mom called the cops on her son, and that kid got arrested in Michigan. Ricky and his crew did not know this. All they knew was that kid suddenly went missing. That’s strange. But they had no idea he got arrested. But then that kid came back out of the blue and really, really, really badly wanted to get in on the action again. Ricky suspected that’s really weird that this kid got a bunch of money from a crypto heist and then disappeared for a while and now really wants back in. They kept that kid at arm’s length, but that didn't matter. Another one of Ricky’s friends was arrested shortly after, who was also present on that same call where the kid’s mom overheard them. Joel Ortiz was arrested for SIM-swapping and stealing millions of dollars in crypto from victims. He pled guilty, and a judge sentenced him to a decade behind bars. Prosecutors said that he was the first SIM-swapper to ever be sentenced to prison in the US, and after hearing about Joel’s arrest, Ricky was worried that he might be next. RICKY: I’ve known Joel. I’ve talked with him and I’ve done stuff with him and stuff where it was like, hold on, this is a huge red flag. I remember I was eating at Ford’s Garage when it happened when I found out that Joel got arrested. So, that’s what kinda raised my suspicion. I’m like, oh shit, Joel got caught. JACK: After hearing Joel went down, you would think that it would give you a spook of some kind and be like, okay, I’m gonna lay low for a couple weeks or clear some stuff or get rid of some evidence. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: But you didn't do any of that. RICKY: Um…no. JACK: Just a day after learning about Joel’s arrest, the dominoes started to fall. There are moments in our life that stand out forever. Maybe it’s when your first child is born or first kiss or playing a video game for the first time. For Ricky, that day was July 18, 2018. On that day, Ricky was still living at home with his mom, and he had broken up with his girlfriend that he had a child with, but he had a new woman and a new child with her. I think the baby was a few months old at that point. The day started just like any other day. Ricky was getting ready to go to work at the parks and recreation department, and his girlfriend left the house just before him so that she could go to work. RICKY: I used to live by a cul-de-sac area. [Music] When she went to work, she’s like, hey, there’s a lot of cops in this cul-de-sac. I was like, okay, come back. Like, that’s weird. That’s off to me. So, when she went around the block the other way, she’s like, yo, they're also on this side of the house, like on this block. I was like, alright, I’m pretty sure they're coming. I walk outside to go — just act like I’m going to work. Like, I knew at that point that they were probably coming for me. I could see them coming down the road. I was like, just try to play it off. I went to go get up in my truck, and they were like, don't go in your truck. Don't run, don't run. JACK: Ricky stayed still, standing next to his truck as officers handcuffed him. OFFICER: You wanna lean against your truck or something? RICKY: Yeah, if — whatever. I mean, just whatever. [Background talk] OFFICER: You have anything on you that might hurt us if we pat you down or whatever? Alright. Just hang tight. You understand right now you're just being detained. JACK: This is body cam audio from Ricky’s arrest by the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office. It’s the very same sheriff’s office where his mom Debbie worked as a nurse. DEBBIE: When they came here that day — and, you know, they — I guess it would be to raid the house, but they were very — doing the search warrant stuff, but they did not break down our doors. They didn't do anything. So, now I kinda get up out of my bed and I look into the kitchen area, and there’s two cops standing in the doorway. They're like, hey, Debbie. I need you to come out here. JACK: They know you? DEBBIE: Yeah, they knew my name, they knew everything. Now, yeah, I knew some of them from coming in and out of work. I think I kept saying, what is going on? What is going on? What is happening? JACK: And when they finally tell you this is what we think is going on, what was your reaction to that? DEBBIE: We have — my reaction to that was, well, isn't Bitcoin — isn't this legal? That was my first reaction; but I thought it was legal. So, I kinda looked at him and he goes, he was not — those coins and the money that he was getting, Debbie, did not belong to him. He was stealing them. That’s when I really realized like, oh, okay. So, now what? JACK: Debbie sat outside the front of the house with Ricky as deputies collected evidence. Some of Ricky’s burner phones, his iPhone, his crypto wallets, and some other SIM cards were taken. RICKY: They took my truck, they took two side-by-sides, they took a trailer I had, the trailer I haul everything. JACK: Ricky was taken away in the back of a squad car to jail. … OFFICER: I have one male adult, 1012. Nothing else is in your pockets? RICKY: No, sir. JACK: They drive off to jail. The twenty-five minute ride is mostly quiet. Ricky is alone with his thoughts, but he does ask the officer behind the wheel what to expect. RICKY: Do you know how all this all goes? Like, do I see a judge and then…? OFFICER: You’ll have advisors. RICKY: I will? Okay. OFFICER: That’ll be done by video, on chat or whatever. RICKY: That’ll be today, right? OFFICER: Should be. JACK: I can't get over how calm Ricky sounds. He had been cooking up these schemes for years to steal things from who knows how many victims, starting with a few hundred dollars in gamer tags to millions of dollars in crypto wallets, and it all came to an end here in the back of the squad car. Maybe he was feeling relief, like his big secret’s out. He doesn't have to lie to his mom anymore or try to walk quietly in the shadows of his double life. But sitting in the back of the car, you have to wonder what else is going through his head. What’s gonna happen to me, and what about my family? What about my money? But he quietly listens as the officer driving him to the jail spells out the next steps for him. OFFICER: I would think it would be this afternoon. That’s when they’ll basically just announce what you're charged with, and then whether you're gonna retain your own attorney or whether you're asking for a public defender. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: And then — but that is — again, I don't know if you're being charged federally. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: Which makes it different, so… RICKY: Alright, thank you sir. JACK: Ricky was booked in the county jail. His mom was so distraught, though. She didn't want to see her son in jail. What mother would? So, she went down to jail to see if she could bail him out. DEBBIE: I just — it had to be done. I wasn't leaving him in jail. JACK: Did he go to the very jail you worked at? DEBBIE: Oh yeah, he sure did. All my nursing staff, friends, they were all like, oh my god, Debbie’s son is here. What’s going on? Then the sergeant — they all knew once I posted bond for him, get him outta here. Yeah, they did do a little bit of, let’s say, courtesy. I shouldn't say courtesy, but they treated him knowing that he was my son. Like, let’s move him along. You know? JACK: Yeah, that must have been embarrassing. DEBBIE: But yeah. Yeah, a little bit embarrassing, a little bit of shocking, embarrassing. The only thing — and I wasn't actually physically working there anymore. I had just left like six months prior. But I mean, it was still fresh. I had worked there for almost ten years. JACK: They said his bail was $110,000. The cost of a bail bond is usually 10% to 15% of the total amount. Debbie ended up paying that to a bail bondsman to get him out. She didn't even hesitate. She just immediately was there for him. Prosecutors charged Ricky with grand theft and money laundering. The case against him dragged on for four years. He had to wear an ankle monitor during that whole time and follow a strict curfew. He pled guilty to federal charges of computer misconduct and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. By the time he went before a judge for sentencing, Ricky didn't know what to expect in the courtroom or how it would affect his family. His mom and fiancé were there during the sentencing. DEBBIE: It was horrible. It was I think one of the saddest days of my life. I remember standing in front of that judge. I just cried and said, look, I know my son did wrong. I know he did wrong, believe me. I can't believe he did all this, but he’s — that’s not my — that’s not the kind of kid he is. It was horrible. JACK: What did the judge say to that? DEBBIE: She was a woman, and I could almost feel her sympathy for me and getting it, but the law is the law, and I agree. The law is the law, and my son broke the law, and he had to pay his consequences. I let him know you did not just do this to yourself. You did this to your whole family. We're all suffering through this. We're suffering more than you are. JACK: The judge sentenced Ricky to four years in federal prison and ordered him to pay $7.6 million in restitution, which is what the courts accused him of stealing. RICKY: I knew it could have been worse and it should have been worse, and I was thankful that I got the forty-eight months. Like, I knew it was coming. I knew it had to happen because all the havoc I caused. I was like, you know, I gotta deal with it. I did what I did and now I gotta do it. I lost — I had to leave everybody, my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. JACK: Okay, so your child was four or five months old when you went away. RICKY: Correct, and that’s super hard because all those — I’ve always said the money, whatever, the money can't buy back those memories that I missed. Like, there’s nothing I could do; his first walk, his first talk, stuff like that, that money can't buy. DEBBIE: It was so hard coming to see him in prison and having to leave knowing that my kid’s in prison. Me and his fiancé, we went and saw Ricky at least once a month if not twice a month. We’d pack up the car, we’d leave early one morning, get there. We drove six hours, whatever it was, with two kids in the car, me and her only. No men, nobody to help us. We drove down there and had to do what we had to do, and then spend the night in a hotel. It was horrible, embarrassing, horrible, a combo of everything. JACK: So many criminal hacker stories go the same way. There’s a video game, a cheat, an underground community, an exploit, a payday, and then the knock on the door. They don't usually have the foresight to see how it will inevitably end. What do those millions of dollars really buy you? A couple of years of wealth that you can't really show anyone? Some screenshots of good old times? The skills to find gaps in security through social engineering? Whatever it is, the windfall was worth a lot less when you factor in what you lose. That’s the real cost. No cryptocurrency can buy back lost time or memories with your children. That’s what Ricky learned. [To Ricky] What was the worst part of this whole experience? RICKY: The worst part was the victims, because they didn't deserve it. So, that was the worst part, dealing with — I was doing terrible things. But I guess you have a chance in prison; you're like, dude — looking back on the shit that you caused — I can only imagine if I was in there and she was with a kid. That could have been used for my — their kids’ college funds or retirement or whatever the case may have been that they had that much money for, and I just came by and took it all. JACK: If it was me, I think I would have been — the saddest or the worst part of it was just not seeing my child in those early day — in those early years. Did that have an affect on you? RICKY: Yeah, that’s the second part of it. The first part was how I ruined innocent people’s lives. The second part now is I went to prison, I affected more people than just myself. I lost — I had to leave everybody, like my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. They were devastated. I know they were devastated, and it hurt me knowing that I hurt them like that. Like, my actions caused all that. JACK: After serving just a little more than two years in prison, Ricky got out early in 2024. These days he’s thinking a lot about the time he has now. Since his release he’s tried to turn his story into something useful, to reach out to the very gamers like him who may follow a darker path of social engineering. He’s spoken at anti-fraud events and security conferences like Black Hat and DEF CON. SPEAKER 6: Ricky, what would have made a difference to you as a teenager that would have stopped you going down this pathway? RICKY: Probably companies who could intervene, like get you before you're — it’s too late. If you had a chance to use your skills for good and after you help companies and whatnot, where they could be like, hey, we offer you a job, said job, into this world where you don't have to do what I was doing. JACK: I agree with that. The people in his bubble at that time were all criminals, and they used their skills for bad. But if he had more exposure to people, mentors, for instance, who could show him that these hacking tricks he knows, the cleverness of his social engineering skills and his OSINT skills, can be used for good and here's how, I think that kind of stuff does influence a lot of people to turn away from their life of crime and to find a new home, to be a productive member of society. So, he’s trying to do that now. He’s trying to build a pen testing company with another former SIM-swapper named Joseph Harris, one of the people Ricky met in the hacker forums. They're hoping to get this company up and running next year. [Outro]: [Outro music] A big thank you to Ricky and Debbie Handschumacher for sharing this story with us, and also thanks to Mark Kreitzman for telling us about one of the worst days of his life. You can learn more about what he’s working on at efani.com. If you liked this episode, go listen to our most popular episode we’ve ever made, Episode 112, called Dirty Coms, which goes into more details about this whole underground world, or listen to Joseph Harris’ story, which is Episode 118, called Hot Swaps. Hey, have you listened to my other podcast yet, LOW? It is wild. A lot of feedback from people are saying, pssh, I’ll pass, which is fine. It’s not for everyone. But I’m getting even more feedback from people saying — well, here, let me actually pull up one of the quotes that came in today. "The end of Episode 1 left me speechless." Someone else wrote, "it has moved me in a way that I did not think a podcast could." I mean, when is the last time you heard a show that moved you in a way that you didn't know was possible? If you need that in your life, open your podcast player and type in LOW, L-O-W. I made it as easy as possible to find. Go find it, go listen to it, and tell me what you think. This show is created by me, the ghost in the groceries, Jack Rhysider. This episode was written and produced by the packet-snacker, Sean Powers, assembled by the fridge phreaker, Tristan Ledger, mixing by Proximity Sound, theme music by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. Alright, question; if you dug up a tomb that was in a pyramid, does it become unencrypted? This is Darknet Diaries.

articles.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
articles.context: A binder is only the first step to developing an antivenom Our results show binding only against recombinant toxins, which are grown in the lab from each toxin’s gene rather...
articles.full_text:
Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field.

In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom.

Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease.

We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report.

Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom.

We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

We share more detail in our technical report, and are making all 211 designs and their data available.

Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible.

Susana Vázquez Torres, Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain.

Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions

Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels, large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death.

There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply.

De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur.

Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo-designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described.

For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots, specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto.

We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences.

To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously.

Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer.

Timothy P. Jenkins, Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark.

Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy

Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins.

Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.2

Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins.

Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work.

Testing Claude's designs in the lab

After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system, which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc, the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results.

Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding.

When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs3—that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.”

Claude’s Cn2 binders likely bind the same site as a toxin-neutralizing antibody

Antibodies and nanobodies remain the standard for de novo designs to beat. Three such molecules have reported affinities (KD) below 1 nM (nanomolar) against Cn2 or AaH II, and they have been shown to protect mice from scorpion toxins.

Our two strongest binders, which we call Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, target Cn2, a neurotoxin from the Mexican scorpion Centruroides noxius. They each bound Cn2 tightly at both Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, with affinities (KD) in the single-digit nanomolar range.

One way to find out whether two molecules (e.g., an antibody and a miniprotein) bind the same site on a target is with a competition experiment, which tests whether both binders can attach to the target at the same time. If the presence of one molecule reduces the other molecule’s binding, then they likely compete for the same binding site.

Our competition experiments suggest our Cn2 binders each attach on or near the same epitope (binding site) as an antibody called LR, which has been reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice. LR’s binding site covers the part of Cn2 that attaches to the sodium channel and causes nerves to misfire. We have not tested our strongest binders, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, in a cellular environment or in live animals, but the fact that they compete with LR suggests that they will likely neutralize Cn2.

A binder is only the first step to developing an antivenom

Our results show binding only against recombinant toxins, which are grown in the lab from each toxin’s gene rather than purified from venom. The two biggest limitations of this study are that we didn’t test any design for neutralization in vitro (against cells grown in the lab) or for efficacy in vivo (in living animals, such as mice).

If we were to advance one design toward a therapy, Cn2-B1 would be one of our strongest candidates. First, though, we would need to confirm the design also binds toxin purified from venom. We would then assess it for function in vitro with patch-clamp recordings (which can measure the electrical current passing through sodium channels) to see whether it stops the toxin from acting on the channel. Then, we would need to test the binder in mice to see whether it actually protects them. Beyond neutralizing the toxin, a treatment must also be safe, stable, affordable, and available where stings occur. Reaching patients will also take cooperation from clinicians, funders, and policymakers.

We are releasing all 211 designs and their binding data so that other researchers can build on our work. We hope this demonstration of Claude’s capabilities, along with the data we are releasing, will help accelerate further research into antivenom design.

Further reading

The following resources provide further technical depth and more detailed information about the results described above:

Technical report;

Data release: all 211 designs, their predicted structures and scores, and experimental data;

Our previous posts on protein design and uplifting biomolecular modeling.

The ballot box meets the bot.
articles.context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
articles.full_text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Securing the agentic insider
articles.context: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge wil
articles.full_text:
In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful.

While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents.

Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised.

Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise.

They are agentic insiders.

Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly.

To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7.

An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime.

In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise.

The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise.

Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence:

Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions.

Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically, the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do.

Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk, a team of Guardian Agents, with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time.

This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners.

Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed. Practitioners provide judgment. That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against.

Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger. And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders.

With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders. There should not be a choice between innovation and safety.

Hayete Gallot leads Microsoft’s work to help organizations operate securely in an AI-driven world. Her scope includes identity, threat protection, compliance and data security at global scale.

The post Securing the agentic insider appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.title: ConnectWise Shuts Off Cloud Services After ‘Unauthorized Access’ to Microsoft 365 Tenants
articles.context: IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365...
articles.full_text:
IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365 tenants.

A Microsoft 365 tenant is a dedicated instance of Microsoft services used by an organization to store their data separately from other organizations using Microsoft services. Each organization using a Microsoft 365 tenant has its own unique identifier assigned to it by Microsoft.

ConnectWise began investigating suspicious activity on October 15. By October 17, the company said that it had identified “unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.”

The discovery has resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident, said a security advisory.

“We understand that this interruption affects your ability to support your customers. We do not yet have a confirmed restoration time and will share a timeline as soon as we can do so reliably,” ConnectWise said in an October 19 update.

The action has been taken due to the discovery of unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

An attacker could potentially abuse this access to gain unauthorized access to customers' Microsoft 365 environments. They would do this by authenticating to the app using the tooling of the tenant in the same way the backup service would, leveraging this access to obtain tokens with the app's existing permissions, therefore providing access to the environment.

With this access an attacker could access the same directories and data as a backup service, putting the tenant users’ corporate data at risk.

“The credential belongs to the application itself, so the attacker inherited the permissions granted to it. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) doesn’t apply because this is an application sign-in, so no user, device, or MFA prompt is involved,” said Justin Kohler, chief product officer at SpecterOps

“Backup tools need broad access to read and restore data. Anyone holding the app’s credential can reach the same mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information the backup service can,” he added.

Cybersecurity analysts at Huntress have been following the ConnectWise incident. In a blog post, they said that in at least one customer tenant being observed, the attacker provided themselves with a Global Administrator role, using this access in an attempt to modify permissions for other applications, including an MSP management application, and Huntress's own security application.

While ConnectWise has said it has yet to discover any indication that partner backup data has been compromised, the company said it will “continue investigating potential unauthorized access.”

There is currently no attribution as to who could be behind the attack. “We cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time. Our focus is on investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers,” ConnectWise said in the advisory.

ConnectWise has also advised its customers to take the following actions to help identify any potential incidents:

Verify the status of the listed application connections and keep affected applications disabled until ConnectWise provides restoration instructions

Preserve available sign-in and audit records promptly, while taking any urgent containment action

Review application and user authentication, application credentials and federation trusts, directory roles, owners, consent grants and recent policy changes

Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding, inbox or transport rules and delegated mailbox access

Investigate any other identities changed or used during suspicious activity; disabling the original applications does not remove those separate access paths

articles.title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26%, Hitting Four Year Low
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity job postings in the US fell by 26.4% year-over-year from January to September 2026, according to analysis by CyberSN.

A total of 235,786 cybersecurity roles were posted on the job market intelligence platform JobSpikr in 2026. This is the lowest amount of US-based cybersecurity jobs advertised in the four years CyberSN has undertaken its analysis, compared to 273,498 in 2023, 244,911 in 2024 and 320,210 in 2025.

There was a particularly significant drop in leadership roles. CISO postings fell from 4632 in January to September 2025 to 2832 in the same period in 2026, a 38.9% reduction.

Other leadership roles that saw substantial dips included cybersecurity director (a 32.5% fall), cybersecurity lead (41% fall) and cybersecurity manager (24.4% fall).

Overall, nine of the 10 cybersecurity functions tracked by the researchers had fewer postings in 2026 compared to 2025. The only exception was research roles, which grew by 26.1%.

The CyberSN researchers said it is not clear whether the sharp decline in job postings reflects less demand for cybersecurity roles from employers or is simply a return from an unusually strong year in 2025.

The report, published on October 16, also highlighted that roles posted in the three quarters tracked in 2026 stayed within 1.5% of one another.

“That is consistent with demand having settled at a lower level rather than continuing to fall,” the researchers wrote.

A significant proportion (39.9%) of postings in 2025 came from small businesses, with 200 or fewer employees. Nearly half (47.3%) were from large firms with 1001 or more employees, and 12.7% from those with 201 to 1000 employees.

AI Security Engineer Postings Surge

AI security engineer roles, grouped in the cybersecurity function of “defense” by CyberSN, jumped by 268.3% in January to September 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The share of job postings that mentions AI or machine learning in the job description was similar in 2026 compared to 2025, 14.6% versus 15.1%, respectively.

Read now: Cybersecurity Job Ads Requiring AI Skills Double

September 2026 also saw a surge in cyber data scientist postings, with 667 compared to 247 in the previous month, August. Of all these roles posted in 2026, 88% mention AI in the job description.
