articles.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
articles.context: In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components
articles.full_text:
Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.1

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2).

In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.

These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.

A new reversible algorithm

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs.

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

A hard first test: modular inversion

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself n times, find n. For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.

The memory demands of divsteps

Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called modular inversion. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer a, find x such that ax ≡ 1 (mod p). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called divsteps. Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.

Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called branch information, is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.

How Claude got around the memory problem

Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

A family of designs

Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).

Optimizing a quantum optimizer

Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.

When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.

A more efficient quantum decoder

The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position x contains several acceptable values of y. The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many x positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed-Solomon decoder.

Reed-Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a syndrome. The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.

Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed-Solomon decoding.

So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp-Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp-Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.

A simplified approach to storage

Switching to Berlekamp-Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.

Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.

What we learned

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones.

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.

articles.title: The AI expectations gap
articles.context: First, the two groups largely agree about what AI can do today but disagree about the pace of future progress
articles.full_text:
Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, Charles I. Jones, Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory

Key findings

US adults expect AI capabilities to advance rapidly in the coming years; Anthropic staff expect even faster progress; 39% of US adults and 91% of staff expect that AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030.

Anthropic staff expect much larger productivity gains from AI on the tasks it is well-suited for. Among US adults who use AI at work, 26% say a task takes a quarter of the time or less with AI, compared to 59% of Anthropic staff.

When it comes to their own job, over half of Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do at least 80% of their current work by 2030, compared with 5% of US workers.

Among both US workers and Anthropic staff, people who expect AI to do more of their own work anticipate higher unemployment. While there are differences in beliefs about future capabilities, the perceived link between how AI might change one’s own job and broader unemployment is very similar for both groups.

Introduction

How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the possibility that future AI models may be able to build their own successors (recursive self-improvement) could further accelerate the rate of progress. How quickly this might materialize and to what extent is unclear. Forecasts vary widely and are fiercely debated.

What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? Is it principally due to differences in beliefs about how quickly AI capabilities will improve? Or does it reflect disagreement about how quickly and in what form those capabilities translate to real-world adoption? Which views on the future path of AI are consistent with rapid economic growth?

This note presents new survey evidence on these questions. In August 2026, we surveyed two groups: a sample of US adults that was nationally representative and Anthropic staff.1 The questions covered, among other things, AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how autonomous it will be, and how difficult it will be for a displaced worker to find a job in a different occupation.2 Anthropic staff build and use frontier AI every day. The second survey therefore shows how people closest to the technology anticipate its future, both in capabilities and in broader economic impact.

We report the following main findings. First, the two groups largely agree about what AI can do today but disagree about the pace of future progress. Anthropic staff expect capabilities to advance faster, AI to be used more widely and with less human involvement, and the time it saves on a task to be much larger. For example, 91% of staff expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared to 39% of US adults.

Second, there are sharp differences concerning people's own jobs. On average, staff members expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work by 2030, compared to 28% for US workers overall.

Third, the two groups seem to reason about the labor market in a similar way: people who expect AI to do more of their own work in the future forecast higher unemployment. And, at the same level of expected AI automation of their own work, both groups forecast about the same unemployment rate.

What people expect AI to do

Capabilities

We first investigate expectations about AI capabilities. We asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level scientific discovery. US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree on what AI can do today, particularly when it comes to more complex tasks. Both groups rank tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty (Figure 1, panel A).

The groups disagree on the path of future AI progress. For example, around a quarter of US adults and Anthropic staff think that AI can design, conduct, and publish scientific studies today. But by next year, 9 in 10 staff expect this to be feasible for AI as compared to just 38% for the general public. By 2030, 39% of US adults expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery (panel C), compared with 91% of staff. What is perhaps the most striking difference, depending on the task, between 19 and 40% of US adults say AI will never be able to do a given task, compared with at most 2% of staff.

In part, differences in views reflect differences in frequency of AI use. Among those who use AI at work regularly (about a fifth of respondents), 56% expect AI to be able to do at least seven of the eight named tasks by 2030. This is substantially higher than among all US adults (41%) and among those who have never used an AI tool (28%), but still well short of the staff view (96%).

Adoption and its obstacles

The impact of AI on the economy is not solely determined by raw capabilities. People and businesses need to actually use AI, which takes time and experimentation. Of the work tasks AI will be able to do, US adults expect that 42% will be done with AI by 2030. Anthropic staff expect noticeably faster diffusion over the next few years, with AI used for 65% of all tasks for which it could be used.

To understand what might hold back AI adoption at work, we asked US adults to choose up to three obstacles from a list of nine that they expect to be the biggest. The general public expects that people's preferences and rules, more than the technological constraints, may be what holds adoption back (Figure 2). “Customers preferring to deal with a person” was the obstacle selected most often, followed by “data privacy and security concerns,” “AI not being reliable enough,” and “laws, regulations or liability.”

Notably, US adults who use AI regularly at work rank data privacy and security concerns first (42% consider it among the top three obstacles, compared with 37% among the rest) and see customer preferences to deal with humans as slightly less important (37% vs. 42%).

How autonomous AI will be

The impact of AI on the labor market will in part depend on whether AI completes complex tasks autonomously or in collaboration with a human. The former tends to displace human workers. Alternatively, when AI complements human capabilities, workers become more productive. To get a sense for anticipated automation versus augmentation in 2030 among Anthropic staff and the general public, we asked how AI and humans will work together on various tasks ranging from email drafting to legal contracting by 2030. At Anthropic, the vast majority of staff say that by 2030 AI will either complete tasks alone or with a worker evaluating the work (Figure 3). By contrast, 4 in 10 US adults instead expect that humans will do most of the work themselves or with some AI help.

Time savings

How much AI raises output depends not only on which tasks it can do and how widely it is used, but also on how much faster and better it does them. A technology that is just good enough to replace workers—what Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) call a "so-so" technology—displaces work without much increase in GDP. By contrast, a technology that completes tasks at a small fraction of cost or in a fraction of time can meaningfully raise GDP.

To measure perceptions about the productivity lift from AI, we asked the general public and Anthropic staff how long a task for which AI is well suited takes with AI, compared with doing it without AI. A task done in half the time corresponds to a doubling of output per hour.3

Anthropic staff report much larger expected savings, with 85% saying that it takes half the time or less. Among US adults who use AI at work, the typical answer is half the time, and 29% say the task takes just as long or longer, while only 5% of staff say so. Among US adults, 26% of those who use AI at work say a task takes a quarter of the time or less, and 21% of those who do not use AI at work say the same. For staff, that share is 59% (Figure 4).

Staff may be describing what they experience at work. As discussed further in How Employment is Changing at Anthropic, Anthropic employees increased productivity on some dimensions after adopting agentic tools: the lines of code engineers added tripled in the month after adopting coding agents and sales representatives closed more deals with clients after adopting AI agents. Output per person also rose in other business functions, like legal and recruiting.

Own work and jobs

How much of their own work AI will be able to do

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we find a large gap in perceptions between the general public and Anthropic staff when it comes to AI’s impact on their own jobs (Figure 5). On average, Anthropic staff members say AI will be able to do 75% of their current work hours by 2030. US workers (respondents who report having a job) put the share at 28% on average, and only 1 in 20 say that AI could do 80% or more of their work hours by 2030.

Across US workers, expectations vary by occupation: AI is expected to be able to do 25% of work hours among manual trades, production and transport workers and 33% for workers in computer, engineering, and science occupations. For this latter group, those who use AI regularly expect only 40%, a belief that is closer to the average US worker than to the average Anthropic staff member (75%).

Own-job exposure and unemployment forecasts

How much of their own work people expect AI to do goes a long way toward explaining what they expect for the labor market. We told respondents that the current unemployment rate was about 4.2% and asked them to forecast the rate in 2030. Figure 6 groups respondents by the share of their own hours they expect AI to be able to do by 2030, and shows each group's average unemployment rate forecast.

US workers who expect AI to be able to do less than half of their work forecast unemployment of 7 to 8%. Above half, the forecast increases with the share of AI-exposed work. Those who expect AI to do 80% or more of their work expect, on average, an unemployment rate of 12.2% in 2030, above its peak during the Great Financial Crisis. Across US workers, ten more percentage points of work affected is associated with 0.4 points more forecasted unemployment. General optimism about AI does not explain this. Holding their own work exposure fixed, the share of the eight tasks a worker expects AI to master is unrelated to the forecast.

Even though their own reported exposure is much higher, the same gradient appears among Anthropic staff, with forecasts closely mirroring those of the general population. Therefore, these two groups do not seem to hold different theories of how AI will simultaneously affect their own jobs and the broader labor market. They have different experiences of what AI capabilities are and, in turn, expectations.

Hiring and re-employment

Even though Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do most of their work, they also expect Anthropic to keep hiring. 95% of Anthropic staff expect headcount to grow over the next 12 months, the median staff member expects it to grow by 66%, and 27% expect it at least to double. These are the personal expectations of staff members in an internal poll and do not represent Anthropic's plans or its view of its headcount. Even so, they show that automating tasks and shedding jobs are different forecasts, at least at a frontier AI lab.

Anthropic staff, however, are slightly more pessimistic than US adults about how quickly workers displaced by AI can find new work. We asked how long it would take a person who loses their job to AI automation in 2030—and who needs to switch occupations—to find a new one.4 The median Anthropic staff member expects that a worker displaced by AI would take 12 months to find a role in a new occupation. This compares to the median US adult response in the range of 7-12 months.

Expectations about AI and their economic implications

Mapping survey responses to model-implied economic scenarios

In Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI we introduced a structured framework for assessing how different future paths for AI capabilities and diffusion might translate into differences in economic outcomes. The model allows us to translate each respondent’s answers across five dimensions — capabilities, diffusion, automation, productivity, and worker transition frictions — into model-implied economic outcomes.5 Across both our US adult and Anthropic staff samples, we identify every respondent who answered all questions related to the key model inputs (3,259 US adults and 1,093 staff). We then evaluate the economic scenario implied by those answers for each respondent, focusing below on implications for GDP growth in 2030.

The median US adult's answers imply GDP growth of 5.4% in 2030, according to the model. The median staff member's answers imply GDP growth accelerating to 17.1% by 2030. There is significant variation within each group, so the distributions overlap widely (Figure 7). Figure A1 in the appendix shows how much each belief contributes to this gap.

Responses from online scenario explorer quiz

Figure 7 also shows the economic scenarios implied by inputs provided by site visitors to an interactive scenario explorer based on this economic model that was published at www.anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios on September 9, 2026.

The interactive explorer asked shorter form versions of the questions we fielded to US adults and Anthropic staff in August 2026. 23,075 visitors completed the survey in the first 48 hours after publication, connecting from more than 140 countries worldwide. These visitors chose to come to a page on Anthropic's website and to take the quiz, so they are likely to be more interested in AI than the general public. Indeed, their answers place them between those of US adults and Anthropic staff: the median visitor's answers imply 12.5% growth.

Inside the lab

One reason staff are more optimistic about AI capabilities may be that they have greater visibility into the development process. The Anthropic Institute recently published a report on progress toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), a process where AI systems increasingly improve their own capabilities (Favaro and Clark, 2026).

To shed light on whether staff themselves expect this to happen, we asked Anthropic staff what share of the work of building an early-2026 frontier model is done by AI today, and what they expect it to be in the future (Figure 8).6 Among surveyed Anthropic staff, the median answer today is 51%, 80% by the end of 2027 and 95% by the end of 2030.

Estimates of the share of work that AI does in AI development vary far more within teams than between them. Still, staff on research teams, who are closest to the work of building models, put AI's share today somewhat higher: 60% on average, against 53% for all other survey respondents. This is consistent with information playing some role, although researchers—by virtue of the nature of their work—may also use AI more in their own work than other employees.

As with the hiring forecasts, these responses are the personal views of staff members in an internal poll fielded to Anthropic staff in August 2026.

Conclusion

US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree about what AI can do today. However, they disagree about how quickly it will improve, how widely it will be used, and how large the productivity gains measured by time saved will be. Through the lens of the model in Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI, the median US adult's answers imply a scenario in which the US economy grows at more than twice its typical rate. Among Anthropic staff working at the frontier of AI development and usage, expectations about AI progress, adoption, and automation of knowledge work imply a transformative and historically unprecedented change to the economy: by 2030, GDP is doubling in size roughly every four and a half years.

Those who expect AI to do more of their own work in the years ahead expect higher unemployment as well. This is true for the general public in the US and among Anthropic employees; on average, Anthropic staff expect faster automation of their own work and, in turn, higher unemployment. We find that this disagreement in expectations is closely tied to differing views between Anthropic staff and the general public about how much of their own work will be automated in the years ahead.

The day-to-day experience with AI varies widely between the two groups. Most Anthropic staff already work alongside AI that does much of their job, whereas few US workers do. Those who do already hold expectations closer to those of Anthropic staff, which suggests that public expectations may shift as AI use spreads. How far they shift will depend on whether AI comes to do as much of the work elsewhere as it does at a frontier lab.

References

Acemoglu, D. and P. Restrepo (2019). "Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor." Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(2), 3–30.

Favaro, M. and J. Clark (2026). “When AI Builds Itself.” The Anthropic Institute. https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement.

Korinek, A., C. I. Jones, S. Sacher, T. Cotter and P. McCrory (2026). "Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI." The Anthropic Institute Working Paper No. 2026-02.

articles.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
articles.context: The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally
articles.full_text:
LAYER BY LAYER

Layers, not one gate

Six layers of checks, with rollback under them

1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.

REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.

4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

Risk

Examples

Human approvals

Low

Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag

None required once automated review and security checks are green

Medium

Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts

One person

High

The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people

Two people

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.

7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

articles.title: How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Managed Agents
articles.context: The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job
articles.full_text:
As a business development representative on Anthropic's Japan team, my job is to show Japanese companies how Claude can simplify and automate their workflows, but until earlier this year, most of mine were still manual. I was spending a couple of hours each morning routing and qualifying leads, then writing emails in Japanese or English. In the time I had left, I was updating our CRM, often a day or more behind. Now my agents prepare most of that before my day starts, and I review it.

The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job. I'd hand Claude one piece of my work at a time, correct what it got wrong, and save those corrections. Over time, that grew into a handful of agents, each covering a different routine.

Word got around quickly, and teammates started asking for my prompts and skills so they could build their own. All I could send them was a zip file with my skills and a few Markdown files from the knowledge base, which they had to upload to Claude and then answer a round of setup questions before anything worked. My own setup was getting harder to keep track of, too. Each agent was a skill, a scheduled task and a shared folder, and I changed them by asking Claude in whatever chat I had open, so the same skill was being edited from lots of different conversations.

I wanted to define each agent once, in one place, and be able to see every change I'd made to it. So I decided to try Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) (beta), our managed agent infrastructure on the Claude Platform.

I was hesitant to try it at first. The docs talk about schedules, tools, and credential vaults, and I'm a sales rep, so I assumed Managed Agents was for developers who can build and maintain the necessary infrastructure. I tried it anyway because my agents already existed, and I only had to move them over.

It turned out I didn't need to be a developer. I described each agent's job in plain language, Claude wrote a few short setup scripts, and I ran them from the terminal on my laptop. (If you're starting from scratch, the Console also has a quickstart with ready-made agent templates.) Since then, there has been no infrastructure for me to look after.

In this post, I'll walk through how I designed and prototyped the fleet, why I moved it to Managed Agents, how Claude Tag picks up anything that falls outside the routine, how it all changed my week, and what I'd tell sellers who want to build their own agents to automate manual, repetitive workflows.

Designing my fleet of agents

I divided up my workflow across several agents and gave every agent one clear job. A single responsibility keeps each one easy to reason about and easy to track, especially when something is off. I also gave every agent a Japanese name, because they mostly work in Japanese. Together they're called the Nakama, "the crew," or more literally, the companions you work with:

Furiwake ("sorting") kicks off first: it reads the daily inbound queue and routes each lead to the right rep on the team, balancing the number of leads and the priority of each one and checking who's in that day, so every lead has an owner before any of us start our day. At the end of each run it posts a report to a dedicated Slack channel (every lead in, every lead assigned) so I can track the handoff.

Sabaki ("handling") triages the leads that are assigned to me: it qualifies each lead, categorizes it against pre-set criteria, takes the defined next step for that category (draft a reply pointing them to to self-serve, craft a customized first email), updates the lead record in Salesforce, and drafts the first-touch email. It sources the draft's contents from the Nakama's shared knowledge base, a memory store (opens in new tab) every agent reads and writes (more on this below).

Henji ("reply") scans my inbox hourly for customer emails that need a response and prepares a draft reply in Japanese or English, depending on the thread, drawing on the same knowledge base as Sabaki. I can review, edit, and send the draft.

Shoudan ("opportunity") reads recent customer interactions and pushes updates into Salesforce, so opportunity records stay current without manual data entry.

Nokori ("what remains") runs at the end of the day: it scans my calendar, reads the attached meeting transcripts, summarizes each meeting, and drafts the follow-ups, again from the same knowledge base.

Each agent runs on a schedule. A sixth agent, the Nakama's coordinator, is the fleet’s operations manager. It updates the agents’ instructions and the shared knowledge base between runs. When I want to change how an agent works, I write what I want in plain language in the Nakama’s Slack channel. Only I can post requests for changes to agents’ instructions and system prompts. The coordinator checks that channel every 15 minutes or so, picks up the request, and makes the update.

Prototyping the fleet in Claude

You don't need Managed Agents to start. I prototyped the whole fleet in Claude first, using the following pieces:

A skill per agent: the instructions for one job.

A scheduled task for each skill, so I don’t need to run it manually.

A shared folder on my laptop as the knowledge base every skill writes its learnings back into: the difference between what it drafted and what I sent, plus anything new it dug up along the way.

On Managed Agents, the skill became the agent's system prompt, the scheduled task became a schedule on the agent's deployment (opens in new tab), and the shared folder became a memory store. I still ask for changes in plain language, but now I do it all in one Slack channel, and each change to an agent's instructions is saved as a new version, so each agent keeps a numbered history of its instructions. I'd suggest starting in Claude and moving your agents to Managed Agents once you have more than you can comfortably keep track of.

Running the fleet on Claude Managed Agents

Three things I got on Managed Agents that mattered most for my workflow:

The agents can run in the background

The agents run on their schedule whether my laptop is open or not, even when it's offline. The schedule is part of each agent's deployment. I could schedule skills in Claude too, but each of those schedules was a task set up in my own app. On Managed Agents, I set the cadence and timezone in the Console, next to the deployed agent's instructions and tools, and I have no cron jobs to maintain on the side. If a run goes wrong, I can open it in the Console and see each step the agent took. And while I'm trying out a change to an agent, the scheduled runs keep using the version that’s deployed, so a half-finished edit doesn't end up in tomorrow's run.

The Nakama shares one memory and learns from my edits

Every agent reads and writes the same memory store (opens in new tab), so any agent can use the others’ learnings. The agents compare the drafts they wrote with the emails I sent, and they save each difference as a note on how I'd phrase it. They also keep whatever new information they dig up while researching an answer, from our internal docs and our official websites. I fix a phrasing once in Henji's drafts, and Sabaki and Nokori stop making the same mistake.

Credentials live in a managed vault with scoped permissions

My agents have access to my email and our Salesforce records, but since these are customer conversations and company records, I wanted that access under control. The credentials live in managed vaults (opens in new tab), which protect credentials agents use to log in to outside services, such as OAuth access and refresh tokens, API keys, and personal access tokens. Each agent’s deployment uses only the vaults its job needs, it never sees the credentials, and I can revoke access in one step.

Handing the next steps to Claude Tag

For most of what the Nakama produces, I only need to read a draft in my inbox and send it, or glance at an updated Salesforce record. But some items need a follow-up step, such as figuring out an upgrade path or a purchasing route, or escalating an issue to another team.

For those, the agents don't stop and wait for me. They hand the item to Claude Tag (opens in new tab) (in beta). Claude Tag is Claude set up as a member of our Slack workspace: anyone in a channel it has joined, a person or one of my agents, can tag @Claude with a request and it picks the request up and works on it in the thread. Once it's configured in your workspace there is nothing new to learn. You tag Claude the way you would a colleague.

In my setup it works like this. An agent posts the action item to the Nakama's Slack channel and tags Claude. Claude reads the thread, checks our rules and the terms that apply, lays out the options, and drafts what's needed. It tags me when a step needs my review or sign-off. When a customer or another team needs to reply first, Claude sets a reminder for itself to check back on a set day. In the thread below, it set a reminder for Tuesday to check whether the customer had replied and whether the deal desk had answered the ticket. When the reminder comes due, Claude checks both and posts where things stand in the same thread. If someone needs a nudge, it drafts the message and tags me to send it.

Claude also posts a morning brief of product and pricing updates. The Nakama coordinator picks up that brief and writes the necessary changes into the shared knowledge base.

What changed in my week

Now that Claude prepares inbound replies and keeps CRM records current (mostly) without my manual input, my role is to review anything that requires human judgment. A written rulebook defines each agent's lane and items like pricing questions, sensitive accounts, or ambiguous asks route to me. Every email draft from Henji, Sabaki, or Nokori arrives with a short summary at the top of what's going on, so I don't have to trace the whole thread to understand the context: I read the summary, confirm, make revisions, and send.

Looking at the weekly log of what the Nakama gets through and counting each task as the time it would have taken me to do manually, the fleet saves me around 60 hours of work. I spend the time that frees up on work that agents can't effectively do (yet): conversations with customers, outbound strategy, cross-functional projects, and helping teammates build their own fleets.

Designing agents to be more efficient

Scheduled agents run every day whether I'm watching or not, so waste can add up, in cost and reliability. Some of the most common mistakes include adding to existing instructions rather than updating them, giving agents more context than they need for their tasks, and running every job on the biggest model at the highest effort level.

Most of what keeps the agents efficient is how I designed the fleet: each agent has one job, so its instructions stay focused on that job; each working agent runs on a schedule, so it wakes up, does its pass, and stops; and the agents share memory, so a correction made once is reused everywhere.

The other big factor is which model each agent runs on. Once an agent's job is well defined, it may not need our most capable model. Furiwake and Shoudan follow a written rulebook, so they run on Sonnet, our smaller model. Sabaki, Nokori and the coordinator run on Opus, our larger model, because their work needs more judgment. The coordinator needs it most, since it edits the other agents' instructions and one bad edit would reach every agent. Henji needs as much judgment as Sabaki, because every customer's email is different, but it also runs more often than any other agent, all through the working day. Running it on Opus every time would be the most expensive option, so I use the advisor strategy (opens in new tab) in Managed Agents: Henji runs on Sonnet, and when it reaches a decision it can't make on its own, it asks Opus for advice. The advisor reads what Henji has done so far and sends back a plan, a correction, or a stop signal, and Henji then finishes the draft for my review. I also set each agent's effort level (how long the model thinks before it answers) separately from its model, and I raise it only where the reasoning is hard, as with Henji's replies.

What I learned

Three things I'd pass on to anyone building their own fleet.

You don't need a detailed prompt every time. Describe the job once, let Claude draft, fix the draft, and let it keep the fix.

The knowledge base matters more than the prompt. Every correction and past interaction is saved where all the agents can read it and write to it, so Claude takes its context from there instead of from a longer prompt. It took a few hundred cheap rounds of drafting, fixing, and saving to get the drafts to sound like me.

Give Claude more room, sooner. At first I kept doing the tasks that I assumed needed me: updating the knowledge base, or editing each agent's instructions by hand. Both worked fine once I let go of them. The agents now write what they learn into the knowledge base themselves, and the coordinator updates the other agents' instructions when I ask in plain English. I had been too cautious with work I could trust the agents to do.

articles.title: A little too OpenAI.
articles.context: Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability.
articles.full_text:
An OpenAI engineer faces charges over an alleged covert recording device. Attackers exploit a PAN-OS firewall flaw and an Ivanti zero-day. Aoki infostealer hunts AI credentials. Researchers uncover critical weaknesses in an AI gateway. CikaBika Bot turns Discord into a command center. Online ads deliver mercenary spyware without a click. Microsoft disrupts a massive Chinese-language phishing operation. And INTERPOL leads an international crackdown on child sexual abuse material. Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Today is Thursday October 15th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

An OpenAI engineer is charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device.

A 35-year-old OpenAI engineer has been arrested and charged with allegedly planting a covert recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed by OpenAI since July 2025, concealed an encrypted recording device inside a television’s USB port, wrapped in toilet paper. Investigators say surveillance footage placed Alfozan near the room, while chatbot queries associated with his spouse’s account included instructions for building and concealing audio recorders. Security personnel subsequently discovered a second recording device in his unattended bag. The conference room reportedly hosted sensitive discussions involving proprietary research, product development, and government relationships. Authorities have not disclosed whether any conversations were successfully intercepted. Alfozan faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

A high-severity PAN-OS firewall vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software, prompting an urgent federal response. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, allows authenticated attackers with network access to execute code with root privileges. Palo Alto Networks says exploitation has been very limited, but CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch affected systems and investigate potential compromises by October 17. The vulnerability affects PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, along with Panorama management systems. Patches are available for supported versions, but no complete workarounds exist. Researchers warn that patching alone isn’t enough. Organizations should review administrative logins, investigate suspicious configuration changes, and restrict management interfaces to trusted networks. Once attackers control a firewall, they potentially control the very device responsible for protecting the network.

CISA urges immediate patching of an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day.

CISA is urging organizations to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances following active exploitation of a critical zero-day vulnerability. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935, allows attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely. Researchers at Volexity say an unidentified threat actor began exploiting the vulnerability October 3, chaining it with additional weaknesses to gain root access. Attackers harvested domain credentials, searched for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, and probed Active Directory. They also covered their tracks by manipulating memory and deleting logs, potentially evading Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool. Ivanti released patches October 13, though a separate privilege escalation flaw remains unpatched. CISA warns that patching alone isn’t sufficient. Organizations should investigate potential compromises, rebuild affected appliances, and rotate exposed credentials and certificates.

Aoki infostealer targets AI credentials.

A relatively new infostealer called Aoki is expanding its appetite for stolen credentials, and AI coding assistants are now on the menu. According to Symantec, newer versions of the malware target authentication tokens, session files, and API keys associated with tools including Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Gemini. Earlier versions focused primarily on browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and password managers. Researchers warn that stolen AI credentials could allow attackers to impersonate developers, run up API charges, and potentially access connected code repositories, cloud services, and development pipelines. Symantec says the malware, first observed earlier this year, remains under active development. The researchers haven’t identified the group responsible, but Aoki’s continued focus on cryptocurrency suggests its operators are financially motivated.

Researchers uncover high-risk vulnerabilities in a popular open-source gateway.

Researchers at Check Point have uncovered two high-risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, a popular open-source gateway that connects enterprise AI applications to providers including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823, could allow ordinary users to gain administrative control of the gateway. One vulnerability could enable remote code execution and potentially complete system takeover. The other could expose API keys through manipulated outbound requests. That’s particularly concerning because AI gateways often centrally manage credentials, permissions, and access to multiple AI services. Check Point says any authenticated user could potentially exploit a vulnerable deployment. The flaws affect LiteLLM versions earlier than 1.83.9, which includes fixes for both issues. Organizations are urged to update promptly.

CikaBika Bot uses Discord for command and control.

Researchers at Darktrace have uncovered a malware campaign distributing CikaBika Bot, a Rust-based remote access trojan that uses Discord for command and control. The attack begins with a document-themed lure that launches hidden PowerShell commands and attempts to bypass Windows security protections. Once installed, the malware collects system information, captures screenshots, and allows attackers to execute commands, manipulate files, and conduct surveillance. It also uses Ngrok to exfiltrate stolen data. Darktrace says the campaign illustrates how legitimate online services can support malicious operations.

A surveillance operation uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware.

Researchers at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab have uncovered a surveillance operation that uses ordinary online advertisements to deliver mercenary spyware without requiring victims to click anything. Dubbed AdFection, the operation allegedly involves Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech, which researchers say facilitates surveillance for spyware vendors including Candiru. Citizen Lab linked the campaign to zero-click attacks targeting at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera. Discover-Tech’s ads appeared on more than 120,000 websites and 70,000 mobile apps between March and June, with activity also observed on sensitive government and international networks. Researchers also identified a related operation, dubbed DARK CARTOGRAPHER, that allegedly exploits mobile carrier vulnerabilities to connect advertising identifiers with phone numbers. Google and IAB Europe have removed Discover-Tech from their approved vendor lists. Citizen Lab warns that the findings expose fundamental security weaknesses in digital advertising, where the machinery built to target consumers can also be used to target them for surveillance.

Interpol leads an international effort against CSAM.

INTERPOL says a coordinated law enforcement operation spanning 17 countries in Latin America and Europe has resulted in 95 arrests targeting the distribution of child sexual abuse material through online messaging groups. Dubbed International Effort Confluencia, the operation involved four investigations between March and September, with authorities executing 127 search warrants. Investigators rescued a five-year-old child whose parent had allegedly been producing and selling abuse material. In Panama, police arrested the administrator of a messaging group with more than 700 members. An Argentine suspect allegedly used sextortion against girls around the world. INTERPOL warns that messaging platforms increasingly facilitate grooming, exploitation, and the commercialization of abuse material. Authorities expect evidence seized during the operation to help identify additional offenders and children at risk.

Character.ai runs out of tokens.

Character.ai’s bankruptcy offers a cautionary tale for the AI industry: attracting millions of users is one thing. Making money from them is quite another. Valued at a billion dollars in 2023, the AI companion company was spending as much as $13.8 million a month on computing costs, while subscription revenue never exceeded $2.8 million. Lawsuits involving alleged harm to users added substantial legal expenses, but the company acknowledges its business was unsustainable even without them. Character.ai tried cutting costs by simplifying its models, laying off employees, introducing advertising, and charging for additional features. Users got a diminished experience, and the company still lost eight to nine million dollars a month. The service remains operational during bankruptcy proceedings. Meanwhile, larger competitors can draw on deep-pocketed investors or established businesses to keep funding their AI ambitions. Character.ai discovered that impressive technology and enthusiastic users don’t necessarily add up to a viable business.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Inside Arctic Wolf and Anthropic’s Trust-First Approach to the Agentic SOC
articles.context: Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a...
articles.full_text:
In the recently released 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey, nearly two out of three security professionals said they have been given AI-generated guidance that later turned out to be wrong. Not from an experimental tool off in a sandbox, but from systems built into the security stack they were told to rely on. Security teams should not have to live with that. They need to trust the systems that protect them, which is why trust had to be engineered into the foundation of our security operations platform and agentic security operations center (SOC), not bolted on afterward.

Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection

In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a pace human-led security teams were never built to match. Speed doesn’t favor both sides equally. If an attacker’s tool fails, or an AI-generated exploit produces an incorrect result, the cost to the attacker is close to zero. They try again. Defenders do not get that luxury. An AI agent that makes the wrong call inside an organization’s environment, missing a real threat or acting on a false one, can mean damage to that business, and a win for the attacker. An agentic SOC that moves fast but gets it wrong only benefits attackers.

Meeting frontline threats like these takes more than speed. It takes frontier protection, defenses built on AI capable enough to match the attacker and trustworthy enough to be allowed to act.

Why We Chose to Collaborate with Anthropic

That asymmetry is exactly why trust has to be core to what we build, and why we made the decision to collaborate with Anthropic to help us achieve that. Their mission is to ensure the world safely navigates the transition through transformative AI, and for us here at Arctic Wolf, safety and trustworthy AI are inseparable. That alignment, more than any single feature, is why working together made sense from the start.

The first result of that collaboration was the Aurora Security Assistant, which we unveiled at the RSA Conference in 2025. Built in part with Claude models, it gives customers natural language access to security insight uncovered by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them get faster answers to complex security questions via a simple, chat-based interface.

Delivering Trust and Safety from the World’s Largest Commercial Agentic SOC

Over the last 18 months, our collaboration has only deepened. Anthropic’s Claude models now run throughout the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, including the agents within the Swarm of Experts, the agentic framework that executes key functions of our SOC. That framework now supports thousands of organizations worldwide and performs more than 200,000 security investigations a week, a scale that makes the Aurora Agentic SOC the largest commercial agentic SOC in the world.

This week, at Arctic Wolf’s annual Security Operations Summit, Arctic Wolf shared the stage with Ash Alhashim, Head of Enterprise Cybersecurity GTM, Anthropic, who spoke to just how far this collaboration has come.

“Arctic Wolf’s team knows security operations deeply, and that shows in how they’ve put Claude to work,” he said from the stage. “We’ve learned a lot from working with them and we’re glad to keep building together.”

Today, the Swarm of Experts in the Aurora Agentic SOC resolves more than 60% of its investigations autonomously, with high confidence. That level of unassisted resolution comes from technology we’ve built, leveraging Anthropic’s models as part of the foundation. The same technology has also helped customers resolve cases 26% faster year over year, which means they are not just getting faster answers but better ones. The occurs because Swarm of Experts draws on real investigations across our entire customer base and on each customer’s own unique environment, so the guidance behind every investigation is tailored to their needs.

Our work together also extends to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted security teams access to Anthropic’s most capable models with reduced blocking classifiers for legitimate cyber work. Arctic Wolf is part of the program and has access at the Defense Access tier, which is built for defensive work such as security operations center and incident response tasks. It is another sign of the trust between our teams, and it helps ensure the models behind the Aurora Agentic SOC can support the demands of real defensive work.

A Collaboration That Will Keep Advancing

In under two years, Arctic Wolf and Anthropic have made incredible strides in advancing agentic security operations together. What began as a single AI security assistant has grown into the reasoning layer behind the world’s largest commercial agentic SOC, delivering faster, more accurate outcomes for thousands of customers around the globe each week.

But the best is yet to come. Arctic Wolf and Anthropic will continue to work together to find new ways to build Claude’s capabilities into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and deliver new innovations, as both the threats and the SOCs built to stop them keep moving at machine speed.

How can Aquasec help?

Aquasec monitors the real behavior of running cloud native workloads, including process activity, network connections, file changes and privilege usage. That production context shows what an application is actually doing under operating conditions rather than relying only on what was known before deployment.

Observation is only the first step. Aquasec enforces policy locally at runtime, including blocking malicious execution, preventing privilege escalation and containing attacker activity. When an attack chain accelerates, local enforcement changes what the workload is allowed to do next without waiting for a separate analysis or approval workflow.

Aquasec Compass extends that operating model into agentic investigation, containment and remediation through the Model Context Protocol, with humans retaining control over consequential decisions. Attackers are using AI to reduce the time and labor inside their operations. Defenders need automation that reduces the time from evidence to bounded action.

Runtime protection does not replace patching, recovery planning or application layer security. It addresses the interval in which an active attack turns one malicious action into the next. In an AI accelerated ransomware operation, that interval is where containment can still change the outcome.

TLS 1.3 introduced some major changes. It uses different cipher suite definitions to earlier TLS versions, and has different configuration options. Some implementations separate TLS 1.3 configuration from previous TLS versions. Please consult your implementation documentation to determine how to configure options specific to TLS 1.3.

The recommended profiles include both post-quantum and traditional algorithms to support the transition to PQC. The recommended symmetric cipher suites are unchanged.

The key exchange algorithms included in the recommended profiles are not the only ones the NCSC considers acceptable. All of the post-quantum key exchange algorithms currently specified for use with TLS 1.3 by the IETF offer appropriate protection for personal, enterprise and OFFICIAL-tier government information.

OpenSSL Configuration

The way preferred algorithms and cipher suites are configured varies between TLS platforms. As an example, for platforms built around the OpenSSL library, the following recommended configuration string for TLS 1.3 servers will enable a set of key exchange algorithms (or ‘supported groups’) that aims to optimise security, compatibility and performance:

*X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768:MLKEM768/SecP384r1MLKEM1024:MLKEM1024/*secp256r1:secp384r1

Client configuration for TLS 1.3

TLS clients should offer key shares and cipher suites that are most likely to be accepted by the server. The configuration of TLS clients is often outside the control of the administrator, but where it is possible to configure clients (for example within a privately hosted enterprise network), the NCSC recommends offering key shares for X25519MLKEM768 and secp256r1.

Using the recommended profiles for PQC migration

To support PQC in TLS, you should:

enable TLS 1.3 and prefer it over TLS 1.2 where possible

enable at least one of the recommended post-quantum key exchange algorithms as soon as your implementation supports them

enable the recommended traditional key exchange algorithms where you still require compatibility with systems that do not yet support PQC

In most cases, it will be appropriate to combine these activities by adopting TLS 1.3 and enabling and preferring the recommended post-quantum key exchange algorithms as a single migration activity.

Migrating the authentication methods used by TLS 1.3 to post-quantum alternatives will depend on the transition of the PKI infrastructure they rely on, and will need to wait until the relevant standards have been confirmed.

For internet-facing servers and clients, maintaining compatibility with systems that do not yet support PQC is important. As a result, support for traditional cryptography cannot be disabled until much later in the overall PQC migration.
